note:
Open questions seeded with a deploy. Keyed on slug: adding one here adds it to the site, and an answer or an edit made on the site is never overwritten by this file. Ordered by priority: the lowest number is the work that gives most back. The top of the list unlocks many records at once or stops a fault recurring; the middle is a life a published source will settle in an evening; the bottom needs somebody standing in front of the house.

**Sorted by area.** Every question carries an `area`, and the file is ordered by it, then by priority: **Missing census**, **Houses to find**, **Street numbering**, **House names**, **Names to settle**, **People**, **Birthplaces and maps**, **The record itself**, **On foot**, **Answered**. The areas are kinds of work, not kinds of subject - a person opens one of them and finds a morning's worth of the same sort of thinking, rather than a hundred and ninety-six of everything.

questions.title: Every gap in every census - and after 1871 and 1881, the cheapest work has moved
questions.detail:
**Rewritten after the 1871 and 1881 rounds went in.** The shape of the record has changed, and so has the answer to what to do next.

## What the record holds, round by round

| round | houses held | of the estate | houses with a **hole** (held both sides) | houses holding **nothing** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1861 | 1 | 0% | - | 411 |
| **1871** | **36** | 8% | 0 | 376 |
| **1881** | **164** | **39%** | 0 | 248 |
| 1891 | 114 | 27% | **52** | 298 |
| 1901 | 145 | 35% | **55** | 267 |
| 1911 | 237 | 57% | 22 | 175 |
| 1921 | 258 | 62% | - | 154 |

**363 of the 412 properties now hold a household in at least one round. 49 hold nothing, ever.**

## What changed, and why it matters

Before these two rounds the record held **5 houses in 1871 and 37 in 1881**. It now holds **36 and 164**. 1881 went from the emptiest round on the spine to the third fullest.

**And that has moved the cheapest work in the whole record.** A *hole* is a house the record holds before and after but not during - the family is usually still in it and you already know the name to search. Filling 1881 out created holes that did not exist before, because a house now held in 1881 and 1911 but not 1891 is a hole where it used to be a blank.

| round | holes before | holes now |
|---|---|---|
| 1891 | 5 | **52** |
| 1901 | 34 | **55** |
| 1911 | 18 | 22 |

**So the order has changed. 1891 is now the best hour in the record**, not 1901 and not finishing 1911. Fifty-two houses where the household is known on both sides, and the 1891 round is the one the record has worked least of the late rounds.

## What to do, in order

**1. The 52 holes in 1891 - and they are six searches, not fifty-two.** Thirty-six of them fall into whole stretches of one street missing the same round, which is an enumerator's round nobody has transcribed rather than houses that went quiet:

| street | houses | which |
|---|---|---|
| **Lenton Avenue** | 9 | 15, 19, 21, 23, 25, 27, 29, 31, 33 |
| **Lenton Road** | 7 | 9, 13, 15, 17, 25, 29, 37 |
| **Lenton Road** | 5 | 4, 5, 11, 19, 31 |
| **Park Valley** | 5 | 1, 2, 3, 5, 7 |
| **Derby Road** | 4 | 117, 119, 121, 125 |
| **Cavendish Crescent South** | 3 | 17, 19, 21 |
| **Western Terrace** | 3 | 1, 3, 9 |

**And six of the 52 have the same family on both sides**, which makes them the cheapest houses in the record - you already know the name to search:

| house | 1881 | 1901 or later |
|---|---|---|
| 21 Cavendish Crescent South | Richard Allen, retired bookseller | Sarah Elizabeth Allen |
| 33 Cavendish Road East | John George Woodward, timber merchant | Frank Woodward |
| 33 Lenton Avenue | Frederick Wadsworth, solicitor | Frederic Wadsworth |
| 25 Lenton Road | Hannah M Hopkins | Hannah Maria Hopkins |
| 1 Park Valley | Martin J Preston, solicitor | Arundel Preston |
| 7 Park Valley | Alfred Wilson, hosiery, 300 hands | Alfred Wilson |

**One lead the tool spotted on its own:** Alfred H Clarke was at 7 Western Terrace in 1881 and a Clarke heads **9** Western Terrace in 1911 - so he may simply have moved two doors, which would close two holes at once.

**2. The 55 holes in 1901.** Same reasoning. Four whole stretches of street are missing the same round, which means an enumerator's district nobody has transcribed rather than houses that went quiet - Cavendish Crescent South, Newcastle Drive, Pelham Crescent, Lenton Road. **A block like that is one search, not six.**

**3. Finish 1911 and 1921.** 175 and 154 houses respectively, and they are the rounds nearest complete. Only a complete round lets you say *this is who lived on the estate in that year*.

**4. The 1,204 unfiled rows from 1871 and 1881.** These are not gaps in the census - they are households the enumerator would not place. **Use the Round filter on the Unfiled Census Records page** to work one at a time. Most want a directory rather than another census page: see [[clumber-road-names-against-numbers]], [[cavendish-road-south-has-no-properties]] and [[derby-terrace-is-ten-houses-and-the-record-holds-one]].

**5. 1861 last.** 117 houses were standing and the record holds one. It is the hardest hand and the vaguest address, but 1871 has now taught the estate's shape, which makes it far quicker than starting cold.

## Where the pivots come from

```bash
railway run python3 census_gaps.py --year 1891
```

It prints, for every house with a hole, **the head when the record last saw it and the head when it next sees it**, and says whether it is the same family - which tells you whether you are looking for a household that stayed or a move that wants the directory.

**One caution for the early rounds.** Names and numbers both moved. The whole of Newcastle Drive was renamed before it was renumbered ([[newcastle-drive-rule-name-before-number]]), Derby Terrace is a block of Derby Road, and Clinton Terrace is numbered on Derby Road too. **Expect to place early households by name, not by number.**

questions.title: The 1901 round is 102 schedules of 243 - what is still to read, and which gap matters most
questions.detail:
**The 1901 enumerator's round runs from schedule 6 to schedule 248, and the record now holds 102 of them.** The rest have not been read. The gaps, as runs:

**8 to 73** - sixty-six households, much the largest hole, and the one that would give Hamilton Drive, Kenilworth Road and Fish Pond Drive their neighbours. Perhaps three hundred people.

**150 to 179** - thirty households, and the run that matters most for a filing already made. A. Hagues reads this stretch as Ernest Jardine, then 6 Clumber Road, then Hesse, then Felixstowe, then the Kippings - which is why the Kipping household is filed at Holly Lodge. Those pages would prove that order or break it. They would also give Clumber Road properly: the record holds two households there for 1901 where the street has eleven properties.

**129 to 134**, **90 to 96**, **212 to 216** - six, seven and five households.

Then single schedules and short runs: 81-84, 98-100, 107, 112-114, 121-123, 141-143, 187, 191, 193, 219, 227, 239, 241-243, 245.

**Why the numbering has holes at all.** Some are houses returned uninhabited, which the enumerator numbered and left empty - six of those are known and recorded in [[empty-houses-census-night-1901]]. The rest are simply pages not yet read.

**The order to take them in**, on present evidence: 150-179 first, because it settles a filing that currently rests on inference rather than on a page; then 8-73, because it is the largest and three streets depend on it.

questions.title: RG12/2682 numbers its schedules twice - one run is very likely District 14, the other is still unnamed
questions.detail:
**Settled:** the 1891 book covers The Park in more than one enumeration district, and each district numbers its schedules from 1. The two runs read so far both pass through 146-177:

| schedule | the Lenton Road run | the Tattershall Drive run |
|---|---|---|
| 155 | The Chestnuts, 5 Kenilworth Road | Bertha Lloyd at Castle Dene |
| 159 | William Martin, 11 Lenton Road | Benjamin North |
| 162 | Samuel Parr, 17 Lenton Road | Edward Hy Fraser |
| 164 | John Alfred Wilson | Frederick Wm Goddard at Charnwood, 10 Cavendish Crescent North |
| 170 | Hannah Maria Hopkins, 25 Lenton Road | Richard B Brindley at Ellington House |

Both runs are continuous and internally sequential, so neither is a misreading.

**Done:** every 1891 source line in the record names its district in words, so a household can still be found from its citation.

## District 14, read from the front of the book

**Enumeration District No. 14**, Registration District **Nottingham**, sub-district **Nottingham South West**, enumerator **Mr Thomas James Palethorpe**. Civil parish **Standard Hill**, Castle ward, Southern Division of Nottingham, ecclesiastically extra-parochial.

Its own boundary, in the enumerator's words: bounded **north by Derby Road, east by Ropewalk Street and Castle Road, south by Lenton Boulevard, Peveril Drive and Park Drive, west by North Road**. Comprising Derby Terrace, Western Terrace, Ropewalk Street, Standard Hill, Castle House and Lodges, Castle Road, Lenton Boulevard *(omitting Brewhouse Yard)*, thence along Peveril Drive to **Clare Valley and Park Valley**, up Park Steps to **Park Terrace, Newcastle Drive, Newcastle Terrace, Tattershall Drive** and all houses within that boundary **to Lenton Road**.

Its summary table: **pages 1 to 28, 195 schedules, 195 houses inhabited, 12 uninhabited, 1 building, 8 tenements of under five rooms, 339 males and 810 females, 1,149 people.**

## Which run it is

**Open, but leaning hard one way.** Two things point at the Lenton Road run:

- **The order fits.** District 14 walks Clare Valley and Park Valley, then Park Terrace, Newcastle Drive and Newcastle Terrace, then Tattershall Drive, then Lenton Road. The Lenton Road run has **Park Valley at 126-136** and **Lenton Road from 159**, with 137-158 unread - exactly the room those streets need.
- **The other run is excluded by the west boundary.** District 14 stops at North Road. The Tattershall Drive run holds **Cavendish Road East, Cavendish Crescent North, Huntingdon Drive, North Road and Park Drive**, none of which District 14 names.

Against it: District 14 names **Clare Valley and Tattershall Drive**, and the Tattershall Drive run opens with both. A district boundary can cut a street in half, so this is not fatal, but it is not settled either.

**Already checked and no help:** page ii of RG12/2682 is the printed *General Instruction to the Enumerator* and carries no district of its own. It does confirm how an empty house is written - *"1 U"* or *"1 B"* in the fourth column - which is what the unoccupied list is built from.

**No more sheets are to be had around this enumerator**, so the other district's front page is not coming. That is not fatal: [[the-cavendish-road-east-ditto-run]] was the thing waiting on it, and it has been answered from the **1894 street directory** instead, which carries a street for every entry and needs no district at all.

**What is left is bookkeeping, not doubt.** The two runs are told apart in every source line by the streets they walk. Giving them their numbers would be tidier, but nothing in the record now depends on it. **If it is ever wanted:** a district number also appears on the head of each enumerator's *page*, not only on the front of the book. Links: [[every-census-gap-and-where-to-start]].

questions.title: The 1861 round: 71 people placed off 1871, 313 still unfiled
questions.detail:
The 1861 enumerator wrote street names and **no numbers**. 1871 covers the same ground *with* numbers, so where a household stands in both rounds the 1871 number places the 1861 one.

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| filed | 47 | **118** |
| unfiled | 385 | **313** |

## What the two walks do

**Park Terrace climbs in both rounds.** Schedule 85 is the one house the 1861 page numbers - *"6 Park Terrace"* - and Robert Hoyles is in it, with Robert Hoyle at 6 in 1871. The runs keep step from there.

**The Ropewalk runs the other way.** 1861 **descends** the numbers where 1871 climbs them: 56, 40, 36a, 36, 34 ... 16 as the 1861 schedules go on.

## The eleven placed

| 1861 sched | house | what places it |
|---|---|---|
| 85 | 6 Park Terrace | the page writes the number, and Robert Hoyle(s) is in both rounds |
| 88 | 8 Park Terrace | Martha Clarke, boarding house keeper, in both |
| 93 | 12 Park Terrace | Henry Wing, solicitor, in 1861, 1871 and 1881 |
| 95 | 13 Park Terrace | Catherine Turner in both |
| 96 | 14 Park Terrace | William Gibson, hosiery manufacturer, in both |
| 105 | 56 The Ropewalk | Joseph Smith in both |
| 108 | 40 The Ropewalk | William Henry Blackmer - **the school of nineteen** |
| 110 | 36a The Ropewalk | Samuel Newham in both |
| **111** | **36 The Ropewalk** | **by the walk, not a name**: a gardener with two in the house, standing between 36a and 34 exactly as Edward Woolley, gardener, with two in the house, stands between them in 1871 |
| 112 | 34 The Ropewalk | Thomas Herbert in both |
| 122 | 16 The Ropewalk | Charles Buttery, retired druggist, in both |

**A head who moved is not evidence of a house.** Nathaniel Dickenson is on the Ropewalk in 1861 and at 6 Western Terrace in 1871; Richard Hall is on the Ropewalk in 1861 and at 10 Park Terrace in 1871. Neither was used.

## What is left

**313 people.** Standard Hill (73-76) has no numbered partner in any round. Park Terrace still has 77-84 below number 6, and 87, 89-92, 94 and 97-99 among the numbered ones - and **more schedules than houses**, which points at service dwellings in the run: schedule 78 is a **watchman** with five in the house and 87 a **coachman** with two, neither of them likely to hold a numbered Park Terrace address.

The Ropewalk run between 34 and 16 is the big remaining prize: [[the-ropewalk-1861-run-between-34-and-16]].

## Two 1871 households placed the same way

Walking 1871 against the rounds either side closed two of its own gaps:

- **Schedule 125 is 11 Park Terrace** (#251). One to one: 11 was the only Park Terrace house between 1 and 17 with no 1871 household, and 125 the only 1871 Park Terrace household with no house. The walk reaches it between 12 and 13, and **11 stands about three metres from 12**, so 12, 11, 13 is the natural order on the ground. William Knight, timber merchant, and seven others.
- **Schedule 113 is Broxtowe House** (#406). A Bradley household standing immediately before 1 Park Terrace, exactly where Broxtowe House falls in the 1891 walk - and Broxtowe House is held by Alfred Bradley in 1891, 1901 and 1911 but had nothing for 1871. The head is on the previous page; the schedule opens with his daughter. See [[broxtowe-house-where]].

**1871 is now 409 filed to 336 unfiled.** The rest of its unfiled households do not match 1881 on a name: the only candidate, William Patterson at 4 The Ropewalk, is claimed by **two** 1871 households at once - schedule 196, a magistrate and silk throwster with four in the house, and schedule 208, a retired silk merchant with eight - so neither was used.

questions.title: The 1921 Derby Road run, placed by its servants - except the Sampsons, who are left unfiled
questions.detail:
**ANSWERED by A. Hagues: assign to what the servants say.** Schedule 56 is **153 Derby Road** and schedule 55 is **151**, as their servants give them, not the Derby Terrace numbers first supplied.

**In 1921 a servant's place of work is the house she lives in**, and on this run of Derby Road it did almost all the work. Seven of the sixteen households place themselves:

| what the servant wrote | places |
|---|---|
| *3 Derby Terrace* | schedule 57 |
| *153 Derby Rd* | schedule 56 |
| *151 Derby Rd* | schedule 55 |
| *Edgmont, 143 Derby Rd* — **seven servants and the manageress** | schedule 52 |
| *Nursing Home, 139 Derby Rd* | schedule 51 |
| *5 Clinton Terrace, 135 Derby Road* — **both numbers, which confirms the record's own mapping** | schedule 49 |
| *131 Derby Rd* | schedule 47 |
| *129 Derby Rd* | schedule 45A |
| *125 Derby Rd* | schedule 44 |

## The Sampsons are LEFT UNFILED

**Their cover sheet has been written over.** It gives the postal address as **129 Derby Road**, but the figures carry the remnants of **133** beneath them, and A. Hagues reads 133 as the original.

**The household itself says 133 twice.** Both the wife and the cook give their place of work as **4 Clinton Terrace**, which the record makes 133 Derby Road.

**But filing them at 133 creates a second problem.** Every other number in the run is forced by the walk - 50 is the only household between 139 and 135, 48 the only one between 135 and 131, 45 the only one between 129 and 125 - so 48 cannot move, and 133 would end up holding two 1921 households with 131 between them in the walk.

**So the household is held unfiled**, with the whole difficulty written on every one of its five rows, rather than filed at either number on a guess. The unresolved address reads *"Derby Road (the cover sheet reads 129 over what may be 133)"*.

**What would settle it:** whether 4 Clinton Terrace was ever two dwellings, and what the Essexes' own schedule - 48, which has no address of its own on the page - actually says.

## Superseded: the reading that prompted all this

**A. Hagues reads 133 beneath the 129 on their cover sheet** - the number was written over, and the remnants show in every figure. That agrees with what the household itself says twice: the wife and the cook both give the house as **4 Clinton Terrace**, which is 133 Derby Road. Filed at #74.

**It leaves one thing odd, and worth a note.** The walk now reads 135, 133, 131, **133**, 129 across schedules 49, 48, 47, 46, 45A - so **133 Derby Road holds two 1921 households**, the Essexes on schedule 48 and the Sampsons on 46, with schedule 47 at 131 between them. Every other number in the run is forced: 50 is the only household between 139 and 135, 48 the only one between 135 and 131, 45 the only one between 129 and 125.

So either 4 Clinton Terrace was **divided into two dwellings** - 129 was divided the same way, carrying schedules 46 and 45A until this correction - or the Sampsons' schedule was collected out of order. Nothing in the record settles which.

## The reading that prompted all this

**Schedule 46, the Sampsons.** Percy Sampson, Levers lace manufacturer, with his wife, a visitor, a cook and a housemaid. **Both the wife and the cook give the house as "4 Clinton Terrace"** - and the record makes 4 Clinton Terrace **133 Derby Road**, which the run gives to schedule 48.

The run itself is not in doubt: 47 is 131 and 45A is 129, both confirmed from the inside, and 46 falls between them at **129**, which the record makes **2 Clinton Terrace**. Two schedules, 46 and 45A, share that house - the page numbers the second of them 45A.

So the Sampsons name their house **two along from where the walk puts it**. Either:

- they wrote it loosely, or the figure is a 2 misread as a 4;
- the record's **Clinton Terrace to Derby Road mapping is out by two below number 5** - but it is confirmed exactly at 5 by schedule 49's servant, which makes a local slip unlikely;
- Clinton Terrace numbers do not run one-to-one with consecutive Derby Road numbers along that stretch.

**Filed at 129 on the run**, with the discrepancy written on every row of the household. One look at the figure in the Sampsons' own hand would settle it.

questions.title: 12 Cavendish Crescent North in 1939 - the Grahams, and a house that wants a round of its own
questions.detail:
**A. Hagues asked for this to be kept where it would not be lost.**

The 1939 Register has a **Graham** family at **12 Cavendish Crescent North**, and the record held one of them as **"? Graham"** - a surname with no forename against a house. **12 CCN wants checking on its own**, rather than as part of a street sweep.

**What the record holds for the house:**

| round | head |
|---|---|
| 1891 | - |
| 1901 | Thomas Page |
| 1911 | Clarissa Page |
| 1921 | Sarah Ann Rayus Hickershot |
| 1939 | the Grahams |

**1891 is a hole**, and 12 CCN is one of the eight houses on that street with no 1891 at all - see [[every-census-gap-and-where-to-start]]. The 1901 pivot is **Thomas Page**.

**Four of the six people in the record whose name is a question mark were on this street**: Graham at 12, Quinn at 10, and two more. Whoever transcribed Cavendish Crescent North wrote surnames without forenames, and the 1939 Register is where most of them sit.

questions.title: Six houses in The Park stood empty on census night 1901
questions.detail:
**The 1901 enumerator marked six houses uninhabited** as he walked: **Blantyre** and **Peveril House** on Cavendish Crescent North, **Ivanhoe** on Peveril Drive, **Thorn Lea** on Pelham Crescent, one house on **Lincoln Circus**, and one on **Park Ravine**.

This is worth having written down because an empty house explains a gap that would otherwise look like a missing page. Thorn Lea in particular is a name the record does not hold against any property, and it held eight people in 1891 under George Elinsley Coke - so it emptied between the two censuses.

questions.title: Cavendish Crescent North in 1881: the record holds nothing at all
questions.detail:
**Six households, about forty people, and not one of them in the record.** The 1881 enumerator's schedules 106 to 111 walk the crescent: Carisbrooke House under John G Woodward, Cavendish Lodge under Alfred Goater the printer employing three hundred hands, James B Walker the lace manufacturer, Thomas Bayley the leather merchant, Thomas Walker the seed crusher, and Hardwicke House under John W Lewis the iron merchant.

**These have been read off the page and set out on a working sheet, but not yet imported.** They want checking first, and two readings in particular: a servant given as Harriett Leush, another as Clara Softy, and a third whose forename reads Omah Swaine.

**One schedule may not belong here at all.** Schedule 110, Thomas Walker's, heads the street 'Road North' rather than Cavendish Crescent North.

questions.title: 11 Cavendish Crescent North and Cavendish House have no 1921 household after the corrections
questions.detail:
Moving four 1921 households to the addresses their own schedules give has left two houses with nothing for that round:

| | | held until now | now |
|---|---|---|---|
| **#27** | 11 Cavendish Crescent North | the five servants, who belong at 1 Cavendish Crescent South | **no 1921 household** |
| **#56** | Cavendish House, Cavendish Road East | Sybil Speed, who belongs at 27 Cavendish Road East | **no 1921 household** |

Neither is likely to have stood empty - Cavendish House had the Sudburys through 1891, 1901 and 1911, and 11 Cavendish Crescent North had Sidney Thompson in 1911. Their 1921 schedules are still to be found. Links: [[sunnyside-park-terrace-or-park-valley]].

questions.title: 1 Duke William Mount has no census household at all — where are the Fishers?
questions.detail:
The house was built c1878-80 for Horace Arthur Fisher, who moved in with his wife Sarah Kate after their first child was born in 1883, and they had six children. Not one census record in this record is filed there — 1891, 1901 and 1911 should each show the family in the house, and 1921 whoever followed them.

Eight Fishers are now in the record from the family account, with names but almost no dates. Any return for the house would date the children, give their occupations, and name the servants who are certainly missing. Note that Horace the son went by Frank, so a page may read Frank Fisher.

questions.title: TO ASK: Sunnyside and Clinton House on the Park Terrace ridge - what was there, and when did it go?
questions.detail:
**This one is written to be taken to other people.** Everything below is what the record can show; the questions at the bottom are what it cannot.

## What the record holds

**Sunnyside was a large house that is gone.** It appears in four rounds:

| round | as the page gives it | household |
|---|---|---|
| **1891** | *Sunny Side*, street written as a ditto of **Park Valley**, schedule 139 | **Fifteen people** - John Howard Bradwell, auctioneer and valuer, his wife, eight children, two visitors and three servants. The largest household on the street. |
| **1911** | | four people |
| **1921** | householders' cover sheets give **Sunnyside, Park Valley** | **Two separate households at once** - Lewis and Julia Ord with three children, and Clarence and Gertrude Parker. Two returns from one address. |
| **1939** | schedule 121 | **A guest house of nine**, under Beatrice Anton, manageress |

**Clinton House is a different house, next door.** The Ordnance Survey sheet names it, in its own grounds running down from Park Terrace, and **it is still standing**. Nobody in this record ever lived in it: the name appears in no census round, no directory volume, and no search A. Hagues has made.

## Where they stand

**On the ridge between Park Terrace along the top and Park Valley at the foot**, with Clinton House to the west and Sunnyside east of it, off Park Terrace by **Sun Drive**.

The census reaches Sunnyside from both sides, which is what a house on a ridge does:

- **from below** - 1891 and 1939 both climb the odd side of Park Valley to 25, take Sunnyside at the turn, and come back down 10, 8, 6, 4, 2
- **from above** - in 1921 Dr Kneebone's household falls between **19 Park Terrace and Sunnyside**
- and in 1891 the very next schedule, 140, **opens Huntingdon Drive**

**Sunnyside carried no number.** No page gives one. A 12 Park Valley was briefly inferred from where the enumerator turned, and has been withdrawn.

**Dougal de Havilland's Park Map marks *Former site of Sunnyside*** off Park Terrace by Sun Drive, around The Studio House and Abbot House. That is the only positional evidence there is for it.

## What is not known - the questions to ask

1. **When was Sunnyside demolished?** It was standing in 1939 as a guest house. The cliff-hugging twentieth-century houses on Park Terrace are on that ground now. Anything between those two dates would be new.
2. **What did Sunnyside look like, and how big was it?** Fifteen people in 1891 and two households in 1921 says large. No photograph, plan or description is in the record.
3. **Who built it, and when?** No architect, no date, no first owner.
4. **Is Clinton House still standing, or was it rebuilt?** The Park Map appears to date the building on its ground to the **1970s** and gives it no name, which suggests the original was demolished too. If so, when - and is anything of it left?
5. **Why does Clinton House leave no written trace at all?** The Dukes of Newcastle were **Pelham-Clinton** and the estate's naming runs through the whole record - Newcastle Drive, Newcastle Circus, Pelham Crescent, Clinton Terrace. Was *Clinton House* an estate name for a building rather than a house anyone called home? The **Newcastle estate papers** are the obvious place, not a directory.
6. **Was Sunnyside ever addressed to Sun Drive?** Sun Drive is on the Park Map as NG7 1BQ and is **not a street in this record at all**, so nothing can be filed to it.

## What is still to do here

The marker for #390 sits on **Clinton House** and wants dragging to the Park Map's *Former site of Sunnyside*. Recorded on the property as known wrong rather than left to look like a placement.

Links: [[sunnyside-park-terrace-or-park-valley]], [[what-is-clinton-house]], [[broxtowe-house-where]], [[james-colvert-or-calvert-wilson]].

**And Clinton House itself may also be gone.** A. Hagues reads the Park Map as dating the building on that ground to the **1970s**, and it carries **no name** there. So the house standing today is very likely a replacement, and Clinton House was demolished like Sunnyside - which would explain the total absence of the name from the directories and from every search made for it. **Two large houses lost off one ridge**, one of them leaving only a map label.

## The 1953 Ordnance Survey settles the position

**Sheet SK5639, revised 1953 and published 1955, labels *Sunnyside* on exactly the ground A. Hagues first placed it** - in its own grounds west of Park Terrace, with Springdale, Ribble Lodge, Grove House and The Spinney beyond it and allotment gardens below. His original marker was right, and the note that briefly called it wrong has been taken off.

**It also dates the loss.** The house was still standing and still named in 1953, so it came down after 1955 - which answers one of the questions this record was asking.

**Sun Drive stays out of the street list.** A. Hagues gives it only one property - Sunnyside itself - so there is nothing to file to it.

questions.title: 1861 and 1871 walk Western Terrace in the same order, twenty schedules apart - and both start before number 1
questions.detail:
**The 1871 numbering is confirmed from outside itself.** The 1861 round walks Western Terrace in the same order as 1871, household for household, **exactly twenty schedule numbers earlier**, and three of the households are the same people:

| 1861 | 1871 | | |
|---|---|---|---|
| 162 **John Wood**, 63 | 142 **John Wood**, 71 | the same man | *before number 1* |
| 163 Alexander Alliott, 55, and **Mary**, 51 | 143 **Mary Alliott**, 61, widowed | the same woman, same house | **1 Western Terrace** |
| 164 William Milton | 144 Thomas Pyper | | **2** |
| 165 Charles Henry Bakewell | 145 Pius Lewenz | | **3** |
| 166 **James Roger Allen**, 67 | 146 **James R Allen**, 77 | the same man | **4** |
| 167 Moseley Samuel Oliver | 147 Reginald W Miller | | **5** |
| 168 Edward Manlove | 148 Nathaniel Dickenson | | **6** |

Mary Alliott is at 1 in 1871 and her son James B Alliott is there in 1881, so the anchor holds across three rounds; James Roger Allen sits four houses along in both 1861 and 1871. The numbering A. Hagues read off the sheet is right.

## What it does not do

**It does not solve the houses before number 1 - it ages the puzzle by ten years.** John Wood stands immediately before the Alliotts in 1861 exactly as he does in 1871, and 1861 has households before him too. So this is not one enumerator's oddity: **two enumerators, a decade apart, both put houses on Western Terrace ahead of its first number.**

That makes the likeliest explanations the ones about the street rather than the clerk: houses at the far end taken first, or houses known by name and never numbered, or a stretch later renumbered.

## What transcribing 1861 would be worth

The record holds **four people in 1861** altogether. The page supplied would place six Western Terrace households by the mapping above without a single inference - the schedule numbers do the work - and would give the record its first real 1861 presence. Schedule 161 is on it too, with its servants but its head on the sheet before, so one more page reaches back further still.

**Next:** transcribe 1861 schedules 160 to 168, then file 163 to 168 as 1 to 6 Western Terrace. Links: [[newcastle-terrace-is-the-low-end-of-newcastle-drive]], [[every-census-gap-and-where-to-start]].

questions.title: ANSWERED - Brampton House is 9 Huntingdon Drive, and the record held the name
questions.detail:
**Settled 2 October 2026 by A. Hagues: Brampton is 9 Huntingdon Drive.**

The 1939 Register named a house the property list had not got. It was read on the page as *Brankston*, corrected to **Brampton**, and made as its own property - wrongly, because **9 Huntingdon Drive already carried Brampton as a former name**. The house is now **Brampton House, 9 Huntingdon Drive**, and the household is in it.

**Leslie Fleetwood Bates**, 42 here, held the chair of physics at Nottingham for twenty-eight years and made the place a centre for the study of magnetism. He is on the notable list, and now he has an address.

**The lesson is the one Gwedon taught the day before.** The record knew the name. It was in `prev_house_name`, where nothing searches and nothing displays, so a page that named the house looked like new information instead of a confirmation. See [[house-names-live-in-prose]].

**Settled:** the 1939 Register, schedule 87, puts **Leslie Fleetwood Bates, CBE, FRS** - Lancashire-Spencer Professor of Physics at Nottingham from 1936 to 1964 - and his wife **Winifred** at **Brankston, Huntingdon Drive**. His biography is written.

**The property list has no Brankston**, so the most distinguished scientist the record holds sits unfiled, with a street and no house.

**Three more named houses on the same short stretch are missing with it**, all from the same enumerator's walk down Huntingdon Drive: **Avalon** and **White Gates** (both marked empty in 1939) and **Ravenswood**, where Fred Noble Smith, a civil engineer in the water department, was living. The record's Huntingdon Drive runs 1 to 10 plus The Cottage at 14, and the register walks **The Cottage, Avalon, Brankston, White Gates, Ravenswood, 7, 5 (Napier), 4, 3, 2** - so the four named houses sit *between* number 14 and number 7 and ought to carry numbers in that range.

**Napier is the clue.** The register writes *Napier* against number **5**, a house the record does have. That is a named house with its number attached on the same page, which shows the enumerator knew both and used whichever the householder gave him. The same is likely true of the four.

**Next:** the 1910, 1913 and 1915 street directories in the record print Huntingdon Drive with names and numbers together - one pass would place all four and file Bates at the same time. Links: [[house-names-live-in-prose]], [[notables-the-1939-register-brought-in]].

questions.title: The record carries two properties for 16 Cavendish Crescent North, and one of them is now empty
questions.detail:
**Settled:** there are two.

| | number | address as written | holds |
|---|---|---|---|
| **#411** | 16 | *16 Cavendish Crescent North*, census-only | 1911, 1921 and 1939 |
| **#31** | 16a | *16 and 16a Cavendish Crescent North* | **nothing** |

#31's own number says **16a** while its address says **16 and 16a**, which is how a household comes to be filed to the wrong one of the pair - and one was.

**What settled which is which.** The 1921 census has **Thomas Berridge Cox and Ada Elizabeth Cox** at #411; the 1939 Register has the same couple at **Crescent Lodge**, which had been filed to #31. One couple cannot be in two properties, so both are now on #411 and #31 stands empty.

**Open:** whether 16a is a separate dwelling that the record should keep, or whether #31 is a duplicate of #411 and should go. The pattern elsewhere on the estate says the first - **18 and 18a** holds two households at once in 1901, and **36 and 36a The Ropewalk** was separated into two on the strength of Edward Woolley being at 36 in two rounds. If 16a is real it wants the same treatment, with its address corrected to *16a Cavendish Crescent North*.

**Next:** a round that names 16a outright would settle it. Failing that, a household filed to #31 in a round where #411 is also occupied would prove they are two houses. Links: [[house-names-live-in-prose]].

questions.title: The 1939 Register marks 2, 25a and 27B Newcastle Drive empty, and the record has none of the three
questions.detail:
**Settled:** the record's Newcastle Drive is **all odd, 1 to 39**, and that is not an accident - it is [[the-newcastle-drive-rule]], where an even number on a document is the old Pelham Terrace sequence and converts as *Newcastle Drive = 39 minus the old number*. The street was renamed by 1881 and renumbered in 1894-5.

**The trouble:** the 1939 Register is forty-five years after the renumbering, so nothing on it should still be on the old sequence. Yet it marks three houses empty that the record has not got:

| schedule | as written | where it sits in the walk |
|---|---|---|
| 206 | **2 Newcastle Drive** | between 1 and 3, both also empty |
| 238 | **25a Newcastle Drive** | the very last entry in the book, out of sequence |
| 225 | **27B Newcastle Drive** | between 27 and 29 |

**25a and 27B are easy** - a letter suffix is what a house gets when a plot is split or a coach house becomes a dwelling, and both sit exactly where their parent number is. They are two more properties the record wants, not a problem with the rule.

**2 is the real question.** It is written plainly, it sits between 1 and 3 in an unbroken walk of four empty houses at the top of the drive, and all four are ticked rather than entered - so the enumerator was reading a list of addresses, not knocking on doors. Under the rule a *2* would be **37 Newcastle Drive**, but 37 is occupied at schedule 235 by Hettie May Green, so it cannot be that.

**Open:** whether Newcastle Drive gained an even side after 1894 that the record has never held, or whether the enumerator's list carried a number that no longer existed.

**Next:** the 1910, 1913 and 1915 street directories are already in the record and carry a street and often a number for every entry - a sweep of Newcastle Drive in those three years would show at once whether any even number is ever printed. Links: [[house-names-live-in-prose]], [[every-census-gap-and-where-to-start]].

questions.title: The coach houses, stables and lodges Land Registry names
questions.detail: Land Registry holds outbuildings sold as houses in their own right: The Coach House on Cavendish Road East, Kenilworth Road, Newcastle Circus, North Road and Tunnel Road; The Stables on Kenilworth Road; Mews Cottage on Hope Drive; Edale Lodge on Clumber Road East, beside Edale House (#82); and Tunnel Lodge on Tunnel Road, which is where Gees Lodge (#408) is provisionally placed. These are the Gartree Lodge kind of building — each is worth checking for a census household that was filed at the big house. From HM Land Registry's price paid data, which records a house name beside the number for every sale since 1995. These are the names in use now, or recently — they may not be the historic ones, and a house name here is a lead, not a record. Under the rule for this record, none becomes a property until a census household is found at it.

questions.title: Miss Churley's school ran through 1 and 2 Western Terrace, and two names on its schedule want checking
questions.detail:
**Settled.** The 1921 census, schedule 60, is a **girls' school occupying two houses**. The record had all five people at 1 Western Terrace; the enumerator brackets his lines across both, and they are now split as A. Hagues reads them:

| | who | |
|---|---|---|
| **1 Western Terrace** | **Frank** and **Louisa Biller**, caretakers of the schoolhouse | and **Margaret Hensley**, 55, **modern language mistress**, born at Hitchin |
| **2 Western Terrace** | **A. Marion Churley**, 45, **Principal of the School** and an employer, born in Birmingham | and Annie Cotton, 17, between maid |

**The school itself runs through both.** Miss Churley and Miss Hensley each give their place of work as **1 and 2 Western Terrace**, while the caretakers give theirs as **1** alone. A school in two houses with a resident principal, a resident modern-language mistress, a between maid and a married pair of caretakers is a good deal of establishment, and the record had none of it as such.

**Two names to check against the image.** The record has them from the National Archives transcription:

- **Biller** - and it is **the only one in the record**. A sweep of every surname beginning Bil-, Bit-, Bir- or But- finds no Biller, Billie or Bittie among the people, and none in the street directories of 1894, 1898, 1910, 1913 or 1915 either; the nearest are Birkin, Burton, Butler and Buttle, and none of them fits a caretaker at a school. **So the name cannot be checked against anything else the record holds**, and the National Archives spelling stands only because there is nothing better to put in its place. My own reading of the image is *Billie* or *Bittie* and is not good enough to act on. A caretaker and his wife are exactly the sort of household that leaves no directory entry, so the absence proves nothing - but it does mean the image is the only witness there will ever be.
- **Annie Cotton** - the schedule reads **Cottam**, which is clearer. Worth noting there is a **Sarah Jane Cottam** in the record, a servant at Pendower in 1921 and 1939.

**Open:** what the school was called, and how long it ran. A principal of forty-five in 1921 with a language mistress of fifty-five is an established place, not a new one, and the directories would name it. Links: [[james-forman-was-transcribed-as-kathleen]].

questions.title: 6 South Road carries four 1939 schedules, two of them empty
questions.detail:
**The RMGB page gives 6 South Road four schedules - 238, 239, 240 and 241 - and marks 239 and 240 empty.** So by September 1939 the house was in flats, four of them, with two standing unoccupied.

| Schedule | | |
|---|---|---|
| 238 | **Elsie L Manning**, 74, widow; **Agneta E Bevan**, 68; **Jemima Gregory**, paid domestic duties | |
| 239 | *empty* | |
| 240 | *empty* | |
| 241 | **Ada M Lowe**, 70; **Clarebell Mills**, 48, housekeeper | |

The record held all five as one household because the index it came from carried no schedule numbers. They are now two.

**Worth knowing:** when the house was divided, and whether the division survives. The record holds 6 South Road in 1881 and 1921 as well, and neither round shows flats. See [[properties-carrying-two-house-numbers]].

Links: [[the-unsourced-1939-batch-holds-married-names]].

questions.title: Every other house on The Ropewalk in 1939 holds a physician or a surgeon
questions.detail:
**Settled:** the 1939 Register walks The Ropewalk from 56 down to 2, and the heads of house read almost as a medical register:

| house | who |
|---|---|
| 54 | Sydney A S Malkin, **orthopaedic surgeon** |
| 48 and 50 | Robert S Hogarth, **surgeon, retired** |
| between 48 and 42 | Vernon T Lieberman, **surgeon** |
| 42 | Rupert A C Rigby, **physician, radiologist** |
| 40 | Joseph W Scott, **physician, consulting**, with Marjory Annie Scott, **medical practitioner** |
| 36 | John D Proctor, **medical practitioner** |
| 26 | Harold J Malkin, **gynaecological surgeon** |
| 24 | Charles Henry Allen, **consulting surgeon** |
| 22 | Patrick J O'Donovan, **consulting physician** |
| 16 | George Ogg Gauld, **medical practitioner** |
| 12 and 10 | Ernst Zuckermann, **medical practitioner** |
| 8 | William T Rowe, **physician** |
| 6 | Frederick Crooks, **surgeon** |
| 4 | Arthur Noel Birkett, **surgeon** |
| 2 | Alexander Mellor, **surgeon, consultant** |

Fifteen houses in one unbroken run, and 52 is a solicitor. Two of them are women in their own right - Marjory Annie Scott and, at 42, a student of radiology.

**Open:** when The Ropewalk became the consulting street, and whether the record's earlier rounds show it forming. The General Hospital stands at the top of it - the register has its **Lodge** at schedule 133 and its **house governor** at Tower House - which is the obvious reason, but the record has not tested it.

**Next:** the same stretch in 1901, 1911 and 1921 is already in the record; counting the medical men in each round would date the change. The street directories would show the brass plates. Links: [[every-census-gap-and-where-to-start]].

questions.title: Derby House, 159 Derby Road and 2 Derby Terrace cannot all be the same house
questions.detail:
**Settled.** Derby Terrace is a named block of Derby Road, and the record already writes it both ways: **#98 is "159 Derby Road (2 Derby Terrace)"** down to **#105, "145 Derby Road (9 Derby Terrace)"**. The 1881 enumerator walks one unbroken run of odd numbers up Derby Road - 113 to 159 - labelling stretches of it Derby Road, then Clinton Terrace, then Derby Terrace. The record's Clinton Terrace properties carry both numbers too, 127 to 139. **The whole run agrees.**

**Open. Three records overlap and at most two can be right.**

| record | says |
|---|---|
| **#97** | Derby House (**1** Derby Terrace) |
| **#98** | **159** Derby Road (**2** Derby Terrace) |
| **#93** | **159 - 161** Derby Road |

If 1 Derby Terrace is Derby House, Derby House is **161** Derby Road - and #93 already claims 159 *and* 161. Meanwhile the 1881 page puts a household at **159** and appears to name it **Derby House**.

Counting settles part of it: schedules 66 to 75 are **ten households** and 141 to 159 is **ten numbers**, so 161 is not on these pages at all. That points to the house name on schedule 75 being the misreading, not the number - the Chief Constable is at 159, which is 2 Derby Terrace, and Derby House is one house further up.

**Next.** Re-read schedule 75's house-name column against the original. Then resolve **#93 against #98** - two properties cannot both hold 159. A note was raised that 159 Derby Road today sits a long way from Derby Terrace, which would mean Derby Road was renumbered at some point; if so that is worth recording on the street, because it is the same trap as [[newcastle-drive-rule-name-before-number]].

questions.title: 13 Park Valley is on the 1881 page and not in the property list
questions.detail:
**Settled.** The 1881 enumerator walks Park Valley downwards - 25, 23, 21, 19, 17, 15, **13**, 11, 9, 7, 5, 3, 1 - and the record holds every one of those numbers except 13. At 13 in 1881 is **Walter Wadsworth, 38, lace merchant**, his wife Elizabeth C, two children and three servants.

Walter Wadsworth is the stepson of Anne Wadsworth of 38 The Ropewalk, where he was living in 1871.

**And 1891 says the same.** The same household is there ten years later - Walter Wadsworth, his wife Elizabeth C and their daughter Hope - between 11 and 15 exactly as before. **Two rounds is not a misreading.**

**Open.** Does 13 Park Valley still exist, was it absorbed into a neighbour, or is it recorded under a name? The property list runs 11 then 15 with nothing between.

**Next.** Create the property by the census-only route, as 4 North Road was, so the household has somewhere to sit. Then check the map and the 1891 round for what became of it. Compare [[house-names-live-in-prose]].

questions.title: Derby Terrace is ten houses on the page and one in the property list
questions.detail:
**Settled.** The 1881 enumerator walks **141, 143, 145, 147, 149, 151, 153, 155, 157 and 159 Derby Terrace**, ten inhabited houses in a row. The record holds **Derby House (1 Derby Terrace)** and nothing else on that street. The 1871 round walks eleven Derby Terrace households and the same one property has to absorb them.

**So nineteen households across two rounds cannot be filed** - among them George B Trueman the lace manufacturer, William Redfern, Henry Lasalle the railway company secretary, John Ellis the colliery manager who became an MP, and George Packer's boys' school.

**Open.** Is Derby Terrace inside The Park's boundary, or is it a neighbouring street the enumerator included because the district ran that way? **That is the question that decides everything else.** The same doubt applies to Clinton Terrace, which the record does hold - all seven of it - under Derby Road numbers.

**Next.** Settle the boundary first, on the Park Estate plan rather than on the census. If Derby Terrace is in, ten properties want creating by the census-only route and nineteen households file themselves. If it is out, the households stay unfiled and should be marked as outside the estate rather than left looking like a backlog. Compare [[1881-clinton-terrace-derby-road-numbers]].

questions.title: 2, 4, 6 and 8 Pelham Crescent are not in the record, but the 1891 enumerator wrote up three of them
questions.detail:
**The record's Pelham Crescent runs 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 10, 11, 12 and upward** - no 2, 4, 6 or 8.

**The 1891 enumerator wrote up schedules for 4, 6 and 8** in a continuous run between houses that do exist, which is hard to explain unless the houses were there. Schedule 9 is Edgar Herbert Hill's at number 4, schedule 7 is Charles Henry Clarke's at 6, and schedule 8 is Alfred Harriman Clarke's at 8. Those seventeen people are in the record but unfiled.

Either the numbering changed, or these are houses that have since gone.

questions.title: Cavendish Road South carries five households and no properties
questions.detail:
**Settled.** The 1881 round puts five households on **Cavendish Road South** - among them **Howard A Allport**, civil engineer and colliery proprietor; **John Manning, Alderman and magistrate**; **Ernest W Enfield, banker, BA Oxon**; and **William J Heslop**, managing director of a hosiery company. Only one of the five carries a house name: **Hucknall Lodge**, where the brewer Edwin P Dawson lived.

**The record has no properties on Cavendish Road South at all.** It holds Cavendish Crescent North and South, Cavendish Road East, and nothing on a Cavendish Road South.

**Open.** Is Cavendish Road South a street the property list is missing, or the enumerator's name for a stretch of something the record calls by another name - Cavendish Crescent South, or Cavendish Road East's southern end? Five households turn on it.

**Next.** Check the Park Estate plan for a Cavendish Road South, and look for **Hucknall Lodge** by name, which is the one fixed point. Compare [[derby-terrace-is-ten-houses-and-the-record-holds-one]], which is the same kind of question and was answered by the record already holding both names.

questions.title: Western House School — sixty-three years, and two nights of it recorded
questions.detail:
**Where it was is settled, and it was in two places.** A. Hagues gives the school's span as **1873 to 1937**, founded by **Miss Louisa Clark on Western Terrace in 1874** and moved in **March 1890** to its final home at **30 The Ropewalk (#327)**. That resolves what looked like a contradiction between two returns: the **1881 census** heads the household 'Western Terrace (Western House), Boarding School' - Louisa Clark, 49, Principal of School, with the governess Isabella Huddleston, the teachers Ellen A. Hartt and Georgeana Barnblem, the pupil teachers Alice A. Eminson and Anna Toepken of Oldenburg, scholars, a cook and a housemaid - while the **1891 census** names it '30 Ropewalk (Western House)'. The school did not move between the two addresses by an enumerator's error; it moved by removal, a year before the later return. So Western Terrace was its home for sixteen years and The Ropewalk for forty-seven. The 1891 census names it outright — schedule 195, "30 Ropewalk (Western House)" — with Louisa Clark, 59, Principal of a Private School, and three resident governesses.

By **1911** the house holds twenty people and is run by **Annie and Florence Green**, sisters from Beverley, both returned as Principal, with six teachers, four servants and eight boarding pupils. The 1911 return does not give the school a name, so whether it was still called Western House under the Greens is unknown.

What is open: who ran it between Louisa Clark and the Greens, and after them to 1937; whether the name changed; and what became of the building. Directories and prospectuses would answer all three. **The Bangkok girls are accounted for.** Their father was almost certainly James Murchie (1865–1929), an engineer who went out to Singapore in 1891 and was sent on to Bangkok by Howarth Erskine Ltd, structural engineers in iron and steel, as their representative and general manager over a works of some six hundred men; he later joined the board, and by 1912 was trading in London as James Murchie & Co. Ltd. Doris Mary and Phyllis Kathleen were born at Bangkok in 1901 and 1903, with Janet Martha born at Much Wenlock in 1899 between them — a wife coming home for one confinement, and daughters later boarded in Nottingham while the family was abroad. The identification is inference and is recorded as such: no return or certificate here names him as their father, and the case rests on the place and the years agreeing. From the Stapleford and District Local History Society. What remains open about the school itself is unchanged: who ran it between Louisa Clark and the Greens, and after them to 1937; whether the name changed; and what became of the building.

questions.title: A boys' boarding school on the Ropewalk in 1861, kept by the Blackmers
questions.detail:
The largest household in the 1861 round - **nineteen people**, schedule 108 - is a school, and the record has not held it before.

**William Henry Blackmer**, 63, born Shoreditch, is returned as *proprietor of houses*. His wife Sarah Ann is 62. Their **three daughters are all governesses** - Sarah 33, Louisa 23, Alice 20 - and a fourth governess, **Jane Square**, 22, boards with them.

**Ten boarding scholars, aged seven to eleven:**

| | born |
|---|---|
| Harry W Lee, 11, and William J Lee, 10 | Sneinton |
| **Charles S Hebden, 10, and William W Hebden, 7** | **Australia** |
| William W Allen, 10 | Arnold |
| Samuel J Claye, 9 | Derby |
| George Deverill, 9 | Nottingham |
| Arthur Pearson, 7 | Chilwell |
| Ernest Leo Price, 7 | Blackheath, Kent |
| George Stringer, 8 | Wakefield |

A cook and a housemaid keep the house.

**Worth knowing:** what the school was called, how long it ran, and which house on the Ropewalk it occupied - the 1861 page gives no number, so it is unfiled with the rest of that street. Boys sent from Kent, Yorkshire, Derby and **Australia** to a small Nottingham boarding school says it had a name that carried.

The estate already holds three schools in the record - [[miss-churleys-school-at-one-and-two-western-terrace]], [[western-house-school]], [[auckland-house-school-when]] - and this is the earliest of them. Links: [[the-1861-round-has-no-house-numbers]].

questions.title: Who built Glendower, 27 Newcastle Drive — and is the Fothergill attribution right?
questions.detail:
The record gives **27 Newcastle Drive** as 'Large detached house c1884, by Watson Fothergill architect', and its architect field says Watson Fothergill. A. Hagues doubts it, and has found something that points elsewhere.

**What the house is.** Glendower, built for **William Foster** of Foster, Cooper & Foster, the furnishing firm. Foster is at 12 Pelham Terrace on the 1891 census — the same house, before the street was renumbered — and the 1898-99 directory names it Glendower. The initials **WF** are inscribed on the front, which A. Hagues notes could as easily stand for the owner, William Foster, as for Watson Fothergill; the same two letters serving both men is exactly the sort of coincidence an attribution can be built on by mistake.

**What points at Bromley.** The Nottingham Journal of **10 November 1881** carries **Albert Nelson Bromley** tendering for builders to work on a furniture depository for Foster's company. So Bromley was working for this client, on this firm's buildings, three years before the house is dated. Bromley was born at Stafford in 1850 and the directory prints him at **15 Newcastle Drive** from 1898-99 through 1915-16 — a few doors from Glendower, on the same street. He is now on the architects' watch list.

**The record already knows his practice, but not the man.** Two property descriptions name later forms of the firm: 'Bromley, Cartwright and Waumsley' for alterations at 3 Cavendish Crescent North about 1933, and 'Bromley and Cartwright' for a flat conversion at 4 Western Terrace about 1948. Albert Nelson Bromley himself appears nowhere in the record — not as a person, not among the sixteen architects, not among the fourteen firms.

**Nothing has been changed.** The architect field still reads Watson Fothergill, because a tender for a different building by the same client is a lead and not an attribution. What would settle it: a drawing or a building notice for the house itself, a dated plan in the estate archives, or Fothergill's own job list, which is well documented and would either include Glendower or not. If it is not his, the field and the history note both want correcting, and Bromley wants adding as an architect in his own right.

questions.title: What was Clumber Court?
questions.detail: Recorded as demolished, with no residents linked to it and no census year at all. Either the links have gone missing or the record was never more than a stub. What stood there, when did it go, and did anyone in the record live in it?

questions.title: The housekeeper at 27 Cavendish Road East gives her place of work as Cavendish Road South
questions.detail:
Betsy Williamson, housekeeper to **Sybil Speed** in 1921, gives her place of work as **"Cavendish Rd S, The Park"**. A housekeeper's place of work in 1921 is the house she lives in, so that reading would put the household on Cavendish Road **South**, not East.

**Filed at 27 Cavendish Road East all the same**, on A. Hagues's reading of the run and on the family: the Speeds stand at 27 in 1891, 1901 and 1911, and the house had no 1921 household at all until now.

**The doubt is only the one letter.** A capital E and a capital S in that hand are close, and "Cavendish Rd E, The Park" would be exactly right. But Cavendish Road South is a real street in this record - Hucknall Lodge stands on it - so the reading cannot simply be dismissed. Worth one look at the original.

questions.title: James Holroyd, house agent: 18 or 20 Barrack Lane?
questions.detail:
The 1911 return heads the Holroyd household **Harlaxton House, 18 Barrack Lane**, and that is where it is filed (#11). Wright's Directory of Nottingham puts him next door, three times over: 1910-11, 1913-14 and 1915-16 each print **"20 Holroyd James, house agent"**, always after Glenroy (F. W. Pare, no number given) and before 28 Simpson. See [1913-14, page 14](https://specialcollections.le.ac.uk/digital/collection/p16445coll4/id/166408), [1910-11](https://specialcollections.le.ac.uk/digital/collection/p16445coll4/id/165758) and [1915-16](https://specialcollections.le.ac.uk/digital/collection/p16445coll4/id/347693).

Neither 18 nor 20 has any other household in the record, so nothing here decides it. Either the enumerator's number or the directory's is wrong, or the lane was renumbered between the return and the directories' canvass. What would settle it: the 1921 return or the 1939 Register for either house, a rate book, or a deed naming Harlaxton House. If it turns out to be 20, move the household with the reassign page and add Harlaxton House as the house name there; if 18, add the house name to #11.

Glenroy is worth placing too: it sits between 10 and 20 in every directory, so it is likely one of 12 to 18.

questions.title: 5 Clumber Crescent South or Clumber Court - which held the Kippings in 1921, and which the McCraiths?
questions.detail:
**The crescent held five households in 1921 and three are settled.** Kirkaldy is at number 3 on the strength of Professor Adam Willis Kirkaldy's will, reported in the Nottingham Evening Post of 28 March 1932, which calls him formerly of 3 Clumber-crescent; the notice does not say north or south, but the north crescent holds only Cedar Lodge and no numbers at all, so the address can only be this one. Lewenz is at number 7, the single house number any of the five schedules gives. Jardine is at number 9, where the family is returned in 1901 and 1911, printed in Wright's Directory from 1910-11 to 1915-16, and still found on the 1939 register; Mary Evanson is cook there in both 1911 and 1921, which fixes that household to the house independently of the enumerator's walk.

**That leaves two houses and two households, and nothing separates them.** The houses are 5 Clumber Crescent South (#79) and Clumber Court (#399). The households are Frederick Stanley Kipping, professor of chemistry at University College, eleven people including the visiting Jinks family and his mother-in-law; and James William McCraith, eleven people including four McCraiths, two visitors and five servants.

**What has already been tried.** Wright's Directory prints two Perry households on the crescent without numbers in 1910-11, 1913-14 and 1915-16 - Mrs John Maddock Perry and John Thorpe Perry - and John Thorpe Perry is returned at number 5 in 1911, so the other Perry household is presumably at Clumber Court; but neither Perry connects to Kipping or to McCraith. Kipping, Kirkaldy, Lewenz and Wigglesworth appear in no volume of the directory at all, so that source is exhausted. The McCraiths come to the crescent from Ellenborough House, 3 South Road, where the record holds them from 1881 with their servant Isabella Richardson; nothing in that line names a house here. Two published lives of Kipping - F. Challenger's Royal Society obituary notice of 1950 and N. R. Thomas's paper in Silicon of 2010 - give his career in full and neither names his Park address. Thomas has him a regular at the Nottingham Park Tennis Club; Challenger places him at 40 Magdala Road, which is not on the estate and whose relation to the 1921 return is unknown.

**Where both households sit now.** The McCraith household is eleven unfiled 1921 rows under the label Clumber Crescent South. The Kipping household was imported with its rows deliberately unfiled under the same label. Neither should be filed by interpolating the walk. See [[clumber-court-stub]].

**Where the Kippings were twenty years earlier, which is new ground for this question.** The 1901 census puts the household on **Clumber Road West** - Frederic Stanley Kipping, 37, professor of chemistry, his wife, two children born in Scotland and Middlesex, his mother-in-law Florence Holland, and two servants. A. Hagues reads the enumerator's round as Ernest Jardine, then 6 Clumber Road, then Hesse, then Felixstowe, and then this household, which places it at **Holly Lodge (#86)**, and it is filed there.

**This does not settle 1921**, and should not be made to. But it does two useful things. It shows the family held a house in The Park long before the return that is in dispute, so the 1921 household is a return to the estate rather than an arrival on it. And it puts **Ernest Jardine on the same 1901 round**, which matters because Jardine is the household already fixed to 9 Clumber Crescent South by his cook in two censuses - so the two families were neighbours of a sort in 1901 as well as in 1921.

**A caveat that belongs with it.** Schedules 150 to 179 are absent from the pages read, so the order of that round is A. Hagues's and cannot be checked against the transcription. If it is ever shown to run otherwise, Holly Lodge is the thing to undo.

questions.title: Pelham Cottage and Pelham Cottages: where on the crescent were they?
questions.detail:
**Three separate 1881 schedules are headed Pelham Cottage** - Fletcher Hind's four, Johnson Marriott's two, and Charles Sidney Hill alone - and two more in 1891 are headed Pelham Cottages, holding Ethel Matilda Pitts's three and Sarah Warriner's five.

The name is in the record nowhere. Small dwellings of this sort often stood behind or beside the larger houses, and the Hinds at least are already in the record, so they may be placeable from another source.

questions.title: Where was William Henry Radford, engineer, in 1901?
questions.detail:
The record files **William Henry Radford (#3200)**, engineer to a lace manufacturer, as head at **Gleadthorpe, 11 Cavendish Crescent North** in 1901, with no age, from the note "engineer 1899 Wright's / lace manu 1901 census". A. Hagues now places the **McConnell** household at Gleadthorpe in 1901, and Wright's Directory agrees with him for 1894-95: "Gleadthorpe, Jno. M'Connell, warehouse manager" ([page 44](https://specialcollections.le.ac.uk/digital/collection/p16445coll4/id/164550)). The same page prints **Wm. Hy. Radford, engineer**, on the line after Gleadthorpe and before Flixton, as a separate entry with no house name, and 1898-99 starts its page with him in the same place ([page 50](https://specialcollections.le.ac.uk/digital/collection/p16445coll4/id/165226)). So he is next door to Gleadthorpe, not in it.

Which house is between Gleadthorpe (11) and Flixton (15): 12 Hazlewood or 14 Park House? Hazlewood is Thomas Page's in the directories, so **14 Park House (#29)** is the likeliest, but only the 1901 return for Radford can say. Once it is known, move #3200's 1901 record there with the reassign page.

He is not the coachman William Hy Radford of the Meyer household on Pelham Crescent in 1901, who is the William Edward Radford at 1 Pelham Crescent in 1911.

**Checked against the 1901 round now transcribed, and it does not answer this.** The pages read cover Cavendish Crescent North at schedules 189 to 195 - Hardwicke House, Haddon House, Peveril House (empty), one unnamed household under Donley Scott Ransom, Blantyre (empty), Cavendish Lodge and Carisbrooke House. **The numbered middle of the crescent, 11 to 15, is not among them**, so Gleadthorpe, Hazlewood, Park House and Flixton are all absent, and so is McConnell.

The only Radford anywhere in the transcribed 1901 rounds is **Wm. Hy. Radford, coachman, 40, born at Colston in Leicestershire**, in Julia Meyer's household at schedule 197 on Pelham Crescent - the very man this question already sets aside as the wrong Radford. So the question stands exactly where it did, and the page that would settle it has still to be read.

questions.title: Thorn Lea is 7 Western Terrace, and Lincoln Villa is 11 - both settled from the directory
questions.detail:
**Two 1891 households on Pelham Crescent are given by name rather than number.** Thorn Lea holds eight under George Elinsley Coke; Lincoln Villa holds eleven under Joseph Bright. Neither name is in the record against any property.

Both are the sort of name that ought to resolve to a number from a directory of the 1890s, and Joseph Bright is already in the record, which may make him the quicker way in.

**Thorn Lea stood empty on census night 1901.** The enumerator marked it uninhabited on his round, so the house survived the decade but lost the Cokes. See [[empty-houses-census-night-1901]].

**The 1901 round moves them, and that is the useful part.** Ten years on, the enumerator reaches Lincoln Villa and Thorn Lea **between 10 Western Terrace and the North Road lodge** - schedule 217 is 10 Western Terrace, 218 is Lincoln Villa, Thorn Lea follows, and 220 is the lodge on North Road. In 1891 both were written up as Pelham Crescent.

**It is the same house, not a name reused.** Joseph Bright, solicitor, is at Lincoln Villa in both years - 51 in 1901 with Frances, Horace, Josephine and Frank, and the same family ten years earlier. So the household did not move and the name did not travel; what changed is which street the enumerator wrote at the head of the schedule.

**So both houses sit near where Pelham Crescent, Western Terrace and North Road meet**, and are addressed off whichever the enumerator was working along. That is a much smaller search than "somewhere on Pelham Crescent", and it is the same corner problem as [[kentmere-ccn]], where a house on the join of two crescents is written up under either.

**Thorn Lea stood empty on census night 1901**, so the Cokes had gone by then - see [[empty-houses-census-night-1901]].

**Answered, and from a source already in the record.** Wright's Directory for 1894-95 prints, on **Western Terrace**: *no. 7, Thorn lea, George E. Coke, of Coke, Mills & Coke*. That is the same George Elinsley Coke the 1891 census gives at Thorn Lea, with a house number against his name.

**So Thorn Lea is 7 Western Terrace.** The reasoning above - that it sat somewhere near the junction of Pelham Crescent, Western Terrace and North Road, addressed off whichever street the enumerator was walking - was sound as far as it went, and is now beside the point. The 1891 schedule heading it Pelham Crescent was simply wrong.

**Lincoln Villa is 11 Western Terrace (#350)**, which the record already carried as that property's house name. The directory confirms it independently for 1910-11, 1913-14 and 1915-16, where Sir Joseph Bright J.P. and his sons Arthur Stanley and Horace Dickinson are all printed at Lincoln Villa, Western Terrace - the same family the 1891 and 1901 censuses give.

**What remains.** Western Terrace runs 1 to 11 in the record, and #346 is 7 Western Terrace. The Coke household of 1891 should be filed there once somebody is satisfied the numbering has not shifted since 1894.

questions.title: John George Woodward in 1881: 33 Cavendish Road East, or Carisbrooke House?
questions.detail:
**The record has him alone at 33 Cavendish Road East for 1881.** The 1881 schedule 106 has him at Carisbrooke House on Cavendish Crescent North with eight others: his wife Caroline, his stepson Lewis H E de Vera, an architect of 28, three grown children, and three servants.

**Both cannot be right.** If the schedule is right, his existing row wants moving rather than duplicating, and the other eight creating alongside it. The stepson is the useful name here, being unusual enough to trace on his own; he is not in the record at all.

questions.title: Two Huntingdon Drive households in 1891 with nothing to number them by
questions.detail:
Schedules **140 and 141** are on Huntingdon Drive and the page gives no number for either. They are left **unfiled**, because the record has no anchor for that street in 1891 - no numbered Huntingdon Drive row in any round to walk back from.

| schedule | household | rooms |
|---|---|---|
| **140** | **George Miller**, coachman, born Dumfries, his wife Annie and five children | **four rooms** - a coachman's cottage rather than a house |
| **141** | **John Ashworth**, timber merchant and employer, wife, four children and two servants | |

**A third house on Huntingdon Drive is marked uninhabited** between 141 and 142. It is not recorded in the unoccupied list, because that list files by property and there is no number to file it against.

An 1891 schedule 160 on the same street is already unfiled in the record - the Loder household - so Huntingdon Drive now has **three** unfiled 1891 households. A directory or a numbered later round would place all three at once.

The record holds 1 to 10 Huntingdon Drive (#143 to #152) and The Cottage at 14 (#405).

questions.title: Arundel House stood from 1870 — why is Stephen Wills not in any census for it?
questions.detail:
T. C. Hine built the house in 1870 for the lace manufacturer Stephen Wills, and the record's only household there is 1921: George Edward Dixon, steward of an institute, with his wife, two daughters and a niece. Searching the census for Wills at the address has come up empty, which is worth thinking about rather than simply repeating.

Things worth trying. The house may not have been **numbered** in the early returns — enumerators often wrote the name alone, so look for *Arundel House, Park Valley* rather than number 1, and for the corner given as Lenton Road, since the house stands on the junction. The record does hold early returns nearby — 15 and 25 Park Valley, and 23 Lenton Road, reach back to 1871 and beyond — so the pages themselves exist and the house should be on them.

It is also worth allowing that **he never lived here**. A manufacturer could commission a house to let, or build it for a son or a daughter. A trade directory for the 1870s would place Stephen Wills at whatever address he actually occupied, and if that is somewhere else, the account's "built for" means built to his order, not lived in by him. The 1871 return, taken within a year of completion, is the one to find first.

questions.title: Does anything of Barrack Yard survive, and exactly where was it?
questions.detail:
Three households were returned at "Barrack Yard, Barrack Lane" in 1911 — twelve people, all filed at 10 Barrack Lane because the enumerator counted the yard on the Barrack Lane round. Elizabeth Baker, a widow of 81, with her daughter and cabinet-maker son-in-law; Joseph Blythe, a sexton, with his wife, three children and a boarder; and Fletcher Hind, a domestic coachman, with his wife, a lace hand drawer, and their daughter, a hosiery machinist. A working court, in a lane otherwise recorded as eighteen numbered cottages.

It is now in the record as #410, placed at the foot of the lane just beyond number 30 and set back off the frontage. That position is worked out from Barrack Lane's own numbering and is provisional. Dougal de Havilland's map carries a note reading "Allegedly known as Barrack Yard" at the same end, around Pelham Cottages and Reveille, by the pedestrian access to Harlaxton Drive — allegedly is his word, and the map is far too coarse to place anything from.

Is the name still known? Does the entry or any of the cottages survive? And is the yard the block Dougal was pointing at, or somewhere else at that end of the lane?

questions.title: Where is Broxtowe House, and why does a Park Valley schedule carry the name?
questions.detail:
**The 1911 index puts it on Park Terrace.** A. Hagues's run of the 1911 Park Terrace households heads the list with **Alfred Bradley at Broxtowe House**, locality *Park Terrace Nottingham* - the first source the record has that gives the house a street at all, where the property list has only *The Park*.

It does not say which house on the terrace, and it does not explain the Park Valley schedule that also carries the name. But it halves the question.

**Settled: the Park Valley household is at 6 Park Valley.** Mary Enfield, 79, her brother Henry, 71, an artist, her companion Jane Chaffer and two servants are filed at Stuart Cottage (#262) on the 1921 return, and A. Hagues confirms the house. Their census rows now carry that address and a source.

**Their schedule is addressed Broxtowe House, and that is not accepted as a name for the house.** A. Hagues cannot see 6 Park Valley as Broxtowe House, so no such name is recorded against #262 and none should be. The address on that schedule is therefore unexplained: an enumerator's or indexer's error, a postal usage that did not belong to the building, or something else. Understanding where it came from is now part of this question rather than evidence for a second house.

**An earlier draft of this question went further than the evidence.** It reasoned first that Stuart Cottage could not be a candidate because it has a name and a listed description of its own, and then, once the household was confirmed there, that the name must have been carried by two houses. Neither conclusion is kept. What is known is narrower: the household is at 6 Park Valley, and its schedule says Broxtowe House.

**The Park Terrace end, which is where the name belongs.** Dr Kneebone's 1921 schedule gives his postal address as 'Broxtow House, The Park', spelt without the e, and his household falls between 19 Park Terrace and Sunnyside. Alfred Bradley, a single cotton doubler of 45, with his niece, a visiting governess and three servants, is returned at Broxtowe House on the 1891 census and is filed at **#406**, between 1 and 3 Park Terrace in that year's walk. On A. Hagues's instruction Kneebone (#1843) is being filed at #406 as well.

**What is still wanted: which building #406 is.** It is a census-only property - no description, no build date, no position beyond the walk order - and it now carries two households thirty years apart. 20 Park Terrace holds no census record at all and remains a candidate for the same ground. The name appears **nowhere in any directory volume, in any spelling**. A rate book, a deed, or an older map would settle it, and might also explain the Park Valley schedule.

questions.title: Which houses did the Weinberg and Smith families live in?
questions.detail: Twenty-two people were filed under 9 Cavendish Crescent North in the 1911 census, which is three schedules, not one household. Four servants with no head belong to Peveril House itself — Weston Fulford Marriott Weston-Webb held the lease and signed the return without being there on the night. The other two are the Weinbergs (nine people, head a shipping merchant and lace manufacturer) and the Smiths (nine people, head a lace manufacturer). The enumerator ran 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 up the crescent, and 10, 11 (Gleadthorpe) and 12 all hold no 1911 record, so the next two houses along are the candidates.

questions.title: Where is Claremont, and can the 1901 census place the Birkins in it?
questions.detail:
The Birkin family account puts Philip Austin Birkin at **Claremont** by the 1901 census. The record holds no house of that name, under any street or former name, and Philip appears in it only in 1911, at 5 Cavendish Crescent North — the house the account calls Blanbyre and the record holds as Blantyre House — where he is returned as a brewery manager.

So either Claremont is a Park house under a name this record does not yet know, or it stands outside the estate. The 1901 return that names it would settle both, and would be the evidence needed before any new property is created: nothing is added here without census data for it.

The same account places his brothers around him — Major Harry Birkin at Lincoln House on Lincoln Circus, Charles Wilfred at The Elms, now Newcastle Court, on Newcastle Circus, and Richard Lesley at Edale House on Clumber Road East. The record holds all three houses; Lincoln House has nobody in it at all.

**Overtaken in part: the record now holds a Claremont.** This question was written when no house of that name was in the record. **#230, 7 North Road**, built 1872, now carries Claremont as both its name and its former name, and the map labels it. So the question is no longer whether a Park house of that name exists, but whether *this* is the house the Birkin family account means, and whether the 1901 return puts Philip Austin Birkin in it. The 1901 household at #230 is William Smith, lace manufacturer, 79, his daughter Emily and three servants - not a Birkin - so either the account means a different house, or it means a different year. Claremont was briefly one of two candidates for Alfred William Stanfield's unnamed Lincoln Circus house. That is now superseded: his house is Lincoln House, on the circus itself. See [[stanfield-lincoln-circus-house]].

questions.title: Gartree Lodge: standing, at 17a Tattershall Drive, and where the map puts it
questions.detail: Both halves answered on the ground by A. Hagues. It stands, it is 17a Tattershall Drive, and it goes by The Lodge now — which is why HM Land Registry's unnumbered "The Lodge" on this street is this house and not the lodge beside the tennis ground. And the position was right: he took the point this record already held, looked at it on Street View, and found the building exactly there. That point had been a calculated guess — the Tattershall Drive end of Gartree House's garden, 28m short of 4 Tattershall Drive along the line between them — so it is worth saying that the guess has been checked rather than merely left standing. The house began as part of the carriage and stable building at the bottom of Gartree House's garden, converted into a separate dwelling and addressed on the street the garden backs onto. In 1921 it held John Raven Erwin Hatton, a chauffeur of 28, and his wife Evelyn, 22 — a chauffeur housed over the stables of the house he drove for. Nothing here is open any longer; mark it answered on this page when you are ready, since an answer belongs to whoever made it rather than to the seed file.

questions.title: Which of the two buildings by the tunnel is Gees Lodge?
questions.detail: Albert Drinkwater, a police constable, lived at "Gees Lodge, Tunnel Rd" in 1921 with his wife Ada and their son Harold. Two small buildings stand between Penrhyn House's garden and the road at the mouth of the Park Tunnel: the northern is still called Penrhyn Cottage, the southern is now called Tunnel Lodge.
