Gees Lodge is recorded on the southern one, since a lodge on Tunnel Road by the tunnel is the likelier of the two, but that is a judgement and not evidence. Is either still known by the older name? And is the reading Gees at all — the hand is loose enough that Cees or Lees are possible.

questions.title: Where exactly does The Hermitage stand?
questions.detail: Two positions are held for The Hermitage and they are 48 metres apart — one placed by hand, one derived. Nothing turns on it except the map, but on a site this small 48 metres is the difference between one building and its neighbour.

questions.title: Lincoln Circus 1 and 2 — which houses are they? The record holds only two on the circus
questions.detail:
**Settled: number 3 is Lincoln House.** Harry Laurence Birkin's household of eight — him at 49, a lace manufacturer, his wife Olive and six servants — is now filed there, on the strength of the family account that puts Major Harry Birkin opposite his brother.

**Settled: number 1 is Gladstone House.** The six returned at number 1 in 1921 are Alfred Charles Radford, 56, a lace and embroidery manufacturer, his wife Nellie, their daughter Doris, a trained nurse and two servants; Wright's Directory prints 'Gladstone house, Radford Alfd. Chas' on Lincoln Circus in 1910-11, 1913-14 and 1915-16. The Radfords' own 1911 household is now filed at Gladstone House.

**Number 2 is open.** Edward Palmer and his wife Alice are returned there in 1921, he as a gardener of 57. Ten years earlier the same two were filed at **Gladstone House**, where he gave the same trade. A. Hagues places the Palmers at The Cottage, Lincoln Circus, which the record does not yet hold; if The Cottage is number 2, a gardener's dwelling on the same ground, both returns agree and nothing needs a gardener living in the big house beside another family.

**Correction.** An earlier draft of this question named Annie Tune among Gladstone House's 1921 household. She is not there: the 1921 household is Wilfred Owen Woodward, his wife Vera Lilian, Harriet Elvina Weselby and Kathleen Edith Pollard. Annie Elizabeth Tune, cook, belongs to 1911 and to a different house — see [[stanfield-lincoln-circus-house]].

What is still wanted is a house for Stanfield, and a name for number 2.

**A cottage has been found in Lincoln House's grounds.** A. Hagues has identified a third building named The Cottage on the OS 1:1250 sheet of September 1953, on the Clumber Crescent North side of Lincoln House, which the record did not hold; it is now **#414**. The other two on that sheet were already held — #409, The Cottage, Tunnel Road, which belongs to Gladstone House, and #407, Penrhyn Cottage. The Palmers, returned at number 2 in 1921 and filed under Gladstone House in 1911, are very probably its household, which would make **The Cottage and 2 Lincoln Circus the same address** and close the number 2 part of this question. Its position is Lincoln House's own approximate one and wants fixing from the sheet.

**The circus is now fully accounted for in 1911.** The Palmers are filed at The Cottage (#414), Gladstone House holds the Radfords, and Lincoln House is answered as Alfred William Stanfield's - see [[stanfield-lincoln-circus-house]]. So every house on the circus has a 1911 household, which is what allowed Stanfield's to be settled by elimination. Whether The Cottage is also the number 2 of this question remains open: the Palmers are returned at 2 Lincoln Circus in 1921, and if that is the same dwelling then number 2 is answered too.

questions.title: Where did the Carr household live in 1921?
questions.detail: Three separate schedules were filed under 19 Park Terrace in the 1921 census: the Clark household (19 Park Terrace itself), the nine doctors at Broxtowe House, and Arthur Carr with his wife, a son of three, a visitor and three servants. The Carrs need a house. The enumerator's round puts them between Broxtowe House and Sunnyside. 20 Park Terrace is empty in the record for that year, and Sunnyside itself already holds two schedules.

questions.title: 13 Park Valley and Sunny Side: two houses the 1891 enumerator walked that the record does not hold
questions.detail:
**There is no 13 Park Valley among the properties**, though the 1891 schedule for it is plain enough and gives Walter Wadsworth and five others. The numbers run 11 and then 15, with nothing between.

**Sunny Side has no property either**, and it held the largest household on the street - fifteen people under John Howard Bradwell.

Both households are now in the record but unfiled, so they can be found and placed once it is known whether these are houses that were later renumbered, renamed, or demolished.

**Sunny Side now has a property** - #415, *12 Park Valley* - and so does a second Sunnyside, #390 on Park Terrace. Whether those are one house is now its own question: [[sunnyside-park-terrace-or-park-valley]].

**Both are now settled.** 13 Park Valley is #396, built on ten attestations. Sunny Side is not a Park Valley house at all - it is Sunnyside on the cliff, #390, and the 12 it was given was an inference from the enumerator's turn rather than a reading: [[sunnyside-park-terrace-or-park-valley]].

questions.title: Penrhyn Cottage and Penrhyn House — one building or two?
questions.detail: The record holds Penrhyn House on Clumber Road East. Penrhyn Cottage turns up separately. Is the cottage the same building under an earlier or a smaller name, a lodge or coach house in its grounds, or a different building altogether? The Park has a number of coach houses turned into cottages and given their own name — Gartree Lodge is one — so a second building is entirely plausible.

questions.title: Is there a house at 14 Huntingdon Drive?
questions.detail: The 1921 census records Sidney Richard Tann, a chiropodist of 42, and his wife Daisy at "Huntingdon Drive (The Cottage)". The road is otherwise recorded only as far as number 10, so the number 14 is a guess and the house may no longer stand. Does anything of it survive, and where was it?

questions.title: The Stables, Lenton Road — which house's stables?
questions.detail:
No census record in the record carries the address, so this comes from outside it. Two Lenton Road houses have a stables or coach house at the bottom of the garden, and both of those gardens back onto Clifton Terrace — the Gartree Lodge arrangement, where the outbuilding takes its address from the road behind.

**21 Lenton Road (#190)** is the stronger: its own listed description reads "Former coach house / stables building at bottom of garden facing Clifton Terrace now separately owned and converted for residential use" — separately owned is what gives a building its own address. **17 Lenton Road, Oakhyrst (#188)** has "Coach house and small outbuilding, now semi-derelict, added in garden area adjacent to Clifton Terrace c1900-1914". Cliff House (#196) has two flats in its converted coach house, but that is a 1959 conversion.

Dougal de Havilland's map carries three stables labels — "The Stables" beside The Chestnuts and 1 Kenilworth Road, and "The Stables 2a" with "Park Stables" over by Parkside and Lenton Avenue — but none of them on Lenton Road, so they are probably other buildings entirely.

Which house did it belong to, is it addressed on Lenton Road or Clifton Terrace, and was anyone ever returned as living there? 15, 17, 25 and 31 Lenton Road all hold people in 1911 and nobody at all in 1921, so there is room in the record for a household that has been filed somewhere else.

questions.title: The Bayley Hospital was at Lenton Abbey, outside The Park — and Newcastle Court took wounded
questions.detail:
**Both halves now answered.**

**Newcastle Court did take wounded.** Claire Birkin (#65) turned her own house, **Newcastle Court, Newcastle Circus (#207)**, into an auxiliary hospital for officers during the First World War. She was awarded the Médaille de la Reconnaissance Française and the Médaille de la Reine Élisabeth of Belgium for that work, and she was also Commandant of the Radcliffe on Trent VAD, president of the Belgian Red Cross committee in Nottingham and chair of the American Red Cross Society. From the Birkin family account, by A. Hagues.

**And the Bayley Hospital was not in The Park.** A. Hagues has placed it: it stood in the grounds of **Lenton Abbey**, off the south side of Derby Road (the A52) at NG9 2SN — west of Lenton, beyond this record's boundary. So the answer to the question as it was put is no: the Bayley Hospital is not one of ours, and none of the Derby Road numbers this record holds (117 to 173, and Rocky Mount) is the building. **Lilian Birkin** was its Matron and Commandant from October 1914; it was one of the first three auxiliary hospitals in England accepted by the War Office, took the first Belgian wounded from Antwerp on 21 October 1914, and more than 1,600 casualties over four years.

A. Hagues cites Historic England list entry 1247537 for Lenton Abbey alongside a sale listing. That entry is not in this record's own copy of the National Heritage List, which holds only the 101 entries inside The Park — correctly, since Lenton Abbey is outside it — and Historic England's site refuses automated requests, so the listing has not been read here. It is recorded on his authority rather than checked.

**What is still open**, and worth pulling: how Lilian and Claire Birkin were related, and whether any Park house besides Newcastle Court took patients. The name Bayley points at the family this record holds at 9 Cavendish Crescent — Thomas Bayley (#1) and his household — and whether they endowed or lent the hospital that carries their name is not known here. The British Red Cross VAD records are searchable and would answer the last of these.

questions.title: Four people on 1939 schedule 36 are still on the unsplit Albury Square record
questions.detail:
When **1 and 2 Albury Square / 3 and 5 North Road** was separated into four houses, every household went to its own number except one.

**1939 schedule 36** - Mary Ellen Hill, Ida Grace, Herbert William Slater and Edward Godfrey - is still sitting on **#1**, which now means *1 Albury Square* alone. Nothing in the entry says which of the four it belongs to.

The other two 1939 households placed themselves by schedule: **schedule 9** is the McConnells at **3 North Road**, **schedule 10** the Holmes household at **5 North Road**. Schedule 36 is a long way from either, so the walk does not settle it.

**1 Albury Square is the likeliest**, since the record already has Selina Hall and Mary Ann Vernon there in 1921 and the property is otherwise empty for 1939 - but the Register page would say. Links: [[a-full-import-undoes-corrections]].

questions.title: Properties carrying two house numbers - four done, five to go
questions.detail:
**The question was A. Hagues's: is it worth looking at every property with two house numbers. It is** - twenty-four carry more than one number or a bracketed alias, and they are not one problem but three.

## 1. Deliberate equivalences - working, leave alone (16)

The **Derby Road / Derby Terrace** pairs (#98 to #105), the **Clinton Terrace / Derby Road** pairs (#71 to #77) and **1 South Road (13 Cavendish Crescent South)** (#301). These are one house with two addresses because the streets were renamed or the house faces two ways, and the record holds them well - #98 alone carries forty-two people. See [[cavendish-crescent-south-has-no-thirteen]].

## 2. Two dwellings sharing one record - these want splitting (4)

| | | holds | |
|---|---|---|---|
| ~~#33~~ | ~~18 and 18a Cavendish Crescent North~~ | | **done 26 September 2026 - split into 18 and 18a** |
| **#36** | 22 and 24 Cavendish Crescent North | 1901, 1911 | two numbers, not a number and a suffix |
| **#196** | Cliff House, Lenton Road (32, 33, 33a, 33b) | four rounds, **52 people** | **four** numbers in one record |
| ~~#1~~ | ~~1 and 2 Albury Square / 3 and 5 North Road~~ | | **done 26 September 2026 - split into four** |

The estate has form: **18, 19 and 20 Park Terrace** and **36 and 36a The Ropewalk** were both separated this week, each on evidence rather than tidiness - Edward Woolley at 36 in two rounds settled the Ropewalk.

## 3. Empty shells duplicating a live property - the real find (3)

| the shell | people | duplicates | people |
|---|---|---|---|
| **#174** 1 Lenton Road (6 and 6a Castle Grove) | **0** | **#382** 6 Castle Grove | |
| **#31** 16 and 16a Cavendish Crescent North | **0** | **#411** 16 Cavendish Crescent North | 1911, 1921, 1939 |
| **#93** 159 - 161 Derby Road | **0** | **#98** 159 Derby Road (2 Derby Terrace) | **42** |

All three hold **nobody at all**, and each names a number another property already holds. They are how a household gets filed to the wrong one of a pair - and one did: the Cox family's 1939 round went to #31 while their 1921 round sat on #411, until the same couple in both turned up.

**Not deleted.** A property that holds nothing today may still be a real dwelling, and #174's address carries a fact worth keeping - that 1 Lenton Road and 6/6a Castle Grove are one building. The question is whether each shell should be **merged into its twin** or **corrected to the half it really is** (16a rather than 16 and 16a).

## What has been done

**#33 is split into 18 and 18a.** The 1901 round has both occupied at once - James Forman heading one, Florence Margaret Allen in the other - which is what proved there were two. **18** went to the Formans: the 1921 schedule counts the house **thirteen rooms** with four servants, and the directories of 1894, 1898, 1910, 1913 and 1915 all print James Forman on Cavendish Crescent North with no suffix, which is how a directory prints a main house. **18a** went to the Allens, who are there in 1911.

**And it exposed a tangle.** Florence Margaret Allen's 1901 row was at 18/18a while her mother **Margaret King Allen's 1901 row is at 17 Cavendish Crescent North** - and the 1894 directory prints *Mrs. Margaret Allen* at **Pendower**, which is 17. Mother and daughter cannot be in two houses. Florence's row now carries the conflict in its source rather than being quietly moved to suit.


**#1 is split into four.** A. Hagues gave the reason the record could not: it is **one building of four storeys**, its two lower storeys entered from **Albury Square** as numbers 1 and 2, its two upper from **North Road** as numbers 3 and 5. Every one of the four had households to go into it - 3 North Road takes the McConnells of 1939, 5 North Road the Manns of 1901 and 1911 and the Holmes household of 1939, 1 Albury Square the Hill household, 2 Albury Square Albert Bland. Only the 1921 pair stay undistributed, because that transcription gives no number within the building.

**#196 Cliff House is NOT split**, on A. Hagues's own condition - split only where there are people to put in each part. There are not. All five of its households, across 1891, 1901, 1911 and 1921, are written simply *Cliff House, Lenton Road*; **not one row names 32, 33, 33a or 33b**. Splitting it would create three empty properties and force a guess about fifty-two people. What the record does show is that **1901 holds two Cliff House households at once** - Christina M. Parr's six and Alice May Parr's six - so it is at least two dwellings, and that is worth knowing without acting on.

## THE REST, which is what is left to do

**One to split, when its households can be told apart:**

| | | holds | what is needed |
|---|---|---|---|
| **#36** | 22 and 24 Cavendish Crescent North | 1901, 1911 | which household had 22 and which 24 - two numbers, not a number and a suffix, so a directory or a walk would do it |

**One deliberately not split, and the reason stands:** **#196 Cliff House (32, 33, 33a, 33b)**, fifty-two people across four rounds, and **not one row names a number**. 1901 holds two Cliff House households at once, so it is at least two dwellings, but there is nothing to put in the other three.

**Three empty shells, each still duplicating a live property:**

| the shell | duplicates | |
|---|---|---|
| **#174** 1 Lenton Road (6 and 6a Castle Grove) | **#382** 6 Castle Grove | merge, or correct #174 to the half it really is |
| **#31** 16 and 16a Cavendish Crescent North | **#411** 16 Cavendish Crescent North | its own number says 16a while its address says 16 and 16a |
| **#93** 159 - 161 Derby Road | **#98** 159 Derby Road (2 Derby Terrace), **42 people** | |

**Next:** #36 when evidence turns up; the three shells whenever A. Hagues wants to decide them. Links: [[two-properties-for-sixteen-cavendish-crescent-north]], [[house-names-live-in-prose]].

questions.title: Newcastle Terrace is 1 to 13 Newcastle Drive, and Pelham Terrace is the far end of the same street
questions.detail:
**Settled.** The 1871 enumerator walks Park Terrace 1 to 17, then seven houses he calls **Newcastle Terrace**, then two he calls **Pelham Terrace**. The middle of that seven - schedule 132, Sigismund Hamel - was already filed in the record as **3 Newcastle Drive**, and it anchors the rest:

| schedule | head | now |
|---|---|---|
| 131 | Thomas L Acton | **1 Newcastle Drive** |
| 132 | Sigismund Hamel | 3 Newcastle Drive *(already filed)* |
| 133 | William G Ward | **5** |
| 134 | Joseph Hewitt | **7** |
| 135 | Alexis C A Baillon | **9** |
| 136 | Thomas Walker | **11** |
| 137 | William J Davidson | **13** |

Fifty-four people filed on it.

## Where Pelham Terrace begins

[[the-newcastle-drive-rule]] converts an **even** Pelham Terrace number as **Newcastle Drive = 39 minus it**, and the record's own paired addresses bear it out without exception:

| Pelham Terrace | 4 | 8 | 10 | 12 | 14 | 16 | 18 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Newcastle Drive | 35 | 31 | 29 | 27 | 25 | 23 | **21** |

So **Pelham Terrace occupies 21 to 37 Newcastle Drive** at the far end, and **Newcastle Terrace occupies 1 to 13** at the near end. The two old names are the two ends of one modern street, and the enumerator uses whichever the householder gave him.

**Open: 15, 17 and 19 Newcastle Drive** fall between the two old names and are claimed by neither. Either the numbering is not quite continuous, or a third name covered them.

**And Pelham Crescent is a different street.** It runs 1 to 19 in its own right and never converts to Newcastle Drive; nothing in the record pairs the two. Worth saying plainly, because Pelham Terrace and Pelham Crescent are one word apart and only one of them is Newcastle Drive.

**Next:** the houses either side of 15, 17 and 19 in an 1881 or 1891 walk would show whether the run is continuous. Links: [[every-census-gap-and-where-to-start]].

questions.title: The 1921 run walks past 32 and 34 Barrack Lane, and the record stops at 30
questions.detail:
**Settled:** the 1921 enumerator walks Barrack Lane in an unbroken run of schedule numbers, and three points of it are fixed by the page itself - a domestic servant's **place of work** is the house she lives in:

| schedule | house | fixed by |
|---|---|---|
| 212 | **16 Barrack Lane** | Florence Taylor's place of work |
| 216 | **26 Barrack Lane** | Alice Richmond's place of work |
| 218 | **30 Barrack Lane** | Maggie Quincey's place of work |

With those three fixed, 213, 214, 215 and 217 fall at 18, 20, 22 and 28, and **24 is passed over** - the record holds it for 1911.

**Open: schedules 219 and 220 are 32 and 34 Barrack Lane, and the property list has neither.** It runs 1 to 30 with an 8a, and then stops. The two houses sit between 30 and Allenfield Lodge in the walk, so they existed in 1921.

**And Allenfield Lodge is a name the record has not got either.** Schedule 221 is headed with it, and it has been filed to **Barrack Yard** (#410), which is what stands at that end of the lane - but on A. Hagues's word rather than on evidence, so every row carries the page's own wording in a `source_address` beside the filed address. If the two turn out to be different places, nothing has been lost.

**Next:** read schedules 219 and 220, create 32 and 34, and settle whether Allenfield Lodge is the Barrack Yard or a house beside it. Links: [[house-names-live-in-prose]].

questions.title: Lynwood, St Ives and Elmsdale are the next three doors past 5 Tattershall Drive - but which numbers?
questions.detail:
**Four houses on Tattershall Drive are named by the 1939 Register and by nothing else the record holds.** A. Hagues confirms all four, so they are now properties #433 to #436 with their households in them - twelve people who had been sitting unfiled. **Every one of the four positions is provisional**, and this is the question of where they actually stand.

## Three of them are a walk, and that is the whole evidence

| Schedule | House | |
|---|---|---|
| 30 | 1 Tattershall Drive | *held* |
| 31 | 3 Tattershall Drive | *held* |
| 32 | 5 Tattershall Drive | *held* |
| **33** | **Lynwood** | **Richard Warwick Bond**, 81, *literary, retired professor*, with Amy Constance Bond, 83 |
| **34** | **St Ives** | **William Parkly Bland**, 62, stockbroker, his wife Florence, his son Donald a chartered accountant's clerk, and a parlourmaid |
| **35** | **Elmsdale** | **Joseph Thomas Roper**, 58, estate agent, with Lilian D and Ethel Margaret Roper, and **Albert Edward Kay**, 68, *fowl dealer, retired* |

The enumerator takes 1, 3 and 5 in order and runs straight on. The three named houses are the next three doors up that side, and then the book leaves the street. **The record's Tattershall Drive runs 1 to 5 and then jumps to 17a**, which leaves exactly the room three more houses would need.

**So the obvious reading is that Lynwood, St Ives and Elmsdale are 7, 9 and 11** - and the record does not say it, because a schedule order is not a street numbering. It is the same inference the record accepted on Clare Valley and refused on Park Drive, and the difference is that this run is unbroken.

## The Lodge is a different problem

**Schedule 38 is not in that run at all.** It falls after 1 and 2 Albury Square and before 10 Cavendish Crescent North, which puts it at the **north** end of the drive. It holds **George William Kerr**, 62, *gardener, domestic*, and Mary Catherine Kerr - a service household, which is what a lodge is for.

**Carnoustie Lodge stands at that end and is not it**: it is separately enumerated at schedule 8, holding the three Broadbent sisters. So The Lodge is a second lodge up there. The likeliest readings are the gatehouse at the Tattershall Drive entrance to the estate, or the lodge belonging to one of the large houses on Albury Square or Cavendish Crescent North.

**Gartree Lodge, 17a Tattershall Drive, is the other candidate** - it held a chauffeur in 1921 and has nothing in 1939 - but it stands at the *south* end, which the schedule order argues against.

## What would settle it

A street directory, which would run the numbers against the names in one column. Failing that, the houses themselves: three of these should still be standing between 5 and 17a, and a name on a gatepost would close it in a morning.

Links: [[questions-for-a-walk-round-the-park]], [[house-names-live-in-prose]], [[park-drive-missing-numbers-5-8-and-10]], [[clare-valley-numbered-from-the-1891-walk]].

questions.title: Park Terrace runs 1 to 20, and the 1939 page writes 38
questions.detail:
**A. Hagues has read the enumerator's address column along the run, and it goes 12, 13, 38, 15.** So **38 Park Terrace** is on the page, between 13 and 15, and it is not a misreading of 14 - 14 Park Terrace is separately enumerated at **schedule 204**, the Lindley household.

The record's Park Terrace runs **1 to 20** and has no 38 in any round. The house is now #442, holding **Edwin M Ratcliffe**, 48, commercial engineer, **Audrey Ratcliffe**, 32, and **William B Callow**, 53, commercial manager, at sub numbers 1, 2 and 4 - so a fourth person is behind the closed band.

## What a 38 could be

1. **A dead numbering.** The record has met this before: the 1891 round heads **Clumber House** as *15 Clumber Road*, a numbering since gone out of use, and the house is on Park Drive. A terrace renumbered at some point would leave exactly this - one house still carrying the old number in an official book.
2. **A different Park Terrace.** Nottingham has more than one, and an enumerator working to a boundary could write the number he was given.
3. **A house divided.** The register visits Park Terrace twice - schedules 143 to 151, then 204 - and **four separate returns stand at 19 Park Terrace**. A subdivided house gets several numbers in practice.

**Against the renumbering reading:** if the terrace had been renumbered, more than one house would show it, and the other fifteen on these pages are all in the 1-to-20 run.

## What would settle it

A street directory for Park Terrace in the 1930s, which would show whether any house carried a number above 20. Or the deeds of whatever stands between 13 and 15 today.

**The position is provisional**, set between 13 and 15 because that is where the walk puts it.

Links: [[properties-carrying-two-house-numbers]], [[questions-for-a-walk-round-the-park]], [[park-drive-missing-numbers-5-8-and-10]].

questions.title: Huntingdon Drive runs 1 to 10 and then 14 - and four named houses want the gap
questions.detail:
**The record's Huntingdon Drive is 1 to 10, then The Cottage at 14.** There is no 11, 12 or 13 - and the 1939 Register names four houses on the street that the property list has not got: **Brampton**, **Ravenswood**, *Avalon* and *White Gates*.

## The enumerator comes down the street

| Schedule | | |
|---|---|---|
| 85 | **The Cottage, 14 Huntingdon Drive** | *held* |
| **87** | **Brampton** | **Leslie Fleetwood Bates**, 42, professor of physics, and Winifred Frances Furze Bates |
| **89** | **Ravenswood** | **Fred Noble Smith**, 56, civil engineer in the water department, and Violet Amy B Smith |
| 91 | 5 Huntingdon Drive | *held* |
| 92, 93, 94 | 4, 3, 2 Huntingdon Drive | *held* |

**The numbers descend**, 14 down to 2, and Brampton and Ravenswood fall between 14 and the numbered run. **Avalon and White Gates are both marked empty** in the register, which is why they have no schedule here - and schedules 86, 88 and 90 are missing from the run, which is what empty houses look like.

So the two named households stand somewhere in **11, 12 and 13** or among 6 to 10, and the record does not say which, because a descending schedule run is not a street numbering.

## Brampton was read as Brankston

The name was first transcribed **Brankston**, which is how it stood in the record and in the import note. A. Hagues settles it as **Brampton**. The earlier reading is kept on the census rows so nobody later takes it for a second house.

**Worth knowing on its own account:** Bates held the chair of physics at Nottingham for twenty-eight years. Where the professor of physics actually lived is a question the record should be able to answer.

Links: [[named-houses-on-tattershall-drive-and-where-they-sit]], [[questions-for-a-walk-round-the-park]], [[house-names-live-in-prose]].

questions.title: Named houses at numbers the record does not hold
questions.detail: Land Registry pairs a name with a number for houses whose number is not in the record: Beech Lodge, 8 Clumber Crescent South; The Mews House, 1, and Ashdown, 7, Clumber Road West; Hardwick View, 11 Hardwick Road; Lenton View, 11a, and Cedar Mews, 1b, Lenton Avenue; West Park Lodge, 36 Lenton Road, with East Park Lodge beside it; and Park View House, 58, and Carrick House, 64, The Ropewalk. Most will be later infill or subdivisions. From HM Land Registry's price paid data, which records a house name beside the number for every sale since 1995. These are the names in use now, or recently — they may not be the historic ones, and a house name here is a lead, not a record. Under the rule for this record, none becomes a property until a census household is found at it.

questions.title: Newcastle Drive got its name thirteen years before it got its numbers
questions.detail:
**Settled.** The record's Newcastle Drive Rule - **Newcastle Drive number = 39 minus the old Pelham Terrace number** - is confirmed a third time by the 1881 round, and this time by a household the record already holds at both ends.

| round | what the page says | who |
|---|---|---|
| 1881 | **14 Newcastle Drive** | John Jardine, 56, lace machine maker employing 162 hands |
| 1891 | **14 Pelham Terrace (now 25 Newcastle Drive)** | John Jardine, 66 |

Ten years exactly, and 39 minus 14 is 25.

**What is new is the timing.** The 1881 enumerator uses **both street names in the same book** - schedule 201 is "4 Pelham Terrace", schedules 203 and 204 are "10" and "14 Newcastle Drive" - while numbering every one of them on the old Pelham Terrace sequence. The Bromley account dates the **renumbering** to 1894-5. So **the street was already being called Newcastle Drive by 1881, and kept the Pelham Terrace numbers for another thirteen or fourteen years.**

**Why it matters.** Any 1881 or 1891 document saying "Newcastle Drive" with an **even** number is on the old sequence and must be converted. An **odd** number is already on the new one. A researcher who does not know this will file half a street wrongly and never notice, because both numbers exist.

**Open.** When exactly did the name change, and was it the estate, the Post Office or the householders who changed it? The 1871 book calls the same ground **Pelham Terrace** and, confusingly, calls the next run **Newcastle Terrace**, which is a third name again.

**Next.** The estate minute books and the trade directories year by year between 1871 and 1895 will show the changeover. Until then the rule holds and is applied with the page's own figure kept in the source line. See [[house-names-live-in-prose]] and [[every-census-gap-and-where-to-start]].

questions.title: Park Drive has no 5, 8 or 10 - and the census pages name two of them
questions.detail:
**Park Drive is numbered 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7 and 9, with Ashley House and Clumber House carrying names instead.** 5, 8 and 10 are missing - and the census pages name two of them.

## What the pages say

| Round | Schedule | Heading | Who |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1881** | 185 | **10 Park Drive** | **Richard J Dexter**, cigar manufacturer *employing 200 girls*, his wife Harriett, **nine sons** aged 4 to 19, two sisters and two servants - fifteen in the house |
| **1939** | 23 | **8 Park Drive** | the **Howitt** household of four with three servants - seven people |

Both are real headings. The 1881 household of fifteen in particular is not a house the record can afford to leave nameless.

## The three readings

1. **They are houses the record holds under a name.** Ashley House and Clumber House have no number, and the record has already found one of these: the 1891 round heads Clumber House as *15 Clumber Road*, a numbering since gone out of use. If Park Drive once ran a number up to 10, Ashley House and Clumber House had numbers too.
2. **They were demolished or absorbed.** Park Drive's houses were converted to flats almost without exception, and Ashley House's garden alone has since taken a bungalow and a pair of semis.
3. **The numbering was renumbered.** 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 9 is not a run on one side of a street; it is a sequence round the triangle, and a sequence that has been edited.

## What will not settle it

**The 1939 schedule order is no help.** Schedules 21 to 26 run 2 Park Drive, 7a Lenton Road, **8 Park Drive**, 4 Park Drive, 3 Lenton Road - hopping a quarter of a mile between streets. The Register was numbered by the returns, not by a walk, so nothing brackets number 8 geographically. The 1881 enumerator *did* walk, so schedules either side of 185 are worth reading for 10.

## What would settle it

A street directory for Park Drive in the 1880s or the 1930s, which would give the numbered run against the house names in one column. Failing that, the rate books.

**8 Park Drive is now in the record as #432**, holding all seven of its people, with a provisional position between 7 and 9 that nothing fixes. If it turns out to be Ashley House or Clumber House it folds into them. The 1881 household at 10 is still unfiled.

Links: [[questions-for-a-walk-round-the-park]], [[properties-carrying-two-house-numbers]], [[every-census-gap-and-where-to-start]].

questions.title: The 1881 Clumber Road numbers are named houses, and one of them is on a different street
questions.detail:
**Settled:** the 1881 enumerator numbers Clumber Road - *1 Clumber Road*, *4 Clumber Road*, *6 Clumber Road* - and the record knows none of those numbers. All four households are named houses instead:

| schedule | as the page writes it | the house | |
|---|---|---|---|
| 147 | **6 Clumber Road** | **6 Maxtoke Road** | a different street, same number |
| 148 | **4 Clumber Road** | **Felixstowe**, Clumber Road West | |
| 149 | **1 Clumber Road** | **Holly Lodge**, Clumber Road West | |
| 150 | Clumber Road, no number | **Linden House**, Clumber Road West | |

**Benjamin Dowson confirms his own.** He heads schedule 148 with fifteen in the house, and the record already held him at **Felixstowe** in 1891 and 1901 - so the placement is corroborated rather than inferred, and his family is there through to 1921.

**And 6 Clumber Road is 6 Maxtoke Road**, which is a different thing again from the corner houses at [[cavendish-crescent-south-has-no-thirteen]]: not one house facing two streets, but a stretch of road that changed its name and kept its numbers. Worth knowing before anybody trusts a Clumber Road number from this period.

**Thirty-one people filed.**

**Still open:** whether Clumber Road's 1881 numbering maps onto Clumber Road West house by house, or only for these four. The 1901 round has two more unplaced on that road - **Richard Challands** with nine in the house and **Francis R. Ellis** at a house read as *Gardenwood*. Links: [[house-names-live-in-prose]].

questions.title: Clumber Road is nine names in the record and three numbers on the census
questions.detail:
**Settled.** The record holds Clumber Road East and West entirely by **house name** - Adam House, Edale House, Jelenice, Penrhyn House, Westwood, St Helier, Holly Lodge, Linden House, Felixstowe - and gives not one of them a number. The 1881 enumerator gives **1, 4 and 6 Clumber Road** and not one house name.

So three households that are certainly on Clumber Road cannot be filed: **Samuel H Sands** the bank director at 1, **Benjamin Dowson** the solicitor at 4 with nine children, and **Adolph Hesse** the Hanover lace warehouse manager at 6.

**Open.** What number is each named house? Until that is known, no numbered Clumber Road record from any round can be filed, in either direction.

**Next.** This is a directory job, not a census one - Wright's gives both a name and a number on the same line. One evening's work would unlock the whole street. Compare [[house-names-live-in-prose]] and [[dougal-map-unmatched-names]].

questions.title: Park Valley jumps from 11 to 15 - and a 1911 household lives in the gap
questions.detail:
**The record's Park Valley runs 1 to 11 and then 15, 17, 19, 21, 23, 25 and Valley House. There is no 12, 13 or 14.** Nothing in the property list has ever occupied those numbers.

**But a 1911 household does.** The schedule of **George Benedict Kohn** - 53, single, lace merchant, export merchant and managing director, born at Beeston - gives a Park Valley number falling in that gap. A. Hagues reads it as 12; the postal address line reads as 12 or 13 and I cannot separate them. He keeps two servants in twelve rooms.

**So the household cannot be filed**, and it is parked in the 1911 transcription rather than put in an import file. Filing it would mean creating a property on the strength of one address line.

**Three things it could be.** The houses existed and were later demolished or absorbed. Or the numbering was revised and what was 12 is now something else. Or the number is a misreading - though 1 to 11 are all accounted for in 1911 by other schedules, which argues against it.

**What would settle it.** Wright's Directory prints Park Valley householders by number and is already in this record: a 12 or a 13 there and the houses existed. The OS 1:1250 sheet would show how many buildings stand between 11 and 15.

**And the head is already half in the record.** George Benedict Kohn is very probably **#3017 Benedict Kohn, born 1858**, a son of the Kohn household at 11 Pelham Crescent on the 1901 round. See [[melbrook-house-park-valley]] for the other Park Valley address question.

questions.title: Pelham Terrace and Newcastle Drive: how do the 1891 numbers convert?
questions.detail:
**Settled: the Newcastle Drive schedules mean Newcastle Drive.** The 1891 enumerator headed schedules 84 to 88 as 13, 11, 9, 7 and 5 Newcastle drive - Kidd, Taylor, Kentish Wright, Birkin and Hill - so those houses are filed on the numbers the return gives. For 1, 3, 5, 9 and 13 the 1894-95 directory independently names the same householder at the same number, and those five are the only numbers that volume prints for the street.

**Settled: the street's history.** Newcastle Drive was formerly two roads, Lower Newcastle Terrace and Pelham Terrace (A. Hagues). Seventeen listed-building descriptions already in the record say 'Newcastle Drive, formerly named Pelham Terrace', and 35 Newcastle Drive carries the name Pelham House. The road was cut below Newcastle Terrace as part of T. C. Hine's plan for the 5th Duke of Newcastle, halving the width of the terrace above to allow Italianate villas with terraced gardens below.

**The working rule: Newcastle Drive number = 39 minus the Pelham Terrace number.** Two independent confirmations:
- **12 Pelham Terrace = Glendower = 27 Newcastle Drive**, and this one is as firm as anything short of a deed. William Foster junior, cabinet maker and upholsterer, is at 12 Pelham Terrace on the 1891 return with his wife Mary, 45. The 1898-99 directory prints 'Glendower, William Foster, of Foster, Cooper & Foster' against the number 12. The 1913-14 and 1915-16 volumes print 'Foster William, (Foster, Cooper & Foster)' at 27 Newcastle Drive. The Park Houses map labels 27 Newcastle Drive **Glendower** (now subdivided as 27, 27B, 27C and 27D). And the record holds Mary Foster, born 1846, at 27 Newcastle Drive on the 1921 return. Same man, same wife, same house name, four sources. 39 - 12 = 27. Glendower appears nowhere in the record as a house name and is worth adding to #221.
- **24 Pelham Terrace = 15 Newcastle Drive**, from a published account of that house. 39 - 24 = 15.

**What the rule predicts for the rest of the 1891 walk**, which began at Tattershall Corner: 4 Pelham Terrace (Edmund Pratt, lace manufacturer) becomes 35, which is **Pelham House**, built 1860 - a named villa for a substantial household, which fits; 6 becomes 33 and was uninhabited; 8 (John Sylvester, baker) becomes 31; 10 (Job Samuel W. Palethorpe, engraver) becomes 29; 14 (John Jardine, lace machinery, of the firm behind Ernest Jardine) becomes 25; 16 (David Shaw Ramsay) becomes 23; and 18, **Wolsley House** (Samuel Maples, solicitor, notary and under-sheriff, of Maples & McCraith) becomes 21. Every one of those houses exists in the record with a build date before 1891. Wolsley House appears nowhere in the record, so that name is untested.

**Where the rule breaks, and why that may be the answer.** The same walk has 19 and 21 Pelham Terrace, and 39 - 19 = 20, an even number on a street numbered wholly in odds. Since Newcastle Drive was *two* former roads, the odd Pelham Terrace numbers may belong to the Lower Newcastle Terrace stretch, or to the opposite side. Until that is understood the rule converts the even numbers only.

**A heading error in the 1898-99 volume, now identified.** That volume prints an even-numbered 'Pelham Crescent' section - 2, 4, 6, 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 20 - which includes Job S. Palethorpe at 10 and Glendower at 12, the very numbers and householders the 1891 census puts on Pelham **Terrace**. These are not crescent addresses. Pelham Crescent does have a real even side: 10 and 12 Pelham Crescent (#279, #281) are a pair of houses of about 1870-75, possibly by John Loverseed, facing the crescent with their basements at garden level on Barrack Lane, and the 1911 census has the Mellers at 10 and the Levis at 12. The later volumes list that side properly, with Mann, Shaw, Ling, Pinder and Pearson. So the 1898-99 compiler put a run of Pelham Terrace houses under a Pelham Crescent heading, and any use of that volume's even-numbered crescent lines has to be checked against the census before it is trusted. The odd-numbered crescent lines, 1 to 19, are unaffected.

**One caveat on the anchor.** The record's 39 Newcastle Drive is Priests House, whose former names include Tattershall Corner - where the 1891 walk starts, with Bernard Wilcockson, solicitor - but its build date is 1911, so the present house is not the one on the 1891 return. The name marks the corner rather than the building.

What would settle the whole street: a rate book, or the 1901 return, which should name the houses under whichever name was then current.

**Settled: the name changed before the numbers did, and the two ranges tile.** A published account of John Jardine (1825-1895) puts him on the 1881 census at **14 Newcastle drive** - the same house the 1891 enumerator heads 14 Pelham Terrace. The record holds no even numbers anywhere on Newcastle Drive, so an 1881 'number 14' cannot be a modern address; the street had taken the name Newcastle Drive by 1881 while the old Pelham Terrace numbers were still in use, and the renumbering came afterwards. That explains why one 1891 page carries both namings, and it makes the street account for itself: the lower end was enumerated in 1891 as Newcastle drive with the modern numbers 1 to 13, which is why those five match the 1894-95 directory; the upper end was still Pelham Terrace with its own numbers 4 to 19, which convert by 39 minus n into 21 to 35; the published 24 to 15 fills 20, 22 and 24 into 19, 17 and 15; and 37 and 39 are left for the corner at Tattershall. No number is claimed twice and none is left over.

questions.title: Nine households at the top of The Ropewalk, beyond where the record's numbering stops
questions.detail:
The record's Ropewalk runs **2 to 56**. Both the 1861 and the 1871 walks hold households **beyond 56**, and they agree with each other.

| round | where in the walk | households | people |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1861** | schedules **100-104**, *before* 56 in a descending walk | 5 | **52** |
| **1871** | schedules **218-223**, *after* 56 in an ascending walk | 4 | ~31 |

**1861:** John Gibson, John Heard, Sarah Hurst, **Henry Linton**, clergyman, born Ireland, and **Major Charles Edward Burt, Royal Artillery**.

**1871:** **Benjamin Dowson**, solicitor, twelve in the house; George Hardick, corn miller; **Richard Birkin**, magistrate, landowner and lace manufacturer, eleven in the house; and **John Gibson**.

## Why it matters

**John Gibson is at that end in both rounds** - first schedule of the 1861 Ropewalk, last of the 1871 one. Two enumerators walking in opposite directions put the same man at the same end, ten years apart. Whatever these houses are, they were standing in 1861 *and* 1871.

**A. Hagues reads the ground above 56 as empty until the 1950s.** Both things cannot be true of the same ground, so one of these is the answer:

- the houses were **named, not numbered**, and the record's list simply stops where the numbers do;
- they stood on the **odd side**, which this record does not hold at all - every Ropewalk property in it is even;
- the top of the Ropewalk was **renumbered into Park Terrace**, whose 1861 run has more schedules than houses;
- they were demolished long before the property list was drawn up, and the 1950s buildings are the *second* thing on that ground.

**Richard Birkin is worth finding on his own account** - one of the great Nottingham lace names, in a house this record cannot place.

Links: [[the-ropewalk-1861-run-between-34-and-16]], [[the-1861-round-has-no-house-numbers]].

questions.title: Clinton Terrace is numbered as Derby Road on the census and as Clinton Terrace in the record
questions.detail:
**Settled.** The record holds seven Clinton Terrace properties and writes each address with both numbers - **1 Clinton Terrace (127 Derby Road)** through **7 Clinton Terrace (139 Derby Road)**. The 1881 enumerator uses **only the Derby Road number**, and calls the street Clinton Terrace. The two run in step, odd numbers, 127 to 139, and six households are filed on that correspondence.

**Open.** The page also gives **119, 121, 123 and 125 Clinton Terrace**, below the record's range, and **115 and 117 Derby Road** above it. Those six houses are not in the property list. Are they part of the same terrace, or a different run that happens to adjoin it?

**Next.** Check the Park Estate plan and the directories for where Clinton Terrace begins and ends. If it runs from 115, six properties want creating. Related: [[derby-terrace-is-ten-houses-and-the-record-holds-one]].

questions.title: WAITING ON 1871 - Berrey and Wilkins, Pelham Terrace, which end of Newcastle Drive?
questions.detail:
**Held until the 1871 round is finished**, at A. Hagues's word. The rest of the round will settle it better than argument will: every house in it that gets a number narrows where these two can be.

**Settled:** schedules 138 and 139 of 1871 are **George Berrey**, lace manufacturer, ten in the house, and **John Wilkins**, textile manufacturer, six. The page says *Pelham Terrace* and gives no number. They come immediately after schedule 137, which is now 13 Newcastle Drive, and immediately before the walk turns into Western Terrace.

**And the run before them is confirmed**, which is worth saying because it was an inference when it was filed. The 1881 round has **Jane Ward at 5 Newcastle Drive**; the 1871 run puts **William G Ward at 5**. The same family at the same number in two rounds, arrived at from opposite directions - 1871 walking up from 1, 1881 walking down from 35.

## Three readings, and the case for each

**21 and 23 Newcastle Drive** *(the likeliest)*. The enumerator changed what he wrote, and that is itself the evidence: he had written *Newcastle Terrace* seven times and then wrote *Pelham Terrace*, because that is what the householders called it. [[the-newcastle-drive-rule]] puts the lowest Pelham Terrace number - 18 - at **21 Newcastle Drive**. The 1881 round backs the name up at that end: *Bruncliffe, 6 and 8 Pelham Terrace* sits between 35 and 29 Newcastle Drive. Against it: 15, 17 and 19 are then passed over without being marked empty.

**15 and 17 Newcastle Drive.** He has just walked 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13 without a break, and these are the next two; 15, 17 and 19 are precisely the numbers claimed by neither old name. Against it: he would have had no reason to change the street he was writing.

**37 and 35.** He jumped to the far end. Against it: he would then have walked back down 33, 31, 29, and the next schedule is Western Terrace instead.

**Nothing has been filed.** Every Newcastle Drive number from 15 to 39 stands empty in 1871, so all three readings are open and the record would accept any of them, which is exactly why it should not be guessed.

**Next:** the 1871 page itself will have written the street at the head of the column and dittoed it; reading the *headings* rather than the households, as with [[the-cavendish-road-east-ditto-run]], would show where Newcastle Terrace stops and Pelham Terrace starts. Failing that, George Berrey is a lace manufacturer who had moved to Clumber Road by 1881 - a directory of the 1870s would name his house. Links: [[newcastle-terrace-is-the-low-end-of-newcastle-drive]].

questions.title: 1 to 4 Clare Valley are numbered from the walk, not from the page
questions.detail:
The 1891 enumerator gives **no number** for any house on Clare Valley. Schedules 142 to 145 have been filed at **1, 2, 3 and 4** on the walk, and the reasoning should be visible rather than buried:

- **Only five houses stood on Clare Valley in 1891.** The four named houses at the cul-de-sac end - Grove House, Ribble Lodge, Springdale and The Spinney - were built between **1905 and 1916**. The five of about 1890 are numbers 1 to 5.
- **There are exactly five consecutive Clare Valley schedules**, 142 to 146.
- **146 was already filed at number 5** (Arthur Lewis, there again in 1901), so the run must climb 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
- **4 Clare Valley is independently attested**: the 1901 page writes "4 Clare Valley" against Lawrence Wilkins at #62.

| schedule | filed at | head |
|---|---|---|
| 142 | **1 Clare Valley** | Frederick Pearson Jr., basket and perambulator manufacturer |
| 143 | **2 Clare Valley**, named *Ivedene* | William Ed Barlow, provision merchant |
| 144 | **3 Clare Valley** | Alfred Jas Blackburn, hosiery machine builder |
| 145 | **4 Clare Valley** | Arthur Cox, wool merchant |
| 146 | 5 Clare Valley *(already held)* | Arthur Lewis, lace merchant |

**It is an inference, and reversible.** If the walk ran the other way the four would be 5, 4, 3, 2 - but 146 is the last of the run and is number 5, which rules that out unless #63 is not 5 Clare Valley.

**Ivedene is a house name the record has not held before**, and it belongs to 2 Clare Valley on this reading. Links: [[sunnyside-park-terrace-or-park-valley]].

questions.title: The 1881 Lenton Avenue enumerator numbered almost nothing
questions.detail:
**Eleven of his seventeen households carry no house number at all**, only the street - among them Joseph Thornley the lace manufacturer employing over two hundred hands, John Heeley with a household of ten, and Thomas C Moore. Those fifty-four people are in the record but unfiled.

**His walk is the only evidence of order that exists.** He wrote the houses up in sequence, and six of them he did number, so the unnumbered ones sit between fixed points. Working out from those six may place the rest without any further source.

questions.title: 10 Pelham Crescent in 1891: the house number can be read two ways
questions.detail:
**Schedule 6 of the 1891 census carries John Henry Brown's household of eleven**, and the house number on the page supports two different readings, neither decisively. The household has been left unfiled rather than filed on a coin toss.

John Henry Brown is a wine merchant, and appears ten years earlier as head of schedule 88 on the same street, also without a usable house number. Placing either household would place the other.

questions.title: 13 Cavendish Crescent South is the house now numbered 1 South Road
questions.detail:
**Answered by A. Hagues.** Eight people are returned on the 1891 census at **13 Cavendish Crescent South** - Roby Eddington Thorpe (#3184), 51, solicitor and farmer; his wife Nelly (#3185), 46; their daughter Dorothea Mary Roby (#3186), 15; **Mary Mundella** (#3187), 58, visiting; and four servants, Ellen Savinge (#3188), Selina Draycott (#3189), Emma Bussenhart (#3190) and Grace Leech (#3191). No number 13 exists in the record or in any directory volume, so they were held unfiled. They are now filed at **1 South Road (#301)**, and 13 Cavendish Crescent South is kept on that property as a former address.

**The house has gates onto both roads.** The record's own description of #301 records 'original gate piers on Cavendish Crescent South and South Road', and a later extension and porch adjacent to Cavendish Crescent South. A corner house with two frontages can be addressed to either, which is the whole of the difficulty.

**The number survives on the outbuilding.** A. Hagues found a street view of the site: the sign reads **13, The Studio**, on a converted range beside a garage, attached to the main house. The record's description of #301 accounts for both - 'plan by H. Butler for garage building for James Curnow c1920' and 'outbuildings altered/rebuilt to form residential accommodation'. So 13 did not disappear; it stayed on the annexe when the principal house was re-addressed to South Road. The studio is a one-bedroom flat today and could never have held a household of eight, but in 1891 it was still an outbuilding, and 13 was the main house's number on its crescent frontage.

**The same thing happened next door.** Ellenborough House, 3 South Road (#302), was returned in 1891 as **7 Clumber Road**, and that is kept on it as a former address. Two houses at the same junction, in the same census, addressed to roads other than the ones they now belong to.

**Supporting, and worth keeping in view:** 1 South Road held no 1891 census at all while both its neighbours did - the Evanses at 2 and the McCraiths at 3 - so a corner house stood apparently empty in a year when an eight-person household nearby had nowhere to go.

**The one thing unchecked.** On the enumerator's south-side page the household falls between number 7 and number 15, where 9, 11 and 13 would be, rather than at the end of a run; 9 and 11 appear nowhere on that page. The schedule numbers either side of the Thorpes would confirm this reading or overturn it. Mary Mundella, visiting, may also connect this household to the Mundella on the lace makers' watch list, which is a separate thread worth pulling.

questions.title: 8 Cavendish Crescent North — the number survives on a door
questions.detail: The record runs 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 on the odd side and 10, 12, 14 upward on the even, with no 8 and no 6. A walk of the crescent found no house numbered 8, but **an old door with 8 on it at the back of the house below**. So the number was in use and the house has since been absorbed, renumbered or demolished. Which house does that door belong to now, and was 8 a separate dwelling?

questions.title: 110 names on Dougal's map have no house in the record
questions.detail:
Mining the map turned up 964 labels. 86 matched a property outright; the 115 that did not are kept in `data/map_dougal_unmatched.json` with their position on the page and a guess at what each one is: **69 look like house names, 33 like subdivisions** — coach houses, mews, lodges, garden flats — and 13 are notes or people rather than places.

**Settled.** Re-running the match today against every house name the record holds, only five of the 115 land: Charnwood, Clumber Lodge, East Lodge, Barrack Yard, and one false hit where *Newcastle House* caught *Castle House* on a shared word. **110 are still unplaced.**

**Open.** The reason is not that the map is wrong. The record knows **412 properties and 64 distinct house names between them**, because the names sit in history prose where nothing can search them and only **17** have been written into the house-names panel. Until [[house-names-live-in-prose]] is worked, most of these 110 cannot match anything even where the house is already held.

**Next.**

1. **The 33 subdivisions first.** A coach house, mews or lodge belongs to the house it was built for, so each one names a **parent property** rather than a new one — the same job as [[households-filed-to-a-part-not-the-house]]. *The Coach House* appears four ways and *The Lodge* three; the position on the page is what separates them.
2. **Then the 69 house names.** This is the single largest source of new house names available, and it wants somebody who knows the estate rather than a search. Some are earlier names — *Arlington House formerly Holmedale* carries its own answer, and *Holmesdale* elsewhere on the map is likely the same house again.
3. **Every label carries its x/y on the map page**, so a name can be placed by what sits either side of it even when the label itself means nothing.

A few are not houses at all and should be dropped rather than chased: *Hard Courts*, *Grass Courts*, *Queen Anne's Bowling Green*, *Rear Car Park*, *Tunnel Road*.

questions.title: Named houses on the 1911 covers, and which ones the record can already place
questions.detail:
**Six 1911 schedules give a house NAME where the property record works in numbers.** A. Hagues placed four of them from his own knowledge of the estate; two are still open.

| named on the cover | street | where it belongs |
|---|---|---|
| **Melbrook House** | Park Valley | **7 Park Valley**, #263 - from the enumerator's address column |
| **Lynwood** | Tattershall Drive | **2 Tattershall Drive**, #307 |
| **St Ives** | Tattershall Drive | **4 Tattershall Drive**, #309 |
| **Clare Valley Lodge** | Clare Valley | **open** |
| **Elmsdale** | Clare Valley | **5 Clare Valley**, #63 - placed by A. Hagues from the ground |
| **Goddards Lodge** | Tattershall Drive | **open** - and it may settle Elmsdale |
| **Ivy Dene** | Clare Valley | **open** - from the 1901 round, not 1911 |

**Two of the open ones explain households the record has never been able to file.**

- **Clare Valley Lodge.** The 1901 round holds George Hill, a Baptist minister of 53, with his wife and six children, parked unfiled under *Lodge, Clare Valley (no house of that name in the record)*. The 1911 cover names the house outright in the householder's own hand, so the Lodge is real.
- **Elmsdale. SETTLED.** It is **5 Clare Valley**, #63 - the corner house, semi-detached with number 4, which is how the record describes that pair. Arthur Lewis the iron merchant and his family had been unfiled since the 1891 round because Wright's Directory gave two streets and nobody could tell which was meant. **Placing it filed seventeen rows** - eight for 1891, seven for 1901 and two for 1911 - and 5 Clare Valley now holds a continuous line through four censuses where it held only 1921. Emma Elizabeth Goddard heads it in **both 1911 and 1921**, which confirms the placing from inside the record.

**Goddards Lodge may answer that.** The 1911 schedule for Goddards Lodge, Tattershall Drive holds a coachman, and Elmsdale on Clare Valley holds **Emma Elizabeth Goddard**. If the house stands on Clare Valley and its lodge on Tattershall Drive, **the directory was right twice** and the contradiction was never one. The grounds would run between the two roads - which is exactly what 2 and 4 Tattershall Drive do, their gardens reaching Huntingdon Drive. **Not proved. It fits the ground.**

**So several properties want creating**, and four households that have never had a house go to them.

**It is not only these streets.** Park Valley has no house names in the record at all and its numbers jump from 11 to 15 - [[park-valley-12-13-14]], [[melbrook-house-park-valley]]. Hamilton Drive has the same trouble in [[1901-house-names-not-in-the-record]].

**The 1911 covers are the cheapest source of house names there is**, because every household has one and A. Hagues is reading them anyway. On why the ones the record *does* know were hard to find, see [[house-names-live-in-prose]].

**A seventh, from the 1901 round.** *Ivy Dene [?], Clare Valley* holds **George Ranson**, 39, a grocer employing others, his wife Emily, their son of 12 and a servant - four people with no house, under a name the property list does not have. The reading of the name is uncertain, which is why it carries a query, but a household of four is worth placing and the 1911 covers may well name it outright.

questions.title: Sunnyside is on Park Valley in 1891 and again in 1939, and the record has it on Park Terrace
questions.detail:
**Two rounds now say Park Valley, and they are forty-eight years apart.**

| round | as the page writes it | household |
|---|---|---|
| **1891** | *Sunny Side, **Park Valley***, schedule 139 | **John Howard Bradwell**, auctioneer and valuer, his wife, seven children, two visitors and three servants - **fifteen in the house** |
| **1939** | *12 **Park Valley** (Sunnyside)*, schedule 121 | a **nine-person guest house** under Beatrice Anton |

The record holds **Sunnyside on Park Terrace** (#390), and Park Terrace is the only one of the three placements with nothing behind it. Two independent enumerators, in different centuries, wrote Park Valley.

**And 12 Park Valley does not exist in the property list**, which is why twenty-four people across two rounds are sitting unfiled - see [[twelve-and-thirteen-park-valley-are-not-in-the-record]].

**Done.** 12 Park Valley was created as **#415** on 24 September 2026 and both households filed against it, twenty-four people in all. The house carries *Sunny Side* as a former name.

**Still open, and smaller than it was:** whether the record's Park Terrace Sunnyside is a second house of the same name or simply wrong. A 1930s street directory would print both streets and settle it.

**Crescent Lodge is settled, and it was not the house I first filed it to.** The 1921 census has **Thomas Berridge Cox and Ada Elizabeth Cox at 16 Cavendish Crescent North**, and the 1939 Register has the same couple at **Crescent Lodge** - so Crescent Lodge is 16, and the 1939 household has been moved onto the same property as their 1921 one. The record carries two properties for that number, **#411 as 16** and **#31 as 16 and 16a**; everything is now on #411 and #31 stands empty. See [[two-properties-for-sixteen-cavendish-crescent-north]].

**Tower House is unchanged and still open.** The 1939 page puts it on **Park Terrace**, schedule 135, under Henry M Stanley the hospital house governor; the record has Tower House at **53 Park Row**. One round only, so it does not have the weight the Sunnyside case now has. Links: [[house-names-live-in-prose]], [[the-cavendish-road-east-ditto-run]].

questions.title: A household from before a house was divided belongs to the house, not to a flat of it
questions.detail:
**Cliff House is one house. 33 Lenton Road is a piece of it.** The property list holds #196 as *Cliff House, Lenton Road (32, 33, 33a, 33b)* and #365 as *33 Lenton Road* - which exists only because Cliff House was divided.

**The Parr household had been filed at both.** 1901 at Cliff House, 1911 and 1921 at 33 Lenton Road, as though a solicitor with eight children and four living-in servants had taken one flat of a divided house. **Twenty-three rows have been moved back to the parent.**

**The general rule, because this will happen again:** a census household from before a house was divided belongs to **the house**, not to one of the parts it later became. Filing it to a part makes the house look emptier than it was and the part look older than it is.

**Where else to look.** Any property in the list whose address carries a bracketed set of numbers - the shape of *Cliff House, Lenton Road (32, 33, 33a, 33b)* - has parts, and those parts may be holding households that belong to the whole. **It is a search worth running once across the list** rather than waiting to trip over the next one.

questions.title: Park Lodge is the last unplaced name on Tattershall Drive
questions.detail: Two of the three are settled. Belwood is the house at the corner with Tennis Drive, which carries the name on its door post and shares NG7 1AD with Ellington and the four flats at Tennis View; Ellington is Ellington House (#312), as expected. The Lodge is Gartree Lodge, 17a Tattershall Drive (#404), which is not what this question first guessed — it supposed The Lodge was the lodge beside the tennis ground that OpenStreetMap calls Park Lodge. From HM Land Registry's price paid data, which records a house name beside the number for every sale since 1995. questions.title: Two small Tattershall Drive households whose covers give no number
questions.detail:
**Two 1911 covers read simply *Tattershall Drive* with no number at all**, and both are households quite unlike the rest of the street.

| head | rooms | trade |
|---|---|---|
| **William Henry Holmes**, 41 | 6 | representative to maltsters and yeast merchants; his retired licensed-victualler father and mother living with him |
| **Walter William Jackson**, 33 | 4 | barman at a public house, with a wife, a daughter of 5 and **a boarder** - George William Knott, 57, a widowed piano maker from London |

**Everything else on the street has nine, ten or eleven rooms and servants living in.** These have six and four, no servants, and one of them takes in a lodger. **The Park held both kinds of household at once**, and the record is thinner on the second kind because the big houses are easier to trace.

**Neither can be filed from the schedule**, because the 1911 schedule carries no address - only the cover does, and these two covers were not completed properly. **The enumerator's address column will settle both**, by reading the running order either side of them.

**The likely candidates are the small houses**, not the numbered ones: Carnoustie Lodge, #311, is described in the record as *one of the smallest pre-1918 houses in The Park*, built about 1878-80 **probably as a coachman's house**; Gartree Lodge and Ellington House are the others on the street. **Do not guess between them.** A third small Tattershall Drive household, at Goddards Lodge, names its house and still cannot be placed - [[clare-valley-missing-houses]].

**Do not file any of the three until the address column is read.**

questions.title: Huntingdon Drive runs past number 10 — the record stops there
questions.detail: The record holds Huntingdon Drive as numbers 1 to 10. Dougal de Havilland's map draws a second run on the north-east side, numbered up the other way: 11 Burnham House, 13 The Magpies, 14 The Cottage, 15 The Coach House, The Hunting Lodge, 17, and 18 The Round House, formerly The Spiral, with Birchwood beyond. Only The Cottage is in the record, and only because a census household carried its name. Are these separate houses with their own numbers, or flats and coach houses belonging to houses already held? If they are houses, the record is missing half a street.

questions.title: 18 Cavendish Crescent North is still missing from the record
questions.detail:
The record held 16a and 18a but neither 16 nor 18 — although the listed-building descriptions of all four houses in that group name **"Nos. 16, 18, 20 and 22/24"** outright. They were built c.1885 as four substantial houses adjacent to each other, and three were later subdivided: the main part kept as one household, the former kitchen and butler's quarters made into a flat. So 16a is the flat of 16, and 18a the flat of 18.

**16 is now in the record as Crescent Lodge (#411)**, created because a census household was returned there. **18 still is not**, because nothing has yet been found living at it. What was 18 called, and is anyone on a return recorded there? And do 16 and 16a front the road differently, which would settle where each should sit on the map?

questions.title: Clinton House and Sunnyside may be one house renamed - the surveys label the same ground differently
questions.detail:
**ANSWERED 26 September 2026, from the Ordnance Survey sheet and Dougal de Havilland's Park Map together.**

They are **two houses side by side on the same ridge**, and the question only arose because Sunnyside's marker had been dropped on Clinton House's building.

- **Clinton House** is named on the Ordnance Survey sheet, stands in its own grounds running down from Park Terrace towards Clare Valley, and **is still there**.
- **Sunnyside** is marked separately on the Park Map as ***Former site of Sunnyside***, further east, off **Park Terrace** by **Sun Drive**, around The Studio House and Abbot House. It is gone.

**So the two contradictions dissolve at once.** Clinton House leaves no trace in the census or the directories because it is a different house that nobody in this record lived in; and Sunnyside is marked as a former site because it was demolished - which is exactly what the record's own weight says, since it held **fifteen people in 1891**, **two households at once in 1921** and a **guest house of nine in 1939**. A large house, lost, with something smaller on part of its ground now.

**A. Hagues was right from the first sentence:** an enormous house on the ground the cliff-hugging twentieth-century Park Terrace houses stand on, with a Sun Drive, Clare Valley or Huntingdon Drive address. The census bears it out - Park Valley from below in 1891 and 1939, Park Terrace from above in 1921.

**What is left to do is only the marker.** #390 still sits on Clinton House and wants dragging to the Park Map's *Former site of Sunnyside*. Recorded on the property as known wrong.

**Sun Drive is deliberately not a street in this record.** It is on the Park Map as **NG7 1BQ**, running between the Clare Valley houses and Park Terrace, but A. Hagues gives it **only one property - Sunnyside itself** - so there is nothing to file to it and adding the street would buy nothing.

Links: [[sunnyside-park-terrace-or-park-valley]].

**And Clinton House itself may also be gone.** A. Hagues reads the Park Map as dating the building on that ground to the **1970s**, and it carries **no name** there. So the house standing today is very likely a replacement, and Clinton House was demolished like Sunnyside - which would explain the total absence of the name from the directories and from every search made for it. **Two large houses lost off one ridge**, one of them leaving only a map label.

## The 1953 survey names that ground Sunnyside

**Sheet SK5639, revised 1953,** labels **Sunnyside** on the plot - the same grounds the older 25-inch sheet calls **Clinton House**. So the likeliest answer is no longer *two houses side by side* but **one house renamed between the surveys**, which would explain at a stroke why Clinton House leaves no trace in any census, directory or search: by the time those records begin, it was being called Sunnyside.

**Against that**, A. Hagues reads the Park Map as dating the building on that ground to the 1970s and giving it no name, and Dougal marks *Former site of Sunnyside* off Park Terrace by Sun Drive. Those two still want reconciling with the 1953 sheet.

**The test is a dated map between the two surveys**, or the Newcastle estate papers.

questions.title: The house names the 1901 census used - seven now placed from the directory, two still missing
questions.detail:
**The 1901 enumerator wrote house names where the record keeps numbers**, and nine of the names he used appear nowhere in the property list, on any street:

**Fairfield**, **Oakleigh**, **Glendale**, **Beechwood** and **Douglas House** on Hamilton Drive; **Lea Hurst** and **Holm Vale** on Fishpond Drive; **Gardenwood** on Clumber Road; and **St John's**, on the stretch between Newcastle Circus and Maxtoke Road.

**These are not small households.** Lea Hurst held ten people under Mary Metcalf, a widow keeping six boarders - a leather merchant, two mechanical engineers, two bank clerks and an architect. Beechwood held nine, among them boarders from Switzerland and Curacao. Oakleigh held nine under Ralph J. Horner, a professor of music, with his son another professor of music.

**Hamilton Drive is the sharpest case.** The record holds sixteen properties there, numbered 1 to 11 with 1a, 1b, 1c, then 24, and Ferndene. The 1901 round gives thirteen households on that street and names five of them, and not one name matches. So either the houses were renamed between 1901 and whenever the record's numbering was set, or the numbered properties and the named ones are different buildings.

**Until a name is tied to a number, every one of these households stays unfiled.** A directory of the 1900s printing a name against a number would place a household of ten at a stroke, and Ralph Horner, professor of music, is the sort of resident a directory prints.

**ANSWERED IN LARGE PART, from Wright's Directory - a source already transcribed in this record.** Reading each house name together with the street it is printed under settles seven of the nine, four of them with a number:

- **Douglas House is 10 Hamilton Drive** - Alfred Clarke, civil engineer, 1894-95 and 1898-99; Benjamin R. Tomlinson, lace manufacturer, by 1910-11.
- **Oakleigh is on Hamilton Drive** - D. M. F. Gaskin, the Corporation water engineer, in 1894-95, and **Ralph Horner, mus. bac.**, in 1898-99. That is the professor of music the 1901 census gives at Oakleigh with his son.
- **Glendale is on Hamilton Drive** - John T. Roseblade, corn merchant's traveller, in both volumes, the same head the 1901 round gives.
- **Lea Hurst is on Fish Pond Drive** - Mrs Mary Metcalf in 1898-99, the widow with six boarders on the 1901 return; Arthur Hutchinson by 1910-11; and by 1913-14 it is Godfrey Walter's **boarding house** outright, which explains the household of ten.
- **Holm Vale is on Fish Pond Drive** - William E. Sisling, insurance manager, with Miss F. Sisling, 1898-99: the same household as 1901.
- **Leslie House is 31 Lenton Road** and **Yeldersley House is 43 Lenton Road** - Henry Clark the lace manufacturer and George Hicking of G. & W. N. H., both the heads the 1901 round gives.
- **Newlands is 33 Lenton Avenue**, which the census sheet already said.

**Two names appear in no volume at all: Fairfield and Beechwood**, both on Hamilton Drive, along with **Gardenwood** on Clumber Road and **St John's**. Beechwood is the lodging house of nine with boarders from Switzerland and Curacao; a house of that kind may have been let rather than owned, which is one reason a directory might pass over it.

**The two "clashes" were not clashes, and I was wrong to call them so.** The directory holds **two Cavendish Houses** - one on Cavendish Road East, Charles Sudbury's and later Mrs Marina Sudbury's, and a separate one on **Fish Pond Drive**, where **Charles O. Terry, insurance broker**, is printed in 1898-99. Terry is the exact head of the 1901 Fish Pond Drive schedule, so that household belongs at a Fish Pond Drive house of that name, not at #56. And **Burton House is on Maxtoke Road**, where Mrs Elizabeth A. Watson is printed in 1894-95 and 1898-99 - the same widow as the 1901 schedule. The record's Burton House on Newcastle Circus (#205) is a different building.

**What is now wanted** is not more sources but the work of matching: several of these names have no property in the record at all - Oakleigh, Glendale, Lea Hurst, Holm Vale, Cavendish House on Fish Pond Drive - and want creating before the households sitting unfiled can be placed against them.

**HAMILTON DRIVE: four numbers now have names against them.** A. Hagues has identified **1c as Ivy Nook** and **3 as Warwick House** from the houses themselves, and photographed the gate piers at **10, which reads WISTERIA HOUSE** today. The record already carried Wisteria House at #123, so the photograph confirms what was held rather than adding to it.

**And that settles Douglas House.** Wright's Directory prints *Douglas house, no. 10* on Hamilton Drive in 1894-95 (Alfred Clarke, civil engineer) and again in 1898-99, and Benjamin R. Tomlinson there by 1910-11. So **10 Hamilton Drive was Douglas House and is now Wisteria House** - one building under two names - and the 1901 household at Douglas House belongs to **#123**: Alice Clarke, a widow of 47 living on private means, with two Naylor visitors and a servant. She is #4257 in the record with an unfiled row, so this is a reassignment rather than an import.

**Alice is very likely Alfred's widow**, the directory having him at that house through the 1890s and the census giving her there alone on private means in 1901. The record holds no Alfred Clarke who fits - the three it has are a lace manufacturer born 1850, a schoolmaster born 1865 and a son born 1882 - so the civil engineer is absent from it, and the relationship is an inference rather than a fact until a marriage or a death notice says so.

**Three named houses on that street still have no number**: Fairfield (John H. Jackson, fruit salesman), Oakleigh (Ralph Horner) and Glendale (John T. Roseblade). The directory gives the street for all three but prints no number against them.

**And Beechwood appears twice on the 1901 round** - once unnumbered under Sarah Wilkinson, and again at schedule 85 as a lodging house of nine with boarders from Switzerland and Curacao. Two houses of one name, or one household my reading of the page split in two. It wants looking at before either is placed.

**The numbers still unaccounted for on Hamilton Drive** are 1, 1a, 1b, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 and 11, against which the round offers Fairfield, Oakleigh, Glendale, Beechwood and six households the enumerator left unnamed.

**The OS sheet adds two Hamilton Drive names and confirms Ivy Nook.** A. Hagues's 1:1250 extract marks **Ivy Nook** on Hamilton Drive, which he places at 1c, and gives **Clovelly** and **The Limes** on the north side beside Ferndene. None of the three is in the property record. It does not name Fairfield, Oakleigh, Glendale or Beechwood, so those four remain without a number from any source - map, directory or census.

**GLENDALE IS A BUILDING OF SEVERAL DWELLINGS, NOT ONE HOUSE.** A. Hagues has read the 1901 return at source on TheGenealogist, and the House column for Hamilton Drive gives, in order: **Glendale** (Alice M Roseblade), **Glendale** (Frank Hodson), **6 Glendale** (Walter Woodward), **7 Glendale** (Florence Cockburn). All on piece 3165.

So the numbers belong to the building, not to the street. **6 Glendale is not 6 Hamilton Drive**, and the two households cannot be filed at #119 and #120 on the strength of those figures - a mistake this note previously made and which is corrected here.

- **6 Glendale** - Walter Woodward, timber merchant and employer, 44; his housekeeper Mary Scotney; a visiting bank manager, William J. Pearce, with Annie E. Pearce; and a servant. Five people.
- **7 Glendale** - Florence Cockburn, 34, born at Rugby; her aunt Elizabeth Horsley on private means; a nephew, Herbert G. Neil, a lace warehouseman born in Scotland; a boarding chemical student, James J. Wedgwood; and a servant. Five people.

**This is why the earlier conflict would not reconcile.** John J. Roseblade at Glendale and Woodward and Cockburn at 6 and 7 are not competing for one house: they are neighbours in one building. The directory printing *Glendale, John T. Roseblade* on Hamilton Drive in 1894-95 and 1898-99 names the building, as directories generally do, without saying which part of it he held.

**A discrepancy in the head.** TheGenealogist gives **Alice M Roseblade** as head of the unnumbered Glendale household; the enumerator's page as read here gives **John. J. Roseblade**, 51, a corn merchant's agent, with daughters Emily, Alice and May Victoria, two French boarders and two servants. Alice is eighteen on that page and a school teacher's assistant, so she is unlikely to be its head. Either the index names a different person of the household, or there are two Roseblade households at Glendale.

**And the count does not agree.** TheGenealogist shows **nine households on Hamilton Drive** for 1901; my reading of the enumerator's pages gives thirteen. Some of mine are very likely on neighbouring streets, carried onto this tab because the schedules gave a house name and no street.

All ten are already in the record with unfiled rows, so they want reassigning rather than importing.

**A possible duplicate at number 7.** The record holds a 1921 resident of #120 as **Florence Coctbrand** - which reads like a misreading of Cockburn. If it is the same woman twenty years on, she is one person entered twice under a mangled surname. Worth checking before the 1901 row is filed, so the two are joined rather than left as strangers in the same house.

**And an unresolved conflict about Glendale.** A. Hagues reads Glendale as covering 6 and 7 Hamilton Drive. But the 1901 round puts **Glendale at schedule 80 under John J.
