Roseblade**, corn merchant's agent, with eight people - and Wright's Directory prints *Glendale, John T. Roseblade* on Hamilton Drive in both 1894-95 and 1898-99. Roseblade cannot be at 6 or 7 on census night if Woodward and Cockburn are.

So either **Glendale is a building name covering more houses than the two**, in the way Ferndene shares a structure with 6 and 7 Peveril Drive, or Roseblade's household sits at another number on the street and the name has moved. Nothing is filed at Glendale until that is settled.

**FOUR OF THE THIRTEEN ARE GLENDALE HOUSEHOLDS.** Set against A. Hagues's reading of the source, my transcription of the Hamilton Drive round names Glendale only once. The source gives four:

- **Glendale** - the Roseblade household of eight, schedule 80.
- **Glendale** - **Frank Hodson**, builder and stone merchant, 47, with his wife Mary, five children from nineteen down to a baby, and a servant. Nine people. My reading has them under the street alone, the schedule number never captured because the page headed them only "Next schedule".
- **6 Glendale** - Walter Woodward's five.
- **7 Glendale** - Florence Cockburn's five.

Twenty-seven people in one building, which for a group of late Victorian villas is entirely plausible and explains why the name recurs across the round without contradiction.

**That probably accounts for the count as well.** TheGenealogist shows nine households on Hamilton Drive against my thirteen; if the four Glendale entries are indexed differently, or if some of my thirteen sit on Peveril Drive or Kenilworth Road - the same corner problem that put Thorndale in two streets at once - the difference closes.

**Beechwood is the one that does not resolve.** My reading has it twice, under Sarah Wilkinson with five people and at schedule 85 under Mary Pearson with nine, and it is not among the four houses the source names on this street. Two houses of one name, one household split by my reading of the page, or a house on a neighbouring street: still open.

**BEECHWOOD, IN FULL, FOR WHOEVER GOES BACK TO THE SOURCE.** The two households my reading gives under this name:

**Schedule 85** - nine people, and not a family at all but a lodging house. Mary Pearson, 37, a professional sick nurse on her own account, is the first named and is entered as a **boarder**, so the head is not among them - the page gives no head at all, which is itself a sign the household was split across a page turn. With her: Arthur H. Niblett, 32, civil engineer, from Gloucestershire; George W. Sellars, 33, lace warehouseman, born Switzerland; **Fritz Firmenich, 26, chemical manufacturer, and Hugo Firmenich, 20, lace warehouseman, both Swiss**; Henry Perevia, 27, commercial traveller, born **Curacao**; Maurice Potter, 43, merchant and employer, from Skirbeck in Lincolnshire; and two servants, Elizabeth Burrows and Florence Tett.

**No schedule captured** - five people, and a family: Sarah Wilkinson, 52, born at Burnaston in Derbyshire, with two sons and two daughters, all four born at Newark, the sons a grocer's assistant and a grocer's warehouseman.

**Firmenich is the name to search.** Two Swiss brothers in one Nottingham lodging house is about as distinctive as an index entry gets, and finding them settles which house Beechwood is, whether the two households share it, and whether the nine-person entry is one household or the tail of another. Henry Perevia of Curacao is nearly as good.

**THE WILKINSONS, AND WHY THEY ARE NOT YET PLACED.** A. Hagues finds a **Wilkinson household at Derby House, 1 Derby Terrace** - but in the **1911** return, not 1901. That is worth setting down carefully, because the two do not automatically join up:

- **Derby House is #97 in the record, and holds nobody in any year.** Whatever is at it in 1911 would be new.
- **The record has no 1911 Wilkinson household at all.** Its only two Wilkinsons that year are Sarah Elizabeth, a domestic servant of 28 at #239, and a Daisy at #34. So a family at Derby House in 1911 is genuinely missing, not misfiled.
- **The 1901 household stands apart.** Sarah Wilkinson, born about 1849, a widow of 52 from Burnaston in Derbyshire, with William 22, Florence 26, Maybell 24 and Stuart 17, all four born at Newark. She would be 62 in 1911.

**Nothing is filed on this yet.** A household ten years later at a house the record does not otherwise hold is a good lead and not a placement: the 1901 schedule would need to name Derby House, or the 1911 one to name the same children, before the two are joined. Until then the 1901 rows keep the Beechwood label my reading gave them, which is very likely wrong - the name probably belongs to the household that follows.

**A visitor my reading lost.** The original transcription of that 1901 household ends with **Alissimon Hopewell, visitor, 36**. She is in the record as **#1143, born 1864** - which matches 36 in 1901 exactly - but only from the **1921** return, as wife of Frank Handley Hopewell at #346. So the record holds the woman and lacks her 1901 row, which my parser dropped when it split the household. Six people, not five.

**BEECHWOOD IS ANSWERED, AND IT IS ONE HOUSEHOLD, NOT TWO.** The 1911 return supplied by A. Hagues gives **Sarah Wilkinson, 62, widow, born Burnaston in Derbyshire - a BOARDING HOUSE KEEPER** - at Derby House, 1 Derby Terrace, with thirteen people under her roof: her daughter Florence, a daily governess; eight boarders; and four servants whose occupations are written out as cook, kitchen maid and housemaids **of the boarding house**.

**That settles what the 1901 page was doing.** My reading split Beechwood into two households: Sarah Wilkinson with four children, and a separate group of nine beginning with Mary Pearson. The second had **no head at all** and began with somebody entered as a *boarder*, which I noted at the time as a sign of a page turn. It was. Sarah is the head; the nine are her lodgers; it is a single household of about fifteen, and she was keeping a boarding house at Beechwood in 1901 as she was at Derby House ten years later.

So the lodgers of 1901 - Arthur Niblett the civil engineer, George Sellars, **Fritz and Hugo Firmenich**, Henry Perevia of Curacao, Maurice Potter the merchant, and the servants Elizabeth Burrows and Florence Tett - belong with the Wilkinsons, and the household wants rejoining.

**She moved between the censuses.** Beechwood is on Hamilton Drive and Derby House on Derby Terrace, so these are two houses, not one renamed. A boarding-house keeper moving premises in ten years is unremarkable, and it means Beechwood still needs a number on Hamilton Drive - but it is no longer a mystery about who lived there.

**The 1911 household is new to the record.** Derby House (#97) holds nobody in any year, and the record has no 1911 Wilkinson household, so all thirteen would be created.

**AND A POSSIBLE NAME FOR IT.** A. Hagues recalls a **Beechdale House** on Peveril Drive near the Hamilton Drive corner, and has someone in Nottingham going to look. One syllable from Beechwood, on the corner that has already put Thorndale in two streets at once. See [[beechdale-house-peveril-corner]].

questions.title: Two girls' schools at 7 Western Terrace — when was each of them there?
questions.detail:
The house held Thornleigh Boarding and Day School for Girls, run by Miss E Leigh about 1900, and Auckland House School, a private boarding and day school for girls, briefly. Neither is dated here, and the record's only household at number 7 is the Hopewells in 1921 — a traveller of 65, his wife, a niece and two boarders — so neither school was there that year.

The 1901 return for the house should show Miss Leigh and her boarders outright, which would date Thornleigh and give the record a house full of women and girls that it does not have. Whether Auckland House came before or after is open, as is where each school went next. No Leigh is in the record at all.

Western Terrace held a third school in the same era: Broadgate took 1 and 2 from 1921 until 1997.

questions.title: Is there a Beechdale House on Peveril Drive - and is it Beechwood?
questions.detail:
**A. Hagues has a recollection of a house called BEECHDALE HOUSE, and places it on Peveril Drive near the Hamilton Drive corner.** Nothing of that name is in the record - not in the property list, not in any census transcription, not in Wright's Directory, and not on the OS sheet. He has asked someone in Nottingham to walk the corner and look for the name on the house itself. This note is here so that whatever they come back with lands somewhere.

**Why it matters more than a stray name usually would.** Beechwood is the one house name from the 1901 Hamilton Drive round still without a number. It held Sarah Wilkinson's boarding house of about fifteen - her four grown children and nine lodgers, among them the Swiss brothers Fritz and Hugo Firmenich and Henry Perevia of Curacao - before she moved the trade to Derby House by 1911. It appears in no volume of the directory and is not among the nine households the source counts on Hamilton Drive. **Beechdale and Beechwood are one syllable apart**, and a name seen on a gate is exactly the kind of evidence that would settle it.

**And that corner is already known to confuse the two streets.** Thorndale is a corner house numbered on Hamilton Drive and built into the Peveril Drive terrace; the 1901 enumerator wrote it under Peveril Drive. A house standing on Peveril Drive at the Hamilton end could reasonably be written under either street, which would explain why Beechwood cannot be fitted to a Hamilton Drive number and does not appear in the street's directory entries.

**Three things the name could turn out to be.**

- **The same house as Beechwood**, either misread by me on the enumerator's page or renamed since. That places Beechwood on the Peveril Drive side of the corner and closes the oldest open question on that round.
- **A different house altogether**, not in the property record. Peveril Drive already holds two named properties with no number - **Parkdale (#299)** and **Peveril House (#300)** - so an unnumbered named house there is the pattern, not the exception. A third would want creating, and the unnamed Peveril Drive households of 1901 (schedules 236, 237, 238, 240, and the one written under Park Dale at 228) are the candidates for who was in it.
- **Parkdale itself, misremembered.** This is the first thing to rule out. **Parkdale is already in the record on Peveril Drive** with no number against it, and it is a -dale name on the same short stretch. Seeing a plate and recalling it a month later as Beechdale is an easy slip and costs nothing to check.

**WHAT WOULD BE MOST USEFUL FROM NOTTINGHAM.** Not just whether the name is there, but:

1. **Which street the house fronts** - the door and the gate, not the side wall. That is the whole Thorndale problem in one observation.
2. **Whether a number is on the house as well as a name**, and what it is.
3. **Which houses stand either side of it**, named or numbered. Two neighbours fix a house in a row even when its own plate says nothing useful.
4. **A photograph of the plate**, which settles the spelling past any argument - dale or wood.

**In the meantime the record claims nothing.** No property is created, no household moved, and Beechwood stays where the 1901 page put it, on Hamilton Drive without a number.

questions.title: Belwood is the corner of Tattershall Drive and Tennis Drive — which households were in it?
questions.detail: Found, or as near as makes no difference. A. Hagues has it on the street: a house at the Tattershall Drive corner with Tennis Drive carries BELWOOD on the post beside its door. The Land Registry postcodes agree — Belwood and Ellington are both NG7 1AD, along with the four flats at Tennis View, while Park Lodge and The Lodge sit apart in NG7 1BX. Ellington House (#312) is already in the record at that end of the street, so Belwood is its neighbour. What stands there now is modern: brick, flat-roofed, tall narrow windows, later 20th century by the look of it, so whatever Dougal de Havilland and the OS sheets recorded has gone and the name was carried over to its replacement. That is worth saying carefully — the name on a modern door is evidence of the site, not proof that the old house stood on the same footprint. What is still wanted is a household. No census entry anywhere in the record names Belwood, or any address on Tattershall Drive, so under this record's rule it stays a name rather than a property until somebody is found living in it. Dougal's map puts Belwood at x 174.0, y 403.3 with Hazelwood beside it at x 187.0, y 408.7 — the map's own coordinates, which nothing in the record can yet turn into a position on the ground.

questions.title: Who ran Broadgate School after Ada Churley, and what happened to the houses in 1997?
questions.detail: Broadgate School occupied 1 and 2 Western Terrace from 1921 until 4 March 1997, initially run by Miss Ada Churley, who is on the 1921 census at number 1 as the principal of a school. Seventy-six years is longer than any household the record holds, and almost all of it is blank here: who ran the school after her, how many children it took, whether it used both houses from the start, and what became of the buildings after it closed. Both are flats now. Anyone who was taught there, or taught there, would settle most of this in an afternoon.

questions.title: Which South Road house is Lindo House?
questions.detail:
The 1891 return puts Julius Meyer, commission merchant, born in Germany, with his wife Alice Ann, five children, a governess and three servants — eleven people — at **Lindo House, South Road**. The return gives no number, and no house of that name is in the record: a search of all 413 properties finds no Lindo at all. The nearest name, Linden House (#87, formerly The Lindens), is on Clumber Road West, a different street, and is already entangled with the Homberger filing. So the household sits unfiled under the address the return gives.

**What the directory adds, and what it does not.** Wright's Directory prints 'Julius Meyrick, of M. Schilling & Co.' on South Road in 1894-95 (page 136, Leicester Special Collections id 164642) and 1898-99 (page 146, id 165322), with no number and no house name, almost certainly the same man under an anglicised spelling. He is printed between Gardenhurst and Parkhurst. That does not yield a number, because the printed walk is not a numeric run: the 1894-95 order is Thorpe, Ellenborough House (3), Gardenhurst (5), Meyrick, Parkhurst (4), Evans. It places him between those two houses on the ground, nothing more.

**The candidates.** South Road holds six houses in the record, numbered 1 to 6 with no gap. In 1891 only number 2 (the Evanses) and number 3 (the McCraiths, Ellenborough House) hold anybody, so **1, 4, 5 and 6 are all empty that year**. Four candidates is too many to choose from on position alone, and filing eleven people on a guess would be costly to unpick.

**What would settle it** is the 1891 enumerator's walk. The census route is geographic, so the schedules either side of Lindo House on the page — particularly its distance from Ellenborough House or from the Evanses at number 2 — would give the position directly. A. Hagues has transcribed the Evans household from that street and year, so the page may already be to hand.

**A loose end found alongside it, now settled:** the record dated Parkhurst, 4 South Road (#303), to 1925, against a directory that prints the house in 1894-95. A. Hagues has corrected the date to 1870. See [[parkhurst-build-date]].

**Being asked on the ground.** A. Hagues is putting the question to the current owners, which is the kind of answer this cannot be reasoned into. Meanwhile the candidates have narrowed: filing the Thorpe household at 1 South Road leaves the street's 1891 occupancy as 1 Thorpe, 2 Evans, 3 McCraith, so only 4, 5 and 6 stand empty. Of those, 4 is Parkhurst and 5 is Gardenhurst, both printed under their own names in the directory with other householders, which leaves **6 South Road** as the single unnamed vacancy. That is a narrowing and not a finding: the Thorpe case ended by showing that a house can sit on a corner and be addressed to another street entirely, so nothing is filed on it.

questions.title: 7 Park Valley is Melbrook House - and Park Valley has no house names at all
questions.detail:
**SETTLED. 7 Park Valley is Melbrook House.** The 1911 householder wrote *Melbrook House, Park* on the cover of his schedule and no number at all; A. Hagues checked the enumerator's address section, which gives **7 Park Valley**. The number is the official address and the name is what the family called it, and they are the same house.

**The action is to add the name to #263** - Map, click the house, House Names, Edit. The year is 1911 from this return; whether it was called that earlier or later is not yet known, so the years are best left open.

**WHAT IS NOT SETTLED IS THE REST OF THE STREET.** Not one of Park Valley's eighteen properties has a house name in the record - where Peveril Drive has Parkdale and Peveril House, and Hamilton Drive has Ferndene. A street of named Victorian villas carrying nothing but numbers is far likelier a gap in the record than a fact about the street, and Melbrook House turning up on the first cover anybody read is the evidence for that.

**Wright's Directory is the place to look**, and it is already transcribed into this record. It prints house names against householders where it has them. One pass down its Park Valley entries would probably name several houses at once.

**And a family question beside it.** The 1901 head of number 7 is **Alfred Wilson, 81**, living on means with his widowed daughter Alice Lynam. The 1911 head is **John Croshaw Wilson, 35**, a hosiery manufacturer. Forty-six years and the same surname in the same house: grandfather and grandson would fit, and nothing in the record says so. *Croshaw* is carried as a middle name by both daughters, which makes the family easy to follow.

See [[1901-house-names-not-in-the-record]] for the same problem on Hamilton Drive.

questions.title: Which house was Newcastle House in 1891?
questions.detail:
Arthur Bee, butler, 48, with his wife Mary, his son Arthur Henry, a clerk in a lace warehouse, and his daughter Mary Corner Bee, a dressmaker, are returned at **Newcastle House** on the 1891 census. All four (#3490-#3493) are in the record **unfiled**, by A. Hagues's decision, because no property of that name exists and the evidence for placing them is all from a later date.

**What points at 19 Park Terrace.** Wright's Directory prints 'Newcastle house, Clark Wm. Froggatt, (Nottingham Mills Co)' on Park Terrace in 1910-11, 1913-14 and 1915-16, and the record has William Froggatt Clark as head of **19 Park Terrace** (#379) on both the 1911 and 1921 returns. Same man, same house name, same street: 19 Park Terrace was Newcastle House in the 1910s.

**Why that is not enough for 1891.** The gap is nineteen years, and a house name can move to a neighbouring building or a number be re-cut in that time. Worse for the inference, the directory shows Clark somewhere else earlier: 'Wm. F. Clark, of Nottm Mills Co.' is printed at **11 Park Terrace** in 1894-95 and 1898-99. So he reached Newcastle House between 1899 and 1910, and in 1891 the house was somebody else's - which is consistent with the Bees being there, but leaves the building unidentified.

**Two other things worth weighing.** #379 is a census-only property: no build date, no description, nothing but returns. And a butler as head of household, with his own grown children working outside the house and no employer's family on the schedule, usually means a lodge, a coach house or rooms over stables rather than the principal house - or a house being kept while its owners were away. Which it was changes what Newcastle House means on this return.

**What would settle it cheaply:** the 1891 enumerator's walk. If the Bees' schedule sits among the Park Terrace numbers near 19, the identification holds; if it sits elsewhere, it does not. The page is in A. Hagues's hands. Failing that, a rate book or the 1901 return for the same stretch would name the house.

questions.title: Park Mount is on Park Drive, and was Otto Homberger’s for twenty years
questions.detail:
**Answered from Wright's Directory, which prints it in every volume held.** *Park mount, Otto Homberger, of Homberger & Co.* appears on **Park Drive** in 1894-95 and 1898-99, and *Homberger Otto (Homberger & Co)* at the same house in 1910-11, 1913-14 and 1915-16. Twenty-one years in one house.

**The 1901 census agrees.** Schedule 222 of that round is headed *Park Drive, "Park Mount"* and gives Otto Homberger, a lace merchant of 49, a German subject naturalised British, with his wife Kate and three servants.

**The record holds no property called Park Mount.** Park Drive has nine - numbered 1 to 9 with Ashley House and Clumber House among them - and none carries the name. So either it is one of those under a name the record has not kept, or it is a house the property list does not hold.

**Kate Homberger is the reason this matters beyond the house.** Her marriage bears on the Dowson household at Felixstowe, and Otto is one of the German lace merchants whose naturalisation the record deliberately keeps in the birthplace field. A. Hagues has said the house may be identifiable on foot.

**Until it is placed**, the 1901 household stays unfiled - see [[1901-house-names-not-in-the-record]] for the others in the same position.

questions.title: Peveril Drive: which house is Parkdale, which is Dudley Lodge, and where is Castle Rock?
questions.detail:
**Settled by A. Hagues, from the 1911 census key and his own knowledge of the street.** The 1911 return names six houses on Peveril Drive that the record held only partly, and two of them had been put on the wrong properties.

- **11 Peveril Drive (#296) is Ivanhoe Lodge** - 'I used to walk past it.' The record already had that as its house name, but also carried **Dudley Lodge** as a former name, taken from the OS 1:1250 sheet. That has been removed: Dudley Lodge is a different house, and the 1911 key lists Ivanhoe Lodge and Dudley Lodge as two separate households on the same page, so one property cannot be both.
- **12 Peveril Drive (#297) is Dudley Lodge.** The record had it as **Parkdale**, sourced to A. Hagues himself; he now corrects that. Parkdale is kept on #297 as a former name only because the record carried it until now - not because the house bore it.
- **Parkdale is #299**, the unnumbered property of that name, which he confirms. The census supports it independently: the household his key places at Park Dale - Woodward, Cole, Barker and Galpin - is already filed at #299 for 1911.
- **Castle Rock is 5 Peveril Drive (#376)**, now named. The modern map shows 1 and 2 Castle Rock beside The Coach House; he judges the census Castle Rock to be the one now numbered 2, number 1 not having existed then. This is the least corroborated of the four - no directory line or OS sheet has been checked against it yet.
- **7 Peveril Drive (#293)** already carries Harlech House as a former name, matching the key's Harlech.
- **Easdale** (the Polley household) has no property in the record and is not created here.

**Why this mattered.** Twenty-two people sat unfiled under a single label, 'PeD1 Peveril Drive', which was a load artefact rather than an address: the first household's tag had been applied to a whole page of five families. A. Hagues supplied the key that splits them, and the house names above are what allow most of them to be placed.

**The 1901 return has now been read, and it tests all of this.** The enumerator walked the drive giving house names and almost no numbers, exactly as 1911 does: Dudley Lodge, Harlech House, Homebush, Thorndale, Castle Rd House and Sunnyside, with only No 3 numbered - August R. von Renesse, a lace warehouse manager and a German subject, keeping house with his mother-in-law and two servants.

**Four of the six confirm the settlement above.** Dudley Lodge, Harlech House and Castle Rd House are the names now held at #297, #293 and (as Castle Rock) #376, and Ivanhoe stood **uninhabited** on census night 1901, which fits a house the record holds at #296. Park Dale, at schedule 228, is Fredk J. Elborough's household of eight and belongs to #299.

**Three names are new to this street, and two of them collide with houses elsewhere in The Park.** Homebush held Edward Sanderson, a widowed shipping and forwarding agent, with three grown children; **Thorndale** held Henry Towle, station master on the Midland Railway; **Sunnyside** held Herbert Norrell, a railway contractor of 29. Two railwaymen next door to one another is the kind of pattern a directory will confirm.

**Homebush has no property in the record at all.** But **Thorndale is carried as a former name of 24 Hamilton Drive (#125)**, and **Sunnyside is a property in its own right on Park Terrace (#390)**. Neither is on Peveril Drive. So either the name was used twice in The Park, or the 1901 enumerator's Peveril Drive round strayed into a neighbouring street, or one of the existing records has the street wrong.

**Thorndale is answered, and it is a corner house - which is why two sources appeared to disagree.** Wright's Directory prints **Henry Towle, M.R. station master, at Thorndale** under **Hamilton Drive** in 1894-95 and 1898-99, with Henry Vickers there from 1910-11. The OS 1:1250 sheet draws **Thorndale in the row with Parkdale, Dudley Lodge, Harlech House and Woodley**, which are Peveril Drive houses.

**Both are right.** The record's own account of #125 settles it: *a semi-detached house adjacent to 8 Peveril Drive, on a prominent corner plot at the junction of Hamilton Drive and Peveril Drive, one of a group also including 8, 10, 12 and Parkdale on Peveril Drive.* It is numbered on Hamilton Drive and built as part of the Peveril Drive terrace, so a directory files it under one street and a map draws it in the other's row.

**A correction to what was written here earlier today.** I recorded that the directory proved Thorndale to be a Hamilton Drive house and that my reading of the 1901 round - which had placed Henry Towle's household on Peveril Drive - was simply wrong. That was too strong. The 1901 enumerator gave the house name and no street, and a house on this corner can honestly be written up under either; the household belongs at **#125** whichever street heads the schedule.

**Sunnyside is still open.** No directory volume prints it, on Peveril Drive or anywhere else. The record holds a Sunnyside on Park Terrace (#390), and whether Herbert Norrell's household of 1901 belongs there, or at a Peveril Drive house of the same name, is unsettled. Nothing should be filed at #390 from this round until it is.

**Homebush is answered too**: the 1898-99 directory prints *Homebush, Jph. Adams, of S. Adams & Sons* on **Peveril Drive**, so the name does belong to this street even though the record holds no property of it. It wants creating before Edward Sanderson's household can be filed.

**Four more 1901 households on the drive carry neither name nor number** - Francis Budd the wine merchant, John C. Wright, Tom King and Albert Ley - and cannot be placed from this return at all.

**THE OS 1:1250 SHEET NAMES FOUR HOUSES THE RECORD DOES NOT HOLD.** Supplied by A. Hagues. Reading the block between Kenilworth Road and Peveril Drive, the sheet gives in order: **Parkdale, Dudley Lodge, Harleck House** (so spelt), **Woodley, Thorndale**. Woodley sits between Harlech House and Thorndale and is in no property record.

Along the north side of Hamilton Drive it gives **Easdale, Ferndene, Clovelly** and **The Limes**. Only Ferndene is held (#298). **Easdale** is the name this question already wanted: the Polley household of the 1911 key has nowhere to go, and here is the house on a map.

**Ferndene's neighbours explain themselves.** The record says #293 is the central section of a building holding *6, 7 and Ferndene*, and #298 says the same - so Harlech House at 7 Peveril Drive and Ferndene are parts of one structure, which is why the map draws them close together and why the numbering runs oddly.

**Still wanted:** a property for Woodley, Clovelly, The Limes and Easdale, and a date for the sheet, which looks like the 1950s revision and so records names a half-century after the censuses this record is built on.

questions.title: Peveril House or Peveril Tower — which name, and when?
questions.detail: 9 Cavendish Crescent North is recorded under both names, and there is a second Peveril House on Peveril Drive. Which name did the Cavendish Crescent house carry, and over what period? The name clash is a live risk: a census address reading only "Peveril House" could be filed against either.

questions.title: Is Yorke Mews its own address, or part of Yorke House?
questions.detail: A walk of the crescent turned up Yorke Mews, with the thought that it belongs to North Road rather than Cavendish Crescent North — made from an extension of the big house on the corner. The map agrees: Dougal de Havilland draws "Yorke Mews — The Lodge" and "formerly Yorke Cottage" immediately beside Yorke House, 6 North Road (#229), with The Coach House just beyond. So it is a mews of Yorke House. What is not known is whether it was ever a separate address with people returned at it, which is what it would take to give it a record of its own. Yorke Cottage is the older name and may be the one to search.

questions.title: 9 Park Valley in 1939 is read as Walding and the record holds the same couple as Spalding
questions.detail:
**Settled:** the 1939 Register, schedule 111, gives **W Arthur Walding**, born 4 December 1871, retired departmental store director, with **Lilian Alice Walding**, born 4 October 1872, at 9 Park Valley.

The record already holds **#635 William Arthur Spalding, born 1872** (1911 and 1921) and **#636 Lilian Alice Spalding, born 1873** (1911). A husband and wife with the same two forenames apiece, within a year on both birth dates.

**Open:** which spelling is right. Two rounds of the record say Spalding against one reading of mine that says Walding, and *Sp* and *W* are an easy pair to confuse in a 1939 hand. But the register is the only one of the three that gives an exact date of birth, so it is not simply the weaker witness.

**Nothing has been changed.** The transcription stands as the page reads, and the pair is on the 1939 variant-spelling sheet for the duplicates page. If they are merged, the question of which spelling the record keeps should be settled first, not decided by whichever row happens to be the keeper.

**Next:** the 1930s street directories already in the record carry a street and a name for every entry - a look at Park Valley in 1913 or 1915 would print the surname outright. Links: [[house-names-live-in-prose]].

questions.title: 126 names in the 1939 Register the transcriber flagged, in three kinds
questions.detail:
Every source line that says a name was hard to read is a name somebody could settle by looking at the page again. Scattered through the record they are invisible; gathered, they are a morning's work. **`~/Desktop/1939 names to check.xlsx`**, a sheet for each kind.

## 1. Name hard to read — 63

The name itself is doubtful. Some are plainly wrong and worth doing first: **Vauckhard** (four of them at 19 Cavendish Crescent North), **Skayman**, **Sankson**, **Stolworth**, **Shreckley**, **Varas**, **Plunk**.

## 2. An amendment written over the name — 61

**This is a feature of the Register, not a transcription fault.** The 1939 Register was kept up to date as an identity register for decades, so a woman who married after 1939 has her **married name written across the original**. The entries flagged here are ones where the later name cannot be made out - and they skew young, exactly as that explanation predicts: of the six youngest, four are girls of 16 or 17 in domestic service, and one is a schoolgirl of 10.

**What they are worth.** Each one is a marriage between 1939 and the 1990s, and the amended name would date it and name the husband. That is a different kind of fact from anything else in this record, and the only place it survives.

## 3. No forename at all — 2

- **#439 Kirk**, 63, bank manager, at 15 Lenton Road with Gertrude E Kirk, also 63
- **#461 Sawer**, 16, domestic servant, at 1 South Road with the Curnow household and a second servant, Ivy Hayes, 18

Both are one glance at the page.

Links: [[a-full-import-undoes-corrections]].

questions.title: Lynam or Lynum at Newcastle Court in 1891?
questions.detail:
The record holds the widow **Elizabeth Lynam (#52)** at Newcastle Court, Newcastle Circus (#207) for 1891, with her daughters Amelia Ann (#54), Helena Gertrude (#57) and Mabel Winifred (#58), and the servants Eliza Thorne (#62) and Emma Louise Skeggs (#63).

The 1891 enumerator's page heads that household *Newcastle Circus "THE ELMS"* — which is right, since #207 carries The Elms as a former name — and the surname there was transcribed **Lynum**, with a u. Same household either way: the daughters, both servants and the widow's age all agree.

So this is only about the spelling. Is the family Lynam or Lynum, and is the page's hand clear enough to settle it? The record's spelling should win unless the page plainly says otherwise, and if the page does say Lynum it is worth keeping as an alias so either spelling finds them.

From image L16848_3.

questions.title: Springdale's land surveyor: Colvert or Calvert Wilson?
questions.detail:
The 1921 schedule for **Springdale, Clare Valley** writes him **James C. Wilson** with **Calvert** added beside it, apparently to spell out the initial. The record's 1911 and 1939 rows both give **Colvert**.

Two rounds to one for Colvert, so the record keeps Colvert and the 1921 row is bound to the same man. Worth settling from a baptism or a directory, since it is his own hand on the 1921 form.

He is a land surveyor to the **Duke of Newcastle**, working from the Newcastle Estate Office in The Park - which makes him the man who surveyed much of the ground this record is about.

questions.title: Springdale's Mrs Wilson is Edith in 1911 and 1921 and Ethel in 1939
questions.detail:
**Edith Wilson**, born Huddersfield, is at Springdale with her husband in 1911 (aged 49) and 1921 (aged 59 years 7 months). The 1939 Register row for the house reads **Ethel Wilson, aged 77** - which is the right age for the same woman.

Almost certainly one person and a misread 1939 entry, but the two spellings are held as two people until the Register page is looked at again. Links: [[james-colvert-or-calvert-wilson]].

questions.title: The Spinney's servant in 1921: Bramley or Barnsley?
questions.detail:
The single servant at **The Spinney, Clare Valley** in 1921 is **Lizzie**, aged 27 years 3 months, born Newton, Derbyshire. The surname is written small and could be **Bramley** or **Barnsley**; entered as Bramley.

Her occupation column was left blank - only the employment column, "Private", and her place of work, "The Spinney, Clare Valley", say what she did. That place of work is what places the household.

questions.title: #3794 William W Lewis is two men, one on Pelham Crescent and one on Lenton Road
questions.detail:
**Settled:** person **#3794, William W Lewis**, born 1829, carries seven census rows, and they are two lives running side by side:

| round | house | age |
|---|---|---|
| 1871 | **3 Pelham Crescent** | 42 |
| 1881 | **3 Pelham Crescent** | 52 |
| 1891 | **3 Pelham Crescent** | 62 |

| round | house | age |
|---|---|---|
| 1881 | **8 Lenton Road** | 49 |
| 1891 | **6 Lenton Road** | 59 |
| 1901 | Lenton Road, unfiled | 69 |
| 1911 | **6 Lenton Road** | 79 |

**He is in two houses in 1881 and again in 1891**, which no man is, and the two ages are three years apart throughout - 52 against 49, 62 against 59. Two men, born about 1829 and about 1832.

**It has already cost a wrong answer.** The tool that places unfiled households by their people picked **3 Pelham Crescent** for the 1901 household, because that is where most of #3794's rows are. The age says otherwise: 69 in 1901 follows 59 in 1891, which is the **Lenton Road** man. Nothing was filed on it.

**Not split here.** `tools_split_welded_people.py` exists for exactly this and takes a reason per split, but which rows go to which man decides two houses and four rounds, and the 1901 household waits on the answer.

**Next:** split #3794 on the ages - 1871, 1881 and 1891 at Pelham Crescent to one man, 1881, 1891, 1901 and 1911 at Lenton Road to the other - then file the 1901 household at **6 Lenton Road**, which is where the second man is in the rounds either side of it. Links: [[eleven-people-the-import-welded-together]].

questions.title: Twelve people carry the notable mark. The 1871 and 1881 rounds brought in fifteen more who should
questions.detail:
**Settled.** The Notable Residents page holds **twelve** people. The two rounds read in one day brought in at least fifteen who belong there, and not one is marked. This is checklist step 8.7, and it is twenty minutes of ticking rather than research - every one of them is already in the record with a house and a round.

| | who | where | why |
|---|---|---|---|
| #6238 | **John Player** | 9 Park Valley, 1881 | tobacco manufacturer employing 80, with William already in the business at fifteen |
| #6298 | **Thomas Forman** | Castle Grove, 1881 | newspaper proprietor and JP, two sons proprietors beside him |
| #5565 | **John E Ellis** | Derby Terrace 1871, North Road 1881 | later MP for Rushcliffe and Under-Secretary of State for India |
| #7082 | **Robert Evans** | 11 Cavendish Crescent South, 1881 | architect and JP, of Evans and Jolley |
| #5631 | **William Felkin** | Clinton Terrace, 1871 | JP, retired lace manufacturer, historian of the trade |
| #3494 | **Richard Birkin** | The Ropewalk, 1871 | 500 hands in the lace and 236 acres |
| #1315 | **Ernest Jardine** | 19 Park Valley, 1891 | later Sir Ernest, MP - already in six rounds |
| #6397 | **William Hy Poyntz** | 2 Derby Terrace, 1881 | Chief Constable of Nottingham, Major of Royal Marines retired |
| #5934 | **Ann J Clough** | 13 Park Terrace, 1881 | **first Principal of Newnham College, Cambridge** - a visitor on census night, not a resident, so she may want a different mark |
| #2 | **Annie Bayley** | Cavendish Crescent North, 1881 | member of the School Board. Thomas #1 is already marked; she is not |
| #4111 | **Dennis Bayley** | Cavendish Crescent North, 1881 | aged two here, knighted later |
| #201 | **Marriott Ogle Tarbotton** | 6 South Road, 1881 | Borough Surveyor and Engineer |
| #7026 | **John Watson** | Burton House, 1881 | magistrate and solicitor |
| #5235 | **Harvey Hadden** | 3 Park Terrace, 1871 | nineteen and keeping house with his brother; the stadium carries his name |

**Two housekeeping notes while you are on the page.** **#201 Marriott Ogle Tarbotton and #7050 Marriot O Tarbotton are the same man**, both 1881 - my reading against the record's. And **#7082 and #7086 Robert Evans are father and son**, both 1881 at the same house, so the elder is the one to mark and they must not be merged.

**Next.** Notable Residents (`/significant`). Marking is one click each; the biographies can wait, and [[significant-people-thin-biographies]] will then show them as lives still to write.

questions.title: Ernest Jardine, later Sir Ernest, keeping his own house at 31
questions.detail:
**Settled.** The record now holds him twice over. In **1881** he is **Ernest Jardine, 21, "Assistant machine maker"**, in his father John Jardine's house - the page calls it 14 Newcastle Drive and the rule makes it **25**. In **1891** he is **31, a lace machinist, head of 19 Park Valley**, with his wife Ada Jane, a son of six and a daughter of three months.

His father is the lace machine maker **employing 162 hands** in 1881. Ernest took the firm on, became **Sir Ernest Jardine, 1st Baronet, and MP for East Somerset**, and is the Jardine of Jardine's of Nottingham.

**Open.** Which rounds after 1891 hold him, and where did he go from Park Valley? And the record should link father and son, and the two houses.

**Next.** A short biography from the published sources, which are plentiful, and a look at 1901 and 1911 for both houses. See [[significant-people-thin-biographies]].

questions.title: Eight people the 1939 round brought in who belong on the Notable Residents page
questions.detail:
**Settled:** the register named these, and none of them carries the mark yet.

| who | what the register says | where |
|---|---|---|
| **Athelstan Popkess** | **Chief Constable** of Nottingham, b. 23 Nov 1896 | 35 Newcastle Drive |
| **Sir Albert R Atkey** and **Lady Euphemia A Atkey** | motor agent, b. 1 July 1867 | 11 Park Valley |
| **Leslie F Bates** | **Professor of physics**, b. 7 March 1897 | Brankston, Huntingdon Drive |
| **Richard Warwick Bond** | *Literary, retired professor*, b. **30 Sept 1857** | Lynwood, Tattershall Drive |
| **Harold J Malkin** | gynaecological surgeon, b. 27 April 1898 | 26 The Ropewalk |
| **Dorothy Kentish-Wright** | **actress, retired**, b. 27 March 1884 | 9 Newcastle Drive |
| **Ursula Kentish-Wright** | social worker and writer, b. 22 Oct 1890 | 9 Newcastle Drive |
| **Werner R Schweizer** | senior lecturer, University College Nottingham | 1 Clinton Terrace |

**Two corrections the register makes outright**, because it gives exact dates where a census gives none: **Richard Warwick Bond was born 30 September 1857**, not 1858, and **Philip A Birkin 24 September 1869**, not 1870. Both are on the notables list already with the year the record had.

**Open:** which of the eight carry enough of a life to be worth writing, and whether any has a Wikipedia article. The two Kentish-Wrights at one house - an actress and a writer, both unmarried, both in their fifties - are the pair most likely to repay a look.

**Next:** *Notable Residents* takes them one at a time, and *Wikidata Review* will say which have articles. Links: [[every-census-gap-and-where-to-start]].

questions.title: John Edward Ellis, MP and Under-Secretary for India, lived in The Park
questions.detail:
**Settled.** The record now holds him twice. In **1871** he is **John E Ellis, 29, "Manager of coal mines", born Leicester**, on Derby Terrace with his wife Maria R and two infant sons. In **1881** he is on **North Road**, 39, a **coal owner and bank director**, with five servants and twin daughters.

This is the Quaker colliery owner who became **MP for Rushcliffe from 1885 to 1910** and **Under-Secretary of State for India**, a leading opponent of the South African war. He was in The Park for at least ten years and the record did not know it.

**Open.** Which house on North Road, and which on Derby Terrace? Neither page gives a number. Is he in the 1891 round? And his father Edward Ellis was MP for Nottingham before him - was the father in The Park too?

**Next.** A short biography from the published sources, which are plentiful. Then the directories for the house, since the census will not give it. See [[significant-people-thin-biographies]].

questions.title: Richard Kohn of 11 Pelham Crescent is bound to a person number the record no longer has
questions.detail:
**Settled:** `people_1901_pelham_crescent.json` binds **Richard Kohn, aged 67 in 1901** at *Pelham Crescent, “No 11”*, to person **#3016**, and no person of that number exists. The importer says so every run and passes him over, so his 1901 row has never been made.

**The record's Kohns**, none of them Richard:

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| #520 | Recha Kohn | b.1834 |
| #521 | Amy Kohn | b.1873 |
| #3017 | Benedict Kohn | b.1858 |
| #3018 | Herman Kohn | b.1860 |
| #3019 | Fanny Kohn | b.1873 |
| #3020 | Charles Kohn | b.1865 |

**#3016 sits immediately before #3017 to #3020**, which is the block the rest of that household came in as - so he was created with them and has since been merged or deleted. Age 67 in 1901 gives a birth year of about **1834**, which is Recha Kohn's year exactly; a husband and wife of the same year is ordinary.

**Open:** whether #3016 was merged into an existing person, and if so which. The id is left in the file unchanged rather than pointed at a guess - a wrong binding would hang a stranger's census row on somebody, which is the fault the post-import checklist warns about at 5.5b.

**Not fixed by name matching.** Taking the id out would make the importer create a *new* Richard Kohn beside whoever he was merged with, which is worse than leaving him out.

**Next:** `person_alias` records the old spelling whenever a merge is done, so a look there for Kohn would name the keeper outright. Failing that, the 1901 return for 11 Pelham Crescent lists the household and the head's name settles it. Links: [[every-census-gap-and-where-to-start]].

questions.title: John Player lived at 9 Park Valley, and the record did not know it
questions.detail:
**Settled.** The 1881 enumerator puts **John Player, 40, tobacco manufacturer employing 80 persons, born Saffron Walden, Essex** at **9 Park Valley**, with his wife **Ann, 57, born Holwell, Leicestershire**, his son **William G Player, 15, tobacco manufacturer's assistant**, a visiting eight-year-old **Ernest Goodacre**, and one servant.

This is the founder of the firm that became **John Player & Sons**, in a Park house, with the elder of the two sons who would run it already working in the business at fifteen. Player died in 1884, three years after this page was written, and the sons took the firm on in 1893.

**Open.** How long was he in The Park, and which rounds hold him? 1871 has not been searched for him. Ann Player was a **Goodacre** - the visiting Ernest Goodacre is the clue - and the Goodacre connection may place the family earlier. Where the family went after 1884 is also unknown to the record.

**Next.** Search the 1871 round for Player at Park Valley, and check whether 9 Park Valley holds him in 1891. Then a short biography, which is well documented in print and needs no archive. Link the house to the man on the property page. See [[significant-people-thin-biographies]].

questions.title: Six women in the record carry Red Cross or VAD service and none of it is sourced
questions.detail:
**Settled:** the record now holds six women with wartime voluntary service, four of them brought in by the 1939 Register:

| | who | born | what the source says | where |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| #2130 | **Dorothea Kentish Wright** | 27 Mar 1884 | served with the VAD (found outside the census) | 9 Newcastle Drive |
| #2057 | Dorris Gwendolen Warner | - | *Red Cross Nurse*, 1921 | - |
| #7425 | Kathleen Mary Pentecost | 9 Jun 1914 | *British Red Cross V.A.D.* | 1 Huntingdon Drive |
| #7479 | Margaret V Hyltonsmith | 9 Jan 1919 | *Nursing member, British Red Cross* | 19 Cavendish Crescent North |
| #7489 | Beryl Plackett | 19 Mar 1921 | *None, V.A.D.* | Cedar Lodge, Tunnel Road |
| #7555 | Joyce Alice Stirk | 1910 | *Lecturer, Red Cross association* | Ribble Lodge, Clare Valley |

The three born 1914 to 1921 were **eighteen, twenty and twenty-five** when the register was taken three weeks into the Second World War, so theirs is that war beginning. Dorothea's and Dorris Warner's point back to the first.

**Open:** not one of the six has a source beyond the word in the occupation column. No detachment, no hospital, no dates.

**Why this is worth a pass.** The **British Red Cross VAD record cards** are indexed by name and give the detachment, the dates, the hospital and often the work done - and unlike most sources for women of this period, they exist *because* the women were volunteers rather than wives or daughters of somebody. For a record that struggles to say what its women did, this is the rare source that answers directly.

**Next:** six names is a morning's work, not a project. It would also make a natural companion to the medal index cards the checklist already runs for the men at stage 8.4. Links: [[the-kentish-wright-sisters-at-9-newcastle-drive]], [[notables-the-1939-register-brought-in]].

questions.title: Thomas Forman, newspaper proprietor, on Castle Grove in 1881
questions.detail:
**Settled.** The 1881 round has **Thomas Forman, 62, newspaper proprietor and Justice of the Peace, born Lincolnshire**, on **Castle Grove** - the street the enumerator never numbers - with his wife Caroline and three grown sons: **Arthur, 32, newspaper proprietor**, **Jesse A, 30, newspaper proprietor and Master of Arts**, and **James, 25, salaried clerk, BA**.

Thomas Forman built the *Nottingham Daily Guardian* and the printing house that still carries the name. Two of his sons are already proprietors beside him at this date.

**Open.** **Which house on Castle Grove?** The page gives the street and nothing else, so the household cannot be filed - see [[castle-grove-has-no-low-numbers]]. A man of this standing will be in the trade directories with a house name, and that would settle both his house and, by elimination, some of his neighbours'.

**Next.** Wright's directory for 1881 and either side, under Forman. A named house on Castle Grove in a directory is worth more than any amount of census reading, because the census will not give one.

questions.title: Thomas and Annie Bayley, and Dennis aged two, on Cavendish Crescent North
questions.detail:
**Settled.** The 1881 round has **Thomas Bayley, 34, leather merchant, born Lenton** on **Cavendish Crescent North** with his wife **Annie, 31**, sons Harold and **Dennis, aged two**, a seven-month-old daughter Muriel, and five servants.

The record already knows all three as names without a house: **Thomas Bayley**, who became **MP for Chesterfield**; **Annie Bayley**, recorded as a **member of the School Board**; and **Dennis Bayley**, later knighted. They were in The Park.

**Open.** **Which house?** The page gives the street and no number. And what is the relation to **John Bayley**, leather dresser employing 400 hands, whom the 1871 round has in The Park with four sons - brother, cousin, or no relation? Thomas would have been 24 in 1871 and is not in that household.

**Next.** The directories for the house number, and a published source for the Bayley family tree. Then link the three of them to it.

questions.title: Robert Evans, architect and JP, at 11 Cavendish Crescent South
questions.detail:
**Settled, and the house is settled too.** The 1881 round has **Robert Evans, 48, "Architect, Justice of the Peace", born West Hallam, Derbyshire** with his wife Sarah, four daughters - **Edith M, Mary, Ethel F and Dorothy** - and a son **Robert, 15, already an architect's pupil**.

The page writes the street as **South Road**. **It is the corner house**, and A. Hagues places it on Cavendish - which the record independently supports: it holds **Robert Evans Sr at 11 Cavendish Crescent South in 1891 and in 1911**, a man of the same name and trade in the same place either side. The 1881 household is filed there, with the page's own wording kept in the source line.

**That also closes a hole.** 11 Cavendish Crescent South was on the 1901 gap list as *same family either side, very likely still there* - 1891 and 1911 both Robert Evans Sr. It now has 1881 as well, and only 1901 is missing.

**The record already knew the four daughters as names with thin biographies and no house.** It did not know their father was one of the architects who built the town, nor that they lived in The Park.

**Still open.** What did Evans build? The firm was **Evans and Jolley**, and the architect side of the record has nothing under his name. And his son Robert, an architect's pupil at fifteen in 1881, presumably followed him.

**Next.** His buildings, which are documented. Then link the five Evanses to the man and the house. See [[significant-people-thin-biographies]].

questions.title: The Chief Constable of Nottingham lived at Derby House
questions.detail:
**Settled.** The 1881 round puts **William Henry Poyntz, 42**, at **Derby House, 1 Derby Terrace** - entered as **"Major, Royal Marines, retired"** and **Chief Constable of Nottingham**, born Dublin. His wife Henrietta, her father a non-practising barrister, and six children are in the house.

**The children's birthplaces are a career.** Chatham, Cork, Friern Barnet, then Nottingham and New Radford - a marine officer's postings followed by the move to the force.

**Open.** How long was he Chief Constable, and is he in the record's other rounds? Poyntz wrote a memoir of police life, and a man in that post leaves a heavy paper trail in the local press and the watch committee minutes. Nothing of him is in the record beyond this page.

**Next.** A short biography from the published sources, and a check of 1891 for whether he was still at Derby House. Link the man to the property. See [[significant-people-thin-biographies]].

questions.title: Was John Alfred Henderson Green the Town Clerk of Nottingham?
questions.detail:
**In 1901 he is a solicitor on his own account. In 1911 he writes *Solicitor (Town Clerk)* and gives his employer as *Nottingham Corporation*.**

That is a move out of private practice into the Corporation, and the question is which post he actually held: **Town Clerk of Nottingham** is a principal office of the borough and a matter of public record, but a solicitor *in* the Town Clerk's department might write the same words. **He answers *worker* rather than *employer***, which leans towards the second reading - though a salaried Town Clerk would also be a worker.

**Easily settled** from a borough list, a directory or the local press, and worth settling: the record already holds the **Borough Surveyor** who laid out The Park and the **Postmaster of Nottingham**, and a Town Clerk would sit beside them.

**He is #4896**, held from the 1901 round as *John A. H. Green* - the full forenames come from this schedule, in his own hand.

**A second marriage.** Married nine years in 1911, so about 1902, with **no children born to that marriage**. But the 1901 household at the same house holds **Dorothy Green, 13**, his daughter, born about 1888. She is 23 by 1911 and not at home.

questions.title: The Feilmanns and Max Loewenstein - Russian-born lace at 29 Newcastle Drive
questions.detail:
**Eight people at 10 Pelham Terrace in 1911, and not one of them was in the record.** It is the most unusual household of the whole 1911 round.

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| **Emilie Feilmann** | 56, widow | born **Russia**; *Resident*, **British by marriage** |
| **Gertrude Feilmann** | 35, single | **Principal of a School**, **employer** |
| **Rose Feilmann** | 34, single | **Vocalist**, own account |
| **Max Loewenstein** | 58, single, her brother | **Lace manufacturer, machine-made lace, employer**; born **Russia**, **naturalised British subject** |
| **Lilian Albert** | 40, widow, boarder | born **New South Wales** |
| three general servants | 33, 25, 21 | |

**Why this matters.** The record has held **one** person born in Russia. Here are two, heading a lace business between them, and the man is **naturalised** - which means there is a naturalisation file with a date, a former name and often a reason for coming.

**Two professional unmarried women in one house is rare anywhere in this record.** A woman who is **Principal of a school and an employer** at 35, and her sister a **professional singer** at 34. Most women in the 1911 round are wives, widows or servants. **Which school Gertrude ran should be findable in a directory**, and a vocalist leaves concert notices in the local press.

**The head's own trade is struck out on the form.** Emilie Feilmann's occupation reads *Lace Manufacturer* with *Employer* beside it, both crossed through. A widow of a lace family answered as a manufacturer and somebody - she or the enumerator - thought better of it.

**Feilmann and Loewenstein are almost certainly a Jewish family in the Nottingham lace trade**, and Nottingham's Jewish community of this period is documented. That is the obvious place to look.

**And the surname wants care.** *Feilmann* is close enough to *Flersheim* and *Hersheim*, already a known duplicate pair in this record, that a careless matcher could bring them together. They are different families.

questions.title: One province, two countries: Alsace at Pelham House in 1911
questions.detail:
**The wife gives her birthplace as *Alsace, France*. The governess gives hers as *Alsace, Germany*. Both are right.**

Alsace was French until 1871 and German from then until 1918. **Alice Lina Manning**, born about 1866, was born in France. **Anna Elizabeth Kuntz**, the governess, born about 1893, was born in Germany - in the same province. The two entries sit four lines apart on one schedule and between them date the annexation without mentioning it.

**The nationality column finishes the picture.** The wife is **British by marriage**. The governess, 18, is entered simply as **German**.

**This is April 1911.** Britain declared war on Germany in August 1914. **What became of Anna Elizabeth Kuntz is worth knowing** - German nationals in England were registered under the Aliens Restriction Act, and many were interned or repatriated. A governess of 18 in 1911 would be 21 when the war began.

**The household is Edward Laurence Manning's**, a solicitor employing others, with two children born at Beeston. **All four Mannings are already in the record** from 1921, by which time they had moved to **5 Lenton Road, Castle Bank**. So the family can be followed either side of the war, and whether the governess stayed with them is a question the 1921 return answers.

**The record spells two of them differently** - **Elise Lina** for the wife where her husband wrote Alice, and **Geoffrey Lawrence Frederic** for the son against this schedule's Geoffrey Frederic Laurence.

questions.title: Eight Parr children at Cliff House, and two sons who do not come back after 1911
questions.detail:
**George Parr the solicitor had at least eight children at Cliff House, and the three censuses never hold the same set of them.** A. Hagues supplied the 1911 and 1921 households; the 1901 one was already here. Laid side by side they make a family that is easy to lose.

| born | | 1901 | 1911 | 1921 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1879 | George Henry, stockbroker | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| 1881 | **William Noel, solicitor** | | ✓ | **gone** |
| 1885 | Cecil Gordon | | | ✓ |
| 1888 | Violet, teacher | | ✓ | |
| 1891 | Christine Nora | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| 1893 | **Edgar Brown, student of practical engineering** | ✓ | ✓ | **gone** |
| 1894 | Wilfred V. | ✓ | | ✓ |
| 1897 | Doris F. | ✓ | | |

**Two sons are in the house in 1911 and not in 1921, and both were of an age to be in the war.** **William Noel** would be 33 in 1914; **Edgar Brown** would be **21**, and an engineering student in 1911 is exactly the man the Royal Engineers wanted. **Neither has a death recorded.**

**This is checkable and should be checked.** The record already searches medal index cards; Commonwealth War Graves would settle it either way, and a solicitor's death is in the probate calendars whatever the cause. **Absence from a census is not death** - Cecil Gordon is missing from two rounds and turns up alive at 36 - so the point is to establish it rather than assume it.

**And the absences cut the other way too.** Cecil Gordon appears only in 1921, Wilfred only in 1901 and 1921, Doris only in 1901. A household of this size sent its children away, and **each gap is a school, a lodging or a post somewhere else** rather than a mystery.

**Two names want the image.** The record has **William Noel** where A. Hagues's index reads *William Nail*, and **Jo Violet** where the index reads *Fox Violet*. Neither pair can both be right and neither reading is obviously the better one. **Vina** or **Vera** Ann Askew, the kitchenmaid of 16, is the same problem.

**One name the record settles by itself.** The 1921 index gives *Winifred Vera Parr*, marked **Son** and **Male**. The 1901 return has **Wilfred V. Parr, son, aged 6**. Wilfred is right and the index has mis-read it - which is worth knowing, because a female forename against a male relationship is exactly what the forename sex review flags, and this one would have been a false alarm.

questions.title: John Stubbins, Stubbing and Stubbings - one man, one job, one street
questions.detail:
**Three spellings, three birthplaces, and a single career.**

| census | held as | trade | where |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1901** | #4752 John **Stubbins**, b.1854 | Corporation porter | **unfiled**, under a bare *Park Row* |
| **1911** | this schedule, 57 | **Municipal door attendant, Guildhall** | **Park Lodge, Park Row** |
| **1921** | #2239 John **Stubbing**, b.1855 | Attendant | **East Lodge, Park Row**, #413 |

**The birthplaces look like the objection and are actually the proof.** Cuckney, Holbeck and Welbeck are **three villages within a few miles of each other on the Welbeck estate** in north Nottinghamshire. A man born in one of them, asked three times in twenty years, gives whichever name he thinks the clerk will know.

**Same street, same employer, the same job dressed up a little more each decade.**

**Two things follow.**

1. **#4752 and #2239 should be merged.** The pair is exactly the *Stubbing/Stubbins* case already named in `docs/post-import-checklist.md` as one the 1901 round created, and it has never been done.
2. **Park Lodge is probably East Lodge**, #413 - and if that is confirmed, it fills 1911 for that property **and** places the **six unfiled 1901 rows** sitting under a bare *Park Row*. **Not filed yet**, because the cover says Park Lodge and the record says East Lodge, and the estate may have had more than one lodge on that road.

**His wife Maggie was born at Carlisle**, they had been married 29 years, and **no children were ever born to them**. Two rooms - the smallest dwelling in the 1911 round.

questions.title: Roy Henderson the baritone, aged 11, at 5 Tattershall Drive
questions.detail:
**The record already claimed him. It now has the evidence.**

The description of 5 Tattershall Drive has long said the house *was once occupied by Roy Henderson (1899-2000), popular English baritone in the 1920s, 30s and 40s* - with nothing behind it, and not one member of the family in the record.

**The 1911 schedule is in his father's hand and puts the whole household in the house:**

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| **Alexander Roy Henderson** | 48 | Congregational church minister, born King Edward, Aberdeenshire |
| **Jean Boyd Henderson** | 43 | born Campbeltown, Argyll; married 19 years |
| **Muriel Henderson** | 17 | student, born Montrose |
| **Dorothy Henderson** | 15 | at school, born Edinburgh |
| **Roy Galbraith Henderson** | 11 | at school, born Edinburgh |
| **Kenneth Harvey Henderson** | 4 | born Nottingham |

**Age 11 in April 1911 and born in Edinburgh agrees with a birth in 1899**, and the middle name Galbraith is on the schedule, not supplied from anywhere else.

**What the household adds that a reference book would not.** His father's calling is why the family is in Nottingham at all, and the children's birthplaces date the move - Montrose, then Edinburgh twice, then Nottingham by 1906 or 1907, so Roy came south as a boy of six or seven. **Four children born, four still living.**

**Worth chasing:** which Nottingham congregation Alexander Roy Henderson served - Castle Gate is the obvious candidate and should be checkable in a directory - and whether the family is in the 1921 return at the same address. A minister is also the sort of man the local press reported, so there may be an obituary.

**And the property description should cite this schedule** rather than standing on assertion.

questions.title: Virginia Compton, lessee of the Grand Theatre, boarding on Derby Road in 1921
questions.detail:
The 1921 schedule for **Edgemont House, 143 Derby Road** has among its boarders a widow of 68, born New York, whose occupation is *theatrical manageress* and whose place of work is the *Repertory Theatre*.

**She is Virginia Frances Compton, born Bateman** - identified by A. Hagues, and the identification explains itself: **she took the lease of the Grand Theatre in Nottingham in 1920** and was trying to build a resident repertory company there. A theatre manager lodging near her work.

She was the daughter of Hezekiah Bateman, the American actor who took on the Lyceum, and of Sidney Frances Bateman, playwright and manager. She married the actor Edward Compton in 1882 and was leading lady, then co-manager, of the **Compton Comedy Company**. In 1914 she founded the **Theatre Girls' Club**. Her children were the novelist **Compton Mackenzie** and the actresses **Fay Compton** and **Viola Compton**.

**What the record would still like to know.** How long the Nottingham repertory venture lasted, whether any of her children were with her in the city, and whether she is in a Nottingham directory at Edgemont House or anywhere else in the town. The Grand Theatre's own records would date the lease at both ends.

Her life is written up on her person page and she is marked on Notable Residents. Links: [[derby-terrace-1921-which-number]].

questions.title: An authoress at Brooklyn House, and a pastor of the Church of the People
questions.detail:
**Settled.** At **Brooklyn House, 21 Park Valley** in 1881: **Fred Bell, 35, "Pastor of the Church of the People", born Sheffield**, and his wife **Annie J Bell, 33, born Darlington**, whose occupation column reads **"Authoress"** - one of very few women anywhere in this round given a profession of her own rather than a dash. Their son Frank, 7, was born in **New York**.

**Open.** What did she write, and under what name? And what was the Church of the People in Nottingham - a congregation, a mission, a hall? The family's movement between Sheffield, Rotherham, New York and Nottingham suggests a preaching career worth following.

**Next.** The British Library catalogue and the newspaper archive under Bell, Nottingham, 1878-1890. A pastor of a named church will be in the local press.

questions.title: John Holland Walker of 15 Park Valley - the Nottingham antiquarian?
questions.detail:
**The 1911 schedule for 15 Park Valley is signed John Holland Walker.** He is 37, born at Leeds, and gives his occupation as **department manager in a wholesale clothing factory** - a worker, not an employer. His wife Lucy Mabel is 36, born at Nottingham; married eleven years with no children born. They keep a cook and a house parlourmaid in eleven rooms.

**A J. Holland Walker of Nottingham wrote a great deal on the town's history** in the early twentieth century, including an itinerary of its streets published through the Thoroton Society. The name is uncommon, the town is right, and a man of 37 in 1911 would be of an age to be writing by the 1920s.

**But the trade does not obviously fit**, and that is the whole of the question: the record should not turn a clothing factory manager into an antiquarian because the names agree. Local historians of that generation frequently had day jobs, so it is not evidence against him either.

**What would settle it:** the Thoroton Society's own membership lists or obituaries, which would give an address; or the Nottingham press. An address at 15 Park Valley against the author's name would close it in one line.

**Nobody of this name is in the record**, so whichever way it goes this household is new.

questions.title: Tinsley Lindley of 14 Park Terrace - barrister, and something else
questions.detail:
**The record holds him at one house across three censuses and says only that he was a barrister.** #1819 Tinsley Lindley, born 1866 at Nottingham, head of **14 Park Terrace** in 1901, 1911 and 1921. He signs the 1911 schedule himself in a clear hand - *Tinsley Lindley* - which is worth saying, because the 1921 transcription made him **Tinster Lindey**.

**The name is very unusual and he was a public figure.** A Tinsley Lindley of Nottingham, born in the 1860s, played football for England in the 1880s while qualifying for the bar. Whether that is this man is not something this record can settle on its own, but the name, the town and the dates all point one way, and the record should either establish it or rule it out - because the coincidence will be noticed again by somebody else.

**What would settle it:** an obituary, a bar admission record, or the Nottingham press, which would have noticed either a famous footballer or a well-known barrister living on The Park.

**Twelve people in this record carry the notable mark.** If this is the same man he is an obvious thirteenth.

**His family is small and settled.** Married about 1896, and the 1911 return gives **one child born alive, one still living** - Victoria, four on the 1901 round and the only child they had. **His wife is in the record twice and neither entry is right**: #1820 *Constance Agnes Lindey* has the forename and not the surname, #4785 *Constance Lindley* the surname and not the forename.

questions.title: Frank Beckitt Lewis, City Architect of Nottingham, at 6 Lenton Road
questions.detail:
**The record has held him since the 1911 return and nobody has looked at him.** **Frank Beckitt Lewis (#815), born Nottingham 1862**, is entered on the 1911 census at **6 Lenton Road** as *city architect*, living at forty-nine in his father's house. The 1901 return gives the same man at the same house, aged thirty-nine, as **"City Architect (Nottm) (own a/c)"** - so he held the office across at least that decade.

**He is the son of a cork cutter.** **William W Lewis (#3794)** is at 6 Lenton Road in 1891 as a cork cutter and in 1911, at seventy-nine, as a retired lace merchant; Wright's Directory prints him there in 1894-95, 1898-99 and 1910-11. Frank is one of seven children, and the only one who left the family trades - his brothers were a cork cutter's assistant and a yarn agent's assistant.

**He is absent from the house in 1891**, aged twenty-nine, which is where a young architect would be: articled, working, or qualifying somewhere else. The 1891 return for wherever he was would give the practice he trained in.

**What is wanted.** The years he held the office, and what he was responsible for. A City Architect of Nottingham in the 1900s is a public appointment with a paper trail - council minutes, the local press, the building control records - and the buildings are likely still standing. Whether any of them are on this estate is the question that matters here.

**And how he was nearly lost.** My transcription of the 1901 page read the enumerator's ditto mark under the surname column as a surname, so he went into the record as **"Frank B."** - a man with no family name, sitting unfiled on Lenton Road. See [[1901-ditto-surnames]]. Four of his household went in the same way, and the house they were in could not be recognised until the surname came back.

questions.title: James Calvert Wilson, land surveyor to the Newcastle Estate
questions.detail:
**The man who surveyed The Park lived on it.** The 1911 schedule for **Springdale, Clare Valley** gives **James Calvert Wilson**, 49, *land surveyor*, and in the industry column beside it: **Newcastle Estate**.

The record already holds him and his household from the 1911 spreadsheet, but with the trade alone. The employer is the whole of the interest. The Park is the Duke of Newcastle's estate; its layout, its plot boundaries and its numbering were the estate surveyor's work, and this record spends a great deal of effort on exactly those things - which house is which number, where one plot ends and the next begins, why a corner house answers to two streets.

**What is worth finding.** How long he held the post, and what survives of his work. Estate plans, plot books, sale particulars and feu or lease papers are the surveyor's output, and any of them would answer questions this record has open - [[park-valley-12-13-14]] asks whether Park Valley ever had a 12, 13 or 14, and an estate plan would simply show.

**Where such papers would be.** Nottinghamshire Archives holds Newcastle estate material; the Manuscripts and Special Collections at the University of Nottingham hold a great deal more of the Newcastle family's papers.

**He is not a Nottingham man.** Born at Huddersfield, his wife too, and both daughters at Burnley - so he came to the post from Lancashire some time between 1895 and 1911. When he was appointed may itself be findable.

**One correction comes with the schedule:** the record has his servant as *Florence Gertrude Wathing*. The schedule reads **Watkins**.

questions.title: Are there two Wilkins daughters at 4 Clare Valley, or four?
questions.detail:
**The record holds four Wilkins girls where the house had two.**

The 1901 round gives Lawrence Wilkins, clergyman, at 4 Clare Valley with **Eleanor, born 1896** and **Jessie, born 1897**.

The 1911 schedule for the same house, in their widowed mother's own hand, gives **Joyce, born 1896** and **Mary, born 1897**.

**Same house, same mother, same birth years, different forenames** - and the record holds all four as separate people: #3339 Eleanor, #3340 Jessie, #3344 Joyce, #3345 Mary.

**Two readings.** Either the girls had several forenames and each source picked a different one - entirely ordinary, and *Jessie* is their mother's name, so a daughter called Mary Jessie or Jessie Mary is likely. Or one of the two transcriptions is simply wrong.

**The 1911 names are the better authority**, being the householder's own writing rather than an enumerator's copy. But the 1901 round is A. Hagues's own reading of the page, so this is not a case of trusting a stranger's index over his work.

**What would settle it:** baptisms at St Mary's or wherever Lawrence Wilkins served, which would give each girl's full name at birth. A birth registration would do as well.

**Whichever way it falls, two merges follow**, and the duplicates page cannot see them: the forenames are entirely different, so nothing buckets them together.

**Two other things from that schedule.** Lawrence Wilkins **died between 1901 and 1911** - his widow heads the house. And the fourth child, **L. A. Wilkins**, a son of 6 in 1901, is absent at 16; the marriage answers say four born and four living, so he was alive and elsewhere.

questions.title: Frances May Pearson and Frances Mays Parson - one woman or two?
questions.detail:
**Two women, born the same year, in adjacent houses, in the same census.**

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| **#416 Frances May Pearson** | born 1887 | 1911, property 190 |
| **#858 Frances Mays Parson** | born 1887 | 1911, property 192 |

**Pearson and Parson are one letter apart. May and Mays are one letter apart.** The birth year is identical and the houses are next door but one.

**Either reading is possible.** Two young women of nearly the same name working in neighbouring houses is perfectly ordinary - service was a local trade and sisters often went into houses on the same street. But so is one woman entered twice from two readings of the same hand.

**The birthplaces would settle it**, and so would the relationship column: two servants are two women, a servant and a daughter are two women, and the same relationship in two houses on one night is impossible.

**The duplicates page cannot decide this** and neither can the variant sweep - both pair on the name and the year, and here the name and the year agree while the house does not. **This one needs the return read.**

See [[duplicate-sweep-keyed-on-house]] for the opposite failure - a pair the matchers miss because they share a house but not a year.

questions.title: Arundel Preston of 1 Park Valley: one man, or a man and his widow of the same name?
questions.detail:
**The 1911 schedule and the record disagree about whether Arundel Preston is a man.**

The record holds **#4027 Arundel Preston, born 1838** - head of 1 Park Valley on the 1901 round at 63, a **widower**, occupation *Gentleman*, born in Wiltshire.

The 1911 schedule for the same house gives **Arundel Preston, head, aged 73, widow**, with the age in the **females** column, born at Tisbury in Wiltshire. It is signed *Arundel Preston*.

**Sixty-three to seventy-three is exactly ten years** and Tisbury is in Wiltshire, so on age and birthplace the two are one person.

**Two readings.** Either the age went into the wrong column and *widow* is loose for widower - both common on a householder's own schedule - or Arundel Preston died in the decade and his widow, also called Arundel, took the house. The second is less strange than it sounds, because **his daughter is Arundel Aplin**: the family uses the name for women. But he was already a widower in 1901, so it would need a second marriage after 63.

**The first reading is much the simpler**, and nothing has been changed on the strength of either. The 1911 row is bound to #4027 by number, which is right either way, and no sex is sent.

**What would settle it:** a death registration for Arundel Preston between 1901 and 1911, or its absence. And the return brings a generation the record has never held - **Arundel Aplin**, a widowed daughter of 42, with granddaughters **Alys Arundel** and **Alfreda Althea Aplin**, 11 and 9. No Aplin is in the record at all.

questions.title: Are the three Brownsword households one family — and does Helena connect to them?
questions.detail:
The record now holds Brownswords in three places and does not say how, or whether, they join up. **John Hind Brownsword** (b.1836) with Mary, Edith Mary and John Anthony at #206, on the 1881 and 1891 returns. **Harry A. Brownsword** (b.1863), a lace manufacturer and an employer, with Mabel and their children Daphne, Norah and Douglas at 15 Lenton Road (#187) on the 1901 return, which came in this morning. And **Arthur Brownsword** (b.1870) at #44 and #206, who is already recorded as a cousin of Helena Brownsword Dowson (#2548).

Helena is the reason this matters. She was a leading Nottingham suffragist, a city councillor and a magistrate, and she has a Wikipedia article; her father was **Alderman Anderson Brownsword**, a Unitarian aligned with the Nottingham Liberal party, who is not in this record at all. Arthur and Harry were born seven years apart and both in Nottingham, and Brownsword is not a common name here. Nothing yet shows the tie, and none should be recorded until something does — a census, a will, a birth registration. Adding Anderson Brownsword himself would likely be the way in.

**A fourth Brownsword household, from the same 1901 round.** At schedule 184, a house called "St John's", **Mary Brownsword**, a widow of 65 born at Melbourne in Derbyshire, keeps house with her son **Arthur Brownsword**, 31, a lace manufacturer and an employer, born in Nottingham, and four servants.

Arthur born about 1870 in Nottingham is the Arthur already in the record at #44 and #206, recorded as a cousin of Helena Brownsword Dowson. **So this gives his mother, and she is a widow by 1901.** If Anderson Brownsword - Helena's father, the alderman who is not in this record at all - died before 1901, Mary is a candidate for his widow, and that would be the tie the question has been waiting for. A death registration for Anderson Brownsword, or Mary's own, would settle it.

questions.title: Henry Handford of Hardwicke House — which of Lord Belper’s daughters did he marry?
questions.detail:
**Answered, and he was.** Munk's Roll — the Royal College of Physicians' lives of its fellows, the entry by G. H.
