Brown from his 1928 obituaries in the Lancet and the British Medical Journal — gives Henry Handford as the son of Dr Thomas Handford of Atherstone, which is exactly where the 1901 census says the man at Hardwicke House was born. He trained at Edinburgh, taking his M.B., C.M. in 1878 with high distinction, then Paris and Vienna; tutored at Queen's College, Birmingham; came to Nottingham as physician to the General Hospital until 1906, strongest in pathology and diseases of the heart; and then spent twenty years as **medical officer of health for the county**, retiring in 1926. F.R.C.P. 1899. A major in the sanitary branch of the R.A.M.C. in the Great War. He died on 24 June 1928.

**What is still open** is his wife. Munk's Roll says only that she was *a daughter of the first Lord Belper* — Edward Strutt, of the Derbyshire cotton family — without naming her. The record holds her as Mary E. Handford, born 1854 at St George's in London, and she brought three grown daughters to the house, Gertrude, Sybil and Dorothy **Gale**, all born at Bedale in the North Riding between 1874 and 1876. So she married a Gale first and was widowed or otherwise free by the time the Handford sons arrived in 1894 and 1896. Which Strutt daughter she was, and who Gale was, neither the census nor Munk's Roll says. Burke's or the Strutt family papers would.

One discrepancy worth knowing: Munk's Roll dates his birth to **1855**, the record holds **1856** from his age on census night, and the second is the sort of year that is a year out as often as not.

**The sons.** Both were killed on the same morning. Captain Henry Basil Strutt Handford and Lieutenant Everard Francis Sale Handford, the boys of seven and five on the 1901 return, served together in the 1/8th Sherwood Foresters and died in the attack on the Hohenzollern Redoubt on 15 October 1915, aged twenty-one and twenty. Neither body was recovered; they are on the Loos Memorial, and a window in Southwell Minster remembers them together. Their brother-in-law Major John Pickard Becher D.S.O., husband of Gertrude Gale, was mortally wounded in the same attack and died on 1 January 1916. By then the family had left The Park for Elmfield at Southwell.

**One correction worth recording.** An account of the brothers gives their mother as a daughter of *Henry* Strutt, first Baron Belper. The barony was created in 1856 for **Edward** Strutt, and Henry was his son and the second baron — born 1840, fourteen years before Mary, so he cannot have been her father. Munk's Roll says simply "a daughter of the first Lord Belper", and that is what the record follows. Which daughter, and who the Gale was she married first, are still the open questions.

questions.title: Derby House: the Wilkinsons found at Newark, and which sister went to Australia?
questions.detail:
**A Lenton memoir describes the house from the outside, and confirms three things the censuses only imply.** A recollection of Hermon Street published at lentontimes.co.uk remembers Derby House, across Derby Road, as an **upper-class boarding house owned by a Miss Wilkinson**, where the writer earned pocket money helping in the kitchen on Sundays. It names the chef as **Mr Bird**; says the property was later taken by **the Lace Marketing Board**; and recalls that during the war the writer's family swapped margarine for **tinned fruit that Miss Wilkinson's sister sent from Australia**.

**Mr Bird is in the record.** **William Alfred Bird**, born 1892 at Carlton in Nottinghamshire, is a servant in the house on the 1921 census at 28 and a manservant on the 1939 register at 47. The memoir gives him the trade the official returns do not: he was the cook. Eighteen years in one house, and now a name with a job attached.

**"A Miss Wilkinson" fits either sister, and the war years point to Maybell.** Sarah, the mother, was keeping the house at 72 in 1921 and is not on the 1939 register, so she had died or given it up by then. On that register **Maybell Martina** is the proprietress and **Florence Allissinon May** is retired, both single - so a wartime recollection of "Miss Wilkinson" is most likely Maybell.

**But then who is the sister in Australia?** The 1901 household holds only two daughters, Florence born 1874 and Maybell born 1876, with sons William born 1879 and Stuart born 1884. Both daughters are in the house in 1939. So either:

- there was a **third daughter**, older or born in the gap between 1879 and 1884, who had left home before the 1901 census and emigrated - the record would have no trace of her at all; or
- **Florence went to Australia after 1939**, which at 65 and retired is possible but unlikely; or
- the memoir means a sister-in-law, or misremembers the relationship, which reminiscence written down decades later often does.

**Nobody in the record connects to Australia** except the Cartwrights of Melbourne and John Kneebone of South Australia, none of them Wilkinsons.

**What would settle it:** the 1881 or 1891 census for the Wilkinson family at Newark, where all four known children were born, which would give the full set of Sarah's daughters before any of them left home. A passenger list or a probate notice naming an Australian sister would do as well.

**And a date for the end of the house:** the Lace Marketing Board's occupation of Derby House would give the year the boarding house closed, which is currently unknown - the record follows the Wilkinsons to 1939 and no further. See [[1901-house-names-not-in-the-record]] for the Beechwood end of the same story.

**THE WILKINSONS CANNOT BE FOUND AT NEWARK IN 1881 OR 1891.** A. Hagues has looked and they are not there under Sarah's name - which is to be expected, because she was not the head of the household in either year. She is a widow by 1901, so in 1881 and 1891 the household stands under her husband's name and she is listed as his wife. **The record holds no Wilkinson man who could be him**, so he died between 1884, when Stuart was born at Newark, and 1901.

**The way in is not Sarah but the unusual names.** *Maybell* for a daughter born 1876, *Stuart* for a son born 1884 at Newark, and above all **Allissinon**, which the 1921 census gives as Florence's middle name.

**And there is an Allissinon already in this record.** **Alissimon Hopewell (#1143) was born at NEWARK in 1864** - the same town as all four Wilkinson children - and is at #346 in 1921 as the wife of Frank Handley Hopewell of Mansfield. She is the visitor aged 36 whom the 1901 reading of the Beechwood household records, and my parser dropped.

**She cannot be Sarah's daughter.** Sarah was born in 1849 and would have been fifteen in 1864. The likelier relation by far is that **Alissimon was born a Wilkinson** - her husband's sister, Florence's aunt, and the woman Florence was named after. That reading fits the 1901 visit exactly: an aunt calling on her sister-in-law and her nieces, in the boarding house her brother's widow was keeping.

**If that is right, it opens the 1881 census.** Alissimon Wilkinson would be seventeen at Newark in 1881, living with her parents - and her father is Sarah's father-in-law, which finds the family without needing Sarah's married surname to be searchable at all. A marriage registration for Hopewell and Wilkinson would confirm the maiden name outright.

**None of this makes her the Australian sister.** Alissimon is in Nottingham in 1921 as Mrs Hopewell, so the sister who sent tinned fruit through the war is somebody else, and remains unaccounted for.

**FOUND: 3 CHURCH STREET, NEWARK UPON TRENT, 1891.** A. Hagues has the family's Newark address at last, through the youngest child: **Stuart Murray Wilkinson**, 7, born Newark 1884, a scholar. His full name is new - the record holds him only as Stuart - and *Murray* is one more distinctive name to search on.

**But the household as indexed is five people and contains no parent.** Stuart is entered as **Son** with nobody for him to be the son of: a visitor, Mary Wilson of Lincoln, 22, living on her own means; and three servants - Sarah Taylor a nursemaid, Mary Ann Baker a housemaid, and Annie Rastall a cook, all from Lincolnshire. **Florence, Maybell and William are absent too**, though they would be 17, 15 and 12.

**So on census night 1891 the parents were away and the youngest boy was left at home with the staff.** A nursemaid and a cook for one seven-year-old says a household of some means, which fits a family that could later keep an upper-class boarding house.

**That is also why no search for Sarah finds them.** She is not in her own house that night. The next place to look is wherever she and her husband were - and if the husband can be named from the 1891 return for 3 Church Street in an earlier year, or from a directory for Newark, the whole family follows.

**This household is not created in the record.** Newark is not The Park, and the estate's census rows are for houses on it; what belongs here is the fact of the address and the names, not a household at a property the record does not hold.

**Still unaccounted for:** the sister in Australia, and whether Alissimon Hopewell - born Newark 1864, and very likely a Wilkinson by birth - is the aunt Florence was named after.

**THE HUSBAND IS NAMED. 2 & 3 CHURCH STREET, NEWARK UPON TRENT, 1881.** A. Hagues has the household ten years earlier, and at its head is **WILLIAM M WILKINSON, 34, born about 1847, a GROCER EMPLOYING 13 MEN AND 5 BOYS**. Sarah is his wife, 32, born in Derbyshire, which agrees with the Burnaston of every later return.

**A grocer of that size explains a good deal.** Eighteen employees is a substantial business, and it accounts for the household of 1891 - a nursemaid and a cook kept for one seven-year-old boy while his parents were away. It also explains what became of the sons: on the 1901 return **William is a grocer's assistant and Stuart a grocer's warehouseman**, both in their father's trade.

**And it confirms the daughters' names.** They are entered by initials: **F A M**, 6, and **M M**, 4 - Florence Allissinon May and Maybell Martina, exactly as the 1921 census spells them out. Their birth years here are 1875 and 1877, a year later than the 1921 and 1939 figures, which is the ordinary drift of census ages.

**There are only two daughters in 1881.** So a third - the sister who sent tinned fruit from Australia - would have to have been born **after 1881**, in the gap between the son of 1879 and Stuart of 1884, or after Stuart. That is a much smaller search than before.

**One oddity in the household.** The son born 1879 is indexed as **N J S Wilkinson**, aged 2, where the 1901 return gives a son **William**, 22, born the same year. Either the initials are misread, or the boy of 1879 died and another son of the same birth year cannot be the same child. Worth a look, since a son who died young would be one more child to account for.

**William M Wilkinson is not in this record.** He died between 1884, when Stuart was born, and 1901, when Sarah is a widow keeping a boarding house at Beechwood - a fall from grocer of eighteen hands to lodging-house keeper that a death and a failed business would both explain. His death registration would date it, and Newark directories of the 1880s would show how long the firm lasted.

**What is still wanted:** a daughter born after 1881, a death for William M Wilkinson, and confirmation that Alissimon Hopewell - born Newark 1864, and very probably his sister - is the aunt Florence was named after.

**WAS SHE EVER AT BEECHWOOD? A. HAGUES DOUBTS IT, AND THE DOUBT IS WELL FOUNDED.** William M Wilkinson died in **1892**. A widow setting up a boarding house at one address and moving to another within twenty years is possible but wasteful, and the simpler reading is that she went to Derby House and stayed - which is where the record finds her in 1911, 1921 and 1939.

**My own transcription is weaker evidence than I have been treating it as.** The 1901 Wilkinson household carries **no schedule number**; it sits in the gap where schedules 81 to 84 are missing from the pages read; and the house name I gave it is written as a bare label in quotation marks, separate from the entry that follows it - *Sch 85, Beechwood, Hamilton Drive*. So the name may have been taken from the household after theirs rather than from their own line. That is exactly the mistake that put Henry Towle's household on Peveril Drive.

**Three other things already told against Beechwood.** The source A. Hagues consulted counts **nine** households on Hamilton Drive in 1901 where my reading gives thirteen; Beechwood is not among the four houses he found named there; and it appears in **no volume** of Wright's Directory, on that street or any other.

**But one thing tells for it.** **Derby House is 880 metres from Hamilton Drive** - most of the width of the estate, and almost certainly a different enumerator's round. If Sarah were at Derby House in 1901 she should not appear in that sequence at all, and the household was transcribed from a page within it.

**The test is simple and is not mine to make.** The 1901 return for **1 Derby Terrace**: if Sarah Wilkinson is there, the Beechwood label is my error and the family has one boarding house, not two. If somebody else is there, she was elsewhere in 1901 and Beechwood - or whatever that page actually calls the house - stands.

**Until that is known, nothing moves.** The 1901 rows keep the label they have, marked as uncertain, and the three Derby House households stand on their own evidence.

**TESTED, AND BEECHWOOD STANDS.** A. Hagues has looked at the 1901 return and confirms it is the Beechwood household. So the label my transcription gave it was right, the doubt above is closed, and **Sarah Wilkinson did keep two boarding houses in succession**:

- **1892** - William M Wilkinson dies, leaving her a widow with four children between eight and eighteen.
- **1901** - Beechwood, on the Hamilton Drive round, with her four grown children at home and nine lodgers: a civil engineer, two Swiss brothers, a commercial traveller from Curacao, a merchant, a sick nurse and two servants. Fifteen people.
- **1911** - Derby House, 1 Derby Terrace, thirteen people, and her trade written out at last as boarding house keeper.
- **1921** - Derby House still, at seventy-two.
- **1939** - Derby House, her daughter Maybell now proprietress, Florence retired.

**Nine years from widowhood to Beechwood, ten more to Derby House** - which on reflection is not a hurried pair of ventures but a trade she moved premises in once, as any lodging-house keeper might, from a house on the estate to a larger one at its edge.

**So Beechwood is a real house and still wants a number.** It is the last name on the Hamilton Drive round with nothing against it, absent from every volume of Wright's Directory and from the nine households the source counts on that street. The Firmenich brothers remain the most distinctive thing in it to search on.

questions.title: The Ashworths had four children and lost one - was it Leslie?
questions.detail:
**The 1911 return states it and no other source would.** Blanche Isabel Ashworth of 9 Park Valley answers the marriage questions: married thirteen years, **four children born alive, three still living, one died**.

Three are in the house - Edna Blanche Wilson (10), Harold John Vincent (8) and Elaine Isabel (5).

**The record holds a fourth.** **Leslie F. H. Ashworth, born 1900** (#4548), from the 1901 round at Park Ravine, where his parents were before they moved. He appears nowhere in the record after that and is not in this house at eleven years old.

**He is very probably the child who died**, and a death registration would date it. A child who lives and dies between two censuses leaves almost no other trace, and without the 1911 marriage questions nobody would have known to look.

**A correction comes with it.** The record has the eldest daughter as **Edith B. W. Ashworth**, born 1901; the schedule writes her **Edna Blanche Wilson Ashworth** - same initials, same year. Edna read as Edith.

**And the father is in the record under a short form**: **#4546 Fredk J. Ashworth**, born 1873, at Park Ravine in 1901. He is Frederick John Ashworth, timber importer, born at Beeston.

questions.title: Three Bradleys on one short street - brothers?
questions.detail:
**Park Terrace holds three Bradley households across four censuses and the record connects none of them.**

- **Charles Bradley**, born 1842, retired surgeon, head of **3 Park Terrace** in 1891.
- **Herbert Bradley**, born 1848, a **boarder at 10 Park Terrace** in 1891, then head of **3 Park Terrace** in 1901, 1911 and 1921 - unmarried, on private means, with a housekeeper and a housemaid.
- **Alfred Bradley**, born 1846, cotton yarn manufacturer, head of **Broxtowe House** on the same street in 1891, 1901 and 1911, unmarried, keeping house with his niece.

**Born 1842, 1846 and 1848, all in Nottingham, all on one short street**, two of them unmarried, and Herbert takes over the house Charles had. Brothers is the obvious reading and nothing in the record says so.

**Alice Margaret Gill is the way in.** She is Alfred's niece, so one of her parents was a Bradley, and a marriage of a Bradley daughter to a Gill would name the generation above all three men. She is in the record across 1901, 1911 and 1921 with her birth year consistent at 1873.

**A fourth Bradley sits apart:** Frederick James, born 1846, at 15 Pelham Crescent in 1901 and 8 Western Terrace after, with a wife and children.

**There is a duplicate to clear first** - the record holds Herbert Bradley twice, #1796 born 1848 and #4923 born 1849, a year apart and so invisible to the duplicates page.

questions.title: Robert Henry Speed is on Park Terrace in 1861, but ten years too young
questions.detail:
The 1861 round has a **Robert Henry Speed, solicitor, aged 28**, on Park Terrace. The record's Robert Henry Speed is a solicitor too, and is at **27 Cavendish Road East** from 1891 to 1911, with the family there long enough that his daughter Sybil is still heading the house in 1921.

**The ages do not agree.** He is 68 in 1891, 78 in 1901 and 88 in 1911 - born **1823** on all three. That would make him **38** in 1861, not 28.

So either:

- the 1861 age is misread - 38 and 28 are one stroke apart in that hand - and this is him, thirty years before the record otherwise picks him up; or
- it is a different Robert Henry Speed, most likely a relative, since the name is not a common one.

**It matters more than a stray age**, because it would put the Speeds on Park Terrace before Cavendish Road East and give the family an extra generation in The Park. The 1861 row is unfiled - Park Terrace gives no numbers that year - so nothing rests on it yet. Links: [[sunnyside-park-terrace-or-park-valley]], [[the-1861-round-has-no-house-numbers]].

questions.title: Which hospital did the nine doctors at Broxtowe House serve?
questions.detail: Nine house surgeons and house physicians, aged 26 to 33, living in one Park house in June 1921 with no patients and no family. Nottingham General Hospital at Standard Hill is the obvious answer on geography alone, and the hospital's own history records it taking houses in The Park, Park Terrace and the Ropewalk as doctors' residences — but dates that to 1969. If a hospital minute book, annual report or staff list names the residence, it would push the practice back nearly fifty years. Five of the nine were women, which in 1921 makes the house worth a note in its own right.

questions.title: Who were the two lace manufacturers at Carisbrooke House in 1891? The surname will not read
questions.detail:
**Schedule 8 of the 1891 census gives Carisbrooke House to two unmarried brothers**, the head 36 and his brother 34, both lace manufacturers and both born in Nottingham, with an aunt of 66 named Ann Ward and two general servants, Georgina Sharp and Eliza Turfitt. The household is straightforward. The surname is not.

**It has been set down as Pheeps, which is certainly wrong** - a placeholder standing in for a hand that will not resolve. It is written the same way twice, once for each brother, so it is not a slip of the enumerator's pen.

**What would settle it.** A Nottingham lace firm run by two brothers born about 1855 and 1857, unmarried and living together in The Park in 1891, should appear in Wright's Directory for 1891-92 or thereabouts. The aunt Ann Ward may be the easier thread: the record already holds a '? Ward' at 17 Cavendish Crescent North, a forename lost the same way, and the two may be the same woman.

questions.title: Frances M. H. Churchill, aged 5, is entered as a daughter of John C. Wright but under another surname
questions.detail:
**At schedule 237 on Peveril Drive in 1901**, John C. Wright, a commercial traveller of 36, is returned with his wife Florence and four children born at Arnold - Dorothy, Rachael and John, all surnamed Wright, and then Frances M. H. **Churchill**, aged 5, also given as Daughter and also born at Arnold.

A stepchild, an adopted child, or a niece written into the wrong column. The birthplace matching the others makes a clerical slip less likely than a real family story.

questions.title: Henry Meade Brown, aged 56 in 1891, is entered as the son of a head aged 53
questions.detail:
**The 1891 schedule gives him as Son, aged 56, in a household whose head is 53.** The age has been checked against the page more than once and is what is written there.

It has been recorded unchanged rather than quietly corrected, because the contradiction is the interesting part. Either the enumerator wrote an age into the wrong line, or the relationship column is wrong and he is a brother or a lodger, or the head's own age is understated.

questions.title: The Holland sisters and the Duvals - are the Bridgwater and Liverpool Hollands one family?
questions.detail:
**Three chemists married three sisters.** Frederic Stanley Kipping married Lily Holland at Bridgwater on 3 March 1888; William H. Perkin junior had married her elder sister Mina at the same church on New Year's Eve 1887; and Arthur Lapworth married Kathleen Holland at St Mary's, Bridgwater, on 14 September 1900. Their father was W. T. Holland, J.P., of Bridgwater in Somerset. Both published lives of Kipping - F. Challenger's Royal Society obituary notice of 1950 and N. R. Thomas's paper in Silicon of 2010 - add that the sisters were granddaughters of Charles Allen Duval, so their mother was a Duval who married a Holland.

**A second Duval-Holland marriage is recorded elsewhere.** Charles Allen Duval (1810-1872) was born at Beaumaris in Anglesey and settled in Manchester as a portrait painter and photographer. His Wikipedia article names a daughter Florence who married Dr Charles Thurstan Holland, the radiologist, of Liverpool - a different Holland from W. T. Holland of Bridgwater, and of a later generation, Thurstan Holland having been born in 1863. That article also lists at least one granddaughter among his children, so its account of the family is not wholly reliable and should not be built on unchecked.

**Why it matters to The Park.** The 1921 return for the Kipping household on Clumber Crescent South gives a mother-in-law, Florence Holland, 78, born in Manchester, which would make her the Duval daughter who married W. T. Holland. If she is, then the Bridgwater and Liverpool Hollands are either one family or two that each married a Duval, and the Kipping, Perkin and Lapworth marriages sit inside a much larger network. If she is not, the Manchester birthplace on that schedule wants another explanation.

**That caution is now spent - the two women are separated.** #1329 is the Kipping mother-in-law, born 1843 at Manchester. The maid of the same name at 23 Cavendish Crescent South is #3692, born 1882 at Nottingham. Nothing further need be untangled before working on this. Duval himself is not created: he died in 1872, eleven years before Kipping was born, and has no connection to the estate. See [[kipping-mccraith-which-house]].

**The 1901 census gives her a second time, and independently.** She is in the Kipping household on Clumber Road West that year as mother-in-law, a widow of 58, born at Manchester - so a birth year of 1843 twice over, twenty years apart, on two different schedules. The Manchester birthplace that the whole Duval argument rests on is therefore not a single clerk's entry that might be wrong, and she was already widowed by 1901, which dates W. T. Holland's death before that.

**A small thing that runs the same way.** The Kippings' housemaid in 1901, **Ellen M Norman**, sixteen, was born at **Bridgwater in Somerset** - the Hollands' own town, and the town where all three sisters were married. A servant of that age carrying that birthplace is likelier to have come to Nottingham with the family than to have been hired here, which is one more thread between this household and Bridgwater.

Duval himself is still not created, for the reason given above.

questions.title: John Loverseed Mann: how are the Manns and the Loverseeds related?
questions.detail:
A probate notice in the Nottingham Weekly Press of 1 May 1908 gives the full name of the man the record holds as 'John L Mann' (#3306) of 5 North Road: **John Loverseed Mann**. A middle name of that kind is usually a mother's maiden name, and it is the first hard link between two families the record had only as neighbours.

**What the record holds of each.** The Manns: John Loverseed Mann, cardboard box manufacturer, late of Thomas Mann and Co. of Postern Place, died 16 March 1908 aged 44; his widow **Alice** carried the business on and is returned at 5 North Road in 1911 as a cardboard box manufacturer in her own right; their son Thomas is with her. Wright's Directory also prints 'Thomas Mann, box manufacturer' on Pelham Crescent in 1894-95 - presumably the firm's founder and very likely his father - and 'John L. Mann, of Mann & Son' on North Road the same year.

**The Loverseeds** are all over the same streets. Edwin Gauntley Loverseed held **2 Western Terrace** from 1894-95 to 1915-16 and is there on the 1911 return with his wife and three daughters. **Sarah Loverseed** had **1 Western Terrace** in 1894-95 and 1898-99, before the Patons. **A. W. Loverseed** was at Pelham Lodge on Pelham Crescent in 1894-95. And the record's own descriptions of **10 and 12 Pelham Crescent** call them 'one of a pair of houses c1870-75 possibly by John Loverseed' - so the name attaches to the building of the estate as well as to living on it.

**What would settle it:** John Loverseed Mann's birth or marriage registration, which would give his mother's maiden name outright, or Thomas Mann's marriage. If the mother was a Loverseed, it ties a box-manufacturing family to a building one across four houses, and may explain how the Manns came to be in The Park at all. Nothing is joined on the strength of a middle name alone.

**Also outstanding:** #3306 is recorded as 'John L Mann' and wants renaming to **John Loverseed Mann**, which an import cannot do.

**Advanced by the 1891 return: they were next-door neighbours.** The census puts **Thomas Mann, cardboard box manufacturer, at 14 Pelham Crescent** with his wife Mary Ann, his son **John Loverseed Mann, 27, a cashier**, his daughter Nellie Annie and a servant - and **Arthur Wellington Loverseed at 16 Pelham Crescent**, immediately adjacent, with his wife Kate, six children and their servant Esther Holland. So the two families were not merely on the same streets: they were side by side, and the Mann son carried the neighbour's surname as his middle name. Arthur Wellington Loverseed, returned as living on his own means, is very probably the 'A. W. Loverseed, Pelham lodge' the directory prints on the crescent in 1894-95. Thomas Mann is created from this page; he was not in the record at all, though the directory prints him as a box manufacturer on Pelham Crescent in 1894-95 and the firm his son died as part of was Thomas Mann and Co.

**It still does not prove the descent.** Mary Ann Mann's maiden name is not on the 1891 schedule, and nothing there says she was a Loverseed. Her marriage, or her son's birth registration, would give it outright. What the page removes is the possibility that the middle name was a coincidence.

**A duplicate found alongside it.** The record holds this man twice: **#3306 John Loverseed Mann**, with the probate biography and the 1908 death, and **#3689 John L Mann**, born 1864, same 1901 household, no biography. They are one person entered under a census short form. Keep #3306, which carries everything, and join them with **Join up people entered under a census short form** on the admin page.

questions.title: Five servants and no family at 1 Cavendish Crescent South - is the signature Henry Crewdson?
questions.detail:
The 1921 schedule for **1 Cavendish Crescent South** lists five servants and nobody else - Daisy Sands, Gertrude Annie Hanson, Zillah Spear, Clara Emily Strauther and Margaret Annie Locke - in a house of **sixteen rooms**. The first two lines are blank and the household is signed from off the page.

**The hand reads Crewdson.** A **Henry Crewdson, solicitor**, is in the record at 25 Lenton Avenue (#169) in 1901 and 1911, with his wife Margaret and, in 1901, four servants of his own. A move across the estate between 1911 and 1921 would fit, and a solicitor's household is the right size for sixteen rooms and five staff.

**Not yet written down as fact**, because the reading of the initial letter is the whole of the case. If it holds, Henry and Margaret Crewdson belong on this household, and 1 Cavendish Crescent South gains its head.

questions.title: Frank William Martin is married on the 1921 schedule but has no wife in the house
questions.detail:
At **3 Cavendish Crescent South** in 1921, Frank William Martin, solicitor, aged 60 years 7 months, is entered as **married** - but the schedule holds only him and two servants, Mildred Musgrave and Elizabeth Williamson.

His wife **Emma Mary Martin** was with him at the same house in 1911, aged 48. Where she was on census night, and whether she was alive, is not in the record.

The same pattern turns up two doors away at [[who-signed-the-schedule-at-1-cavendish-crescent-south]], where a whole family is off the schedule and only the staff are counted - April 1921 seems to have caught several Park households away from home.

questions.title: Three birthplaces in the record carry the wrong county
questions.detail:
**Long Eaton is written as Nottinghamshire.** It is in Derbyshire, just over the county line.

**Heckington is given as Leicestershire.** It is in Lincolnshire.

**Stourbridge appears twice, once as Staffordshire and once as Worcestershire.** It was in Worcestershire.

These matter more than they look, because birthplaces are geocoded for the Origins map and a wrong county sends the pin to the wrong place - or, where the name exists in both counties, to a village nobody in the record ever came from.

questions.title: What is the colour key on Dougal de Havilland's map?
questions.detail: The map colours the houses, and the colouring appears to encode the architect or the building period. Reading it off the scan gave forty suggestions that all fell into a single class, which is almost certainly wrong — the yellow road markings were being read as the yellow of one of the periods. Does a printed key exist, or does anyone remember what the colours meant? With the key, the map would name the architect of a great many houses at once.

questions.title: Five birthplaces land in the wrong country and the page does not say which is meant
questions.detail:
The sanity check catches birth places that end up outside the British Isles without naming anywhere abroad. **Four were plain enough to position by hand** - Blackheath (it answered Dover, Delaware), Buckingham (Virginia), Huntingdon (Pennsylvania) and Stratford, Essex (Newark, New Jersey).

**Five are not, because the census text is ambiguous:**

| as the page has it | where it lands | the trouble |
|---|---|---|
| **Ashton** | Ashton, Iowa | No county. Ashton-under-Lyne, Ashton-in-Makerfield and Ashton, Northamptonshire are all candidates |
| **Newton** | Newton County, Texas | No county, and Newton is one of the commonest village names in England |
| **Radburn, Wales** | a road in Sydney | No Radburn in Wales. **Radyr** near Cardiff is the nearest sounding place, but that is a guess |
| **South, Lincolnshire** | Lincolnshire, South Carolina | The name is cut off. South Somercotes, South Kelsey, South Witham and a dozen others begin that way |
| **Wellington, Lincolnshire** | Wellington, New Zealand | **There is no Wellington in Lincolnshire.** Shropshire, Somerset and Herefordshire all have one |

**Each needs its page**, and in most cases the rest of the household will settle it - the county the other people in the house were born in usually decides which Ashton or Newton is meant.

**Three more the check flags are right and should be left alone:** the **Falkland Islands**, **New South Wales** and **Marquise, France** genuinely are outside the British Isles. They are the check doing its job, not errors.

Positioned places go in `data/geocode_manual.json`, which wins over the geocoder at the next deploy.

questions.title: E Winifred Goldsmith's birthplace reads Shropshire and Devizes, which do not agree
questions.detail:
The servant at **4 Clare Valley** in 1921 gives her birthplace as the county **Shropshire** and the town **Devizes**. **Devizes is in Wiltshire**, not Shropshire.

One of the two is wrong, and there is no telling which from the schedule alone. Held as written until the original is looked at again or she is found in an earlier round.

questions.title: The house names the record knows are buried in prose, where nothing can search them
questions.detail:
**There is a `property_names` table and it holds fifteen rows.** For 361 properties.

This came to light the hard way. Two 1911 covers named **Lynwood** and **St Ives**, neither appeared in the property list, and both were written up as houses the record had never held. **A. Hagues placed both immediately** - 2 and 4 Tattershall Drive. The record knew them all along.

**It knew them in the history paragraph**, in sentences like *One of a pair of semi-detached houses c1890. Also known as 'Lynwood'.* That is prose. Nothing on the site can search it, no house page shows the name as a name, and a cover reading *Lynwood* matches nothing.

**St Ives is worse, because the record had already used the name to make a decision.** Dougal de Havilland's Park Map was read at this property and the label sampled was **4StIves** - which is how **T C Hine** came to be accepted as its architect. The name was good enough to attribute a building and still not good enough to find the house by.

**A sweep of the history text turns up 54 properties carrying a quoted house name** - Charnwood, Gleadthorpe, Hazlewood, Brightlands, Cuylerholme, Selsoe, Ferndene, Parkdale, Iveston, Avoca, Fairholme, Oakhurst, Greylands, Newlands, Fern Lodge, Ivanhoe Lodge, Claremont, Napier House, Barton House, Kenilworth House, Redcliffe House, Elmhurst, Overdale and more. **Fifteen are in the table. Roughly forty are not.**

**The fix is mechanical and worth doing before the next round of covers.** Lift the quoted names out of the history text, check each one by eye - the sweep also catches *Bowl*, *Plan for Nottingham Park* and other things that are not house names - and write them into `property_names`, which already has the year_from / year_to columns for a house that changed its name.

**Then every cover name is a lookup instead of a puzzle**, and the open ones in [[clare-valley-missing-houses]] are genuinely open rather than merely unsearchable.

questions.title: The National Archives 1921 transcription put a household in the wrong house and changed its head's name and sex
questions.detail:
**Settled.** Schedule 195 of the 1921 census reads **James Forman, Head, M, 65 years 9 months, Printer, Employer, Sherwood Street, Nottingham**, and is signed *James Forman*. The record held that household as **Kathleen Forman, female**, at **16 and 16a Cavendish Crescent North**.

All six people matched on age to the year, so there is no doubt it is the same household:

| the schedule | the record had |
|---|---|
| **James** Forman, 65, M | **Kathleen** Forman, 65, F |
| Ethel Forman, 58 | Ethel Forman, 58 |
| Alice May **Brazier**, 29 | Alice May **Bray**, 29 |
| Lydia Perkins, 15 | Lydia Perkins, 15 |
| Jane Blinder, 32 | Jane Blinder, 32 |
| Mary Kate Bennett, 31 | Mary Kate Bennett, 31 |

**Corrected, and moved to 18 and 18a Cavendish Crescent North**, which is where A. Hagues places it and where the record independently agrees: **James Forman heads that house in 1901**, and the street directories of **1894, 1898, 1910, 1913 and 1915** all print *James Forman, of T. Forman & Sons* on Cavendish Crescent North.

**Why it is worth a question rather than a quiet fix.** This is not a hard hand or a faded page - the schedule is a householder's own clear writing, signed. If the National Archives transcription can turn a signed James into a Kathleen and move the household two doors, then **every row in the record sourced to *National Archives 1921 Census* is a transcription nobody here has checked**, and the 1911 and 1921 rounds came in that way wholesale.

**Next:** the rounds that carry that source line are worth spot-checking against the images, starting with heads of household whose sex looks wrong for their name or their trade. A printer and employer entered as a woman in 1921 is exactly the shape of the fault, and the *Forename Sex Review* page already lists candidates. Links: [[nineteen-people-from-1901-without-a-surname]].

questions.title: Every full import undoes corrections made since the files were written - what to check afterwards
questions.detail:
**The Import button runs every `people_*.json` file, not only the new one.** The older files still say what was true when they were written, so anything corrected since is quietly put back. Importing 39 people on 27 September 2026 brought **thirty-one stray rows** with it, **none of them from that file**.

## The three ways it goes wrong

**1. A corrected birth year mints a second person - on every run.**
The 1939 file works `born_year` out as *1939 minus the age on the page*, which is **a year early whenever the birthday falls after the census date**. With `match_born_year` set, the importer finds nobody of that name and year, and makes a new person. Eight had accumulated: Noel Parker Woodward, Richard Warwick Bond, John Hammersley, Alice Mary Vogel, George Pearson, Lucy Mabel Walker - and two where the record had since given the person their **full middle name**, so even the name stopped matching: *Leslie F Bates* against **Leslie Fleetwood Bates**, *Winifred Frances Bates* against **Winifred Frances Furze Bates**.

**The guard is `person_alias`.** Folding the duplicate back leaves the old name and year behind as an alias, and the importer checks there when the name-and-year lookup misses. That is why a **merge** is safe and a **split** is not.

**2. A split is undone.** `tools_split_welded_people.py` moves a row to the person it belongs to, but the name in the file still points at the person it was taken *from*. Ten rows came back this way - the Lewis cork cutter and his wife, Elizabeth G Lewis twice over, and the Clare Valley wife who had landed on the **five-year-old Margaret Lewis of The Chestnuts**.

**3. A property split is undone.** Thirteen rows reappeared on the unsplit **#1**, because three files still pointed there after Albury Square and North Road were separated into four houses.

## What to do after every import

1. **People in two places in one round.** Was 29, now 16 - and the sixteen are older name-welds, not import damage. Any rise means a split has been undone.
2. **`tools_split_welded_people.py`** with no `--apply`. It should report nothing outstanding.
3. **People created with an id above the last import's.** A single-row new person whose row duplicates an existing person's is this bug, not a discovery.

## The durable fix, applied where it was found

**Bind by `id` rather than by name.** A person number survives a rename *and* a corrected year, and the importer never invents anybody from one. Schedule 146 at 5 Clare Valley, the Lewis cork cutter across four files, and the Albury Square and North Road entries are all bound this way now.

**Worth doing generally:** any file whose people the record has since corrected should carry numbers instead of names. Links: [[elizabeth-g-lewis-is-several-women]], [[henry-wing-was-two-men]].

## Checked again after the Derby Road import, 29 September 2026 - and it had all happened again

The import brought **119 new census rows** and, with them, **eight people the record already had** and **twelve duplicate rows**. None of it came from the new file.

**Three of the duplicates were my own fault**, and the mistake is worth naming. `build91b.py` looked up every name in the record and, where it found one, forced a new person with `born_year` worked out from the age on the page - on the assumption that *a name already in the record means a different person*. For George Miller the coachman, his wife Annie and John Ashworth the timber merchant, that was wrong: the birthplaces and the 1901 round say they are the same people. The file now binds them by number.

**A tool rather than a list.** `tools_fold_import_duplicates.py` finds them by shape - a person created after a given id, holding exactly one census row, where someone else of the same surname and a similar forename already holds a row for the same round, house and age - folds the new one away and leaves an alias. It is the alias that stops the importer making a third copy.

**Property splits leak the same way.** Five people at 36 and 36a The Ropewalk came back at 36 after the split had moved them to 36a, because `people_1881_standard_hill_part1.json` still named the unsplit house. Fixed at source.

**And the Lewis split had been undone completely** - both people the split tool made were gone and their rows were back on the welded originals. It has been re-run, and the four files that name those two now bind them by number. Note that the split tool gives the people **new numbers** each time it has to redo the work, so the files need rebinding whenever it does.

**Count of people standing in two places in one round: 19 before this clean-up, 10 after.** The ten that remain are older name-welds - Mary Shaw is in three houses at once in 1881 - and want the pages rather than a tool.

questions.title: Nineteen people from the 1901 round entered without a surname - all now resolved
questions.detail:
**An enumerator writing a household does not repeat the surname.** He writes it against the head and rules a ditto mark down the column for everybody under him. My transcription of the 1901 pages read that mark as what stood in the column, so nineteen people went into the record with a **middle initial in place of a family name** - *Frank B.*, *Ellen T.*, *Annie E.*, *Marjorie P.* - each one a person with no surname, sitting unfiled, and unrecognisable as a member of the household they were returned in.

**They are resolved.** Every one has been traced back to the head of the house they were returned under - by schedule number where the page gives one, and where it does not, by the house number written into the address and the head the record already holds filed there.

| entered as | belongs to | already in the record |
|---|---|---|
| Annie E., Arthur E., Marjorie P., Kathleen W. | Joseph Blythe, coachman, **6 Lenton Avenue** | yes - all four |
| Henry C., Arthur J. | Henry Thompson, gardener, **8 Lenton Avenue** | yes - both |
| Margaret A., Katharine J. | Helen M. Parkin, **14 Lenton Avenue** | yes - both |
| Alice M. | Henry Rawson, **12 Lenton Avenue** | yes |
| Lisle N. | William Robinson, **21 Lenton Avenue** | yes |
| Margaret E. | William Bowers, **Lenton Avenue** | no - wants renaming |
| Amy M. | Arthur Forman, newspaper proprietor, **13 Lenton Road** | yes |
| Ellen T., Frank B., Elizth B., Edith C. | William W Lewis, **6 Lenton Road** | yes - all four |
| Mary D., Geoffrey C. | Louisa Heather Williams, **Lenton Road** | no - want renaming |
| Jane A. B. | William Martin, **Hamilton Drive** | no - wants renaming |

**Sixteen of the nineteen are duplicates**, not new people: the record already held them, under their proper names, from a neighbouring census. Only three want a rename - Jane A. Martin, Margaret Bowers, and Mary and Geoffrey Williams.

**One of them matters more than the rest.** *Frank B.* is **Frank Beckitt Lewis**, City Architect of Nottingham. See [[frank-beckitt-lewis-city-architect]].

**And the error was worth having**, because undoing it named three whole households and the houses they were in - Lewis at 6 Lenton Road, Williams on Lenton Road, Bowers on Lenton Avenue - each of which the record already carried in the censuses either side of 1901, and none of which could be matched while the family name was missing.

**The transcription rule this sets.** A ditto mark is not a value. Where a page repeats the surname by ruling it down, the surname carried down from the head is what belongs in the column - which is how this record already handles the 1891 and 1911 rounds.

questions.title: THE RULE, and the 1939 amended names - all 61 settled
questions.detail:
**The 1939 Register was not a census.** It was an identity register, kept up to date for decades - which is why a woman who married after 1939 has her **married name written across the original**, and why the online indexes show the *later* name. **Ivy Burton**, cook at Penrhyn House on 29 September 1939, is indexed as **Ivy Luke** because somebody wrote LUKE over Burton years afterwards.

## The rule

**A person is named as the page named them on the night.** The amendment is a real and valuable fact, but it is a fact about what happened *afterwards*, not the name of the woman who was in the house.

So for every one of these:

| | |
|---|---|
| **first_name / last_name** | the name on the night — **Ivy Burton** |
| **person_alias** | the amended name, `made_by = '1939 amendment'` — so a search for **Luke** still finds her, and a re-import cannot make a second person |
| **maiden_name** | **cleared**. Burton is not her maiden name in this record; it is her name |
| **the census row's source** | says the page is amended, and that the indexes show the later name |

## Why round this way and not the other

1. **The record's job is who was in the house that night.** She was Ivy Burton.
2. **Every other person is named as their page named them.** Naming one woman by a name from decades later makes her the odd one out and quietly changes what a census row means.
3. **The alias keeps her findable** under the name the indexes use, which is the only real argument for the other way round.
4. **It turns a silent overwrite into a dateable fact.** *Burton became Luke* is a marriage between 1939 and whenever the amendment was made. Recorded as a name, it is invisible; recorded as an amendment, it is evidence.

## How many

**Two carry a maiden name from the 1939 round today**, and only one was this problem - Ivy. But **61 more have an amendment the transcriber could not make out**, and every future page will bring more, because a legible amendment is the easy thing to transcribe as the surname.

**The signature to watch for:** a 1939 person with a `maiden_name` set and no other round. That is almost always this, and `fix_1939_amended_names.py` takes them one line at a time.

Links: [[names-the-1939-register-flags]].

## How big it is, and how to work it — settled 30 September 2026

**A. Hagues asked whether the documents should go through again.** They should not. Here is what the record already knows and the cheapest way to close the rest.

### The 61 flagged rows - and the index that reads what the page cannot

Their note reads *"the name written **under** the amendment cannot be read"* - so the surname in the record **is** the amendment, and the 1939 name is gone beneath it. **Sixty of the sixty-one are women.**

**Every one of those 61 rows was marked**, so it says on its face that the surname is later than the household it sits in, and the record stops claiming a 1939 name it does not have.

**But they are not beyond recovery, and that was wrong when first written.** The Register's own index carries the name under the amendment even where the page will not give it up - it is printed as *Edward (Howitt)*, the amendment first and the name on the night in brackets. Schedule 23 at 8 Park Drive proved it: **Ethel M Howitt** and **Amy M Jenkins** were both among the 61, and the index named them both. The index also supplies **forenames lost under repair strips**, which is a second use for it.

So the 61 are a worklist, not a loss. Fifty-nine remain. `tools_clear_settled_amendment_flags.py` takes the note off each row as its name is recovered, since the note contradicts the line beside it once the name is known.

**The one man among them is worth a look on his own account:** *John Garwell, 11, at 12 The Ropewalk.* A boy's surname is not amended by marriage, so his is adoption, a correction, or a misread.

### The realistic pool is smaller than it looks

**281 women aged 12 to 50** are in the 1939 round. Only the ones whose page shows a strikethrough matter, and 57 of those are already flagged. The index's bracketed form is the quickest way to read any of them.

### The worksheet - the route chosen, 1 October 2026

**`~/Desktop/1939 names - fill in.xlsx`**, written by `amended_names_worksheet.py`.

**Everybody in the round is on it - all 720 - in the order the record received them**, house by house and schedule by schedule, so it can be worked straight down the page beside the images rather than jumped around. Sorting the likely cases to the top was the wrong shape for the job: the pages come in runs, and a sheet that reorders them makes every row a search.

Two blank columns, **NAME ON THE NIGHT** and **AMENDED TO**, are the only ones to touch. A row needs both filled before anything is done with it, so a half-finished sheet is safe to hand back at any point. Tinting carries the reading, not the order: the 61 whose surname *is* the amendment are the darkest, the 281 women of marrying age are warm, everyone else is plain. Sheet two is the 61 on their own.

### What goes in the two columns

**NAME ON THE NIGHT** is the whole name as the page has it, forename included - *Meryl Vera Wardle*. **AMENDED TO** is the surname written over it afterwards.

**One column or two decides what happens:**

| | |
|---|---|
| **Both filled** | an amendment. The name goes back, the later name is kept as an alias, the maiden name is cleared |
| **Only NAME ON THE NIGHT** | a plain correction. The name was read wrong and nothing was written over it; the earlier reading is kept as an alias so a search for what the indexes say still finds them |

So an ordinary misreading needs nothing in AMENDED TO. That column means *somebody wrote on the page*, not *this name changed*.

### More than one marriage

A woman who married, then divorced or was widowed, then married again carries every name she was amended to, **separated by a comma, earliest first and the latest last**: *Monsarrat, Hart*. Each becomes an alias in its own right and the order between them is kept, because that order is the only thing in the record saying which marriage came first.

**Meryl Vera Wardle**, 35, at 5 Western Terrace on 29 September 1939, is the worked example - indexed as *Marjorie Vera Hart*, two marriages and a misread forename deep. Her name on the night also places her: she is in a house with George Oral and Edith Wardle, 65 and 60, which the indexed name had hidden.

`fix_1939_amended_names.py --sheet "<path>"` takes the filled rows straight off it and does the whole rule for each.

**Or simply say so in passing.** A line like *Ivy Luke = Burton* is enough; they can be applied in batches. No document needs re-sending either way.

### Twenty-six the record already knew about - settled 1 October 2026

**The reading had been done and the rule had not been applied.** Twenty-six 1939 rows carried a source line saying in as many words *"entered as Lewis and amended later to Wormington"* - both names read off the page by the transcriber - while the record went on calling her by the name somebody wrote over her afterwards. They are now put back, with the amendments kept as aliases.

Among them: **Barbara Rushton**, amended twice, Lazareff written above Rushton and Beaumont above that; and **Audrey J Plackett** of Cedar Lodge, who had been sitting in her own family's household under a married name.

`fix_1939_recorded_amendments.py` finds them **by the shape of the source line**, not by a list, so it keeps working as more pages are read. Two are deliberately left: Meryl Vera Wardle, already done, and **Meryl Hope M Owen**, whose line reads *"Taylor and amended to Owen, or the other way about; both are written"* - the direction is not known, so nothing is done.

**This is the lesson, not the twenty-six.** A rule written into the record is not the same as a rule applied to it. Anything that says *"entered as ... and amended ..."* in a source line is an instruction nobody carried out.

### The whole round worked, 1 October 2026

A. Hagues took the sheet of all 720 and filled in **144 rows**. Applying them changed **128 people** - married names taken off, forenames put right, and every amendment kept as a name the woman can still be found under.

**All sixty-one are settled.** Every row whose note said the name under the amendment could not be read has now been read - including **John Garwell, 11, at 12 The Ropewalk**, the single male among them, where A. Hagues confirms there is nothing underneath: the name is John Garwell and it stands as the page has it. The transcriber's mark was wrong, which is worth knowing about the other marks.

**Two of the sixty-one were not amendments at all.** *Enid Kodley* is **Edith Feetham** and *Violet Selby* is **Violet Wilmott** - the hand the transcriber took for an amendment was the name itself, badly written. Both keep the earlier reading as an alias.

**Everything was bound by person id**, in the database and in the import files. The sheet's "name as recorded" column went stale the moment a name went back, and half of these people had already been corrected earlier the same day - matching on names would have missed every one of them. That is the lesson for any sheet that goes out and comes back.

**Barbara Rushton's first married name is Azareff**, not Lazareff as this record had read it.

questions.title: The variant-duplicate check calls a shared street "near proof", and after 1871 it is not
questions.detail:
**Settled.** `variant_duplicates.py` grades a pair higher when both people **carry the same address**, and calls that "near proof". That held while almost every census row was filed to a house. It does not hold now.

The 1871 and 1881 rounds brought in **1,204 unfiled rows**, and an unfiled row carries a **street**, not a house - "Pelham Crescent", "The Ropewalk (no number given)". Dozens of unrelated people share those strings.

**What it produced.** For 1881 it reported **136 pairs carrying the same address on both sides - near proof**. Among them: **John Scott Wells** against **John R Ellis**, both at "Pelham Crescent", which are plainly two men. Restricting the same question to pairs sharing an actual **property_id** gives **thirteen** pairs, and they are all real - see [[1871-1881-duplicates-from-a-letter-or-two]].

**Open.** The tool needs to treat a filed address and an unfiled street label differently: same `property_id` is evidence, same `unresolved_address` is not. Until it does, its top band is noise whenever a round has been read off the page rather than an index.

**Next.** Change the grading so the address bonus applies only where both rows have a `property_id`, and say "same street" rather than "same address" for the rest. Checklist step 5.6 should say so too.

questions.title: Two dates on the estate history where the map and the archive disagree
questions.detail:
The estate history now follows the University of Nottingham's archive wherever it disagrees with Dougal de Havilland's Park Map, on A. Hagues's instruction — they hold the Newcastle family papers. Six dates changed that way, and each entry keeps the map's own date beside it. Four are straightforward. **Two are not.**

**The castle, 1087.** The archive's timeline begins the first castle in 1087. The map says 1068 and credits William the Conqueror, ordering it raised by his son Peverel. The difficulty is that William died in September 1087, and 1068 — after the northern campaign — is the date usually given. 1087 may be the archive's own slip, or may refer to something later than the first earthwork. Worth checking against the printed timeline or the Newcastle papers themselves.

**The sale to Oxford, 1939.** The archive dates the 8th Duke's sale to Oxford University 1939. Both the map *and* the Nottingham Park Estate's own published history say **1938** — so here the archive stands alone against two sources, one of them the estate's own account of itself. This is the one correction where following the archive may be the wrong call.

The other four, for completeness: Cavendish's purchase of the ruin 1663 not 1662; the first house — St Mary's vicarage — 1809 not 1810; forty to fifty houses built by 1832 rather than fifty by 1834; and T. C. Hine appointed surveyor in 1854, not 1851 where the map places it alongside the 4th Duke's death.

questions.title: Parkhurst, 4 South Road: the 1925 build date was wrong, and is now 1870
questions.detail:
**Settled.** The record dated 4 South Road, also known as Parkhurst, to **1925**. Three things contradicted it, and A. Hagues has corrected the date to **1870**.

- **The property's own history text**, in the same record, reads 'One of a pair of houses (with 3 Clumber Crescent South). Possibly by architects Hine & Son **1870-75**.' The field and the prose beside it disagreed.
- **Its pair.** 5 South Road, Gardenhurst (#304), is dated **1870** and described in the same terms - one of a pair, possibly Hine & Son 1870-75. Two houses built together should not be dated fifty-five years apart.
- **The directory.** Wright's prints 'Parkhurst, Mrs. Sarah A. Gamble' on South Road in **1894-95** and **1898-99**, and 'Parkhurst, Walker Joseph' in 1910-11. People were living in the house three decades before 1925.

The 1925 figure may have come from a later alteration rather than nothing at all: the history notes the house is now converted into flats, and the description records an early twentieth-century lean-to and a later single-storey extension in the yard toward Clumber Crescent South. If a date for the conversion turns up, it belongs in the history text rather than in the build date. Kept here so that 1925 is not entered again from whatever source first supplied it.

questions.title: ON FOOT: what a walk round The Park would settle
questions.detail:
**A list to take out of the house.** Every one of these is a question the record cannot answer from paper and a pair of eyes could settle in a minute. Kept together so they can be done in one round rather than one at a time.

## The Ropewalk

1. **The small building between 4 and 2** (#430). It held **William Hurst, solicitor**, and three others in 1861, it has no number on the page and none in the record, and it still stands. **Does it have a number or a name now?** Is it a coach house, as it looks?
2. **Number 2 - is it visibly two houses?** The listing calls it *formerly 2no. townhouses c1835-40*, and the 1861 enumerator walks it as **2 and 2a**, ten people in each.
3. **Do 30, 32 and 32a exist as separate front doors?** They hold a household in 1861 and nothing in any other round, which is odd for three houses.
4. **What is above 56?** Both the 1861 and 1871 walks have households beyond where the record's numbering stops, and both put **John Gibson** at that end. A. Hagues reads the ground as empty until the 1950s. See [[the-ropewalk-top-end-beyond-the-numbering]].

## Derby Road and Clinton Terrace

5. **4 Clinton Terrace / 133 Derby Road - one dwelling or two?** The Sampsons' 1921 schedule has been written over, 129 on top of what looks like 133, and the Essexes are already at 133. If the house is two dwellings the difficulty disappears. See [[derby-terrace-1921-which-number]].
6. **Does Clinton Terrace run one-to-one with the odd Derby Road numbers?** The record says 1 to 7 Clinton Terrace are 127 to 139 Derby Road, and an 1921 servant confirms 5 = 135 by writing both. Worth checking the door numbers along the row.

## Park Terrace and the ridge

7. **Which present-day house is Clinton House - or was it rebuilt?** A. Hagues reads the Park Map as dating the building there to the 1970s and giving it no name. If so it went the way of Sunnyside. See [[what-is-clinton-house]].
8. **What stands on Sunnyside's ground now?** It was still there and still named on the 1953 Ordnance Survey, so it came down after 1955. See [[sunnyside-and-clinton-house-what-to-ask]].
9. **Sun Drive** - A. Hagues gives it as a real road with **only one property on it, Sunnyside**, which is why the record does not hold it as a street. Worth confirming there is nothing else along it.

## Houses the record holds as one and may be two

10. **Cliff House, Lenton Road** (#196) - the record carries it as 32, 33, 33a and 33b in one property, with **52 people** across four rounds. Are there four doors? See [[properties-carrying-two-house-numbers]].
11. **22 and 24 Cavendish Crescent North** (#36) - two numbers in one record, two rounds of people, and no evidence either way.
12. **16 and 16a Cavendish Crescent North** (#31) - A. Hagues confirms it is **one house of about 1885 now split into two households**, which is why #411 has just been folded into it. Worth a look at whether the split shows from the street.
13. **Park Drive's numbering** - the record holds 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7 and 9, plus Ashley House and Clumber House unnumbered. Do any of the three unnumbered or converted houses still carry a **5, 8 or 10** on a gatepost or a door? The 1881 and 1939 pages head households at 10 and at 8. See [[park-drive-missing-numbers-5-8-and-10]].
14. **Tattershall Drive between 5 and 17a** - **Lynwood**, **St Ives** and **The Lodge** are names the 1939 enumerator used in a straight run past number 5, and **Elmsdale** with them. Do any of those names survive on a gate, and what numbers do the houses carry now? See [[named-houses-on-tattershall-drive-and-where-they-sit]].
15. **Huntingdon Drive between 10 and 14** - the street has no **11, 12 or 13**, and the 1939 enumerator names **Brampton** and **Ravenswood** in that gap, coming down from The Cottage at 14. Do the names or the numbers survive? See [[huntingdon-drive-has-no-11-12-or-13]].
16. **The Park Row entrance** - **Tower House** and **East Lodge** stand together there. How many lodges are at that entrance? The 1939 enumerator takes a house called **The Lodge** between the hospital's lodge and Tower House. See [[the-lodge-on-park-terrace-is-probably-east-lodge]].
17. **Between 13 and 15 Park Terrace** - the 1939 enumerator writes **38** for the house there, and the street runs 1 to 20. What number does it carry now? See [[park-terrace-has-a-number-38]].

## How to use this

Anything settled here is worth more than a paper source, because these are the questions where the record has run out of documents. Add to the list as it grows.

questions.title: PROVED - the unsourced 1939 rows hold married names, not names on the night
questions.detail:
**A page settles what the record had only inferred.** The 1939 Register's **RMGB** district - a second district covering Lenton Road, Lenton Avenue, Hamilton Drive and Lenton Boulevard, which the record's RMGC book does not reach - puts the amendment question beyond argument.

## 17 Lenton Road, schedule 143

| The record holds | The page has on the line | Written above it in a later hand |
|---|---|---|
| Edith **Kirk** | Kirk | — |
| Phyllis **Sleigh** | *Hodkin* (reading uncertain) | **SLEIGH** |
| Annie **Mason** | **Padgett** | **MASON** |
| Lilian **Gannon** | **Barefoot** | **GANNON** |

**Three of the six women in one house.** The record is calling each of them by a name written over her years after the night, and the woman who was not amended is held correctly. Next door at **19 Lenton Road**, schedule 144, the record has **Sarah J Thorpe**; the page has **Wyld** on the line with *Thorpe* above it.

## Why this matters beyond the fifteen houses

It is the first time the rule has been **read off a page** rather than reasoned from a household. Everything the record has done with amended names - putting twenty-six women back, the bracket convention, Ivy Burton - rested on inference. This is the evidence.

It also explains the rule's shape: **what is written over the name is what the indexes carry**, which is why an index-built import gets it wrong every time and a page-built one does not.

## What is wrong, and how much

**46 rows across the record had no source line at all** and are now flagged on their face. They came from an index, so they carry no schedule number, no sub number and no district - and their surnames cannot be trusted. The houses are on **Lenton Road**, **Cavendish Crescent North and South**, **South Road** and **Clumber Crescent South**.

**One correction is not an amendment at all**: the record's *Minnie Dunant* at 19 Lenton Road reads **Durrant** on the page.

## The bigger gap underneath

**Lenton Avenue has no 1939 round whatsoever** - twenty-four houses, every one of them holding 1881, 1891, 1901, 1911 and 1921, and nothing for 1939. **43, 45 and 47 Lenton Road** are the same. The RMGB pages cover exactly that ground, so the street's missing round is sitting in this district.

Links: [[how-to-handle-a-1939-amended-name]], [[the-1939-index-bracket-which-name-is-underneath]], [[every-census-gap-and-where-to-start]].

questions.title: ANSWERED: Eleven people were in two houses at once. Ten were welds; one is a misfiling
questions.detail:
**Done.** `tools_split_welded_people.py` made **eleven new people and moved fifteen census rows**, and no original lost a row that was its own. Every split was read off the page rather than guessed - a wife of 65 and a cook of 22 are not the same woman, and a solicitor born at Gotham is not a soda-factory clerk born in Nottingham.

| was | is now |
|---|---|
| **Mary Shaw** in three houses | Charles Shaw's wife at Rock House, and two cooks - one of 22 born Kimberley, one of 36 born Rowsley |
| **Elizabeth G Lewis** in three | John W Lewis's wife at Hardwicke House; Henry Lewis's at The Chestnuts; and the cork cutter's, born Tewkesbury, who keeps both her rounds |
| **William W Lewis** in two | the hosiery manufacturer of 3 Pelham Crescent, born Tewkesbury, 1871 to 1891 - and **William Lewis the cork cutter**, born Nottingham, who keeps 1881, 1891, 1901 and 1911 |
| **George Parr** in two | the solicitor, born Gotham, from 1871 to 1921 - and **George P Parr**, Samuel Parr's clerk son at Oakhurst |
| **Emily S Johnson** in two | Samuel Waite Johnson's daughter at Lenton House - and **Samuel George Johnson's wife** at 17 Pelham Crescent. Two Samuels, two Emilys |
| **Mary Clarke**, **Elizabeth Brown**, **Sarah Bates** | the housekeeper of Park Terrace, and servants of 18, 22, 44 and 18 who were never one another |

## The eleventh is not a weld and is not fixed

**John George Woodward (#404) is one man with two 1881 rows**, both his own:

- **1 Cavendish Crescent North** - Head, 52, timber merchant, **with his wife, his stepson, three children and three servants**. This matches the 1881 page, which names the house **Carisbrook House, Cavendish Crescent North**.
- **33 Cavendish Road East** - Head, 52, timber merchant, **alone**.

The second looks like a misfiling, and his son **Frank Woodward is at 33 Cavendish Road East in 1901**, which is probably where the address came from. **But removing it empties that house for 1881 and turns a household into a gap**, so it is a deletion somebody should make deliberately rather than a script.

**Next.** Decide whether the lone row at 33 Cavendish Road East goes. If it does, [[every-census-gap-and-where-to-start]] gains a hole there and loses a false household, which is the right trade.

questions.title: ANSWERED: Seventeen people entered twice because my reading and the record's differ by a letter
questions.detail:
**Done. Thirty-two pairs merged**, by `tools_merge_duplicates.js`, which calls the **same** `mergePeopleInto` the site's own merge button calls - the function was lifted out of server.js into `merge_people.js` so the two can never drift apart. Every merge left an alias behind, so a file still written in the old spelling finds the keeper instead of making the person a third time.

Among them: **Frederick Wadsworth and his son Frederick A**, both doubled at 33 Lenton Avenue; **Harriett and Annie Husband** at 2 Park Terrace; **Martha Clarke** at 8 Park Terrace; the three **Lasalles** at 153 Derby Road; the **Thekers** at 54 The Ropewalk; and **Alfred and Sarah Dawson** at 11 Park Valley, whose surname the 1891 page had already settled against my Cawson.

## Nine are held back, in `data/duplicate_merges.json` under `held_back`

A letter or two is not enough when it is a father and son, or two surnames that happen to sit close:

- **Henry Wing and Henry M Wing**, 12 Park Terrace - father and son, the son nine in 1871
- **the two James B Gibsons**, 24 The Ropewalk, born 1843 and 1878 - and only the elder can be the James R Gibson of 1871
- **two George Derrys** at 10 Barrack Lane, and only one of them is George Perry
- **Ward and Wood**; **Wiss and Moss** - two letters apart and two different names
- **Skelton and Shelton** - both real surnames; one letter apart is not evidence
- **Anne S and Anna L Heaton**, born a year apart at 19 Lenton Road - as likely two sisters as one woman

**Next.** Those nine want an eye on the page, not a script.

---

**Settled.** The 1871 and 1881 transcriptions were read off the enumerator's page; the spellings already in the record for those houses came from an index. Where the two disagree by a letter or two, the importer could not see they were the same person and made a second one.

**Seventeen pairs, each sharing a forename and a house** - not merely a street label, which is what makes them near-certain rather than suspicious. **Keep the one carrying a birth year**; it is the older record and other things point at it.

| house | keep | merge in |
|---|---|---|
| 2 Park Terrace | #5233 Harriett **Husband** (1871) | #5899 Harriett **Husbands** (1881) |
| 2 Park Terrace | #5234 Annie **Husband** (1871) | #5901 Annie **Husbands** (1881) |
| 8 Park Terrace | #3530 Martha **Clarke** (1881) | #5252 Martha **Clark** (1871) |

questions.title: ANSWERED: Twenty-five more duplicates, where the surname matches and only the forename differs
questions.detail:
**Done. Thirty-two pairs merged**, by `tools_merge_duplicates.js`, which calls the **same** `mergePeopleInto` the site's own merge button calls - the function was lifted out of server.js into `merge_people.js` so the two can never drift apart. Every merge left an alias behind, so a file still written in the old spelling finds the keeper instead of making the person a third time.

Among them: **Frederick Wadsworth and his son Frederick A**, both doubled at 33 Lenton Avenue; **Harriett and Annie Husband** at 2 Park Terrace; **Martha Clarke** at 8 Park Terrace; the three **Lasalles** at 153 Derby Road; the **Thekers** at 54 The Ropewalk; and **Alfred and Sarah Dawson** at 11 Park Valley, whose surname the 1891 page had already settled against my Cawson.

## Nine are held back, in `data/duplicate_merges.json` under `held_back`

A letter or two is not enough when it is a father and son, or two surnames that happen to sit close:

- **Henry Wing and Henry M Wing**, 12 Park Terrace - father and son, the son nine in 1871
- **the two James B Gibsons**, 24 The Ropewalk, born 1843 and 1878 - and only the elder can be the James R Gibson of 1871
- **two George Derrys** at 10 Barrack Lane, and only one of them is George Perry
- **Ward and Wood**; **Wiss and Moss** - two letters apart and two different names
- **Skelton and Shelton** - both real surnames; one letter apart is not evidence
- **Anne S and Anna L Heaton**, born a year apart at 19 Lenton Road - as likely two sisters as one woman

**Next.** Those nine want an eye on the page, not a script.

---

**Settled.** [[1871-1881-duplicates-from-a-letter-or-two]] found seventeen pairs whose **surnames** differ by a letter. It could not find these, because here the surname matches letter for letter and it is the **forename** that differs - an initial against a full name, or one reading against another. My own check had the same blind spot: it insisted the surnames differ.

**The test used.** Same property, same surname, forename within two letters, birth years within two where both are known - **and never present in the same census year at that house**, because two people under one roof in one year are a family, not a duplicate.

## Two on the list must NOT be merged

**#3648 Henry Wing b.1831 and #5265 Henry M Wing** at 12 Park Terrace are **father and son**. The son is nine in 1871 and nineteen in 1881.

**#6021 James B Gibson b.1843 and #6024 James B Gibson b.1878** at 24 The Ropewalk are likewise father and son - the son is three in 1881. Only the elder is a duplicate of **#5717 James R Gibson**, and even that wants a look, because 1871 reads R and 1881 reads B.

**Why the test let them through.** Neither pair happens to sit in the same census year at that property in the record as it stands - the father is there in one round and the son in another - so the rule that catches families did not fire. **A same-house, same-surname pair always wants an eye on it before merging.**

**Next.** Merge on the Duplicate People page, leaving the two flagged pairs alone.

questions.title: ANSWERED: Ageing faster than the calendar proves something is wrong, not what
questions.detail:
**Done, and the answer was not the one expected.**

Seventy-seven people had census rounds disagreeing about their birth year by more than five years. `tools_split_by_birth_year.py` split **fifty-six** on the first test - grouping the rows by the birth year each age implies - including a grandfather and grandson both called **John Jardine**, 56 in 1881 and 6 in 1891.

A **second test** was then added: nobody ages nineteen years in ten, so a step that outruns the calendar is a fault the grouping cannot see. It found exactly the nine expected.

## And eight of the nine were not welds at all

**The calendar test proves that something is wrong. It cannot say what.** Ageing faster than the calendar means either two people welded together **or one person whose age was written down wrong** - and only the household around them tells you which.

| | the two rounds | what the household says |
|---|---|---|
| **John Langham** | 41 then 57 | **with his wife Martha and son Thomas C in every round** |
| **Thomas C Langham** | 2, 17, 31 | son beside John and Martha each time |
| **George Shepperley** | 40 then 59 | a chemist on Western Terrace both times, same son beside him |
| **Henry Hill** | 41 then 57 | son of the house on Pelham Crescent, same trade |
| **Hannah E Heath** | 30 then 48 | cook at 5 Lenton Road in both rounds |
| **Samuel Maples** | 50 then 77 | a solicitor of that name, twenty years apart |
| **Florence A. Wilkinson** | 26 then 30 | daughter of the house, Sarah Wilkinson beside her throughout |
| **Katherine Flersheim** | 34 then 48 | Hermann Flersheim's wife in every round |

**Only #2779 Florence Green was a weld** - 28 at 7 Lenton Avenue in 1901 and 47 at 30 The Ropewalk in 1911, two houses and no household in common. She is split.

**The record keeps the ages the pages give.** They are not corrected, because the page says what it says. The eight are listed in `data/age_conflicts_checked.json` with the reasoning, and the tool skips them, so nobody is offered the chance to invent eight people again.

**The thirteen who aged *slower* were never touched.** People rounded their age down. Frederick Pearson ages four years in one decade and ten in the next - one man who guessed once.

questions.title: SUPERSEDED - this read the 1939 bracket the wrong way round
questions.detail:
**Wrong, and superseded by [[which-side-of-the-bracket-is-the-night-name]].** This entry concluded that the bracketed name was the name on the night. A. Hagues has settled it the other way: the name on the line is the night name and the bracketed one is the marriage that followed. Kept for the reasoning, which shows how a household can look like proof and not be one.

---

**The Register's index prints amended names in a bracket** - *Ethel M Edward (Howitt)*, *Amy M Oakland (Jenkins)*, *Alice James (Mees)*, *Acho (Victoria) Wright (Richardson)*. One of the two is the name the page had on 29 September 1939 and the other was written over it afterwards. **Which way round matters for every one of them**, and the record has settled it one way on evidence that is good but not conclusive.

## The record reads the bracket as the name on the night

The evidence is **Ethel M Edward (Howitt)** at 8 Park Drive, schedule 23:

| | |
|---|---|
| The household | **John Arthur Howitt**, married; **Sybil Howitt**, 55; **John Kenneth Howitt**, 28 - then her, at sub number 4, before three servants |
| Her birth | 7 August 1912, with John Kenneth born 13 February 1911 - a year apart, which is what siblings look like |
| Her occupation | *unpaid domestic duties*, the family phrasing, where subs 5, 6 and 7 are all *domestic servant* |

She is a **Howitt**, in the Howitt household, in the family's place on the page. So the bracketed name is the one on the night, and *Edward* is the later marriage. The record's own transcription agrees: her row is one of the sixty-one whose note says the name **under** the amendment could not be read - so the readable name, the one outside the bracket, is the amendment.

## The forename case, settled 1 October 2026

*Acho (Victoria) Wright (Richardson)* at 2 South Road had a bracket on the **forename** as well, and that looked like a hole in the rule, because a forename is not amended by marriage.

**A. Hagues settles it: the amending hand sometimes rewrites the forename along with the surname.** The clerk entering a married name writes the whole name afresh, so the forename outside the bracket is that clerk's hand rather than a name the woman was ever called. **Acho is not a name. She was Victoria throughout**, and she is entered as **Victoria Richardson**, her name on the night, with **Victoria Wright** kept as the married name.

So the bracket means the same thing in both positions, and the rule holds unchanged: **what is in the bracket is what the page had on the night**.

## Worth watching for

An odd or unreadable forename sitting outside a bracket is now a signal in its own right - it is the amending clerk's writing, and the forename in the bracket is the real one. Anywhere the record holds a 1939 forename that reads like nothing, it is worth asking whether an amendment is sitting on top of it.

Links: [[how-to-handle-a-1939-amended-name]], [[questions-for-a-walk-round-the-park]].
