questions.title: ANSWERED - The Lodge on Park Terrace is East Lodge on Park Row
questions.detail:
**Settled 1 October 2026.** A. Hagues confirms it: schedule 134 is **East Lodge, Park Row (#413)**, and the Geddes household is filed there. #441 is folded in and gone.

The reasoning the record would not assert on its own is below, and it held.

**Schedule 134 of the 1939 Register is headed "The Lodge, Park Terrace"** and holds **Bert Geddes**, 47, *chauffeur*, and **Hannah Geddes**, 48. The record had no such house.

## The case for East Lodge

| | |
|---|---|
| **The book's order** | schedule 133 is the **General Hospital Lodge**, 134 is this house, 135 is **Tower House** - the enumerator is walking the Park Row entrance |
| **The street is already proved unreliable here** | the same page calls **Tower House** *Park Terrace*, and Tower House is **53 Park Row**. That is settled - see below |
| **The ground** | **East Lodge, Park Row (#413)** stands beside Tower House, about eight metres from it, and is **listed with it** |
| **The round** | East Lodge has **no 1939 household** in the record |
| **The trade** | a chauffeur is a service household, which is what a lodge is for |

## Why the record does not say it

Because none of that is the house's name. The page says *The Lodge*, and East Lodge is a different name on a different street. The record has been wrong before by letting a plausible neighbour swallow a named house, and a lodge at the Park Row entrance is exactly the sort of building there might be two of.

**There is a loose end on the same house already:** a 1911 row is filed as *"Park Lodge, Park Row (probably East Lodge, #413 - wants confirming)"*. Two rounds now want the same confirmation, which is an argument for settling East Lodge properly rather than one household at a time.

## Tower House, by contrast, is settled

The 1939 page puts **Tower House on Park Terrace**; the record has Tower House at **53 Park Row**. They are one house, and the **office** proves it: 1939 has **Henry M Stanley**, 46, *hospital house governor and secretary*; 1921 has **Peter Morrison Maccoll**, 47, *house governess and secretary*, at 53 Park Row. The General Hospital's house governor lived at Tower House in both rounds - a house tied to the post. Schedule 135 is filed there, and *Tower House, Park Terrace* is kept on the property as a street the house has been called by.

**What would settle The Lodge:** a directory or rate book listing East Lodge's occupier in 1939, or the Geddes name against either address. Failing that, the ground - how many lodges stand at that entrance.

Links: [[named-houses-on-the-wrong-street-in-1939]], [[questions-for-a-walk-round-the-park]], [[house-names-live-in-prose]].

**Still open on the same house:** the 1911 row filed as *"Park Lodge, Park Row (probably East Lodge, #413 - wants confirming)"*. The 1939 round is settled; that one is not.

questions.title: Albert Nelson Bromley designed 15 Newcastle Drive and died in it - answered
questions.detail:
**ANSWERED, by A. Hagues.** The head of 15 Newcastle Drive in 1901 and 1911 is **Albert Nelson Bromley FRIBA (15 July 1850 - 16 August 1934)**, one of Nottingham's most prolific architects. **He built the house himself, about 1888, and died in it forty-six years later.**

**Sources:** Ken Brand's account for the [Nottingham Civic Society](https://nottinghamcivicsociety.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/an_bromley.pdf), and [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Nelson_Bromley).

## What he was

Born at Stafford and brought to Nottingham as a child after his father's death, he was articled to his uncle **Frederick Bakewell**, an architect and a founder of the Nottingham Architectural Association. After more than a year drawing his way round Europe in 1872-73 he joined Bakewell in partnership, and their entry won the Corporation's competition for workmen's dwellings in Bath Street - **Victoria Buildings, the town's first council housing**, opened 1877.

From 1876 he practised alone. He became **principal architect to the Nottingham School Board**, and from 1895 architect to **Jesse Boot's company** for more than thirty years - the terracotta store on High Street is his, as is a run of branch shops built deliberately in the older manner of each town. Banks, telephone exchanges, warehouses and factories followed, in Nottingham and well beyond it. **T. Cecil Howitt, who designed the Council House, was his pupil from 1903.**

## Two things this settles for the record

**1. #215 has no architect and should have him.** The property is held as *one of a pair of houses c1890* with the architect field empty. **He designed it for himself, about 1888.** That is a house on this estate designed by a notable architect, uncredited.

**2. It proves the Newcastle Drive Rule at a number we had never tested, and dates the renumbering.** He built **24 Pelham Terrace**; Brand's account says it became **15 Newcastle Drive** when the roads were renumbered, **in 1894-5**. **39 - 24 = 15.** The rule was worked out from the record's own 1891 rows for the even numbers 4 to 18; this confirms it from outside, extends it to 24, and **puts a date on the change for the first time**.

## And the record still has his name wrong

**#4717 is held as Albert V. Bromley.** It is **Nelson**, in his own handwriting on the 1911 schedule and in every published account. **An architect matched on a wrong initial is an architect who never gets matched to his buildings**, so this correction earns more than most.

## A client of his was on the estate the same night

Bromley designed a warehouse on St Mary's Gate for **J. B. Walker** in 1900. **James B. Walker**, #4107, lace and lace curtain manufacturer, is heading a Castle Grove household in this same 1911 round - see [[castle-grove-has-no-low-numbers]]. **Architect and client, both living in The Park.**

His practice also designed additions to the **Eye Infirmary on The Ropewalk**, where [[colonel-herbert-indian-medical-service]] was consulting surgeon - though that work came in the late 1920s, after Herbert had left the town.

## Still worth doing

**Which other Park houses are his.** The estate was building through exactly his years and he lived on it; the record credits him with nothing. **Building applications survive** and Brand's account shows how much can be recovered from them.

**His daughter.** Married 1878, one child: **Kathleen Bromley**, #4719, born 1879, at home aged 22 in 1901 and gone by 1911 - so married, and findable under another name.

questions.title: ANSWERED - 9 Clumber Crescent South is Gwedon
questions.detail:
**Settled 1 October 2026.** The house is **Gwedon**. A. Hagues reads the name off the page; my own reading of the image had it as *Gwelen*, which was wrong.

**Schedule 244 of the RMGB district is headed with the house name** where the record had only *9 Clumber Crescent South*. The eight people in it are the ones the record already held there - **Ernest Jardine**, HM Government contractor, **John Jardine**, managing director of an HM gas firm, **Edna W Forthington**, and five domestic servants.

**The lesson is the one the morning kept teaching.** A name read off a page image by me is a guess with a shape; read off the original by A. Hagues it is a fact. Gwelen and Gwedon differ by two letters and only one of them is a house.

Links: [[house-names-live-in-prose]], [[the-unsourced-1939-batch-holds-married-names]].

### The record already had it

**Gwedon was in the property's `name` field all along** - not in its address, not in `house_name`, with no history behind it, so nothing on the site ever showed it. The page did not tell the record anything it did not hold; it made the record look at what it held.

**`house_name` is now filled in from `name` for twenty-four properties** that had one and not the other, so a house name is in one place rather than two.

**Six names still do not appear in their address**, where the record's own habit is *Castle Rising, 3 Lenton Road*:

| | |
|---|---|
| #20 | **Castle Lodge** - 7 Castle Grove |
| #29 | **Park House** - 14 Cavendish Crescent North |
| #77 | **Hampden House** - 7 Clinton Terrace (139 Derby Road) |
| #395 | **Tower House** - 53 Park Row |
| #404 | **Gartree Lodge** - 17a Tattershall Drive |
| #419 | **Bowling Green** - 35 Lenton Road |

Three of those are deliberate - Tower House, Gartree Lodge and Hampden House all carry a number the record needs to keep in front. **Castle Lodge, Park House and Bowling Green are not**, and whether their addresses should read the way Ribble Lodge's does is a decision for A. Hagues, not a tidy-up to make quietly.

questions.title: ANSWERED - Sunnyside is one house on the cliff, and it never had a number
questions.detail:
**ANSWERED by A. Hagues from the Ordnance Survey sheet and the modern map, 26 September 2026.** There would not be two houses of that name so close together. The two records are now one, **#390**, and #415 is gone.

**The disagreement was never really one.** Park Terrace runs along the top of the cliff, Park Valley along the foot, and Sun Drive lies on the other side. A house on that drop is reached from all of them:

| round | what the page gives | reached from |
|---|---|---|
| **1891**, sched 139 | *Sunny Side, Park Valley* - John Howard Bradwell, auctioneer, **fifteen in the house**, the largest household on the street | below |
| **1921**, Dr Kneebone's schedule | falls **between 19 Park Terrace and Sunnyside** | above |
| **1921**, both cover sheets | *Sunnyside, Park Valley, Nottingham*, signed L. C. Ord and C. Parker - **two households at once** | below |
| **1939**, sched 121 | between 25 and 10 Park Valley, run as a guest house of nine | below |
| **Park Map** | a *Sunnyside* label on Park Terrace | above |

**Confirmed from the pages either side, 26 September 2026.** Schedule 139's street column is a **ditto of Park Valley**, carried down from 21, 23 and 25, with *(Sunny Side)* written beneath as the house name - and **schedule 140 opens Huntingdon Drive**. So Sunny Side is the last house on Park Valley before the enumerator turns off it, which is exactly the ground A. Hagues pointed at. See [[clare-valley-numbered-from-the-1891-walk]].

**And the number 12 is withdrawn.** It was never on any page. In 1891 and 1939 alike the enumerator climbs the odd side of Park Valley to 25, takes Sunnyside **at the turn**, and comes back down 10, 8, 6, 4, 2. The house stands on the turn, and 12 was the next even number above 10 - an inference from walk order that had hardened into an address. #390 carries no number.

**Broxtowe House splits the same way on the same ground** - a Park Valley schedule for a name that belongs at the Park Terrace end. Twice on one cliff is a pattern, not a coincidence: [[broxtowe-house-where]].

Links: [[what-is-clinton-house]], [[park-valley-13-and-sunny-side]], [[properties-carrying-two-house-numbers]].

## The 1953 Ordnance Survey settles the position

**Sheet SK5639, revised 1953 and published 1955, labels *Sunnyside* on exactly the ground A. Hagues first placed it** - in its own grounds west of Park Terrace, with Springdale, Ribble Lodge, Grove House and The Spinney beyond it and allotment gardens below. His original marker was right, and the note that briefly called it wrong has been taken off.

**It also dates the loss.** The house was still standing and still named in 1953, so it came down after 1955 - which answers one of the questions this record was asking.

questions.title: ANSWERED - 35 Lenton Road was Bowling Green, and the stables behind 33 were a dwelling for thirty years
questions.detail:
**ANSWERED.** Two properties created on 26 September 2026, both census-only, both from the enumerator's own words.

**#419, 35 Lenton Road - *Bowling Green*.** The 1881 page names it outright at schedule 133, walking 37 (Rock House), **35**, the stables, then 33. **Edward and Sarah Ballard**, two in the house. It appears in no later round, and the **1953 Ordnance Survey shows a bowling green, tennis courts and a pavilion** over that ground - so the house is lost and the name survived it, or the name came from the green in the first place.

**#420, The Stables, Lenton Road.** A coachman's dwelling behind 33, and the record calls it something different every time:

| round | as the page writes it | who |
|---|---|---|
| 1881 | *rooms attached to the stables* | **William Todd**, coachman, and his daughter Carry |
| 1891 | no number at all | **Joseph Newbold**, coachman, and Lizetta |
| 1911 | **The Stables, Lenton Road** | Joseph Newbold, 51, Lizetta, and two daughters |

**Joseph Newbold is there in 1891 and again in 1911** - twenty years in the stable rooms, and by the end of it a daughter working as a typist.

**They were made two properties rather than one**, although the request was for 35. They are consecutive but separate schedules in 1881, and the stables outlived the house by thirty years with three households to the other's one. Merging them later is easy; separating them once they are merged is not.

**Still open:** whether *Bowling Green* is the house's name or the ground's. And a coachman's dwelling is worth knowing about generally - the record holds another at **North Road, the house attached to the stables**, with Moses Bates in it in 1881. Links: [[the-hermitage-lenton-road-is-not-in-the-record]], [[house-names-live-in-prose]].

questions.title: ANSWERED - The Hermitage was already in the record under the other street it stands on
questions.detail:
**ANSWERED, and nothing needed creating.** The Hermitage is **#392, The Hermitage, Hermitage Walk**, already held as a lost house and already positioned from the OS 1:1250 sheet at the west end of Hermitage Walk above Rock Holes. It is now marked demolished and has its history written.

**Why it looked missing.** Its rounds sit on two different streets, which is what a house reached by a footpath does to a census:

| round | as the page heads it |
|---|---|
| 1881 | *The Hermitage, **Lenton Road*** - the road the enumerator was walking |
| 1901 | *The Hermitage (The Park)*, filed to **Hermitage Walk** |
| 1911 | held already |

A search of Lenton Road could never find it, and the census runs sheet showed it as an unfiled house between 33 and 31 because that is where the 1881 walk puts it.

**And the two rounds are one family.** The 1881 head is **John W Leavers**, silk hosiery merchant, 63, with his wife **Sarah**, 56. In 1901 **Sarah Leavers keeps the house alone at 76**, a widow, with a visitor of 72 and five servants including a butler. Twenty years, and the same woman.

**The 1881 household is filed**, so the house now holds 1881, 1901 and 1911.

**Still open on that walk:** schedules 130 (**Richard Challands**, thirteen in the house) and 131 (**Joseph Wilson**, seven), both before Rock House at 37 and both written *Lenton Road* with no number. Links: [[thirty-five-lenton-road-is-a-lost-house]], [[house-names-live-in-prose]].

questions.title: ANSWERED - Cavendish Crescent South has no 13 because that house is addressed to South Road
questions.detail:
**ANSWERED.** Cavendish Crescent South runs **1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11** and then jumps to **15, 17, 19, 21, 23, 25**. The missing 13 is not missing: it is the corner house, and it takes its address from **South Road** instead. The record now holds it as **#301, 1 South Road (13 Cavendish Crescent South)**.

**Roby L Thorpe, solicitor, shows it.** In **1881** the enumerator writes only *Cavendish Crescent South*, with no number, and the household sat unfiled for that reason. In **1891** the same man is at **1 South Road**, where the record already had him. Same solicitor, same house, two streets. The 1881 household is now filed, so the house holds 1881, 1891, 1911 and 1939.

**This is the fourth of these in the record**, and they are worth recognising as a class rather than solving one at a time:

| the house | its two names |
|---|---|
| #301 | 1 South Road / 13 Cavendish Crescent South |
| the Derby Terrace run | 145 to 159 Derby Road / 2 to 9 Derby Terrace |
| the Clinton Terrace run | 127 to 139 Derby Road / 1 to 7 Clinton Terrace |
| Newcastle Drive | 1 to 13 Newcastle Terrace / 21 to 37 Pelham Terrace |

**A corner house is why an unnumbered street name on a census page is not a dead end.** The enumerator writes the street he is walking; the householder answers with the address he uses. Where a number is missing from an otherwise continuous run, look for a house facing the other way before assuming the number never existed. See [[the-cavendish-road-east-ditto-run]], where the same habit sent eleven households to the wrong street.

Links: [[newcastle-terrace-is-the-low-end-of-newcastle-drive]], [[house-names-live-in-prose]].

questions.title: ANSWERED - 1, 2, 3 and The Lodge, Castle Grove created, and thirty-four people filed
questions.detail:
**ANSWERED.** Four properties created on 26 September 2026, all census-only, each named outright by an enumerator:

| | house | named in |
|---|---|---|
| **#421** | 1 Castle Grove | 1911 (the Borden household) and 1939 (Robert J Willatt, solicitor) |
| **#422** | 2 Castle Grove | 1911 (the Herbert household) and 1939 (George Lawson, estate agent) |
| **#423** | 3 Castle Grove | 1939 (Charles William Shelton, valuer) |
| **#424** | The Lodge, Castle Grove | **1881** (Thomas Marriott) and 1911 |

**Thirty-four people filed** across 1881, 1911 and 1939. The record's Castle Grove now runs 1 to 7 with its Lodge.

**Positions are placeholders.** Castle Grove is a close of houses round a green, so its numbers cannot be extrapolated along a line the way a terrace can. All four sit beside 4 to 7 and say so, for correction on *Positions vs OpenStreetMap*.

**Still open: the 1881 run is not numbered.** Seven households walk the grove at schedules 230 to 237 and only The Lodge is named - John G Good, John Patterson, Hannah Simons, **Thomas Forman**, Frederic Dobson and John Brown are all written *Castle Grove* with no number. A Peveril Drive household at schedule 235 interrupts the run, so even the order is not a clean count.

**Seven Castle Grove households were read from the 1911 schedules and not one of them can be filed.** The property list holds **4, 5, 6, 6a and 7**. The covers give **1**, **2**, **The Lodge**, and four with **no number at all**.

| cover | head | rooms |
|---|---|---|
| **1 Castle Grove** | Harold Borden, cycle manufacturer, born San Francisco | 9 |
| **2 Castle Grove** | Herbert Herbert, late Lt-Col, Indian Medical Service | 10 |
| **The Lodge** | William Hall, coachman | 5 |
| no number | Samuel M. Taylor, **American Consul at Nottingham** | 11 |
| no number | James B. Walker, lace and lace curtain manufacturer | 12 |
| no number | Kate Mary Snook, widow, of James Snook & Co, drapers | 11 |
| no number | Frederic William Dobson, lace dyeing and dressing | 9 |

**That is 44 people with nowhere to go**, and it is not a 1911 problem: **eight rows already sit unfiled from the 1921 round** under *Castle Grove - no name or house number in 1921 census*. **Whatever fixes one fixes both.**

**The shape of the gap is clear.** The list starts at 4. **Numbers 1, 2 and 3 are missing from the record and two of them are named on covers**, so they existed. The Lodge is an eighth property again.

**Three things would settle it**, in order of cost: the **enumerator's summary book** for the piece, which lists every schedule in order with its address; a **trade directory**, which names Castle Grove householders; and the **1921 covers**, which would place the eight unfiled rows and probably name the same houses.

**Until then the seven stay on the unfiled page**, each under its own name so they can be told apart. See [[clare-valley-missing-houses]] for the same fault on another street.

**The 1939 Register settles that they existed.** Schedules 95, 96 and 97 of the RMGC register are **1, 2 and 3 Castle Grove** - Robert J Willatt, solicitor; George Lawson, estate agent; Charles William Shelton, estate agent and valuer - and schedules 99 and 100 mark **5 and 6 Castle Grove** empty, so the enumerator walks 1 to 7 in order with nothing missing. Three houses the property list has not got. See [[house-names-live-in-prose]].

questions.title: ANSWERED - Castle Mount is 20 Cavendish Crescent North
questions.detail:
**ANSWERED, and by the 1921 census twice over.** Schedule 194 is the household of **Percy Pinder, draper and employer**, which the record already held at **20 Cavendish Crescent North**. The schedule names the house without being asked to:

- **Mary Rooke the cook, Dora Pollard the housemaid and Adelaide Carr the governess** all give their place of work as **Castle Mount, The Park, Nottingham**.
- **Beryl Pinder, twelve**, gives her birthplace as **Castle Mount, The Park, Nottingham**.

The name is now on the property as a former house name, and the six 1921 rows carry the evidence in their source lines.

**And it closes an entry that had nowhere to go.** The 1939 Register marks **Castle Mount** empty at schedule 44, and that could not be recorded because the record had no such house. It is now recorded as 20 Cavendish Crescent North standing empty in 1939 - which fits, because the record holds nobody there for that round.

**A name still to correct:** the schedule writes the cook **Rooke** and the record has her as **Rook**. Links: [[house-names-live-in-prose]].

questions.title: ANSWERED - the Pendower solicitor is John Thorpe Perry, and I had made a second one of him
questions.detail:
**ANSWERED, and a duplicate of my own making has been undone.** The 1939 Register at schedule 48 reads the second forename as **Shaw**, and the household was entered as *John Shaw Perry*. It is **John Thorpe Perry**, whom the record already held.

**The two servants settle it.** **Sarah Annie Cuff**, housekeeper, and **Sarah Jane Cottam** are with him in **1921 and again in 1939** - the same two women, eighteen years apart, in the same house. A man does not acquire an identical pair of servants under a different middle name.

| | 1921 | 1939 |
|---|---|---|
| head | John Thorpe Perry, 61, solicitor, retired | John Thorpe Perry, 79 |
| housekeeper | Sarah Annie Cuff, 45 | Sarah Annie Cuff, 63 |
| servant | Sarah Jane Cottam, 22 | Sarah Jane Cottam, 40, cook |

**And he goes back further than that.** The **1861** census has **John Thorpe Perry aged one** at Park Terrace, in the household of John Maddock Perry, merchant - so the record now holds him from a baby of one to a retired solicitor of seventy-nine, seventy-eight years apart, and Pendower is where he ended.

**Pendower is 17 Cavendish Crescent North**, which the 1939 walk suggested and the 1921 census confirms outright. Links: [[the-kentish-wright-sisters-at-9-newcastle-drive]].

**Applied to the record, 4 October 2026.** The answer had been written up but never carried out - *John Shaw Perry* was still in the record as a separate person, and his 1939 row still sat loose at *Pendower, Cavendish Crescent North* while his two servants sat at 17. He has been folded into John Thorpe Perry, his row rehoused at **17**, and **Pendower** is now the house's name in the property list. The street list A. Hagues sent the same day names the head of Pendower as **John Thorpe Perry**, which is the confirmation from outside the household.

questions.title: ANSWERED - Castle Lodge is 7 Castle Grove, and it is lived in to this day
questions.detail:
**ANSWERED by A. Hagues, who knows its present occupant.** Castle Lodge is a house in its own right - the gate lodge built into the wall beside the arch at the entrance to Castle Grove - and it is **number 7**.

So *The Lodge, Castle Grove*, which the 1881 and 1911 enumerators write, and *7 Castle Grove*, which the 1921 and 1939 rounds give, are one house. They were held as two properties for a few hours on 26 September 2026 and are now one, #20, named **Castle Lodge**:

| round | as the page writes it | household |
|---|---|---|
| 1881 | The Lodge, Castle Grove | Thomas Marriott and four children |
| 1911 | The Lodge, Castle Grove | William Hall, his wife and daughter |
| 1921 | 7 Castle Grove | Sidney James and his wife |
| 1939 | 7 Castle Grove | Herbert W Fletcher, head waiter, living alone |

**The doubt was worth having and worth dropping.** The argument for two houses was the photograph - a turreted gatehouse in the wall looks unlike a numbered house on a close. The argument for one was that the two names never share a round. The second was right, and the first was a picture of the same building. Links: [[properties-carrying-two-house-numbers]].

questions.title: ANSWERED - Elizabeth G Lewis was three women, and a re-import had put two of them back together
questions.detail:
**ANSWERED 26 September 2026.** #4124 held five census rows with three different ages in the same round. It is now three people, each internally consistent:

| | holds | born |
|---|---|---|
| **#4124** Elizabeth G Lewis | 1881 and 1891 at #398, aged 49 and 59 | 1832 |
| **#7111** Elizabeth G Lewis | 1881 at The Chestnuts, 5 Kenilworth Road, aged 38 - Henry Lewis's wife | 1843 |
| **new** | 1881 at 8 Lenton Road aged 51, 1891 at 6 Lenton Road aged 61 - the cork cutter's wife, born Tewkesbury | about 1830 |

**But the interesting part is why it had come back.** Two of those rows had *already* been split off, by `tools_split_welded_people.py`, and were sitting on the wrong person again.

**A split is not protected the way a merge is.** When two people are merged, a row in `person_alias` records the name that went away, and the importer looks there before making anybody - so a later import of the same file finds the surviving person instead of recreating the old one. A **split** has no such guard. The importer matches on the name, the name still belongs to the person the row was taken *from*, and re-running the source file puts it straight back.

So `tools_split_welded_people.py` is not a one-off: **its splits have to be re-checked after every import that touches the same names**, and the two rows removed here were exactly that - recreated with higher row ids than the split that had moved them.

**Found the same way as the rest**, from the variant-spelling sweep after the 1861 import. Two other pairs it raised were not duplicates at all and were left alone: Edward Alexander Manlove is the *son* of Edward Manlove at 6 Western Terrace, and William Bruce Milton, aged five, is the son of William Milton, Perpetual Curate of New Radford, at 2 Western Terrace.

Links: [[henry-wing-was-two-men]], [[clare-valley-numbered-from-the-1891-walk]].

questions.title: ANSWERED - Henry Wing the solicitor and Henry Wing the automobile engineer are grandfather and grandson
questions.detail:
**ANSWERED 26 September 2026.** The record held one Henry Wing, **born 1890**, appearing in the **1861** census. Both could not be true.

The rows separate cleanly on relationship and age:

| round | as | age | where | born |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1861 | **Head**, attorney and solicitor | 30 | Park Terrace | **1831** |
| 1871 | **Head**, solicitor | 40 | 12 Park Terrace | 1831 |
| 1881 | **Head**, solicitor | 50 | 12 Park Terrace | 1831 |
| 1901 | **Son** | 11 | Kentmere, Pelham Crescent | **1890** |
| 1911 | **Son**, automobile engineer | 21 | Cavendish Crescent North | 1890 |

Three decades of a solicitor heading the same house, and a boy two generations later. #7163 keeps the 1861, 1871 and 1881 rows and is now **born 1831**; the 1901 and 1911 rows have gone to a new person born 1890.

**And a third Henry.** #5265, *Henry M Wing*, is the son at 12 Park Terrace in 1871 aged 9 and in 1881 aged 19, a solicitor's articled clerk - born about 1862, between the two. Three generations of the name, which is what made the weld so easy for a name-matching importer.

**The 1861 row is the earliest of them and is unfiled**, Park Terrace giving no numbers that year - but the solicitor is at 12 Park Terrace in 1871 and 1881, which makes 12 the obvious candidate. Links: [[the-1861-round-has-no-house-numbers]], [[elizabeth-g-lewis-is-several-women]].

questions.title: ANSWERED - the Cavendish Road East ditto run turns onto Cavendish Crescent North at schedule 161
questions.detail:
**ANSWERED.** The 1891 enumerator wrote **Cavendish R<sup>d</sup> East** once at schedule 153 and carried it down the column as ditto marks to 164. It is wrong for the back half of the run.

**What settled it:** the **1894 street directory**, three years after the census, which gives a street for eight of the twelve households by name.

| schedule | household | 1894 directory entry | street |
|---|---|---|---|
| 153 | Edward Hardy | *Overdale, Mr. Edward Hardy* | Cavendish Road East |
| 154 | Charles Sudbury | *Cavendish house, Charles Sudbury, of C. & F. Sudbury* | Cavendish Road East |
| 155 | Bertha Lloyd | *Castle Dene* | Cavendish Road East |
| 157 | Robert Hy Speed | *R. H. Speed, solicitor* | Cavendish Road East |
| 158 | Parker Woodward | *Parker Woodward, solicitor* | Cavendish Road East |
| 159 | Benjamin North | *Allandale, Bjn. North, whlsl drgst* | Cavendish Road East |
| **160** | **Charles Loder** | - | **Huntingdon Drive, written plainly and not dittoed** |
| 161 | James Smith | *Crescent lodge, James Smith, of E. Smith & Sons* | **Cavendish Crescent North** |
| 163 | Thomas Page | *Hazlewood, Thomas Page, firm of Jonathan Page* | **Cavendish Crescent North** |
| 164 | Frederick Wm Goddard | *Frederick Wm. Goddard, lace mfr* | **Cavendish Crescent North** |

**The turn is schedule 160** - the one household in the run the enumerator did not ditto. He finished Cavendish Road East, took the Huntingdon Drive cottage, came onto the crescent and went on writing the street he had left.

**The house names close it independently of the directory.** The property record holds **Charnwood as 10 Cavendish Crescent North** and **Hazlewood as 12** - one from a walk of the crescent, one from the house's own listed-building description, neither from a census. Goddard is at Charnwood (164) and Page at Hazlewood (163), so with Fraser at 162 the enumerator walks the crescent **downwards: Crescent Lodge, 14, 12, 10**. The 1894 directory prints those same houses in the opposite order, which is what a directory does.

**The record was right and the page was wrong.** Edward Henry Fraser was already held at **14 Cavendish Crescent North** for 1891, and that is where schedule 162 belongs. The 1939 Register has his son **Cecil Edward Fraser, born 22 February 1884** - the seven-year-old of this very household - still at 14, and the 1910, 1913 and 1915 directories have him there too.

**Four houses filed:** 154 to Cavendish House (#56), 159 to Allandale, 23 Cavendish Road East (#50), 162 to 14 Cavendish Crescent North (#29), 163 to **Hazlewood, 12 Cavendish Crescent North** (#28) - the pivot that house had been waiting for.

**One correction to an earlier reading.** Charles Sudbury was at 5 Tattershall Drive in 1881 with ten in the house and that had looked like a reason to doubt his Cavendish Road East line. It was not: he moved, and the 1894 directory puts him at Cavendish House with the same firm. The doubt was right about the run and wrong about him.

**Still open, but smaller:** Castle Dene and Crescent Lodge are not in the property list, and four households in the run carry no number or house name at all. Their **street** is now certain. See [[house-names-live-in-prose]], [[two-schedule-series-in-rg12-2682]].

questions.title: ANSWERED in part - Dorothea Kentish Wright wrote for the stage, and Ursula acted in it
questions.detail:
**ANSWERED.** The search for Dorothea as a performer came back empty because she was not billed as one. **The Stage Yearbook for 1912/13** records *Fantasy*, **her** adaptation of a poem by **John Drinkwater**, staged at the **Mechanics' Hall, Nottingham, on 28 September 1912**:

| part | played by |
|---|---|
| Pierrot | Laurence Heyworth |
| Harlequin | Kenneth Varvill |
| **Pierrette** | **Miss U. Kentish-Wright** |

Pierrette is **Ursula**, her sister, then twenty-one. Dorothea was twenty-eight. So the 1939 Register's *retired actress* sits on a real theatrical life; the surviving notice simply names her as author rather than cast, which is why no billing could be found.

**A Drinkwater adaptation in 1912 is early.** He was thirty and two years from *The Storm*; the Birmingham Repertory Theatre he helped found had opened only that February. Whoever chose the text was reading new work, not revivals.

**Both are now in the record properly.** *Fantasy* and the 1929 Breton edition are entered in the bibliography against their authors and tied to **9 Newcastle Drive** - where the record holds Dorothea in 1891, 1901, 1921 and 1939 and Ursula in every round from 1891 to 1939. Neither sister ever lived anywhere else that the record knows of. Both biographies are written.

**Still open:**

- **Was Fantasy the only one?** A first adaptation at twenty-eight, performed in a public hall and noticed in the trade yearbook, rarely stands alone. The Stage Yearbook ran for decades and is indexed by author.
- **Which poem of Drinkwater's?** The entry names him but not the poem. His 1911 collection *Poems of Men and Hours* is the likeliest hunting ground.
- **Dorothea's war.** Her VAD service is recorded and unsourced - see [[the-vad-women-of-the-1939-register]].
- **Neither is marked notable yet.** Both carry a note; the mark is a click on *Notable Residents*.

**Next:** The Stage Yearbook for the years either side of 1912/13, and the British Library catalogue under Kentish Wright for Ursula. Links: [[notables-the-1939-register-brought-in]], [[house-names-live-in-prose]].

questions.title: ANSWERED - Sir Albert Atkey of 11 Park Valley, MP, Lord Mayor, and the city's first motor trader
questions.detail:
**ANSWERED.** His biography is written. **Sir Albert Reuben Atkey (1 July 1867 - 9 November 1947)** of **11 Park Valley**:

| | |
|---|---|
| Sheriff of Nottingham | 1910 |
| MP for Nottingham Central | won 1918 as a Coalition Conservative, the seat's first member |
| lost it | 1922, by **22 votes**, to the Liberal Reginald Berkeley |
| tried again | 1923, beaten by 1,805; never stood again |
| Lord Mayor of Nottingham | 1928 |
| received the Prince of Wales | 22 May 1929, to open the Council House |
| knighted | 1935 |

He founded **A. R. Atkey Ltd**, the first motor traders in Nottingham, and never left the trade: the 1921 census enters him as *Motor Agent, Member of Parliament* in that order, and the 1939 Register still has him a motor agent at seventy-two.

**The record had the fact all along.** *Member of Parliament* sat in his 1921 occupation column and nobody had followed it up - which is an argument for reading the occupation field of the notable rounds as a finding list rather than a data column.

**Dates mended.** The record carried a bare year of birth; it now has the day, and a death date it did not have at all.

**Lady Euphemia has her title.** The 1939 enumerator was given no column for one and wrote *Lady* after her name regardless, which is good enough.

**Still open:** his Wikipedia article is not linked - that is a pass of *Wikidata Review*. And neither Atkey is marked on *Notable Residents* yet; both carry a note. Links: [[notables-the-1939-register-brought-in]], [[yrette-joyce-atkey-is-not-a-forename]].

questions.title: ANSWERED - Yrette Joyce Atkey is Yvette, one letter wrong and not a name cut short
questions.detail:
**ANSWERED.** She is **Yvette Joyce Atkey**, aged 8 in the 1921 census at **11 Park Valley**, the house of [[sir-albert-atkey-and-the-twenty-two-votes|Sir Albert Reuben Atkey]] and Lady Euphemia. Corrected in the record by A. Hagues.

**Where the reasoning went wrong, which is the part worth keeping.** *Yrette* was read here as the tail of a longer name with its first syllable lost, and Harriette and Henriette were offered as the shape it might have had. That was the wrong kind of fault to look for. Nothing was missing at all: a single **v** had been read as an **r**, and the name was complete the whole time.

**The general lesson.** A forename that looks wrong gets tested for the damage transcription usually does - a lost prefix, a ditto mark taken for a value, an initial standing alone. It should first be tested for the damage a *pen* does: one letter substituted for another that looks like it. **v and r, n and u, c and e, l and t** are the usual pairs. A check for forenames within one letter of a known forename would have answered this without a question being written at all, and would be a cheap thing to add beside the existing name checks.

**She still matters to the house.** She is the only child at 11 Park Valley in 1921, so she is how the Atkeys carry on past it; her married name is the thread out of The Park. Links: [[notables-the-1939-register-brought-in]].

questions.title: ANSWERED - Leslie Bates degaussed ships for the Admiralty, and called it cloaks and daggers
questions.detail:
**ANSWERED**, by the obituary Professor W. F. Nash wrote for *The Times* of 25 January 1978, reprinted in *Contemporary Physics* **19:2 (1978), 97-98**, doi:10.1080/00107517808210874.

Bates advised the **Inter-Services Research Bureau** through the Second World War, and the work was **degaussing**: demagnetising ships so that magnetic mines would not detect them. It was **Admiralty** work, and it is exactly what fifteen years of ferromagnetism fitted him for.

**He called it “cloaks and daggers”** - his own phrase, recorded by a colleague. The joke lands because *Inter-Services Research Bureau* was the cover name for the Special Operations Executive; the question asked whether he had been doing SOE work, and the answer is that he was doing Admiralty physics **under** that roof, and knew perfectly well how the letterhead read.

**The souvenir survives.** He kept a large ship's compass in his room afterwards, and it stood, when the obituary was written, in the foyer of the Nottingham University physics department. Worth knowing whether it is still there - it is the only physical object anywhere in this record that a resident brought home from a war.

**A guess withdrawn and a guess confirmed.** This question previously offered “magnetic detection, mines and fuses” as guesses and said so. Mines was right; it was the ships being protected rather than the mines being made.

**And his CBE has its reason.** The record had the year, 1966, and nothing else. It was for the twenty-one years he spent as Senior Scientific Adviser for Civil Defence in the North Midland Region. Links: [[brankston-huntingdon-drive-is-not-in-the-record]].

questions.title: ANSWERED - 13 and 12 Park Valley created, and fifty-one census rows filed behind them
questions.detail:
**ANSWERED.** Both houses now exist as **census-only** properties, built on the evidence below and nothing else.

| | house | rounds filed | people |
|---|---|---|---|
| **#396** | **13 Park Valley** | 1881, 1891, 1901, 1911, 1939 | 24 |
| **#415** | **12 Park Valley**, formerly Sunny Side | 1891, 1939 | 24 |

**Fifty-one census rows filed** that had been sitting unplaced.

**Settled beyond any doubt.** The property list holds Park Valley as 1-11, 15-25 and Valley House. **There is no 13 and no 12**, and 13 is one of the best-attested houses in the record.

**Five census rounds, twenty-seven people:**

| round | household | |
|---|---|---|
| **1881** | **Walter Wadsworth**, 38, lace merchant | wife, two children, three servants |
| **1891** | Walter Wadsworth, 48 | Hope, the daughter of 3 in 1881, is 13 |
| **1901** | **Stuart Hartshorn**, 33, lace manufacturer | entered in the record as *Sigt.* - see below |
| **1911** | **Benedict Kohn**, 53, lace and export merchant | two servants |
| **1939** | **Wright J Featherstone**, organising lecturer | six in the house |

**Five directory years, with its neighbours either side every time:**

| year | 11 | **13** | 15 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1894 | Alf. Dawson | **Thos. Hopkinson, wholesale chemist** | John Tom McCraith JP |
| 1898 | Alf. Dawson | **Stuart Hartshorn, lace manufacturer** | John Tom McCraith JP |
| 1910 | Mrs Sarah Dawson | **George Benedict Kohn** | John Holland Walker |
| 1913 | **Albert Reuben Atkey** | **George Benedict Kohn** | John Holland Walker |
| 1915 | Albert Reuben Atkey | **George Benedict Kohn** | John Holland Walker |

Ten independent attestations from 1881 to 1939, and in every directory year the houses on both sides of it are printed by number. The occupants chain cleanly from one source to the next - Hartshorn is in the 1898 directory and the 1901 census, Kohn in the 1910 directory and the 1911 census and again in 1913 and 1915.

**The neighbours confirm themselves too.** Atkey at 11 in 1913 and 1915 is the same Sir Albert the record holds at 11 Park Valley in 1921 and 1939. John Holland Walker at 15 in three directories is the retired clothing merchant the 1939 Register puts at 15.

**Done.** The house was created on 24 September 2026 and the people filed against it.

## Two things that fall out of the search

**Sigt. Hartshorn is Stuart Hartshorn.** #4824 is entered as *Sigt.*, aged 33 in 1901 at 13 Park Valley, a lace manufacturer. The 1898 directory gives **Stuart Hartshorn, lace manufacturer**, at that same house. *Sigt.* is not a forename; it is Stuart misread. **Not changed here** - a person's name is A. Hagues's to correct.

**And there may be only one Stuart Hartshorn.** The record holds three: **#3291** Stuart, with no birth year and no census at all; **#4824** *Sigt.*, born about 1868; and **#7933** Stuart, born **30 June 1865**, at 21 Newcastle Drive in 1939, a retired lace bleacher. Three years between the birth years is the ordinary wobble of an age worked back from a census, and the trade is the same family of trades. Worth putting on the duplicates page.

**12 Park Valley** is the separate case, resting on 1891 and 1939 - see [[named-houses-on-the-wrong-street-in-1939]]. Links: [[every-census-gap-and-where-to-start]], [[house-names-live-in-prose]].

**The positions are approximate and meant to be corrected.** 13 sits at the midpoint of 11 and 15, which stand either side of it. 12 is extrapolated one house beyond 10 along the line from 8 to 10, the enumerator's own walk being 12, 10, 8, 6, 4, 2. Both are open to correction on *Positions vs OpenStreetMap*, and both say so in their own record.

**What is still open is the name, not the house.** The record holds a **Sunnyside on Park Terrace** as well, and which street carries the name is not settled - see [[named-houses-on-the-wrong-street-in-1939]].

questions.title: ANSWERED - it is East London in the Eastern Cape, and the wife on the line above proved it was not England
questions.detail:
**ANSWERED.** **#2505 Henry Godfrey Andrews**, 27, mechanical director in 1911, was born at **East London** in the Eastern Cape - the port on the Buffalo River. Confirmed by A. Hagues. The record now carries *East London, South Africa* in place of the page's bare *London, South Africa*, on his census row and on his person record alike.

**The question was whether the country column had gone wrong for London, England. It had not, and the proof was on the same page:**

| | |
|---|---|
| Henry Godfrey Andrews, head, 27 | **London, South Africa** |
| **Dorothy Agnes Andrews, his wife, 26** | **London, Middlesex** |

The enumerator wrote both Londons in one household and distinguished them. A man does not write *Middlesex* against his wife and then leave his own London to be guessed at. The record had also been holding his birthplace as **South Africa** on his person record all along, entered from a source other than the census.

**The geocoder had him in the wrong province.** *London, South Africa* answers to a hamlet in Ward 7, Bushbuckridge, **Mpumalanga**, nine hundred miles from the coast. Under the corrected name it finds East London at once, in Buffalo City, and no hand position is needed - the one put there while the reading was still an inference has been taken out again.

**Why it mattered.** The Origins map is read as a map. A pin in the north-east veld and a pin at the mouth of the Buffalo River tell different stories about who came to The Park and how they got here.

**Every birth place in the record is now positioned but one**, and that one is *At sea*, which names nowhere.

**Left open, and small:** his daughter Joan was born at Upper Parkstone in Dorset about 1908, so the family had crossed by then. The record holds two other South African births - **Port Elizabeth** in 1921 and **Johannesburg** in 1901 - and whether those three connect is not known. Links: [[every-census-gap-and-where-to-start]].

questions.title: PART ANSWERED - 46 of the part-filed people joined their households, 31 held back
questions.detail:
**46 people filed**, each joining the house the rest of their household was already in, across 1871, 1881, 1891 and 1901.

**Thirty-one households were held back, and they are more interesting than the ones that went through.** In every one the loose rows name a *different street* from the house their household is filed at. That is not a filing error to be tidied away - it is the record telling us two names belong to one place, or that somebody has been filed wrongly. The pattern repeats:

| the loose rows say | the house is on |
|---|---|
| Derby Terrace | Derby Road |
| Pelham Terrace, Newcastle Terrace | Newcastle Drive |
| Cavendish Lodge, Glenhurst, Oakleigh, Glendale, Beechwood, Lea Hurst, Holm Vale, Harpenden, Leslie House, Fairfield | a numbered street |
| Fish Pond Drive | Newcastle Drive |
| Kenilworth Road | Park Terrace |

Most are a **house name against a street name** and simply need the pairing recorded. A few are two genuinely different streets and mean somebody is in the wrong house.

**Next:** work them a street at a time rather than one household at a time - Kenilworth Road against Park Terrace is five households at once. Links: [[house-names-live-in-prose]].

questions.title: ANSWERED - the whole 1861 Ropewalk numbered, 136 people placed
questions.detail:
**ANSWERED by A. Hagues, 27 September 2026,** who numbered the run off the enumerator's page.

The interval argument held exactly. Schedules **113 to 121 are 32a down to 18**, with **Braithwaite at 22** - which was the one corroboration the record could offer before the numbering arrived, and it was right. The doubt about 30, 32 and 32a holding no household in any round was misplaced: they held one in 1861 and had simply never been filed.

**And the run carries on below 16**, which had not been looked at: 123 to 131 are 14, 12, 10, 8, 6, 4, the unnumbered corner building, 2 and 2a.

| sched | house | head |
|---|---|---|
| 113 | 32a | Moritz Jacoby, lace merchant, born Germany |
| 114 | 32 | George Berrey, lace manufacturer |
| 115 | 30 | John Jackson, coachman |
| 116 | 28 | William Patterson, born Scotland |
| 117 | 26 | Nathaniel Dickenson, pawnbroker - 14 in the house |
| 118 | 24 | James Wallis, clothier |
| **119** | **22** | **Francis Braithwaite** - and 22 has Mary Braithwaite in 1881 |
| 120 | 20 | Edward Stegemann, lace manufacturer, born Germany |
| 121 | 18 | Richard Hall, landed proprietor |
| *122* | *16* | *Charles Buttery - the anchor, already filed* |
| 123 | 14 | Thomas Shaw, lace manufacturer |
| 124 | 12 | Cuthbert Orlebar, clergyman |
| 125 | 10 | John Tom Yeatman, barrister at law |
| 126 | 8 | Frances Cook, householder |
| 127 | 6 | Luke S Mason, lace manufacturer |
| 128 | 4 | Edward Monk, landed proprietor |
| **129** | **unnumbered** | **William Hurst, solicitor** - see below |
| 130 | 2 | John Scott Wells, hosiery manufacturer |
| **131** | **2a** | **Sarah Wise, schoolmistress** - see below |

**And 38 fell out on its own.** Schedule 109 is the only household between 108 at 40 and 110 at 36a, and 38 the only number between them: Jonathan Reckless, lace manufacturer.

## Two properties the record did not hold

**#429, 2a The Ropewalk.** The listing for 2 The Ropewalk records it as *"formerly 2no. townhouses c1835-40"*, and the 1861 enumerator walks them as two households - ten people at 2 and ten more at 2a, the last schedule on the street before the walk turns into Derby Road.

**#430, the unnumbered building between 4 and 2.** A small building at the corner that still stands, which A. Hagues reads as a coach house - though it holds **William Hurst, solicitor**, and three others. It has no number on the page and none in the record. **It wants a proper name and a number if one can be found**, and its position is only the midpoint of 4 and 2.

## What is left on the Ropewalk in 1861

Seven households, **52 people**, all above 32a:

- **schedules 106 and 107** sit between 56 and 40 - two households for six numbers (54, 52, 48, 46, 44, 42), so the walk alone will not place them. Hugh Bruce Campbell, *Solicitor and Distributor of Stamps*, and Walter Browne, solicitor.
- **schedules 100 to 104** are above 56, beyond where the record's Ropewalk numbering stops. John Gibson, John Heard, Sarah Hurst, **Henry Linton, clergyman, born Ireland**, and **Major Charles Edward Burt, Royal Artillery**.

Links: [[the-1861-round-has-no-house-numbers]], [[blackmers-school-on-the-ropewalk-1861]].

## And the 1871 round, checked against it

With 1861 numbered, five 1871 households placed on the head being the same person or family:

| 1871 sch | head | house | |
|---|---|---|---|
| 204 | Edward Stegeman | **20** | Stegemann there in 1861 |
| 205 | Joseph Braithwaite | **22** | Braithwaites in 1861, 1871 **and** 1881 |
| 208 | William Patterson | **28** | Patterson there in 1861 |
| 209 | Violet Jacoby | **32a** | Jacoby there in 1861; the schedule says only 'The Park' |
| 197 | Edward Munk | **4** | Edward Monk there in 1861 |

**The 1871 walk places nothing on its own** - its numbers are read off the page and jump about, 18 then 16 then 24. Only the names carry it.

**Left unfiled on purpose:** schedule 196, *William A Patterson, magistrate and silk throwster*. There are two Pattersons in 1871 and only one in 1861, and 1881 has William A Patterson at **4** - the house schedule 197 has just been given. One of the two wants the page.

questions.title: ANSWERED - Naunton is Starston, and St Mary's is collapsed both ways
questions.detail:
Three loose ends from the birth-place corrections of 27 September 2026.

## 1. ANSWERED: it is Starston

**A. Hagues reads it as Starston**, the village near Harleston - which *is* in Norfolk, as the page says, and which no Naunton is. Positioned at 52.4107, 1.2842 and corrected at source as well as in the record.

**Her surname is still open.** The 1891 schedule for 4 Clare Valley was flagged as hard to read in two places, and only the birthplace has been settled. **Louisa Berns**, mother-in-law in the Cox household and so Louisa Cox's mother, may be reading as something else.

## Superseded: why it was a problem

*Nauton, Norfolk* was corrected to **Naunton**, and the geocoder can find no such place in Norfolk. The Nauntons that exist are in **Gloucestershire** (near Stow-on-the-Wold) and **Worcestershire** (Naunton Beauchamp). The nearest thing to it in East Anglia is **Naughton, Suffolk**.

The entry is **Louisa Berns**, mother-in-law in the Cox household at 4 Clare Valley in 1891, aged 55 - and both her surname and her birthplace were flagged as hard to read when the schedule was transcribed. The whole line may want a second look rather than just the place. See [[clare-valley-numbered-from-the-1891-walk]].

## 2. ANSWERED: both halves collapsed

**A. Hagues: collapse them.** The 45 rows of *"St Mary, Nottingham"* have joined the 19 of *"Nottingham St Mary's, Nottinghamshire"* in plain **Nottingham, Nottinghamshire**, which now stands at 2,501 rows. The record makes one distinction where it was making two.

## Superseded: the two spellings

**"Nottingham St Mary's, Nottinghamshire"** - 19 rows - has been collapsed to plain **Nottingham, Nottinghamshire**.

But **"St Mary, Nottingham"** - **45 rows** - is the same parish written the other way round, and it is still standing. It was deliberately left alone when the earlier rewrites were made, on the grounds that it is not the same value.

**They should match, one way or the other.** Either both collapse to Nottingham, or both keep the parish. Forty-five rows is too many to leave sitting on the other side of a distinction the record no longer makes.

## 3. Stoke Village is Stoke Damerel - and is already right

**Settled by A. Hagues.** *Stoke Village* is the parish of **Stoke Damerel**, the old parish covering Devonport in Plymouth. The record already holds it as **Stoke Damerel, Devon**, so nothing needed doing.

questions.title: Lieutenant-Colonel Herbert Herbert FRCS, who gave his name to Herbert’s pits - answered
questions.detail:
**ANSWERED, by A. Hagues.** The head of 2 Castle Grove in 1911 is **Lieutenant-Colonel Herbert Herbert, FRCS (25 February 1865 - 19 March 1942)**, an ophthalmic surgeon of international standing. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_Herbert)

**He has an eponym.** The corneal scars left by trachoma are called **Herbert's pits**, and he was the first to describe them, in 1903. He also devised the **trap-door sclerotomy** for glaucoma, published one of the earliest papers on superficial punctate keratitis, and was **the first to record eosinophils in conjunctivitis**. His books on cataract surgery rest on **five thousand extractions performed in India**. He is counted one of the four pioneers of ophthalmology in the Indian Medical Service.

**The Nottingham question is answered, and it is the reason he is here.** He retired from the IMS in **October 1907**, returned to England in 1908, and was appointed **surgeon and then consulting surgeon to the Midland Eye Infirmary, Nottingham**. **The infirmary brought him to The Park.**

**The schedule agrees with the life at every point**, which is worth saying because it is not always so:

| the schedule | the life |
|---|---|
| aged **46** | born 25 February 1865 |
| born **Birkenhead, Cheshire** | born at **Tranmere**, part of Birkenhead |
| **married 11 years** | married 1899 |
| **4 born, 4 living** | two sons and two daughters |
| youngest born **Bombay**, aged 4 | still serving in India until October 1907 |

**His name is neither an error nor a joke.** He was born **Herbert Sherwood**, son of a barrister and judge; his surname was changed to Herbert at the age of twelve, most likely to his mother's own. **He could not change his Christian name, so he became Herbert Herbert.** Any matcher that assumes a forename and a surname must differ will mishandle him, and now there is a reason to record beside the warning.

**Commissioned 1887; major 1899; lieutenant-colonel March 1907.** Before the eye work he served in the Middle East and the Gulf of Aden, was professor at the Grant Medical College and surgeon at the Jamsetjee Jeejeebhoy Hospital in Bombay, civil surgeon at Kheda, and **wrote on the cholera epidemics of the 1890s** - including a paper read at the International Congress of Hygiene at Budapest in 1894.

**He rejoined the IMS for the First World War**, serving on hospital ships, at the Indian Hospital at Brockenhurst and in India, then settled at West Worthing and consulted to Worthing Hospital and the Sussex Eye Hospital at Brighton. Vice-president of the Ophthalmological Society of the United Kingdom. He died at Rugby, aged 77.

**What is still open is the house.** The cover gives **2 Castle Grove**, and the property list does not hold a number 2 - see [[castle-grove-has-no-low-numbers]]. **His address should be findable**: a consulting surgeon to a Nottingham infirmary is listed in the medical directories of the day, and those give a private address.

questions.title: Samuel McIntire Taylor, United States Consul at Nottingham - answered
questions.detail:
**ANSWERED, by A. Hagues.** The head of an unnumbered Castle Grove household in 1911 is **Samuel McIntire Taylor (24 July 1856 - 7 December 1916)**, American lawyer, politician and diplomat, **United States Consul at Nottingham from 1910 to 1911**.
[Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_McIntire_Taylor)

**The census caught the only full year he was here.** He held Nottingham for one year. Had the count fallen either side of April 1911, he would not be in this record at all - and The Park would have housed a serving foreign consul without anything to show for it.

**A political career first, and a well-connected one.** Republican member of the **Ohio House of Representatives** from 1888, then **Secretary of State of Ohio, 1893-1897**, serving under Governor **William McKinley**. McKinley, once President, appointed him to the consular service - so the posting that brought him to Nottingham came from the man he had worked under at Columbus.

| post | years |
|---|---|
| Glasgow | 1897-1906 |
| Callao, Peru | 1906-1910 |
| **Nottingham** | **1910-1911** |
| Birmingham | 1913 until his death |

**He died in post**, of influenza, at Birmingham in December 1916, and is buried at Urbana, Ohio. Educated at Ohio Wesleyan University and the Cincinnati Law School.

**Everything on the schedule agrees.** Aged **54** on 2 April 1911, against a birth in July 1856. **Married 27 years**, so about 1884 - the year he finished law school. **One child born, one living**: Miriam, 16, born in the United States about 1895, when he was Secretary of State and before Glasgow. His wife **Myrtle A. Taylor**, 49. Two English servants.

**One lesson for the importer.** The age gives a birth year of **1857**; he was born in **July 1856** and had not had his birthday. That is precisely the fault written up at 5.5b in `docs/post-import-checklist.md`, and here it is caught against a real date rather than a suspicion. His record carries the true date.

**What is still open**: the house. **The cover gives only *Castle Grove, The Park***, and seven 1911 households on that street cannot be placed at all - see [[castle-grove-has-no-low-numbers]]. **A consul's address should be the easiest of the seven to find**, because a consulate is published: a Nottingham directory for 1910 or 1911, or the United States consular register, will give the street and number outright. **That would place one of the seven and may place its neighbours.**

questions.title: Clumber House on Clumber Road: answered, 15 Clumber Road is a former name
questions.detail:
Settled by A. Hagues from the census image. The record holds **Clumber House on Park Drive (#239)**, built about 1870–75. The 1891 census heads the Gregory household there twice as Clumber Road — once plainly, and once on a second page as **15 Clumber Road** with *"Clumber House"* written beneath it. Same family both times: William Godfrey Gregory, a lace manufacturer of 57, his wife Harriett, William, Ellen Augusta, Charles Arthur and Kate.

The house keeps Park Drive, and **15 Clumber Road is recorded on it as a former name**. The house has more than one frontage — its own description notes the original coach house was reached from Cavendish Crescent South — so an enumerator walking the Clumber Road round would address it that way.

This does not settle the other numbered Clumber Road entries on these pages. The record holds Clumber Road East, Clumber Road West and Clumber Crescent, every one of them by house name or Crescent number, and no numbered Clumber Road anywhere. Whether that numbering was a wider convention the estate later dropped is still worth knowing.

questions.title: Which house on Huntingdon Drive is Greendale? — answered: 4
questions.detail: Settled by A. Hagues: Joseph Spray's biography gives his address as Greendale, Huntingdon Drive, The Park, and Companies House records put Greendale at 4 Huntingdon Drive. The record already linked the Sprays to number 4 from 1911. 4 Huntingdon Drive now carries the name; press Record what you found to close this.

questions.title: Kentmere: answered, it is on Pelham Crescent, not Cavendish Crescent North
questions.detail:
In 1911 William Wing, a solicitor of 47, lived at 'Kentmere, Cavendish Crescent North' with his wife Sara, his sons Henry, an automobile engineer, and Richard, an articled clerk, a cook and a housemaid. The four Wings are in the record (#668, #669, #670, #671) with that census and **no property**, and they stay unfiled by A. Hagues's decision until the house is identified. The name is on neither OpenStreetMap nor Dougal de Havilland's map.

**The directory confirms the name and the street, but gives no number.** Wright's Directory prints 'Kentmere, Wing William, solicitor (H. Wing & Son)' on Cavendish Crescent North in 1910-11 and 1913-14, 'Kentmere, Wing Henry' in 1913-14, and 'Kentmere, Wing Mrs. Sarah W' in 1915-16. So the house was called Kentmere for at least six years, and the family held it after William. Every one of those lines is printed without a number, as this crescent's named houses usually are.

**The firm ties the family to Park Terrace.** H. Wing & Son is the practice of Henry Wing, magistrate and solicitor, who is at 12 Park Terrace on the 1891 return with his daughter, his married granddaughter, her infant son, his sister-in-law and two servants, and whom Wright's prints at that number in 1894-95 and 1898-99. William, born about 1864, is the son of the firm's name.

**Correction: the earlier answer here was wrong.** This question used to reason that Kentmere was most likely number 1, now Carisbrooke House, 'which holds nobody in 1911'. It does hold a household in 1911: William Bradshaw and four others are filed at #21 that year. Since the enumerator reached the Wings *before* Bradshaw, Kentmere sits ahead of number 1 in the walk, at the North Road end, and cannot be number 1 itself.

**What is actually empty on the crescent in 1911**, for whoever picks this up: numbers 9 (#25), 10 (#26), 16a (#31) and 17 (#32). All four sit further along the crescent than the walk allows, so on present evidence Kentmere is a house the record does not hold at all, rather than one of these. Names on this crescent did change - 10 was formerly Charnwood - so a renaming is possible. A rate book, a deed, or the 1901 return for the same stretch would settle it.

**Answered by the 1901 return, which is what this question asked for.** Schedule 196 of the 1901 census reads **"Pelham Crescent, 'Kentmere'"** and gives William Wing, solicitor, 37, an employer, born in Nottinghamshire, with his wife Sarah W, 37, born at Sedgley in Staffordshire, his sons Henry, 11, and Richard, 8, and two servants, Maud Randeris and Kate Lansdall.

That is the same household the 1911 return puts at 'Kentmere, Cavendish Crescent North', ten years on and with the boys grown into an automobile engineer and an articled clerk.

**So the house is on Pelham Crescent.** The two crescents run into one another, and a corner house addressed both ways is a far smaller thing than a family moving and carrying the name with them. The reasoning above about which Cavendish Crescent North house could be Kentmere is therefore beside the point, and the four Wings (#668, #669, #670, #671) should be filed on Pelham Crescent once the number is known. The 1901 enumerator reached Kentmere at schedule 196, between "Carisbrooke Ho" at 195 and Julia Meyer's household at 197, which on the 1891 walk is the 1 Pelham Crescent end.

questions.title: The McCraiths at 7 Clumber Road: answered, it is 3 South Road
questions.detail:
Settled by A. Hagues from the census image. The record files the McCraith household at **3 South Road, Ellenborough House (#302)** for 1891, and the enumerator's page heads that same household **7 Clumber Road**. They are not two properties: the wife, both boys, the three-month-old Kenneth York and all four servants — Isabella Richardson, Elizabeth Smith, Lucy Else and Mary Jane Atkins — agree name for name with what the record already held.

So the house stays 3 South Road, and **7 Clumber Road is kept on it as a former address**, where it is searchable alongside Ellenborough House.

The page's *Jameston McCraith* is answered too: it is the enumerator running **James Wm** together, not a different forename. Two other hands on the same page were settled by the record rather than by reading — the page's *Hannett York* is **Kenneth York McCraith, b.1891**, and *Lucy Elso* is **Lucy Else, b.1869**, both already held at this house for 1891.

Still open, and not covered by this answer: the other numbered Clumber Road addresses on these pages — 3, 4, 5, 9 and 32 — which the record holds at no number at all.

questions.title: Stanfield's house on Lincoln Circus: answered, it is Lincoln House
questions.detail:
**Answered by A. Hagues: Lincoln House (#403).** Alfred William Stanfield (#3554) is now a resident of it. The case is elimination rather than a document, so the whole of it is set out here.

**What was known.** Wright's Directory prints him on Lincoln Circus in 1910-11, 1913-14 and 1915-16, every time without a house name or number, and his obituary gives only 'his residence, Lincoln Circus, The Park'. He died there on 25 September 1918, a barrister and J.P. of 82 keeping three living-in servants.

**What closes it.** The circus holds three properties, and in 1911 two of them were full: Gladstone House had the Radfords, and The Cottage - identified only this week from the 1953 OS sheet - had the Palmers. **Lincoln House was the only empty house on Lincoln Circus that year**, in the very year his servants were returned at an unnamed house on it, with the cook Annie Elizabeth Tune signing the schedule for her absent master. He is also the only Lincoln Circus resident the 1910-11 directory prints with no house against his name.

**Nothing contradicts it.** Harry Laurence Birkin's household of eight is at Lincoln House on the 1921 return, three years after Stanfield's death, so the two do not overlap. Annie Elizabeth Tune is cook at 8 Western Terrace with the Bradleys by 1921 - a servant moving on when the household she kept was broken up by its master's death, which is what the dates require.

**What it rests on, and what would overturn it.** No schedule names Lincoln House as his address. If the 1911 enumerator's round for the circus is ever read and puts his three servants at another house, the resident link is the thing to undo. Two earlier candidates are superseded: Claremont (#230) and 1 Duke William Mount (#106) were suggested because both stood empty in 1911, but neither is on Lincoln Circus and neither was needed once the circus itself was found to have a vacancy.

**Still outstanding:** the three servants - Annie Elizabeth Tune (#595), Alice Ada Wright (#596) and Florence Swaly (#597) - have 1911 census rows still unfiled under 'Lincoln Circus (house not named)', and want reassigning to #403. Lincoln House is demolished and its position in the record is approximate.

questions.title: ANSWERED - the whole of Huntingdon Drive named, from the 1939 run
questions.detail:
**The whole 1939 run on Huntingdon Drive, from the Genealogist's index**, supplied by A. Hagues. It is the first time the record has seen the empty houses named, and it closes the street down to one question.

| Schedule | The page | The record |
|---|---|---|
| 85 | The Cottage | **14 Huntingdon Drive** - Charles William Slight, chauffeur gardener |
| 86 | **Avalon** | *empty* - no such house in the record |
| 87 | **Brampton** | **9 Huntingdon Drive** - Leslie Fleetwood Bates, professor of physics |
| 88 | **Whale Yates**, which must be **White Gates** | *empty* - no such house in the record |
| 89 | **Ravenswood** | Fred Noble Smith, civil engineer, water department |
| 90 | 7 | **7 Huntingdon Drive** - *empty* |
| 91 | **Napier** | **5 Huntingdon Drive** - the record carries **Napier House** |
| 92 | 4 | **4 Huntingdon Drive** - William C Sallis |
| 93 | 3 | **3 Huntingdon Drive** - Thomas Walker Saxton |
| 94 | 2 | **2 Huntingdon Drive** - Claude Harry Newham |

## What it settles

**Napier is 5 Huntingdon Drive** - the index and the record's own former name agree, with nothing else needed. That and Brampton make two of the street's six recorded house names confirmed off this one page.

**Ravenswood is not 7.** The record holds *Ravenswood* as a former name of 7 Huntingdon Drive, and the enumerator gives 7 its own schedule, ticked and left blank, on the night Ravenswood holds a household. An empty house and an occupied one are not the same house.

## Settled, 2 October 2026

A. Hagues settles the last two: **White Gates is 8** and **Ravenswood is 6**. With Avoca separated from Avalon, every house on the street is named and placed.

| | |
|---|---|
| 1, 2, 3, 4 | numbered, no name recorded |
| **5** | **Napier House** - the index and the record's own former name agree |
| **6** | **Ravenswood**, formerly **Avoca** - the Smiths |
| 7 | numbered; *empty* that night. **Not Ravenswood**, which the record had wrongly carried here |
| **8** | **White Gates** - *empty*; written *Whale Yates* in the index. It had no recorded name of any kind before this |
| **9** | **Brampton House** - the Bates |
| **10** | **Avalon**, also **Kenmare House** and **Kenmore** - *empty* |
| **14** | **The Cottage** |

**Nothing on Huntingdon Drive is unplaced.** The three empty houses are marked empty for 1939 so the gap tools stop offering them, and every name the register gives is written the same way, in front of the number.

**What the street cost to close:** one page of an index, and three corrections to the record - Brankston was Brampton, Ravenswood was one house out, and Avalon and Avoca were two houses rather than one name read twice.

Links: [[huntingdon-drive-has-no-11-12-or-13]], [[house-names-live-in-prose]].

questions.title: Five 1911 Park Terrace names where the index and the household schedule disagree
questions.detail:
**A. Hagues ran the 1911 Park Terrace list against the record and nothing is missing** - every household in the index is in the record, and the record holds five more besides (10, 14, 15, 17 and Sunnyside).

What the run did turn up is five heads of house whose names the index and the schedule read differently. Each is noted on its own census row.

| House | The record, from the household schedule | The 1911 index |
|---|---|---|
| 1 Park Terrace | **Mary Ely Patterson** | Mary **Elizabeth** Patterson |
| 6 Park Terrace | William Henry **Foster** | William Henry **Fister** |
| 7 Park Terrace | John **Tom** McCraith | John **I** McCraith |
| 9 Park Terrace | **Bernard Orme Halford** | **Harford Bernardorme** |
| 11 Park Terrace | Amelia Mary **Nicolls** | Amelia Mary **Niscott** |

**Number 9 is the one worth looking at.** *Bernard Orme Halford* and *Harford Bernardorme* are not two readings of one hand so much as one name taken apart and put back in the wrong order - the index has read the forenames as a surname and the surname as a forename. Which way the page has it decides whether the record holds a Halford or an Orme.

**The record's readings come from the household schedules themselves**, which are the better source, so none of these is changed on the index's word. The schedule settles each one in a glance.

Links: [[broxtowe-house-where]], [[the-unsourced-1939-batch-holds-married-names]].

questions.title: Four index runs checked against the record - what is missing, and what is doubled
questions.detail:
**A. Hagues ran four street lists from the Genealogist against the record.** This is what a complete street looks like when it is checked rather than assumed, and it is the cheapest audit the record has had.

## 1911 Park Terrace - nothing missing

Every household in the index is held, and the record has five more besides (10, 14, 15, 17 and Sunnyside). Five heads read differently - see [[park-terrace-1911-the-index-against-the-schedules]]. **And the index gives Broxtowe House a locality: Park Terrace.**

## 1881 Lenton Road - one household, and two transcribed twice

**Missing: a household at 13 Lenton Road headed by *Mary A Spencer*.** The record holds only John P Cox there. It also holds a **Mary A Spencer, 27, cook**, in William Martin's household at **11 Lenton Road**, schedule 245 - so either the index has put her under the wrong house, or there are two women of the name and the record has the servant and not the householder.

**23 Lenton Road is in the record twice.** *William Ebenezer Dobson*, 54, magistrate and lace dresser **employing 108 hands**, with three children; and *William E Dobson*, 54, the same magistrate **employing 105 hands**, with six children, a stepdaughter and five servants. Two transcriptions of one household, the second much fuller, and **the hands count differs by three** - which is the sort of detail that decides which reading to keep.

**Lenton House, 27 Lenton Road is in twice as well** - *Samuel Waite Johnson*, 49, who carries a biography, and *Samuel W Johnson*, 49, who does not.

## 1881 Western Terrace - one household missing, one house number wrong

**Missing: *Charles Henry Clarke* at 8 Western Terrace.** The record holds nothing at number 8 in 1881.

**George Shepperley is at 2 in the record and 4 in the index.** Both cannot be right, and 4 already holds Louis Simon in both.

**Henry Bursell in the index is Henry Birstall in the record**, at number 3.

**Western House is on Western Terrace.** The record has the boarding school unfiled - *Western House, Western Terrace*, schedule 77, ten people under **Louisa Clark** - and carries *Western House* as a former name of **30 The Ropewalk**, where Louisa Clark is in 1891. So either the school moved in the decade between, or the two names are one building on a corner. See [[western-house-school]].

## 1861 Western Terrace - one household missing, one headless

The index gives nine households; the record has six filed as 1 to 6 and two unfiled. **Mary Woodhouse and Thomas Ashwell head two of the index's first three**, and neither is in the record as an 1861 head.

**Schedule 161 has four servants and no head at all** - a cook, two housemaids and a nurse. One of those two names belongs at the top of it. **The other household is missing outright.**

**Two names read differently:** *Bemrley Samuel Oliver* in the index against **Moseley Samuel Oliver** in the record, and *James Reger Allen* against **James Roger Allen**.

## What this says about the method

**Four streets, four rounds, and the record was wrong in six places** - two households missing, two households doubled, one house number in dispute and one schedule with its head unread. None of it was visible from inside the record. A street list costs one search and finds all of it.

Links: [[every-census-gap-and-where-to-start]], [[western-house-school]].

questions.title: ANSWERED - the second book is RMGB, and schedule 83 is 7 Hamilton Drive
questions.detail:
**Settled 2 October 2026.** The page header reads **ED letter code RMGB**, district 430-3, sub-district 26, and the address column gives the house: **7 Hamilton Drive**. So the two schedule 83s belong to two different books, and the record's RMGC one at Ribble Lodge was never in question.

**Muriel Langtree is at 7 Hamilton Drive**, not Ribble Lodge. She had been posted there from an index on the strength of a schedule number that belongs to the other book. She has her trade back - school teacher - and her birth year stands: the page reads **7 March 1918**, where the index transcription gave 1915.

**And the Cotter beside her is explained.** Sub number 7 is **Ronald H Cotter**, 24 and single; she is 21 and single. The amendment written over her name afterwards is his.

**The whole household is new to the record** - eight people in a boarding house kept by **Horatio Nelson**, 61, with his wife Helen: a shorthand typist in the civil service, an export despatch clerk, a secretary to the Trent Navigation, a supervisor in ladies' fashion, a binder and the school teacher.

**Hamilton Drive had nothing but a 1921 round in the record.** Sixteen properties, one census between them, and RMGB holds the 1939 for all of it. That is the next street to read.

Links: [[the-unsourced-1939-batch-holds-married-names]], [[every-census-gap-and-where-to-start]].

questions.title: ANSWERED - the index's bracket follows no rule, because transcribers differ
questions.detail:
**There is no rule to find.** A. Hagues settles it: *"it changes depending on who has transcribed it, so there is no true rule"*. The bracket records that a woman was known by two names and says nothing about which came first, because different transcribers put them in different orders.

**This entry was written twice with a confident answer and was wrong both times** - once saying the bracketed name was the name on the night, once saying it was the married one. The evidence looked decisive on each occasion because it came from one household at a time.

| The index writes | The night name | Where it falls |
|---|---|---|
| Alice V **Lowe** (Perry) | Lowe | **outside** |
| Gladys **Smith** (Hollingworth) | Hollingworth | inside |
| Alice A **Allen** (Sutton) | Sutton | inside |
| Mabel J **Baldwin** (Gose) | Gore | inside |
| Phyllis **Sleigh** (Meakin) | Meakin | inside |
| Annie **Mason** (Padget) | Padget | inside |
| Lilian **Gannon** (Brailford) | Brailsford | inside |

## The proof, in one woman

**Alice V Lowe of 1 Hamilton Drive is rendered both ways by the same index.** One run of schedule 156 writes her **Lowe (Perry)**; a later run of the same schedule writes her **Perry (Lowe)**. Same woman, same line, brackets reversed. Nothing about the order survives even within one entry, let alone across a book.

## What to do instead

**Ask, or read the page.** A. Hagues says which way round each schedule runs as it comes. Nothing goes into the record from a bracketed index entry on its own.

**Nothing already entered rests on a guess about it.** The 128 names came from two labelled columns; everything given as *"X then Y"* states its order; and the four turned round on 2 October went on A. Hagues's word.

**The wider lesson is about this record and not about brackets.** A convention read off one household looks like a rule and is a coincidence. Four women at 8 Park Drive made a rule that seven women on Lenton Road broke.

Links: [[how-to-handle-a-1939-amended-name]], [[the-rmgb-index-address-column-is-unreliable]].

questions.title: The 1939 index writes one address for a run of different houses
questions.detail:
**Three consecutive schedules of ED letter code RMGB all carry the address *41 Lenton Road* in the index**, and they are three different houses. A. Hagues reads them off the page:

| Schedule | The index says | The house is |
|---|---|---|
| 91 | — | **47 Lenton Road** - Lily Creedon, wages clerk |
| 92 | 41 Lenton Road | **45 Lenton Road** - Gordon R Johnson, tea salesman |
| 93 | 41 Lenton Road | **43 Lenton Road** - Susan F Jackson, chemist's warehouse |

**The run descends and the index does not follow it.** The enumerator writes the address once and rules it down the column with ditto marks; the index takes the mark for a value, so a whole run inherits one house.

**The record made a property out of it before the correction came.** *41 Lenton Road* was created as #443 and is gone again - Lenton Road runs to 37 as Rock House and then jumps to 43, and nothing has shown that 39 or 41 exist at all.

## What to do with an index address

**Treat it as a street and not a house.** It is reliable for which road and worthless for which door, exactly as the ditto-mark surname problem is reliable for a household and worthless for a name. Where a run of schedules shares an address, the numbers want reading off the page or off the walk.
