**This is the second index column to fail this way.** The Huntingdon Drive run gave *Fister* for Foster and *Sayton* for Saxton; the Park Terrace run turned Bernard Orme Halford into Harford Bernardorme. An index is a finding aid, and this record uses it as one.

Links: [[index-runs-checked-against-the-record-october-2026]], [[the-unsourced-1939-batch-holds-married-names]].

questions.title: Three women skate for a living on Hope Drive in 1939 - where, and for whom?
questions.detail:
**The 1939 Register puts three professional ice skaters within two doors of each other**, and the record has nothing like it in any other round.

| House | | |
|---|---|---|
| **8 Hope Drive** | **Iris Poett**, 27 | *professional ice instructress* |
| **6 Hope Drive** | **Joan Walker**, 21 | *professional ice skater* - the page writes *Slater* |
| **6 Hope Drive** | **Doris Allen**, 25 | *ice actress and instructress* - the page writes *Inspectress*, and *instructress* is the likelier word beside Iris Poett's |

**Three women, two houses, one trade.** On a street of boarding houses this reads as a troupe lodged together rather than a coincidence - and *ice actress* is a performer's word, not a teacher's.

## What it is almost certainly about

**Nottingham Ice Stadium opened in 1939**, months before the register was taken. A new rink needs instructors and a show needs a cast, and both would want lodgings nearby. **The record does not assert the connection** - no source here names an employer - but it is the obvious thing to test, and it would date the lodging-house trade on Hope Drive to the rink's opening.

## What would settle it

The stadium's own opening programmes or the Nottingham press for 1939, which would name its instructors and its ice show company. Any of these three names in them closes it.

**Doris Allen became Long**, which is a marriage to find as well.

Links: [[every-census-gap-and-where-to-start]].

questions.title: THE MAP IS NOT all_props.json - 312 of 435 positions differ
questions.detail:
**I raised 7 Peveril Drive as a house three hundred metres off its own street. It was never off its street.** The map was right; I had read the wrong file.

## Where a position actually lives

| | |
|---|---|
| **`coords` table** | what the site draws. 402 properties, each placed by hand and stamped with who placed it and when |
| **`data/all_props.json`** | a seed. Where `coords` holds a row, **the file's lat and lng are ignored** |

**312 of 435 properties have a file position more than 40 metres from the one on the map**, and some are most of a mile out - the Derby Road terrace is 700 to 850 metres adrift in the file and correct on the map. So the file's positions are not a second opinion about where a house is; they are stale, and reading them as if they were the record's answer produces exactly the false alarm above.

## What this changes

**Nothing on the site.** The map has been right all along.

**It changes what I may say.** A claim about where a house stands has to come from `coords`, not from the file - and any check of one house against its neighbours has to compare like with like.

**It does not make the file harmless.** **35 properties have no `coords` row at all**, and for those the file is all there is - which includes every property made today: 8a and 8b Hope Drive, 38 Park Terrace, Lynwood, St Ives, Elmsdale, The Lodge, Cedar Lodge and Allendale. The provisional positions written into the file for those are what the map will draw, so they are worth placing properly.

## What would settle it

**Decide which is the record.** Either the file is brought into line from `coords` so the two agree, or its lat and lng are dropped for anything that already has a hand position, so nothing can read a stale number and believe it.

Links: [[questions-for-a-walk-round-the-park]].

**It has cost real work four times this week.** Gwedon, Brampton, Iveston and Kenilworth House were each treated as a new name off a census page, and each was already here - one of them got a duplicate property made for it before the mistake surfaced.

## What to do with them

**The record's own habit is to put the name in front of the number** - *Castle Rising, 3 Lenton Road*, *Ribble Lodge, Clare Valley*, *The Chestnuts, 5 Kenilworth Road*. Three of these have been written that way already because the work of the week ran through them: **Iveston** at 1 Kenilworth Road, **Kenilworth House** at 3, and **Yew Tree House** at 2.

**The other thirty-five are A. Hagues's call**, because it changes how every one of those houses reads on the site, and because a few of them want the number kept in front for good reason - the record learned that the hard way with Tower House at 53 Park Row.

**The cheap half costs nothing and is not a display change:** whatever is decided about the address, a name in `house_name` ought to be searchable. If it were, none of this week's four would have been missed.

questions.title: Everard L Guilford, born 1882 - is he the Nottinghamshire antiquary, and is he a Guilford of The Park?
questions.detail:
**Schedule 134 of the 1939 RMGB book, on Kenilworth Road, holds Everard L Guilford, born 17 November 1882**, with Margaret M Guilford and a son of 20 who is an undergraduate at **Emmanuel College, Cambridge**. His own trade cannot be read.

## He looks like a Guilford of this estate

The record already holds the family:

| | |
|---|---|
| 1871 | **Francis Leavers Guilford**, 28, engineer and ironfounder, at **15 Park Terrace**, with Ada and a son of 0 |
| 1881 | the same household at **8 The Ropewalk**, Francis L now 37, with sons **Francis C**, 10, and **Henry C**, 8 |

**A son born in 1882 fits that family exactly**, and *Leavers* is the name Everard carries as his middle initial. The record has no other Leavers Guilford.

## And the name is a known one

**Everard Leaver Guilford** wrote on Nottinghamshire - the county volume in a well-known guide series, among other things - and the dates would fit a man born in 1882. **The record does not claim it.** A shared name is not an identification, and nothing on this page says what he did.

**What would settle it:** the author's own dates and an address, from the books' own matter or an obituary. If it holds, the record gains a writer on Nottinghamshire who grew up in The Park and came back to it - and the connection to the ironfounding Guilfords would be worth having either way.

**The house is not identified.** The page gives no house, and the walk puts him next along from The Chestnuts at 5 Kenilworth Road, where the record's Kenilworth Road stops.

Links: [[questions-for-a-walk-round-the-park]], [[house-names-live-in-prose]].

questions.title: Lomax R B Palmer, architect and surveyor, lived in The Park in 1939 and is in none of its architect pages
questions.detail:
**Schedule 137 of the 1939 RMGB book, on Kenilworth Road, holds Lomax R B Palmer, born 15 July 1881, architect and surveyor**, with Emilie Palmer and a servant.

**The record's architect pages do not have him.** There is no Palmer among the architect firms or works, and no other Palmer in any census round of this estate is an architect - the five the record holds are a gardener, a book-keeper, a telephone mechanic, a warehouse apprentice and a wife.

**The name is distinctive.** *Lomax* as a forename, with two further initials, is not a name that will be confused with another man.

## Why it is worth following

This record already treats the architects of The Park as a subject in their own right - Hine & Evans, S. Dutton Walker, Fothergill, Albert Nelson Bromley, Robert Evans. **A practising architect living on the estate in 1939 belongs in that account**, and if he built anything here the houses will carry his name.

**What would settle it:** the RIBA directories or the Nottingham trade directories for the 1930s, which would give his practice and his address, and the Nottingham planning records for anything he put up.

**The house is not identified.** The page gives no house, and the walk is on Kenilworth Road between The Chestnuts at 5 and 9 Lenton Road.

Links: [[questions-for-a-walk-round-the-park]].

questions.title: Six Wardles in three houses on the 1939 round - one family or three?
questions.detail:
**The Wardles are barely in the record before 1939 and then there are six of them in one night.**

| House | | |
|---|---|---|
| **5 Western Terrace** | **George Owen Wardle**, 65 | sales manager, ladies' gown factory |
| | **Edith Wardle**, 60 | **director**, ladies' gown factory |
| | **Meryl Vera Wardle**, 35 | voluntary social service worker |
| **Lenton House, 27 Lenton Road** | **Mary E Wardle**, 60, widow | |
| | **Whiltock Wardle**, 27 | clerk, tobacco |
| **8 Park Drive** | **Francis O Wardle** | domestic servant |

**Before this the record holds two**: Mary B Wardle at 6 The Ropewalk in 1861, and an Elizabeth Wardle, housemaid, unfiled in 1881. Nothing in 1871, 1891, 1901, 1911 or 1921.

## Why it is worth asking

**Edith Wardle is a woman directing a factory in 1939**, with her husband working as its sales manager - the record holds few enough of those to want her family traced. And **Meryl Vera Wardle** is already one of the week's set pieces: indexed as Marjorie Vera Hart, two marriages and a misread forename deep, and put back by A. Hagues.

**Three households of one uncommon surname on one estate on one night is not usually a coincidence** - but a servant in one house and a gown director in another may be no relation at all, and the record should not join them because the name is rare.

**What would settle it:** the Nottingham directories for the gown firm and its partners, and a birth or marriage for Whiltock Wardle, whose forename is odd enough to find.

Links: [[how-to-handle-a-1939-amended-name]].

questions.title: John V Whitaker, chief tuberculosis officer for Nottingham, at 3 Lenton Avenue in 1939
questions.detail:
**Schedule 164 of the 1939 RMGB book holds John V Whitaker, 31, at 3 Lenton Avenue**, returned as **chief tuberculosis officer and assistant medical officer of health** - written on the page as *Chief T B Officer Assistant Med Officer Health*. His wife Rosamond is with him; her forename cannot be read beyond its ending.

## Why he belongs on the notable list

**It is a public office, not a trade.** The record already marks people for holding one - the Chief Constable at Derby House, the Town Clerk, the city architect - and an assistant medical officer of health for Nottingham is of that kind. **Tuberculosis was the city's great public health work of the period**, and the officer in charge of it was running sanatorium admissions, contact tracing and the dispensary service for the whole borough.

**He is 31 and holds it in the autumn of 1939**, with the war about to make every part of it harder.

## What would settle it

The Nottingham medical officer of health's annual reports, which name their own staff, and the Medical Register. Both would give his full name, his qualifications and the years he served.

**The record carries no other medical officer of health**, so this is the first.

Links: [[notables-the-1939-register-brought-in]].

questions.title: ANSWERED - Henry Thomas Herbert Piaggio, the first Professor of Mathematics at Nottingham
questions.detail:
**Settled 3 October 2026.** He is **Henry Thomas Herbert Piaggio** (2 June 1884 - 26 June 1967), and the record now carries his life.

**He came to the college as a lecturer in 1908 and became its first Professor of Mathematics in 1919** - so the chair did not exist until he held it, and the subject at Nottingham was his to shape from the start. He had been at the City of London School and St John's College, Cambridge. His *Elementary Treatise on Differential Equations and their Applications* ran through edition after edition.

The 1939 Register finds him at **5 Lenton Avenue**, 55 and unmarried, with his sister Edith keeping house and one servant.

**He is the second professor of that college on this estate in 1939.** Leslie Fleetwood Bates holds the chair of physics at Brampton House, 9 Huntingdon Drive, on the same night - and Bates held his for twenty-eight years as Piaggio held the first mathematics chair. Two foundational chairs, a few streets apart, both of them living in The Park.

Links: [[notables-the-1939-register-brought-in]].

questions.title: Two households in one book both carry schedule 123
questions.detail:
**ED letter code RMGB cannot number two schedules 123, and the record now holds two.**

| | |
|---|---|
| **Ferndene, Hamilton Drive** | Frederick May, electrical engineer, with Eunice and two sons |
| **11 Lenton Avenue** | John T Fraser Ashby, hosiery machine designer, with Margaret and two grown children |

Both came from A. Hagues's own readings of the same book, days apart. **The people and the houses are not in doubt in either case** - only the number.

## What it is likely to be

**A slip in one of the two readings**, which is the ordinary explanation and costs nothing to correct.

**Or the book restarts its numbering.** Some registers begin again at a new district boundary or a new enumerator's section, and this book has already shown it does unexpected things - it writes one address down a run of four houses, and it renders one woman's names in both orders.

## Why it matters beyond tidiness

**This record files people by schedule number.** Muriel Langtree was put in the wrong house for exactly this reason - an index gave a schedule number that belonged to the other book, and she went to RMGC's schedule 83 instead of RMGB's. A duplicated number inside one book is the same trap one step closer.

**What would settle it:** the page numbers. Ferndene sits in a Peveril Drive run around schedules 118 to 130; 11 Lenton Avenue sits in a Lenton Avenue run around 163 to 173. One of them is a long way from 123.

Links: [[two-schedule-83s-and-one-muriel-langtree]], [[the-rmgb-index-address-column-is-unreliable]].

questions.title: The Park is full of civil servants in September 1939 - were government offices moved here?
questions.detail:
**Twenty-one people in the 1939 round are civil servants or ministry staff, and five of them lodge in one guest house.**

## 19 Pelham Crescent, schedule 208

Lucy Dena Hanley keeps a guest house of thirteen. Four are her own family. Of the nine lodgers, **five are civil servants**:

| | |
|---|---|
| **Dorothy Aldridge**, 49 | clerical, **Ministry of Labour** |
| **Annie Clarkson**, 58 | civil servant, clerical |
| **Violet M Woolmer**, 48 | civil servant, clerical |
| **Annie D Mackenzie**, 49 | civil servant, **higher executive** |
| **Elizabeth B McDonald**, 45 | **civil service audit, travelling** |

All five are single women between 45 and 58, lodging together. That is not a coincidence of a boarding house; that is a department.

## And they are all over the estate

**Ministry of Labour** at Cedar Lodge and 6 Hamilton Drive. **Ministry of Health** at 9 Park Terrace, twice, and at 54 The Ropewalk. **Ministry of Mines** at 1a Hamilton Drive. **War Office** at 5 Clinton Terrace. A **food office** at 8 Hope Drive. Clerical officers and shorthand typists on five more streets.

## The thing to test

**Government departments were dispersed out of London at the outbreak of war**, and Nottingham took some of them. The register was taken on **29 September 1939**, three weeks after war was declared - exactly when that movement was happening.

**The record does not claim it.** No page here names a department's location, and a provincial city always has some civil service of its own. But **five single women of one grade in one guest house** is the shape of a staff billeted together, not of five people who each happened to find lodgings on the same crescent.

**What would settle it:** the Nottingham press for September and October 1939, or the departmental records of which offices were evacuated and where. Either would turn twenty-one scattered people into one event.

Links: [[every-census-gap-and-where-to-start]].

## A second house of them, found 4 October 2026

**North Lodge, schedule 203** - a boarding house of thirteen kept by Clara Burdett, widow - holds **seven more**: a **tax inspector** (John B Heslin, 31), a **third class officer of the Ministry of Labour** (Mary M Hall, 28), a **senior staff officer of Inland Revenue** (Harry R Portman, 42), **two civil servants** (Conelian K De Farrars, 47, and David L McKenna, 54, whose department is written D R N O), a **student at a Home Office laboratory** (Eric W Montgomery, 24) and a **private secretary**.

That is now **two boarding houses on the estate**, 19 Pelham Crescent and North Lodge, each holding five to seven government staff on the same night. Twelve people in two houses is no longer a coincidence of lodgings.

Links: [[north-lodge-and-pelham-cottage-are-not-in-the-record]].

questions.title: Is Glenhurst, Park Drive the same house as Elmhurst, Cavendish Road East?
questions.detail:
**The 1891 census household of Arthur Alfred Dawson is in the record twice, under two house names, and one of them is a house the record does not otherwise hold.**

## One family, written as two houses on one night

| at Elmhurst, Cavendish Road East (prop 57) | at Glenhurst, Park Drive (schedule 152) |
|---|---|
| Arthur Alfred Dawson, 35, head | Arthur Alfd Dawson, 35, head |
| Harriett E Dawson, 33, wife | — |
| Ethel 6, Claude R 4, Leslie 1 | Arthur H 11, Percy A 10, Mabel E 9, Violet E 7 |
| Mary Walker, 30, servant | Mary Walker, 28, servant |
| Emily Gooch 22, Elizabeth Asling 19, servants | — |

The children interleave as one family of seven: **11, 10, 9, 7, 6, 4, 1**. The head is 35 on both sides and a **lace warehouse manager** on both. A servant called **Mary Walker** stands on both.

**The record itself already joins them.** Harriett E Dawson (#360) is the wife at Elmhurst in 1891 *and* the wife of the Arthur A Dawson who kept Holles Crescent in 1881 (schedule 169), whose sons Arthur H and Percy A are the two eldest boys at Glenhurst. So the two households are one household by the record's own links.

## Which house, though

- **Glenhurst does not exist anywhere else in the record.** No property of that name, and nothing on Park Drive carries it.
- The Glenhurst row is the **better sourced**: RG12/2682, schedule 152, read from the enumerator's page, in the **Tattershall Drive and Cavendish Road East** district - which is where *Elmhurst* stands.
- The Elmhurst rows carry **no source at all** and no schedule number, and the family is at Elmhurst again in 1901.

## The thing to test

Either **Glenhurst is a misreading of Elmhurst** - El- for Gl-, -mhurst for -nhurst is an easy hand to mistake, and the district fits - and the street was taken from a ditto in the address column, which this index is known to run on; **or** Glenhurst is a real house on Park Drive the record lacks, the Dawsons were there in 1891, and the Elmhurst rows are the misfiled ones.

**What would settle it:** a second look at schedule 152's address on the page, and Wright's Directory for 1891-92 under both Park Drive and Cavendish Road East. If Wright's prints Dawson at Elmhurst, the two fold into one and the fourteen rows become one household of thirteen.

**Held until then:** the two Arthur Dawsons (#359, #7286) and the two Mary Walkers (#365, #8919) are left unfolded, because folding them would decide the address before the evidence does.

Links: [[the-index-address-column-runs-on-ditto-marks]], [[house-names-that-never-display]].

questions.title: Jemma M Bell of 19 Park Valley and Maria Bell of 15 Cavendish Crescent South - one woman?
questions.detail:
**Both are born in Grantham, Lincolnshire, and both are the stepmother of the same Florence.**

| | 1881, 19 Park Valley, schedule 217 | 1891, 15 Cavendish Crescent South, schedule 67 |
|---|---|---|
| name | **Jemma M Bell** (#6214) | **Maria Bell** (#7218) |
| age | 29 | 38 |
| place | wife | head, *living on her own means* |
| born | **Grantham, Lincolnshire** | **Grantham, Lincolnshire** |

The same children are in both houses: **Henry** (4, then 14) and **Frank** (2, then 12). **Florence** is *daughter* of the head in 1881 and *stepdaughter* of the head in 1891 - and at 29 in 1881, Jemma M cannot have borne a girl of 14, so she was already the stepmother then. William Bell, draper, is dead by 1891 and his widow keeps house on her own means.

The **M** of *Jemma M* is most likely Maria, and she went by it once widowed.

**What would settle it:** the marriage of William Bell to a Grantham-born wife between 1867 and 1876, or a burial for Jemma and a second marriage. **Which name should lead** is the part only you can call - the record can hold the other as an alias either way.

Links: [[two-william-bells-a-draper-and-a-coachman]].

questions.title: Two William Bells were held as one - a Park Valley draper and a Lenton Avenue coachman
questions.detail:
**Settled, 3 October 2026.** The record had #3138 keeping 19 Park Valley as a **draper** aged 41 in 1881 and heading a house on the even side of Lenton Avenue as a **coachman** aged 40 in 1891. A man does not get a year younger in ten.

The even side of Lenton Avenue was the **mews** - five of its six heads that year were coachmen, living over the yards that stabled the horses of houses like 19 Park Valley. The two households share nothing but the surname: the draper's wife is Jemma M of Grantham with Florence, Henry, Frank and a newborn; the coachman's wife is Mary, nine years older, with Annie, Nellie and a different Florence.

The 1881 import had bound its head **by name alone** and found the coachman. The draper is now **#8926**, and `data/people_1881_standard_hill_part2.json` points at him by number. The Coachman trade, written in five times over, is reduced to one.

**Two more of the same family came apart with it:** a second **Florence Bell** made by the 1891 round folded into #6215 (14 in 1881 and 24 in 1891 both give 1867), and the **1891 Frank Bell** row moved from the New-York-born boy of 21 Park Valley, who would have been 17, to his namesake next door at 19, who is 12.

Links: [[jemma-m-bell-and-maria-bell]].

questions.title: Is the Ethel Hardstaff who served at 21 Lenton Avenue the same woman as the Ethel Hardstaff of 1911 and 1921?
questions.detail:
**One person in the record holds a servant born in Nottinghamshire and a wife born in Somerset.**

| round | aged | place in the house | born |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1901 | 22 | **servant**, nurse (domestic), 21 Lenton Avenue | **Hucknall Torkard, Nottinghamshire** |
| 1911 | 34 | **wife** | **Huntspill, Somerset** |
| 1921 | 45 | **wife** | **Huntspill, Somerset** |

Hucknall Torkard is eight miles north of Nottingham; Huntspill is in the Somerset levels, a hundred and fifty miles away. A woman gives one birthplace or the other, not both.

The ages do not quite settle it either: 22 in 1901 works back to 1879, 34 in 1911 to 1877, 45 in 1921 to 1876.

**What raised it.** The 1901 household had been transcribed twice, and the second copy produced *Ethel M. Hardstaff* beside *Ethel Dora Hardstaff* - same age, same trade, same birthplace, same house. The two were folded together on 4 October 2026, which left the Somerset rows and the Nottinghamshire row on one person and made the disagreement visible.

**What would settle it:** the marriage that made the 1911 wife a Hardstaff, or a baptism at Hucknall Torkard about 1879. If they are two women, the 1901 servant wants separating out, as the two William Bells were.

Links: [[two-william-bells-a-draper-and-a-coachman]].

questions.title: Is Frank B. Lewis of Lenton Road the Walter Bickerton Lewis of 1891?
questions.detail:
**The only one of William W Lewis's four children on the 1901 page who could not be matched to the household the record already holds.**

The other three are certain, and the initials are what prove them: **Elizabeth B.** is Elizabeth **Beatrice**, 25 in 1891 and 35 in 1901; **Edith C.** is Edith **Constance**, 19 and 29; **Ellen T.** matches Ellen Frances at 33 and 43. Each works out exactly ten years on.

**Frank B., 39, does not.** The 1891 household at 6 Lenton Road holds two sons - **Walter Bickerton Lewis**, 27, and **Percy Enfield Lewis**, 24. Walter would be 37 in 1901, not 39, and *Frank* is not *Walter*. But **B. is Bickerton** in that family, which is the one thing pointing at him.

So he is in the record as **Frank B. Lewis**, a new person, rather than folded into Walter on a guess.

**And one loose end on the same page:** Ellen T.'s middle initial is **T.** where the record has Ellen **Frances**. The age and the place in the household are exact, so she was folded, but the initial is unexplained - a third forename, or an F read as a T.

**What would settle it:** the Lewis family in the 1911 return, or baptisms at a Nottingham parish between 1860 and 1872 for William W and Elizabeth G Lewis's children.

Links: [[ethel-hardstaff-a-nottinghamshire-servant-and-a-somerset-wife]].

questions.title: When was 33 Lenton Avenue divided? One family of ten in 1921, five households in 1939
questions.detail:
**The 1939 Register gives 33 Lenton Avenue five separate schedules - 186, 187, 188, 189 and 190 - where every earlier round gives one household.**

| round | the house holds |
|---|---|
| 1881 | 9 people, one household |
| 1901 | 8 people, one household |
| 1911 | 5 people, one household |
| 1921 | **10 people, one household** |
| **1939** | **8 people, five households** |

The five in 1939:

| schedule | who |
|---|---|
| 186 | Arthur Eric Roe, garage proprietor, 36, and Irene Doris Horney, 35 |
| 187 | Alan J McClatchie, warp knitter in artificial silk, 31, and Doris S, auxiliary nurse, 29 |
| 188 | Vernon E E Cramphorn, tailor's shop assistant, 29, and Nora N, 23 |
| 189 | H William Forsyth, 26, something registered medical |
| 190 | Charles N Dorrington, manufacturer of ladies' wear, 40 |

Four of the five are couples or single men in their twenties and thirties, in trades - knitting, tailoring, garage keeping, ladies' wear - a long way from the one large family the house held before. **That is a house let out in flats or rooms**, and the change happened between 1921 and 1939.

**What would settle it:** Wright's Directory for the 1920s and 1930s under Lenton Avenue, where a divided house usually starts printing several occupiers at one number, or a rating valuation. Numbers 29 and 31 either side each kept a single household in 1939, so the division was this house and not the street.

Links: [[every-census-gap-and-where-to-start]].

questions.title: Irene Doris Horney (Roe) at 33 Lenton Avenue - which way round is the bracket?
questions.detail:
**The index gives her as Horney (Roe), and the bracket in this register carries no fixed meaning** - it has held a married name, a maiden name and a mere respelling, depending on who transcribed the page.

She is at **33 Lenton Avenue, schedule 186**, born 16 February 1904, 35, unpaid domestic duties - in the house of **Arthur Eric Roe**, garage proprietor, 36, born 30 May 1903.

**She is entered under Horney, with Roe as the 1939 amendment**, on this reasoning: a woman already married to Arthur Eric Roe would have been written *Roe* on the night, so Horney is most likely the name the register was taken in and Roe the name she took afterwards. That would make her his housekeeper in September 1939 and his wife later.

**But the other reading is open:** that she was Mrs Roe already and the index has printed her maiden name first, which it does elsewhere on these pages.

**One word from you settles it**, and the record will swap her round with the name kept as an alias either way.

Links: [[the-1939-bracket-has-no-rule]].

questions.title: Peppercorn or Pepperdine? Five surnames read two ways at 29 and 31 Lenton Avenue in 1881
questions.detail:
**Both houses were transcribed twice** - once reading the street without numbers, once reading the same two schedules again from RG11/3367 and placing them at 29 and 31. Seven people were therefore in the record twice, under spellings close enough that no tool bucketing on the surname could see them. They were folded together on 4 October 2026, keeping the numbered row that cites the piece.

**But the fold had to keep one spelling and alias the other, and the page is what should choose:**

| schedule 114, 29 Lenton Avenue | |
|---|---|
| Reuben, 31, head | **Peppercorn** or **Pepperdine** |
| Mary, 32, wife | born **Wellingore** or **Welbourn** |
| Herbert, 3, son | as his father |
| Johanna, boarder, born Scotland | **McEwan** or **McBean**, and **26** or **21** |
| Henry, boarder, born Tattershall | **Maplethorpe** or **Maplesthorpe**, and **22** or **27** |

| schedule 113, 31 Lenton Avenue | |
|---|---|
| E Thornley, 20, daughter | **Jemmina** or **Jemmima** |
| Frances, 26, servant | **Piggins** or **Piggin** |

The record currently shows the first of each pair, with the second as an alias. **There is only one schedule 113 and one schedule 114**, so these are two readings of one line in every case, never two people - the ages that disagree are misreadings, not evidence of a second boarder.

**What would settle it:** a look at RG11/3367 for those two schedules. Wellingore and Welbourn are both Lincolnshire villages four miles apart, so Mary's birthplace needs the page as much as her surname does.

Links: [[two-william-bells-a-draper-and-a-coachman]].

questions.title: Tinsley Lindley, OBE, had been entered twice - once as Finlay - and so had his wife
questions.detail:
**Settled, 4 October 2026.** The checklist names *Lindey beside Lindley* as one of the five variant-spelling duplicates the 1901 gap round made, and both halves of this couple were still doubled.

**His Honour Tinsley Lindley, OBE** (27 October 1865 - 31 March 1940), the England footballer and county court judge, headed **14 Park Terrace** in 1901, 1911 and 1921. The 1939 round put him in again as **Finlay Lindley**, 73, *barrister at law*, at the same house - a T read as an F. He died six months after the register was taken, so that line is the last the record has of him, and it was sitting on a stranger.

His wife was split the other way about: **Constance Agnes Lindey** held 1911 and 1921, **Constance Agnes Lindley** held 1901 and 1939. Neither pair overlapped in any round, so both folded without anything having to be chosen between. She now carries her husband's spelling, with Lindey kept as an alias.

Tinsley Lindley's record now runs unbroken from 1901 to 1939.

Links: [[two-william-bells-a-draper-and-a-coachman]].

questions.title: ANSWERED - schedule 193 is 9 Cavendish Crescent North, and 254 is 9 on the South side
questions.detail:
**Mostly answered, 4 October 2026.** A. Hagues read the walk off the pages: **191 Hardwicke House, 192 Haddon House, 193 no number, 194 and 196 both 7 Cavendish Crescent, 195 number 5** - all of them on the **North** side.

That filed three of the four and turned up something else:

## 7 Cavendish Crescent North held two households

| | who |
|---|---|
| **s194** | **Henry Holliwell**, lace manufacturer, 63, his wife Annie C, and two domestics |
| **s196** | **Mary E Littlewood**, 85, with Sarah Coates and Agnes Stanley - the two servants she had at 1 Cavendish Crescent North in 1921 - and a housemaid |

Two full households at one address, numbered **194 and 196 with number 5 between them**. That is the second house in this stretch of the walk shown divided, after **33 Lenton Avenue**, which holds five. Mary Littlewood moved into it from 1 Cavendish Crescent North some time after 1921, bringing her servants with her - a woman of 85 giving up a whole house for part of one.

## What is still open: schedule 193

The index gives **no number at all** - only the street. The household is **Miriam Raflowitch, 49, a lace manufacturer in her own right**, with Arthur Spooner, lace machine fitter, 54, Ethel Spooner, 53, and two domestics. It is in the record unfiled.

The walk puts it on the North side, between Haddon House and number 7. **Eight houses on that side have no 1939 round**, and it must be one of them:

| house | who had it in 1921 |
|---|---|
| 1 (Carisbrooke House) | Agnes Salt and four others |
| ~~3 (Cavendish Lodge)~~ | **ruled out 4 October 2026 - it is schedule 257** |
| 9 | Agnes Dobson and seven others - **but see schedule 254 below** |
| 18 | Alice May Brazier and five others |
| 18a | nothing in the record |
| 20 | Adelaide Carr and five others |
| 22 and 24 | nothing in the record |
| Haddon House | Bernard Swanwick Wright - **but this is schedule 192** |

Haddon House is spoken for by 192 and **number 3 by schedule 257**, so **six candidates remain**. A house taken by a lace manufacturer who heads her own household is more likely one of the larger ones - 1, 3 or 9.

## And now a second household, tangled with the first

**Schedule 254** gives *9 Cavendish Crescent* and no side. It is Wilfred O Woodward, a civil servant of the **Ministry of Supply, area officer for Timber Control No 3**, his wife Vera L, their daughter Helen R, 17 and already articled to a firm of chartered accountants, a domestic, and **Emma Radford, cook, 76** - the record's own, general servant at 1 Pelham Crescent in 1901 and housekeeper there in 1911.

**The two questions lock together.** *9 Cavendish Crescent North is one of the seven houses schedule 193 could be.* If 193 is 9 North, then 254 must be 9 South; if 254 is 9 North, then 193 is one of the other six. Neither number 9 holds a Woodward in 1911 or 1921, so the record cannot break the tie on its own.

One point of evidence, and it cuts towards the South for 254: **the enumerator did Cavendish Crescent North in one pass, schedules 191 to 196** - Hardwicke House, Haddon House, 193, 7, 5, 7 - and did not do a number 9 in it. A house revisited sixty schedules later is odd, unless 193 *was* the number 9.

**What would settle either:** the address column on those two pages, or Wright's Directory for the late 1930s under both sides, where Raflowitch and Woodward are both uncommon enough to find.

Links: [[when-was-33-lenton-avenue-divided]].

## Number 3 ruled out, 4 October 2026

**Schedule 257 is 3 Cavendish Crescent North**, settled by elimination: 3 Cavendish Crescent *South* already has its 1939 round at schedule 95, early in this same book, and 3 North had none at all. It is **Albert E Yeomans, office manager in tobacco**, who is almost certainly kin to the **George E Yeomans, tobacco manufacturer**, at number 5 - schedule 195, two doors up, eight years older, same trade. The record held no Yeomans family before today and now holds two on one crescent.

---

## Schedule 254 is settled - 9 Cavendish Crescent **South**

**4 October 2026.** A. Hagues read the page: the Woodward household is at **9 Cavendish Crescent South**, not North. All five rows have been moved off *9 Cavendish Crescent (the side is not given)* and onto the house.

| | who |
|---|---|
| head | **Wilfred O Woodward**, 53, civil servant - Ministry of Supply, area officer, Timber Control No 3 |
| | Vera L Woodward, 49 |
| daughter | Helen R Woodward, 17, articled pupil to chartered accountants |
| domestic | **Marjorie E Slack**, 27 - later Bingham, later Barber |
| cook | Emma Radford, 76, widowed |

The index spells the maiden name **Glack**; A. Hagues read it as **Slack** from the page, and the record follows him. Both later surnames are held as aliases, so she is findable under all three.

**That leaves only schedule 193.** It is now the one Cavendish Crescent household in the record with no house against it. Do not confuse it with [[thorsmore-cavendish-crescent-north]], which is a house with no household - the opposite gap on the same street.

---

## ANSWERED - 193 is 9 Cavendish Crescent North

**Both halves of this question are now closed, and the two of them turned out to be about two different number nines.**

A. Hagues sent *9 ccn* with the schedule 254 block pasted beneath it - the same block he had sent that morning under *9 ccs*. The heading was the new thing. **254 stays at 9 Cavendish Crescent South**, where the walk keeps it, and **193 is 9 Cavendish Crescent North**.

**Three independent things say so.**

**The walk.** 191 is Hardwicke House, 192 is Haddon House, then 193, then 194 at number 7, 195 at number 5 and 196 at number 7 again - the divided house. An enumerator coming off Haddon House onto the odd side reaches **9 before 7**.

**Elimination.** A. Hagues closed 1 and 18a as blank the same evening. That left **9 as the only house on the street with nothing at all for 1939**, and 193 as the only household on the street with no house. One gap, one spare.

**His own reading of the run**, given weeks earlier: *191 Hardwick 192 Haddon 193 no number 194 & 196 7 cc 195 5* - every one of them North.

**So Miriam Raflowitch, lace manufacturer in her own right, kept house at 9 Cavendish Crescent North** with Arthur Spooner, a lace machine fitter, Ethel Spooner as housekeeper, and two domestics.

**Cavendish Crescent North is now complete for 1939** - nineteen houses, fourteen with a household and five ticked and left blank at 1, 18, 18a, 20 and Thorsmore. See [[thorsmore-cavendish-crescent-north]].

questions.title: North Lodge and the three Pelham Cottages, found and added
questions.detail:
**Both settled, 4 October 2026, on A. Hagues's identification.**

## North Lodge is 2 North Road

The house the record also holds as **The Gate House**. Schedule 203's thirteen people are filed there.

What that house became is worth recording. In 1911 and 1921 it was **Percy Lambe Huskinson's** - his wife Muriel Katherine, his brother Ernest, and three or four servants. By September 1939 it is a **boarding house of thirteen** kept by **Clara Burdett**, widow, 65, and **seven of its lodgers are government staff**. One of The Park's gate lodges had become a billet.

## The Pelham Cottages are three, on Barrack Lane

They stand between what the modern Ordnance Survey names **Hamilton Mews** and **Journey's End**, a little north-west of Hardwicke House, and the OS still shows the three small buildings numbered **1, 2 and 3** - which is the row. They are now properties **449, 450 and 451**.

| | schedule | who |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | 205 | **Florence M Onion**, widowed certified teacher, 40, with her daughters of 18 and 17 - a GPO telegraphist and a chemist's clerk |
| **2** | 206 | **Arthur William Smith**, joiner, 70, widowed - the cabinet maker the record has held since 1901 |
| **3** | 207 | **Edith Annie Hind**, 60, single, hosiery shirt machinist - in the record since 1881, aged two, as Fletcher and Sarah Hind's daughter |

Two of the three were people the record already held, which is what confirms the row: a cabinet maker and a hosiery machinist, both followed across four decades, both ending up in a cottage on Barrack Lane. The Onions were already on the lane too - Winifred Onion, insurance agent, was at 1 Barrack lane in 1921, and schedule 204, next door to these, **is** 1 Barrack lane.

**One thing still wants doing: the positions.** All three were placed by reading A. Hagues's map screenshot against Hardwicke House, so they are good to **about twenty metres** and want dragging into place on Dougal's Map.

Links: [[which-side-of-cavendish-crescent]], [[the-park-is-full-of-civil-servants-in-1939]], [[the-coords-table-is-the-map-not-the-file]].

questions.title: Charlotte Carvell was parlourmaid at Lincoln Villa in 1921 and a domestic there in 1939 - but ten years apart in age
questions.detail:
**Everything matches except the age, and the age is out by a decade.**

| | 1921 | 1939 |
|---|---|---|
| name | Charlotte Carvell (#1136) | Charlotte Carvell, later Holt |
| house | **11 Western Terrace** | **Lincoln Villa, 11 Western Terrace** |
| work | parlourmaid | domestic |
| aged | **37**, so born about 1884 | **45**, born 23 February **1894** |

The surname is uncommon, the house is the same house, the work is the same work, and the household is the same Bright family she served in 1921. One reading would make her the same woman with a decade mis-stated on one of the two returns. The other would make her two women of one uncommon name in one house eighteen years apart.

**She is entered as a new person, not bound to #1136.** The post-import checklist is explicit that a name match with a birth year badly out is how a stranger's record gets hung on somebody - the record's Robert Hutchinson was born 1831, not 1879 - and a ten-year gap is exactly that case. Better two people the page can join than one the page would have to split.

**What would settle it:** the 1921 return's own age column re-read, or a baptism for Charlotte Carvell in either 1884 or 1894.

Links: [[two-william-bells-a-draper-and-a-coachman]].

questions.title: Christabel Mary Ellis, and the cook called Barrett - both settled
questions.detail:
**Settled, 4 October 2026, by A. Hagues.**

**She is CHRISTABEL MARY ELLIS.** The record held her as *Christabel M.* from the 1901 page and the 1939 index gave her as *Mary C (Christabel)*, which had looked like a woman registered Mary Christabel. It is the other way about: the record's order was right all along and the M is Mary. She is now written out in full, with *Christabel M.* kept as an alias.

She is #4165, born **27 December 1887** - the register's own date, which is the one thing the 1939 Register does better than any census, and it replaces the 1888 the record had worked back from an age. Daughter of **Francis R. Ellis, colliery director**, of *Gardenwood, Clumber Road* in 1901. In 1939 she is 51, single, of private means, at **17 Pelham Crescent** with her widowed mother Katharine A., 81, and her sister Alice M., 52 - neither sister ever married. Her mother's and sister's exact birth dates were taken from the register at the same time.

**The cook is EMMA BARRETT.** The index wrote her *Banett*, which is not a name. She is 57, single, born 1 March 1882, and the record held no Barrett who could be her - the nearest were a commercial traveller's family at 1 Park Drive in 1891 and a housemaid at 13 Lenton Road in 1881. So she is new, under the right name, with *Banett* kept as an alias.

**One thing the household still raises:** it returns **two cooks** among five people, Emma Barrett and Ada Tongue, 54. One of the two is more likely a housekeeper the register has written down by her former place.

Links: [[jemma-m-bell-and-maria-bell]], [[frank-b-lewis-of-lenton-road]].

questions.title: Ethel Hall of Haddon House - and proof the 1939 bracket flips inside one book
questions.detail:
**Settled, 4 October 2026, by A. Hagues: Hall is the maiden name, Annison the first marriage, Marks the second.** So she was **Ethel Hall** on the night of 29 September 1939, aged 20, and the two brackets are her two later marriages in order.

## Why this row matters beyond itself

**It proves the bracket runs both ways inside a single enumerator's book.** Two rows, both RMGB, both read from the same pages:

| | the index writes | the name on the night | direction |
|---|---|---|---|
| **s198** 7 Western Terrace | Eileen **Archer (Almond)** | **Almond** - she is twelve and in her parents' Almond household, sharing her mother's birthday | surname field = LATER, bracket = register |
| **s192** Haddon House | Ethel **Hall (Annison) (Marks)** | **Hall** - her maiden name | surname field = REGISTER, brackets = later |

The two are **opposite**. A possible mechanical reason is the number of amendments - one amendment printed latest-first, two printed earliest-first - but nothing in the rows proves that, and it is not a rule to lean on.

**The working rule stays what A. Hagues has said all along: there is no rule, and each one is told.** What the record can do is check the reading against the household, which is what settled Eileen Archer at twelve and Helen U H Martlow at fourteen - neither of whom could be carrying a married name.

## The rest of the row

It was malformed two further ways. The index ran the name columns together so the **surname field was empty**, and it gave her **sex as Male** - a woman called Ethel doing domestic duties in a household of four other women. Both corrected.

She is in the record as **Ethel Hall**, born 13 December 1918, with **Annison** and **Marks** held as first and latest married names.

Links: [[the-1939-bracket-has-no-rule]], [[irene-doris-horney-or-roe]].

questions.title: Samuel R Trotman of 3 Pelham Crescent was the City Analyst - when, and for how long?
questions.detail:
**A public office the record has never held before.** The 1939 Register returns him at **3 Pelham Crescent**, aged 70, as *City Analyst Retired*, born 21 March 1869.

The **City Analyst** is not a job title but an appointment. Under the Sale of Food and Drugs Acts a corporation had to appoint a public analyst, and he was the chemist it trusted with its food, its milk, its water and its poisons - the man whose certificate convicted a dairyman for watering milk or a grocer for adulterating tea. In a city the size of Nottingham it was a position of standing.

**The record held no Trotman at all** before this round, so everything about him is open: when he was appointed, how long he served, and whether he is the Trotman of any published analysis.

In the house with him are his wife **Mary G**, 64, his son **John**, 31, a supervisor at a tobacco works - returned married, though no wife is with him - and a cook, Elizabeth Martin, 44.

**What would settle it:** Nottingham corporation minutes or the city's annual reports, which name the public analyst year by year; the Nottingham press, where an analyst's prosecutions were reported; and Wright's Directory, which lists corporation officers.

**He may belong on Notable Residents.** Twelve people carry that mark. A city's public analyst is at least as much a public figure as a city architect, and the page already holds one of those.

Links: [[the-park-is-full-of-civil-servants-in-1939]].

questions.title: Albert Ball VC was holding his father's census records
questions.detail:
**Found and put right, 4 October 2026, while checking a Ball in another household.**

Record #469 carried the flying ace's dates and his Wikipedia article - **born 14 August 1896, killed 7 May 1917** - and two census rows that cannot be his:

| round | aged | at | trade |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1911 | **47** | 43 Lenton Road | Real Estate and landagent |
| 1921 | **58** | 43 Lenton Road | Land Agent |

A boy born in 1896 is fourteen in 1911, not forty-seven, and was two years dead by 1921. Those rows are his **father's** - Albert Ball the elder, land agent, born about 1863 by both ages. He is now **#9065** and holds them.

#469 keeps the ace's dates and his article, and ends with **no census row at all** - which is right. He is in neither return: fourteen and away in 1911, dead by 1921. The record's only trace of him is the house he grew up in.

**His mother was in twice as well.** The wife of 43 Lenton Road is **Harvell Mary Ball**, 46, in 1911 and **Mary Harriett**, 57, in 1921 - the second with her forenames run into the name columns so that *Harriett* became her surname. *Harvell* is not a name, and the 1921 row supplies what it should be. The two are joined as **Harriett Mary Ball**, with both old forms kept as aliases. Their daughter **Lois Beatrice**, 19 in 1911, was already right.

**What is still open:** the elder Albert Ball's own dates and the offices he held. The record holds neither, and has no source for them.

Links: [[two-william-bells-a-draper-and-a-coachman]].

questions.title: Anna E Hirschfield, refugee, at Felixstowe - the first the record has
questions.detail:
**The 1939 Register carried a field for what it called special interest groups, and hers reads REFUGEE.** She is the first person in this record to carry it.

**Anna E Hirschfield**, born 22 November 1876, widowed, 62, at **Felixstowe, Clumber Road West**. Her occupation is written *No Occupation - Refugee*. Her line is RG101/6178A, item 21, line 24. The page spells the address *Felexdive Chamber Road*.

**She had a schedule of her own - number 223** - in a house whose other household, schedule 224, is Helena G Firth's with a cook, a parlourmaid and a housemaid. So she was not a servant and not a guest counted with the family: the register treated her as a household in her own right, lodging in part of the house.

The register was taken on **29 September 1939, three weeks after war was declared**.

**Nothing else about her is known to the record** - not where she came from, when she arrived, nor whether she stayed. Her surname is one commonly borne by Jewish families of Germany and Austria, and The Park already held the **Weinbergs** of Hardwicke House and the **Flersheims** of 13 Pelham Crescent, but the record cannot say she was connected to either.

**What would settle it:** the Nottingham refugee committee's papers; the alien registration cards at The National Archives, which survive for a sample; the Nottingham press for 1938 and 1939; and the rest of the RMGB book, since a household taking in one refugee often took in more.

**And a thing to watch for as the round goes on:** whether any other RMGB household carries the same flag. If The Park was taking in refugees in 1939 it would sit beside what this record already shows of government staff billeted on the estate that same month.

Links: [[the-park-is-full-of-civil-servants-in-1939]].

questions.title: Stowe House is 6 Maxtoke Road - found by the family who owned it
questions.detail:
**Answered, 4 October 2026.** An account A. Hagues supplied names the **Hesse family** as former owners of Stowe House and describes its 1911 household: **Marie Hesse, a naturalised Belgian widow of 60**, her lady's companion **May Reid**, a cook of 29 and a housemaid of 17.

**That is 6 Maxtoke Road's 1911 return, exactly** - Marie Augustine Hesse, 60, head; May Catherine Reid, lady's companion; Gertrude Whittaker, 29, cook; Emily Julia Whitehead, 17, housemaid.

**And the map agrees.** 6 Maxtoke Road stands about a hundred metres from **Felixstowe** and **Holly Lodge**, which are schedules 222, 223 and 224 of the RMGB book - exactly where the walk put schedule 225.

So the house is renamed **Stowe House, 6 Maxtoke Road**, and the 1939 household is filed in it: **Arthur C Ball**, managing director; his wife **Doris M**; **Joan M Ball, 18, a V.A.D. at a general hospital**; a nurse and domestic; a cook whose forename the index cannot read; and a sixth line the register keeps closed.

## The house now runs 1881 to 1939

| round | who |
|---|---|
| 1881 | **Adolph Hesse**, manager of a lace warehouse, his wife Marie, their baby son Frederick, three servants |
| 1911 | **Marie**, widowed, with her companion and two servants |
| 1921 | Marie at 70, her companion of twenty years, a housemaid |
| 1939 | the **Ball** family |

## And the Hesses are joined up

Marie was in the record **twice** - as *Marie A Hesse* for 1871 and 1881 and as *Marie Augustine Hesse* for 1911 and 1921. Joined, so she now runs from twenty years old to seventy in one house.

The account also gives what no census could: **Adolph died in November 1905**; their son **Frederick died at fifteen**, about 1896; and in his memory they founded the **Frederick Hesse Endowment Fund**, of which some **£38,700** went to the **Nottingham Children's Hospital** - a sum its reports were still naming in the mid-1930s, forty years after the boy died. All three now carry lives written from it.

**The account names no author and is not A. Hagues's own writing**, which their source lines say.

Links: [[north-lodge-and-pelham-cottage-are-not-in-the-record]], [[the-park-at-war-september-1939]].

questions.title: The Park three weeks into the war - volunteers, a refugee, and departments billeted on the estate
questions.detail:
**The 1939 Register was taken on 29 September 1939, twenty-six days after war was declared, and this round of the RMGB book keeps catching it.** Four separate things, none of which the record held before.

## Women volunteering

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| **Joan M Ball**, 18 | **V.A.D. at a general hospital** | Stowe House. A Voluntary Aid Detachment nurse, and she had turned eighteen five weeks before the register was taken |
| **Joyce M Crane**, 24 | **British Red Cross volunteer** | 5 Clumber Crescent South |
| **Irene Medd**, 23 | **casualty ambulance driver** | 11 Hope Drive. Born 29 February 1916, so she had had five birthdays |

**Three** of them now, and the third is from the other book - the RMGC side of Hope Drive. Two are daughters of the house; Irene Medd lodges in a shared house with a tailor's cutter, a typewriter mechanic and a dressmaker of 64. None existed in this record before, and no other round of it holds a V.A.D., a Red Cross volunteer or an ambulance driver at all.

**And the third one matters for a different reason:** it is in the **RMGC** book, where the first two were RMGB. So this is not one enumerator noticing something. It is the estate.

## A refugee

**Anna E Hirschfield**, 62, widowed, alone at **Felixstowe, Clumber Road West** with a schedule to herself - occupation *No Occupation - Refugee*, and the register's own flag, *Special interest groups: Refugee*. The first person in this record so marked. See [[a-refugee-at-felixstowe-in-september-1939]].

## Government staff billeted on the estate

Twelve civil servants in two boarding houses - five at **19 Pelham Crescent** and seven at **North Lodge**, including a tax inspector, a Ministry of Labour officer, an Inland Revenue senior staff officer and a Home Office laboratory student. See [[the-park-is-full-of-civil-servants-in-1939]].

## And a man who had already been to one war

The same estate had sent **Albert Ball VC** from 43 Lenton Road, dead at 20 in 1917. See [[albert-ball-vc-was-holding-his-fathers-census-records]].

**What would settle the shape of it:** the Nottingham press for September and October 1939; the Red Cross and St John V.A.D. service records, which survive and are indexed by name; and the rest of the RMGB and RMGC books, which between them cover the whole estate. **Four finds in one book is a pattern worth testing against the other.**

Links: [[every-census-gap-and-where-to-start]].

questions.title: Sir Jesse Hind and Dame Lilian kept Newcastle Court in 1939
questions.detail:
**Answered the same day it was asked.** The page was headed **207**, and 207 is the **property number** - **Newcastle Court, Newcastle Circus** - not a house number on a street, which is what it had been read as. A. Hagues uses the same shorthand elsewhere; North Lodge was given as *228*.

**Sir Jesse Hind**, solicitor, 73, and **Dame Lilian Frances Hind**, 70, of private means. They kept **39 Newcastle Drive** in 1921 with five servants, and by 1939 had moved to Newcastle Court - a house that suits them: Charles Wilfred Birkin, lace manufacturer, kept it in 1901 with **seven servants**, and before him Elizabeth Lynam, widow, through 1881 and 1891.

They have **six domestics**, the largest staff in this stretch of the walk, and **four of the six are teenagers**: Ada Burton and Mary Newton at 17, Edith Newton and Kathleen M Crookes at **15**. Edith and Mary share a surname and are nineteen months apart, so most likely sisters. Mildred I Smith, the eldest at 62, turned 62 on the very morning the register was taken.

**Both titles are new to the record**, which had held them untitled from the 1921 round. When he was knighted, and for what, the record still does not say - a Nottingham solicitor's knighthood would be in the Gazette, and he is worth testing against Notable Residents.

Links: [[samuel-r-trotman-city-analyst]], [[the-park-at-war-september-1939]].

questions.title: Nine continental names in The Park in September 1939 - how many were refugees?
questions.detail:
**The register flags only one of them, and that is the question.**

Anna E Hirschfield at Felixstowe carries the 1939 Register's own marker - *Special interest groups: **Refugee***, occupation *No Occupation - Refugee*. She is the only person in this record so flagged. But the same round holds eight more people whose names are not English:

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| **Anna E Hirschfield**, 62, widow | Felixstowe, Clumber Road West | ***flagged refugee***, a schedule to herself |
| **Hans Fischer**, 56 | 39 Newcastle Drive | managing director |
| **Horst W Fischer**, 20 | 39 Newcastle Drive | clerk at a silk works |
| **Mariaon Alice Fischer**, 19 | 39 Newcastle Drive | unpaid domestic duties |
| **Marion Rhea Portalski**, 19 | 39 Newcastle Drive | unpaid domestic duties |
| **Ernst Zuckermann** | 12 The Ropewalk | **medical practitioner** |
| **Sibylle Zuckermann** | 12 The Ropewalk | unpaid domestic duties |
| **Maria Stepkova**, 38 | 2 Newcastle Circus | domestic |

**Three separate shapes, and each is a known way out of Europe.** A whole family at one address with a German forename for the son, *Horst*. A doctor and his wife - **continental physicians were admitted to Britain in numbers after 1933**, and a medical practitioner in lodgings on The Ropewalk fits that. And a single woman in domestic service with a **Czech** surname in its feminine form, six months after Germany took Czechoslovakia - **the domestic service visa was the commonest route out for women**, and Britain issued thousands.

The Weinbergs of Hardwicke House are a different case: the record holds them from 1911, so they were settled here long before.

**What would settle it:** the alien registration cards at The National Archives, which survive as a sample and name the holder's nationality and arrival; the Nottingham refugee committee's papers; and the 1939 Register's own flag on the rest of the estate - **the RMGC book has not been read for it**. If more of these households carry it, The Park was taking in refugees in numbers, and that sits beside what this round already shows of civil servants billeted here and women volunteering.

Links: [[the-park-at-war-september-1939]], [[a-refugee-at-felixstowe-in-september-1939]].

questions.title: Nine houses are marked empty in 1939 on a note that gives no evidence - and one of them was wrong
questions.detail:
**The record says nobody was in these houses on 29 September 1939, and for nine of them it does not say how it knows.**

A good unoccupied note cites the page: *"20 Hope Drive, schedule 103 - the Register marks it empty"*, or *"3 Western Terrace, schedule 4, the third of three empty in a row before 4 Western Terrace"*. Those name a schedule, so they can be checked.

These nine say only **"1939 census"** or **"1939 Census records show"**:

| house | |
|---|---|
| 5 Cavendish Crescent South | |
| 7 Cavendish Crescent South | |
| 7 Clumber Crescent South | |
| 15 Lenton Avenue | |
| Dundee House, 17 Lenton Avenue | |
| 19 Lenton Avenue | |
| 23 Lenton Avenue | |
| 10 Pelham Crescent | |
| 11 Pelham Crescent | |

**A tenth was found wrong on 4 October 2026.** *21 Lenton Avenue* carried the same stub - and the record holds **schedule 176** there: Wilfred H Wilson, managing director of a bleaching and finishing works, with an assistant manager, a cook, a parlourmaid and a butler, five people fully sourced to RG101/6178A. The mark was removed.

**That one error is the reason to doubt the other nine.** A stub note cannot be told apart from a guess.

**Two of them bear on an open question.** If **5** and **7 Cavendish Crescent South** really were empty, that is quiet support for schedules 195 and 196 belonging to the **North** side, which is where A. Hagues placed them - and so for schedule 193 and schedule 254 both being North too. If the marks are wrong, that support falls away.

**What would settle it:** the RMGB and RMGC pages for those streets. An empty house is not missing from the Register - it is written in and ticked, with a schedule number of its own - so each of these nine either has a ticked blank schedule or it has a household nobody has read yet.

Links: [[which-side-of-cavendish-crescent]].

questions.title: Ferndene is filed on Hamilton Drive, and two things say it is on Peveril Drive
questions.detail:
**The record holds it as property 298, *Ferndene, Hamilton Drive*. Both pieces of 1939 evidence put it on Peveril Drive.**

**The index says so.** A. Hagues's full index of Peveril Drive for 1939 lists twenty-one heads, and *Frederick May, **Ferndene*** is one of them. The same list gives **Kenilworth House** and **The Chestnuts** under Peveril Drive too, though the record has both on Kenilworth Road - so the index is naming houses by the drive they face.

**The schedule run says so, and more strongly.** Ferndene is **schedule 123**, and it sits inside an unbroken Peveril Drive stretch:

| | |
|---|---|
| s117 | 6 Peveril Drive |
| s118, 120, 121, 122 | Peveril Drive, no number given |
| **s123** | **Ferndene** |
| s125, 126, 127 | Peveril Drive, no number given |
| s128 | Eskdale, Peveril Drive |
| s130 | Parkdale, Peveril Drive |

An enumerator does not step off a street for one house and back again. **Ferndene is between number 6 and Eskdale.**

**What this does not settle** is whether the house should be re-addressed or whether it stands on a corner and was always known both ways - which is what Kenilworth House and The Chestnuts appear to do. **Changing a property's street is a decision for A. Hagues**, because the map draws from the file.

**And it bears on the two schedules numbered 123.** The record holds schedule 123 twice: Ferndene, and 11 Lenton Avenue. If Ferndene belongs on Peveril Drive then the two are certainly different houses in different stretches of one book, which is what the two-books-one-number problem looks like from the inside.

Links: [[the-seven-unnumbered-peveril-drive-schedules]].

questions.title: Nine Peveril Drive households with no house, and eight houses in that book
questions.detail:
**The run is now unbroken from schedule 114 to 130, and the arithmetic no longer closes - there is one household more than there are houses.**

## The run

| schedule | house | head |
|---|---|---|
| 114 | 1 Peveril Drive | Wilfred Spiers |
| 115 | 2 | Florence Lewin |
| 116 | 3 | Albert E Tarr |
| 117 | 6 | Kitty Poole |
| **118** | — | Daniel J Hunter |
| **119** | — | **ABSENT** - the Register records the household away on the night |
| **120** | — | L D V Smith |
| **121** | — | Edward A Jennings |
| **122** | — | James McCoy |
| 123 | **Ferndene** | Frederick May |
| **124** | — | **Lilian A Butler**, 38, married - the rest of the household is closed |
| **125** | — | John R Jacques |
| **126** | — | Florence Jennison |
| **127** | — | Edwin E Shaw |
| 128 | Eskdale | Edwin A Polley |
| **129** | — | **Ada Vaugham**, 83, widow |
| 130 | Parkdale | Gertrude Farmer |

## What does not fit

**Nine schedules need a house** - 118, 119, 120, 121, 122, 124, 125, 126, 127 and 129, of which 119 is ABSENT rather than a household, so nine households and one empty house.

**And the street is split between two books, which is what makes the counting hard.** 2a Peveril Drive is **schedule 62 of the RMGC book**, not part of this run at all - Chrristopher Burton, master tailor, who had 3 Peveril Drive in 1911 and 2a in 1921. **1a Peveril Drive is schedule 61 of the same book**, and **33 Peveril** is schedule 50 of it. So RMGC holds at least three addresses on this drive while RMGB walks 1, 2, 3, 6, Ferndene, Eskdale and Parkdale.

**That leaves eight houses for the nine unhoused RMGB schedules**: 4, 5, 7, 8, 10, 11, 12 and Peveril House. Nine into eight.

One of the nine must be **sharing a house**, which this round has seen twice - **7 Cavendish Crescent North** holds two households and **33 Lenton Avenue** holds five. **Or there is another Peveril Drive address the property list has not got**, as 1a was until 4 October 2026.

**What would settle it:** the address column on schedules 118 to 129, or Wright's Directory for the late 1930s under Peveril Drive, which prints occupiers against numbers.

Links: [[is-ferndene-on-peveril-drive-not-hamilton-drive]].

questions.title: Hope Drive in 1939 - ordnance men, pile drivers and a boarding house of thirteen
questions.detail:
**Hope Drive is the first street the record holds complete for 1939, and finishing it changed what the war looks like on this estate.** Until now the war showed in the big houses - civil servants billeted in guest houses, a refugee lodging at Felixstowe. Hope Drive shows it in the lodgings.

## 15 Hope Drive - three Royal Ordnance Factory men

Schedule 71 is **Ida Limb's lodging house**, and three of its men are ROF:

| | |
|---|---|
| **Leslie A Howe**, 46 | **progressman**, Royal Ordnance Factory - the man who chased work through a factory to keep it to time |
| **James Mahon**, 38 | electrical and mechanical engineer, representative, ROF |
| **James Booth** | the same words again, and the index gives him **no birth date at all** |

Mahon and Booth are returned in almost identical words, so the two were sent here together. The record already held eight others on ordnance work in this round - on Hamilton Drive, Hope Drive, Lenton Avenue and Peveril Drive - which makes **eleven**.

## 21 Hope Drive - a boarding house of thirteen, four of them pile drivers

Florence M Simpson keeps it. **Edward Birch, Arthur J Hutchins, George T Lisney and Charles Martin are all returned *piling winchman***, men who drove piles working a winch. Four of one trade under one roof in September 1939 is a gang, and a gang of pile drivers that month was putting in foundations for something. A **Ministry of Mines** clerk lodges with them, and an electrician, a joiner and a sign writer.

That is the **third boarding house** this round has turned up whose lodgers are in war work, after 19 Pelham Crescent and North Lodge.

## And a casualty ambulance driver at number 11

**Irene Medd**, 23, in a shared house with a tailor's cutter, a typewriter mechanic and a dressmaker of 64. See [[the-park-at-war-september-1939]].

**What would settle what they were building:** the Nottingham press for September and October 1939, and the Royal Ordnance Factory records. ROF Nottingham was at Kings Meadow; the Central Ordnance Depot at Chilwell is already named in this round, on a Peveril Drive man's entry. **Four pile drivers lodging together names a site, if the site can be found.**

Links: [[the-park-at-war-september-1939]], [[the-park-is-full-of-civil-servants-in-1939]].

questions.title: The Park was enumerated across at least THREE books in 1939, on two different pieces
questions.detail:
**Until 4 October 2026 the record's whole 1939 round came from one piece: RG101/6178A, under the letter codes RMGB and RMGC.** Two houses on Barrack Lane have now come in from a third book, and it is not even on the same piece.

| book | piece | what the record holds |
|---|---|---|
| **RMGB** | RG101/6178A | 132 schedules, 80 to 257 |
| **RMGC** | RG101/6178A | 178 schedules, 5 to 236 |
| **RMGA** | **RG101/6177J** | **2 schedules, 25 and 26** |

Rockville and Rock House, both Barrack Lane. Gertrude L Ford's line is RG101/**6177J**/003/25.

**What that means for the work.** A third district covering part of the estate has barely been looked at, and because it is on another piece it would not turn up in any search of 6178A. The 72 houses the record still has no 1939 round for are therefore not all waiting on the two known books - **some number of them are in RMGA**, and Barrack Lane is where its two known schedules fall.

Barrack Lane is also the street with the most houses still missing: **15 of the 72**. That is unlikely to be a coincidence. If RMGA is the Barrack Lane book, reading it would close the single biggest hole in the 1939 round at a stroke.

**And a fourth may exist.** RMGA, RMGB, RMGC is a sequence, and nothing says it stops at C.

**What would settle it:** the ED description for RMGA, which lists the streets each enumerator walked, and the piece list for RG101/6177J. Both are at The National Archives and both are indexed.

Links: [[which-side-of-cavendish-crescent]], [[the-park-at-war-september-1939]].

## And the books run past the estate boundary

**A page of one of these books can hold streets that are not The Park at all.** On 4 October 2026 a fragment turned up carrying *Goldschmid, Emil, manufacturers agent, born 28 July 1872* - a name that looked like the **Goldschmidts of 13 Pelham Crescent**, the German-born Alderman Edward Goldschmidt's family, whom the record follows from 1871 to 1901 and who have no son in it. He was on **Castle Boulevard**, outside the estate, and A. Hagues said so before anything was written down.

**That is a caution for the walk.** Reading a house's street off the schedules either side of it has settled several addresses in this round - Ferndene on Peveril Drive, Bancroft on Barrack Lane, 5 Clumber Crescent South - and it works because an enumerator walks a street at a time. But it stops working at the edge of the estate, where the same walk carries on into roads the record does not hold. **A schedule number alone never proves a household belongs here.**

The same lesson was learnt once before, when eighteen people on **Standard Hill** had to be taken out again.

questions.title: Two properties both claim 159 Derby Road, and one of them has never held anybody
questions.detail:
**The record holds 159 Derby Road twice over.**

| | address as the file writes it | what it has ever held |
|---|---|---|
| **prop 98** | *159 Derby Road (2 Derby Terrace)* | 1871, 1881, 1921 **and 1939** - twenty people in 1871, seven in 1939 |
| **prop 93** | *159 - 161 Derby Road* | **nothing, in any round** |

Prop 98 is the real house, and the Derby Terrace numbering proves its address: the terrace runs 2 to 9 against Derby Road 159 down to 145, and every one of those is in the record - 157 is 3 Derby Terrace, 155 is 4, and so on. So **159 Derby Road is 2 Derby Terrace**, and prop 93 is a shell that duplicates it and claims 161 besides.

**It came up on 4 October 2026** when A. Hagues reported 159, 161, 163, 165 and 167 Derby Road all empty in 1939. Of those five the record holds only 159 - and 159 **is not empty**: it holds **schedule 203 of the RMGC book**, seven people, Myra Witherspoon's boarding house, which is itself one of the war households this round keeps finding:

> a **gun fitter, R.A.F.**; a **Second Lieutenant of 112 Light Anti-Aircraft Battery, R.A.**; two structural-engineering draughtsmen; a customs and excise civil servant; and a solicitor's articled clerk.

**161, 163, 165 and 167 are not in the property list at all**, so there was nothing to mark empty.

**What would settle it:** whether 161 Derby Road is a separate house that should be added, or whether prop 93 is a mis-entry that should go. The Ordnance Survey and Wright's Directory under Derby Road would show how far the Derby Terrace run goes and what stands beyond it. **Removing a property is A. Hagues's call.**

Links: [[the-park-at-war-september-1939]].

questions.title: A BBC orchestral conductor and a singer, lodging on Barrack Lane in September 1939
questions.detail:
**Eric H Warr, 34, is returned *Orchestral Conductor Music Staff BBC*, and his wife Viola G, 33, is returned *Singer*.** They are at **4 Barrack Lane**, schedule 20 of the RMGA book.

**They are the first people in this record's whole 1939 round in music or broadcasting of any kind.** The trade columns hold no other conductor, no musician, no singer, nobody from the BBC.

**Why that is more than a curiosity.** This round keeps finding people dispersed out of London at the outbreak of war and lodged on this estate:

| | |
|---|---|
| twelve **civil servants** | in two boarding houses - 19 Pelham Crescent and North Lodge |
| a **Ministry of Supply** timber officer | 9 Cavendish Crescent |
| a **Ministry of Mines** clerk | 21 Hope Drive |
| eleven **Royal Ordnance Factory** workers | across five streets |
| a **Second Lieutenant, 112 Light A.A. Battery** and a **gun fitter R.A.F.** | 159 Derby Road |

**The BBC dispersed too.** Its departments were moved out of London from September 1939 - variety to Bristol, other services elsewhere - and a conductor on its music staff lodging in a rented house in Nottingham that month is the same shape of fact as the civil servants.

**What would settle it:** BBC staff records and the BBC Written Archives at Caversham, which hold wartime department movements; the Radio Times for late 1939, which names conductors and orchestras by place; and the Nottingham press. **If the BBC put an orchestra or a music department in or near Nottingham, Eric and Viola Warr are the evidence of it, and there will be more of them in the rest of the RMGA book.**

**And in the same household:** Sylvia J, 17, in domestic service, given as *Wooley (Woyciehouski)* - a Polish name, Wojciechowski. Poland was invaded on 1 September 1939, twenty-eight days before the register was taken. The record cannot say whether the two facts are connected, and she is entered under the Polish spelling with the anglicised form held beside it so neither is lost.

Links: [[the-park-at-war-september-1939]], [[continental-names-in-the-park-in-1939]], [[the-park-was-enumerated-across-three-books-in-1939]].

questions.title: Barrack Lane in 1939 is complete - and the ninth address was the empty one
questions.detail:
**Answered the same day, 4 October 2026.** The count was one short because an **empty house is still an address**.

A. Hagues's search of the 1939 Register returns **nine Barrack Lane addresses in piece RG101/6177**, and the record held eight households. The street list names all nine:

| head | house |
|---|---|
| Ethel E Woollatt | "Bancroft" |
| Gertrude L Ford | "Rock House" |
| Harry Smith | "Rockville" |
| Emma Mee | Cottage |
| Alice L Fitzhugh | 4 |
| **— none —** | **6** |
| John H Clarke | 8 |
| George F Houston | 10 |
| George Lynch | 12 |

**The ninth is number 6, listed with no head** - the house A. Hagues had already read as empty and the record had already marked so. Eight households and one empty house make nine addresses, and Barrack Lane is complete for 1939.

**That is the whole point of the unoccupied table put plainly.** An empty house is not missing from a census: it is written in and ticked, with a schedule number and a line of its own. The record now says so in step 1.4 of the post-import checklist, and this is the proof.

## One disagreement left, and it is a name

The index renders the head of **10 Barrack Lane** two ways: **Houfton** on the household page, which is what A. Hagues sent and what the record holds, and **HOUSTON** on this street list. The two differ only by a long s read as an f. Houfton is kept, because the household page is the fuller source and because Houfton is a Nottinghamshire name - Percy Houfton the architect was one - with Houston held as an alias. **The page itself would settle it.**

## And the rest of the lane is closed

Thirteen Barrack Lane properties the record holds have **no 1939 round and never will**: the Register does not list them, so they were not separate dwellings that year. 2, 3, 8a, 14, 16, 18, 20, 22, 24, 26, 28, 30 and Barrack Yard, each with a note saying why.

Links: [[the-park-was-enumerated-across-three-books-in-1939]], [[nine-houses-marked-empty-in-1939-on-a-stub-note]].

questions.title: Which 1939 book covers Fish Pond Drive? Its schedule numbers are taken by two others
questions.detail:
**Four Fish Pond Drive households are in the record and only one of them can name its book.**

| house | schedule | book | |
|---|---|---|---|
| **11a** | 269 | **RMGB**, RG101/6178A | the page gives the code in full, and it pushes RMGB's known range from 257 to 269 |
| **4** | 77 | **not known** | RMGC's schedule 77 is *4 Clare Valley* |
| **6** | 78 | **not known** | RMGC's schedule 78 is *3 Clare Valley*, ticked and left blank |
| **2** | 26 | **not known** | RMGC's 26 is *Castle Rising, 3 Lenton Road*; **RMGA's 26 is *Rock House, Barrack Lane*** |

**Schedule 26 is used by three books at once**, which is the clearest statement yet of what the two-books-one-number problem really is - it was never only two.

**And the numbers do not sit together.** Number 2 is schedule 26, numbers 4 and 6 are 77 and 78, and 11a is 269. An enumerator walks a street at a time, so 4 and 6 belong together and 2 does not belong with them, nor 11a with any of them. **Fish Pond Drive is split across at least two books and possibly three.**

The three unnamed households are entered **with the book left unstated** rather than guessed at. The record was bitten once on 4 October 2026, when Bancroft went in under RMGC and turned out to be RMGA - and a schedule number means nothing without the book it belongs to.

**What would settle it:** the ED letter code on the pages for schedules 26, 77 and 78, which the full record view gives, as it did for 11a. One look at any of them names the book.

Links: [[the-park-was-enumerated-across-three-books-in-1939]].

questions.title: George Philip Dunn was born in 1878 - and the correction found a second man of his name
questions.detail:
**Settled, 4 October 2026, by A. Hagues from the page: 1878.**

The record had him at **4 Park Drive**, schedule 25 of the 1939 Register, born **14 September 1888** and aged **51**, returned *Inspector, Board of Education, retired*. The day and month were right and the decade was not. He is born **14 September 1878** and was **61** when the register was taken.

**The trade was what flagged it.** A Board of Education inspector retired at 51 is early; at 61 it is ordinary. The record's age of 51 was self-consistent with its own wrong birth year, so nothing internal would ever have caught it - only reading the page against the occupation did.

**That is worth remembering as a check**: where a person is returned *retired* and the age looks young for it, the birth year is worth a second look. His wife Winifred, born 7 November 1891 and aged 47, was right either way and is untouched.

## And the correction exposed a second man of the same name

Putting the year right made an older row impossible. The record had an **1891 row aged 3** on his record - and a man born in 1878 was **twelve** in 1891, not three.

That row belongs to a different George Philip Dunn: the son of **George Dunn, coachman**, and Maryann, of Lenton Avenue, returned at 3 with his baby sister Hilda. A coachman's son born about 1888 is not the Inspector of the Board of Education born in 1878, and the two were being held as one person.

The coachman's son is now his own record and keeps the 1891 row. The inspector keeps 1939 and **the record holds nothing of him before it**.

**This is the third conflation of the day found the same way** - a person whose two rows cannot both describe one life. The others were **Albert Ball VC** carrying his father's census rows, and **William Bell**, a draper of 41 in 1881 who was a coachman of 40 in 1891.

Links: [[three-bernard-wrights-and-a-family-held-six-ways]].

questions.title: Three Bernard Wrights in 1939 - two of them father and son, and three of the family held twice
questions.detail:
**A. Hagues warned on 4 October 2026 that the 1939 round holds three different Bernard Wrights, and it does.** Checking the warning showed that two of the three are **father and son**, and that the record was holding three members of one family twice over.

| | aged | where | trade |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Bernard Swanwick Wright** | 63 | Haddon House | solicitor and colliery director |
| **Bernard Joseph Maxwell Wright** | 34 | 2 Park Drive | solicitor - **his son** |
| **Bernard Wright** | 25 | 21 Lenton Avenue | **butler** - no relation |

## What joined them
