**24 Barrack Lane in 1911** held the whole family: Bernard Swanwick Wright, his wife **Florence Mary**, his daughter **Kathleen Florence** and his son **Bernard Joseph Maxwell**, with three servants. By 1921 they were at Haddon House.

## Three folded

| held twice | and as |
|---|---|
| *Bernard John Wright*, solicitor at 2 Park Drive | **Bernard Joseph Maxwell Wright** - the index's *Bernard J M* is what names him |
| *Florence M Wright*, entered as new at Haddon House | **Florence Mary Wright**, in the record from 1901 |
| *Margaret Edn Wright* | **Margaret Edna Fraxer**, same birth date, same schedule, same house |

The family now runs **1901 to 1939** unbroken: 24 Barrack Lane, then Haddon House, with the son keeping his own house at 2 Park Drive and practising his father's profession.

**And the warning stands.** The butler of 21 Lenton Avenue is nobody's kin, and the duplicate checks must not be let near him: born 1914, where the other two are 1876 and 1905.

Links: [[two-william-bells-a-draper-and-a-coachman]].

questions.title: Ethel M at 8 Park Drive is entered as Edward, and the household says Howitt
questions.detail:
**She is 27, single, and living with John Arthur Howitt, his wife Sybil and their son John Kenneth.** The index gives her as **Edward (Howitt)**, and the record entered her under *Edward* with *Howitt* as the 1939 amendment.

**Every household this round has settled on its own evidence points the other way.** A single woman in her family's house bore the family's name on the night:

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| Eileen **Archer (Almond)** | 12, in her parents' house | **Almond** on the night |
| Helen U H **Martlow (Yeomans)** | 14, her father's house | **Yeomans** |
| Barbara Rona **Tippett (Sherwin)** | 8 | **Sherwin** |
| Ruby **Limb (Cooper)** | 14 | **Limb** - but there the bracket was the LATER name |
| Irene Doris **Horney (Roe)** | 35, her brother's house | **Roe** - corrected on A. Hagues's word |

So Ethel M was most likely **Howitt** on the night, and Edward the name she came to later. **But the register has no rule** - Ruby Limb's page runs the other way round - and this household was entered earlier on A. Hagues's own reading, so it is flagged rather than turned round.

**The same question applies to the two servants** in that house, though less sharply, because neither is kin to the Howitts: **Amy M Oakland (Jenkins)** and **Alice James (Mees)**, both single, are entered under the surname in front.

**One word settles all three**, and the aliases are already held either way.

**Filled in at the same time**, from A. Hagues: John Arthur Howitt was born 12 March 1885 and is 54, a **printer** - while his son John Kenneth is a **master** printer at 28, so the son held the higher standing in the trade. And Francis O Wardle, whose entry had only a year, was born 11 April 1898 and is 41; *Francis* for a woman is most likely Frances.

Links: [[the-1939-bracket-has-no-rule]], [[irene-doris-horney-or-roe]].

questions.title: ANSWERED - Louisa M Riley was at Castlethorpe
questions.detail:
**The Register's street list for Newcastle Circus shows three households in piece 6178, and two of the three are now placed.**

| head | house the Register gives | where the record puts it |
|---|---|---|
| **Sir Jessie Hind** | **The Elms** | **Newcastle Court** - whose history in this record says it was *"formerly known as 'The Elms'"* |
| **John C Wright** | **2** | 2 Newcastle Circus |
| **Louisa M Riley** | *— none given —* | **still unfiled** |

**That leaves exactly two houses.** Newcastle Circus holds five properties in the record. Mevell House has its own 1939 household at schedule 20 of another book; Newcastle Court and number 2 are now taken. So Louisa M Riley is at **Burton House** or **Castlethorpe**, and nothing else is available.

Her household is schedule 248: herself at 66, a widow on private means, with what reads as her daughter's family - **Winifred H L Grey**, 38, her husband **Malcolm R**, a wages costing clerk, and their daughters of 18 and 15 - and **May Beecroft**, 46, the servant.

**What is known of the two candidates:**

| | 1921 | |
|---|---|---|
| **Burton House** | **Edgar Lyon Paget**, a manager for W. Hollins & Co, spinners and manufacturers | detached house of about 1875, possibly by George Hine, now flats |
| **Castlethorpe** | the record holds no head for it | detached house of about 1875, possibly by George Hine, now flats |

**What would settle it:** the address column on schedule 248, or Wright's Directory for the late 1930s under Newcastle Circus - two named houses and one surname is a short search.

**And the Hind house is now doubly confirmed.** A. Hagues gave it as property 207, which is Newcastle Court; the Register calls it The Elms; and the record's own account of the house says those are one place. The two agree without either having been made to.

Links: [[where-did-sir-jesse-hind-live-in-1939]].

---

## 5 October 2026 - narrowed to two, and neither will budge

**A. Hagues has confirmed that Burton House and Castlethorpe are the only two still open on the street, with one household to place between them.** Newcastle Circus now stands: 2 Newcastle Circus at schedule 249, Mevell House at 20 of RMGC, Newcastle Court at 245, and these two with nothing.

**Three ways of deciding it were tried and all three failed.**

**The walk.** 245 is Newcastle Court, 246 and 247 go off to Lincoln Circus, 248 is the household in question and 249 is 2 Newcastle Circus. The enumerator leaves the street and comes back, so the order says only that 248 is reached before number 2.

**The ground.** From 2 Newcastle Circus it is **49 metres to Burton House and 51 to Castlethorpe** - a two-metre difference, which decides nothing. Lincoln House and The Cottage both sit at rounded placeholder coordinates, so distances from them are worth less still.

**The households.** Neither house holds a Riley, a Grey or a Beecroft in any earlier round. Burton House ran John Watson in 1881, the Ransoms in 1911 and the Pagets in 1921. Castlethorpe ran the Brownswords from 1881 to 1891, Herbert Francis Lancashire in 1911, and in **1921 three servants and no family at all** - Selina James, Emma Griggs and Bessie Louisa Abrey, which is a house being kept up for an absent owner.

**The household to place** is Louisa M Riley, 66 and widowed, on private means, with the Grey family of four - Winifred, Malcolm a wages costing clerk, and two daughters - and May Beecroft, a domestic servant of 46. A widow with private means and a married daughter's family under her roof.

**What would settle it:** the house column on the page for schedule 248, a probate or directory entry for Louisa M Riley in the 1940s, or the 1939 entry for whichever of the two houses stood empty - because the one that is not hers must be ticked and blank, and that blank will carry its own schedule number.

---

**ANSWERED, 5 October 2026.** A. Hagues sent the page and placed the household at **Castlethorpe**. The six rows are housed there, and **Burton House** is now the one house on Newcastle Circus still with nothing for 1939.

**The page gives the street and no house**, so the three dead ends above were not going to be got past from the record alone - which is worth remembering. When the walk, the ground and the earlier households all fail, it is because the answer is not in them.

**The family with her is GREIG, not Grey**, written plainly four times. Winifred H L, Malcolm R, Barbara R and Elizabeth Mary have all been renamed, and their citations say why. The record had held them as Grey since they were entered.

**And the same page closed 5 South Road.** It is written into the street between 2 Newcastle Circus at 249 and 9 Park Drive at 251, ticked and struck through, at **schedule 250**. The record already had it down as empty, but on a note that said only *1939 census* and gave no evidence - one of the nine stubs in [[nine-houses-marked-empty-in-1939-on-a-stub-note]]. That one now has its page.

questions.title: Schedule 154 was sent as 2 Park Terrace, and the walk says 19
questions.detail:
**A. Hagues sent schedule 154 - Alan James Fraser, 30, clerk, and Kathleen May Fraser, 27, bookkeeper - headed *2 Park Terrace*. The record already holds that household at *19 Park Terrace*, and three things say 19 is right.**

**19 Park Terrace is divided into four.** Schedules 153, 154, 155 and 156 of the RMGC book are all at that one address:

| schedule | who |
|---|---|
| 153 | Matthew Vernon James Plunkett, engineering representative, and Ethel E, **embroidery designer** |
| **154** | **Alan James Fraser**, clerk of wages accounts, and **Kathleen May**, bookkeeper |
| 155 | Isabel C Morgan, 45, certificated assistant teacher |
| 156 | James Orrell, 62, shoe and leather merchant, and Ronald J H, clerk to a foreign shippers' agency |

A single schedule at a different address sitting between three at one address is not how an enumerator walks.

**The walk either side agrees.** 148 is 13 Park Terrace, 150 is 15, 151 is 16, then the run of four at 19, then 158 onward is The Ropewalk. There is no room in it for a number 2 or a number 3.

**The record's own citation says 19.** Both Fraser rows read *schedule 154, 19 Park Terrace, ED letter code RMGC*.

**So the household has not been moved.** A. Hagues has twice today corrected an address of this kind himself - *10 Fish Pond Drive* proved to be 10 Hamilton Drive, and *6 fp* at schedule 78 proved to be 3 Clare Valley, ticked and blank. This looks like the same slip, but it is his page and his call.

**2 and 3 Park Terrace are both still open for 1939.** Number 2 was Kate Elizabeth Reid's in 1921, and before her Frances Mary Wing lived there in 1911 - the solicitor's daughter who is doing light domestic work at 9 Western Terrace by 1939. Number 3 was **Herbert Bradley's**, engineer, retired.

**This also makes 19 Park Terrace the fourth divided house this round has found**, after 33 Lenton Avenue with five households, 7 Cavendish Crescent North with two, and Felixstowe with two.

Links: [[when-was-33-lenton-avenue-divided]].

questions.title: ANSWERED - Thorsmore is schedule 45, and it was the gap in the walk all along
questions.detail:
**A. Hagues sent the 1939 street list for Cavendish Crescent North. Every building on it is in the record except one - *Thorsmore*.**

The list names four houses by name rather than number, and the record can place three of them:

| on the list | the record |
|---|---|
| Crescent Lodge | **16 and 16a**, schedule 42, the Cox household |
| Fligton | **15**, schedule 47, the Lymberys |
| Pendower | **17**, schedule 48 - see [[john-thorpe-perry-not-john-shaw]] |
| Castle Mount | **20**, schedule 44, ticked and blank |
| **Thorsmore** | **nothing at all** |

**Thorsmore has no head on the list**, which on this street means the household is either closed or the house stood empty - 18 and Castle Mount are blank in exactly the same way, and both are already written up as ticked and left blank.

**So which number is it?** The property list holds nineteen houses on this street. Taking out everything the list accounts for, and everything that already has a 1939 household, what is left is **1**, **9**, **18a** and **22 and 24**. One of those is Thorsmore - unless Thorsmore is a house the property list has never held at all, which is how Pelham Cottage and Stowe House both began.

**It is not schedule 193.** That household has four living people in it, so it would carry a head on the list. Thorsmore carries none. They are two different gaps on the same street - see [[which-side-of-cavendish-crescent]].

**What would settle it:** the Thorsmore row's own page image, which gives the schedule number, or a street directory of the late 1930s.

---

**ANSWERED the same day, from the page itself.** A. Hagues sent the Register page for schedules 41 to 49. Three houses run together down the left margin, each with a tick and every column after it struck through:

| schedule | house |
|---|---|
| 43 | 18 |
| 44 | Castle Mount |
| **45** | **Thorsmore** |

**So Thorsmore is schedule 45** - the empty number in the middle of the walk that [[schedule-45-missing-from-cavendish-crescent-north]] had asked about an hour earlier. The two questions were the same question from opposite ends: a house with no schedule and a schedule with no house.

**The number is still not proved.** The page gives Thorsmore no number, only its name. The walk puts it last on the even side, after 20 and before the enumerator crosses to 11, and **22 and 24** is the only even house on the street with nothing else against it - so that is where the record has put it, and the note on it says plainly that the identification is not proved. A directory of the late 1930s would settle it.

---

**CONFIRMED, and the record knew all along.** Property 36, *22 and 24 Cavendish Crescent North*, has carried **Thorsmore** in its **prev_house_name** field since long before this round - alongside *Ravenscourt*. The identification made above from the walk alone, and written up as not proved, was already recorded in the property list. It is proved.

**The same field confirms two more from the same page.** 15 Cavendish Crescent North has carried **Flixton** and 17 has carried **Pendower**, both independently of anything read this round.

**The lesson is bigger than these three.** `prev_house_name` was a field nothing in the working process consulted. When a household names a house the property list does not appear to hold, that field should be the first thing checked - before the walk, before the ground, and certainly before a new property is made. See [[check-prev-house-name-before-making-a-property]].

questions.title: ANSWERED - schedule 45 is Thorsmore, ticked and left blank
questions.detail:
**The RMGC enumerator walks Cavendish Crescent North in two clean runs, and schedule 45 is the hinge between them - and it is empty.**

| schedule | house |
|---|---|
| 39 | 10 |
| 40 | 12 |
| 41 | 14, Park House |
| 42 | 16 and 16a, Crescent Lodge |
| 43 | 18 - ticked and blank |
| 44 | 20, Castle Mount - ticked and blank |
| **45** | **nothing in the record** |
| 46 | 11 |
| 47 | 15, Fligton |
| 48 | 17, Pendower |
| 49 | 19 |

**Even numbers up, then odd numbers up.** 45 sits exactly where the enumerator turns round at the top of the even side and comes back down the other. The record's own property list has **22 and 24 Cavendish Crescent North** as a single building, and no 1939 household in it - which is the house the even run would reach next.

**It may be another blank.** Two of the six houses either side of it are ticked and left blank, so a third would be no surprise. But nothing in the record says so yet, and an empty house is written into the Register with a schedule of its own - see [[six-barrack-lane-proves-empty-houses-are-written-in]].

**Note also that 13 is missing from the odd run** - 11, 15, 17, 19 - but the property list holds no 13 on this street, so there may never have been one.

---

**ANSWERED from the page.** Schedule 45 is **Thorsmore**, ticked and struck through like 18 and Castle Mount either side of it. The guess written above - that 45 would turn out to be another blank, and that the even run would reach 22 and 24 next - was right on both counts. See [[thorsmore-cavendish-crescent-north]].

questions.title: Schedule 229 is number 1, and it breaks an otherwise perfect walk down Cavendish Crescent South
questions.detail:
**A. Hagues has read schedule 229's House column as *1*, and that fixes one problem and raises another.**

**What it fixes:** the old import had put both schedule 229 and schedule 231 at *19 Cavendish Crescent South*. Two schedules cannot be one house unless the house is divided, and nothing else says this one is. Moving 229 to number 1 leaves 231 alone at 19.

**What it raises:** the rest of the run is a clean walk down the odd numbers.

| schedule | house |
|---|---|
| 227 | 25 |
| 228 | 23 |
| **229** | **1** |
| 230 | 21 |
| 231 | 19 |
| 232 | 17 |

**Number 1 is at the far end of the crescent from number 23.** An enumerator walking 25, 23, 21, 19, 17 does not step down to number 1 and back again.

**Three things could explain it.** The household is only two people - Henry J Holmes, a taxi driver, and Frances M, a house furnisher's secretary - with no servants, which on this street is unusual and reads more like a flat or a lodge than a whole house. The enumerator may have doubled back for a schedule handed in late. Or the House column may read **1** as part of a longer entry the index has cut short.

**The record now follows A. Hagues' reading.** The paste also spells her *Francis*; the record has *Frances*, which is how the name is usually written for a woman, and that has been left alone.

questions.title: 18 Park Terrace stood empty, but the walk has no schedule left to give it
questions.detail:
**A. Hagues has read 18 Park Terrace as empty on the night. The trouble is that the RMGC walk down Park Terrace is already full.**

| schedule | house |
|---|---|
| 148 | 13 |
| 149 | 38 |
| 150 | 15 |
| 151 | 16 |
| 152 | **17 - ticked and blank** |
| 153 | 19, flat 1 |
| 154 | 19, flat 2 |
| 155 | 19, flat 3 |
| 156 | 19, flat 4 |
| 157 | **56 The Ropewalk - ticked and blank** |
| 158 | 54 The Ropewalk |

**There is no gap.** 151 is 16 and 152 is 17, so the enumerator went straight from one to the other without writing an 18 between them - and an empty house is not skipped, it is written in and ticked, which [[six-barrack-lane-proves-empty-houses-are-written-in]] established on Barrack Lane.

**Three ways out of it.**

- **18 is part of 19.** Number 19 is divided into four flats, which is unusual enough on this street to suggest the two houses were knocked together or re-numbered. If 18 and 19 are one building by 1939, the four flats account for both.
- **18 is in a different book.** Park Terrace has not yet been shown to split between books, but Hope Drive, Barrack Lane and Peveril Drive all do.
- **The tick A. Hagues read sits on a line numbered elsewhere.** The three blanks on the Cavendish Crescent North page - 18, Castle Mount and Thorsmore - run together down the margin in a block, and a block like that is easy to read one line out.

**The record marks it empty on his word**, with a note saying the schedule is not yet known. **Park Terrace is otherwise complete for 1939.**

questions.title: A Register entry that says refer to page 18 can be transcribed twice and invent a household
questions.detail:
**Muriel Langtree was in the record at two addresses on the same schedule number, and only one of them is a house she ever lived in.**

The record had her at **7 Hamilton Drive**, schedule 83. An import file had her at **Ribble Lodge, Clare Valley**, also schedule 83. A. Hagues read the page: her entry **says refer to page 18**, and she appears there again - so the second sighting is a cross-reference, not a second household, and it had been transcribed as though it were one.

**This is a kind of fault worth watching for.** The 1939 Register carries these pointers wherever a person was counted somewhere other than where they were entered - someone away on the night, in hospital, or moved between the enumeration and the writing-up. A transcriber working line by line sees a name with an address beside it and makes a household of it. The signs are:

- **the same person at two addresses on one schedule number** - a schedule is one household, so this cannot be right;
- **a household of one** at a named house that has a full household elsewhere in the same book;
- **a page reference written into the entry**, which is the thing itself.

**The Ribble Lodge row has been removed from the file.** Ribble Lodge, Clare Valley is now a house with nothing for 1939 again, and it is on the list of houses still to find. Links: [[nine-houses-marked-empty-in-1939-on-a-stub-note]].

questions.title: Cliff House and 33 Lenton Road may be the same building held twice
questions.detail:
**The property list holds two entries that both claim number 33.**

| | |
|---|---|
| **#196** | *Cliff House, Lenton Road (32, 33, 33a, 33b)* |
| **#365** | *33 Lenton Road* |

Cliff House's own address says it covers 32, 33, 33a and 33b, so a separate 33 is either a part of it held twice or a different house the name has swallowed.

**A. Hagues named both as empty on the same reading of the 1939 Register**, which is consistent with them being one building ticked once and counted twice in the record - but also with them being two genuinely separate blanks side by side. Both are marked empty for 1939, which is the safe answer either way: if they turn out to be one house, folding them loses nothing.

**What would settle it:** the schedule numbers. One tick with one schedule is one house; two consecutive schedules are two. The Register page A. Hagues read will say.

See [[properties-carrying-two-house-numbers]].

questions.title: Clinton Terrace and Clifton Terrace are two streets, and the 1939 households belong to Clinton
questions.detail:
**A. Hagues sent three 1939 households headed *1 Clifton Terrace*, *3 Clifton Terrace* and *4 ct*. All three are already in the record at **Clinton** Terrace, and the walk says Clinton is right.**

The RMGC enumerator goes down Derby Road and straight into the terrace without a break:

| schedule | house |
|---|---|
| 186 | 119 Derby Road |
| 187 | 121 Derby Road |
| 189 | 125 Derby Road |
| **190** | **1 Clinton Terrace (127 Derby Road)** |
| 191 | 2 Clinton Terrace (129) |
| **192** | **3 Clinton Terrace (131)** |
| **193** | **4 Clinton Terrace (133)** |
| 194 | 5 Clinton Terrace (135) |
| 196 | Hampden House, 7 Clinton Terrace (139) |

**The Derby Road numbers settle it.** Clinton Terrace's houses carry Derby Road numbers running 127, 129, 131, 133, 135, 139 - consecutive odd numbers continuing the run the enumerator was already walking. Clifton Terrace is a separate street, and the record holds three houses on it - **1, 3 and 4 Clifton Terrace** - every one of which still has **nothing at all for 1939**.

**So two things follow.** The three households are correctly filed and nothing has moved. And the three Clifton Terrace houses remain genuinely open - whatever is in the Register for them has not been found yet, and they should not be closed on the strength of these schedules.

**If the index itself says Clifton**, that is an index fault worth knowing about, because it would misdirect anyone searching that street. The enumerator's own page is the authority. See [[the-walk-fails-at-the-estate-boundary]].

questions.title: Three people at Clinton Terrace where the index and the record do not agree at all
questions.detail:
**Most of the index's spellings at schedules 190 and 192 are the ordinary kind - Fernie for Ferris, Slaton for Staton, Fork for Cork, Hodgson for Hodson, Carr for Kerr. All of those are now held as variants, so a search under either finds the person. Three are not that kind.**

## The lodger at 1 Clinton Terrace

| | record | index |
|---|---|---|
| name | **Elmer Bonser** | **Sydney Defeyser** |
| born | 24 January 1894 | 24 January 1894 |
| work | assistant manager, dance hall | assistant manager, dance hall |
| status | **Divorced** | **Single** |

The date and the work are identical, so it is one man - but *Bonser* and *Defeyser* are not two readings of one word, and the marital status differs too. One of them is reading a different line.

## John Bradby Pearl

The record has him born **5 September 1902**, the index **5 September 1904**. Day and month agree; only the year is out.

## John Chambers

The record has him born **31 March 1927**, the index **31 December 1900** - twenty-seven years apart, with only the day in common. At 1927 he is a hosiery worker of twelve, which is on its own a reason to doubt the record's reading.

**What would settle all three:** the page image for schedules 190 and 192. Links: [[clinton-terrace-is-not-clifton-terrace]].

questions.title: ANSWERED - Emmeline D. L. Sampson was Doris Hockmer, a servant at the house he died in
questions.detail:
**Tom Percy Sampson's will, reported on 20 October 1950, gives Emmeline D. L. Sampson an annuity of £260, the use of his effects for life, and a life interest standing between his collection and Nottingham Castle Museum. The record has never heard of her.**

**The difficulty is that she is not his wife, so far as the record knows.** The 1939 Register has him at 4 Clinton Terrace with **Lilian Lucy Sampson**, born 15 June 1875, both of them married - and the 1921 census has him on the same Derby Road house with a wife called **Lilian**. Eleven years later the person with a widow's provision is an Emmeline.

**Three readings, and the record cannot choose between them.**

- **Lilian Lucy died and he remarried.** The provision reads exactly like a widow's.
- **Emmeline is a sister.** His father Walter brought up at least three daughters at 29 Lenton Avenue - the record holds **Flora**, born 1881, and **Effie**, born 1885 - and an unmarried sister living with a widowed brother would be given the use of his effects in just this way. It also holds **Ellie E Sampson**, born 1884, whose name is close enough to want checking.
- **Lilian Lucy and Emmeline are one woman.** Two forenames, two different ones used at different times, is ordinary enough - but *Lucy* and *D. L.* do not obviously meet.

**What would settle it:** a death registration for Lilian Lucy Sampson between 1939 and 1950, or a marriage for Tom Percy Sampson in the same years. Probate records for Emmeline herself would give her dates.

Links: [[sampson-bequest-to-nottingham-castle-museum]].

---

**ANSWERED the same day, and by the house itself.** A. Hagues sent schedule 259, **5 Holles Crescent** - the house Tom Percy Sampson died in - and the first of the two women entered there is:

> **Doris (E D L) Sampson (Hockmer)**, born 16 October 1898, domestic, single

**E D L.** The initials are Emmeline D. L. Sampson's. A. Hagues confirmed Hockmer as the maiden name, so on the night of 29 September 1939 she was **Doris Hockmer, a domestic servant of 40**, and *Sampson* is the married name written in afterwards.

**So the second reading above was wrong and the first was right.** She is not a sister. Tom Percy Sampson left 4 Clinton Terrace some time after 1939, married the woman in service at 5 Holles Crescent, and died in that house in April 1950 - and it is her life interest that stood between his collection and the Castle Museum. **Lilian Lucy Sampson must have died between 1939 and that marriage**, which is now the thing to look for.

**The household has no head.** Only Doris Hockmer and Marjorie Nixon, a hairdresser's receptionist of 21, are entered, both single and both in work - which means the head's own record is still closed. Whoever that was, Tom Percy Sampson was not yet in the house.

She is in the record as **Doris Hockmer**, with *Doris Sampson* and *Emmeline D L Sampson* held as variants, so a search under any of the three finds her.

questions.title: The Sampson Bequest - a Park lace manufacturer's collection went to Nottingham Castle Museum
questions.detail:
**Tom Percy Sampson of 5 Holles Crescent died in April 1950 and left his china, pictures, silver, gold and articles of vertu to Nottingham Corporation, to be shown at Nottingham Castle Museum as the Sampson Bequest.** Reported in the Nottingham Evening News, 20 October 1950; the estate was £52,983.

**The record now holds him from 1901 to his death**, after a probate notice joined four separate entries into one man - see the commit that folded *Peray Sampson* into him.

| | |
|---|---|
| 1901, 1911 | son at **29 Lenton Avenue**, his father Walter's house, already a lace manufacturer at 23 |
| 1921 | head of **133 Derby Road**, a Levers lace manufacturer, with his wife Lilian |
| 1939 | **4 Clinton Terrace** - the same house - with Lilian Lucy, a cook-housekeeper and a housemaid |
| 1950 | died at **5 Holles Crescent**, aged 72 |

**The firm is W. Sampson Ltd. of Ruddington, and the W is his father** - Walter Sampson, born 1847, whom the record already holds at 29 Lenton Avenue in 1901, 1911 and 1921. So the record now has two generations of the firm in two Park houses.

**What is worth chasing.**

- **Does the Sampson Bequest still exist as a named collection?** Nottingham Castle Museum's accession records for 1950 and 1951 would say what came in, and whether it is still shown under his name. If it is, this is a Park house with a public legacy still on display.
- **The life interest** means the collection may not have reached the museum until Emmeline D. L. Sampson died - see [[who-was-emmeline-d-l-sampson]].
- **5 Holles Crescent**, where he died, has nothing for 1939 and the record loses the house after 1911. When did he move there from Clinton Terrace?
- **Westwood, Clumber Road East** was his nephew **William M. Jones's** house, who took the business. The record has the Warner family there in 1921 and 1939, so Jones comes later.

His nieces were **Margaret Jones** and **Kathleen Booth**, another nephew **Howard English**, and his solicitor **Henry N. Hanson** of Nottingham. None of them is in the record.

questions.title: Two Lymbery households in The Park in 1939, and the ages fit a mother and son
questions.detail:
**The 1939 Register has the name twice, in two houses half a mile apart, and the record has not joined them.**

| | |
|---|---|
| **2 Lenton Road**, schedule 265 | **Agnes Lymbery**, 89, widowed, retired, with a housekeeper and a domestic servant |
| **Flixton, 15 Cavendish Crescent North**, schedule 47 | **Robert S Lymbery**, 54, retired lace manufacturer, and **Louise**, 54 |

**Agnes is already in the record from 1921**, in the same Lenton Road house, with her husband **Richard Henry Lymbery**, born 1846. He is gone by 1939 and she is widowed, so he died between the two rounds.

**A son born to Richard Henry and Agnes would be about Robert's age.** She was born in 1850, he in 1846; Robert S was born in 1885, when they were 35 and 39. The surname is uncommon - the record holds nobody else of it - and both households are lace money in The Park.

**But nothing says so.** No census has Robert in his parents' house: the record's Lenton Road rounds for 1881, 1891, 1901 and 1911 hold the Trueman, Townroe and Preston families, so the Lymberys arrive at number 2 between 1911 and 1921, by which time a son born in 1885 would long have left.

**What would settle it:** a birth registration for Robert S Lymbery around 1885 naming Richard Henry and Agnes, or Richard Henry's probate, which would name his children. Agnes died some time after September 1939, aged at least 89, and her own probate would do the same.

**Note the index spells her Lymbury.** The 1921 census and the rest of the family give Lymbery, and the record follows that.

questions.title: Penrhyn Cottage is almost certainly 23 Cavendish Road East, and the record holds both
questions.detail:
**The property list has *23 Cavendish Road East* with nothing at all for 1939, and *Penrhyn Cottage, Cavendish Road East* with a household. The walk says they are the same building.**

| schedule | house |
|---|---|
| 58 | Allendale, Tunnel Road |
| **59** | **Penrhyn Cottage** |
| 60 | 25 |
| 61 | Bishop's House, 27 |
| 62 | 29 |
| 63 | 31 |
| 64 | 33 |

**The run is the odd numbers going up, and 23 is the only one missing from it.** Penrhyn Cottage sits in exactly the place 23 would occupy - the first house on Cavendish Road East the enumerator reaches, coming off Tunnel Road, immediately before 25.

**The record knows 23 Cavendish Road East well enough in other rounds** - Benjamin North's household in 1891, Richard Henry Swain's in 1911, and William C Church with two others in 1921 - and then loses it entirely for 1939, which is not how an enumerator works. A house is either written in with a household or written in and ticked.

**This is the third of its kind this week**, after [[thorsmore-cavendish-crescent-north]] and [[cliff-house-and-thirty-three-lenton-road]]: a named house and a numbered house held as two properties when the Register is describing one.

**What would settle it:** the schedule 59 page, which may give a number alongside the name, or a directory of the late 1930s listing Penrhyn Cottage against a number. **If it is confirmed, the two properties should be folded**, which would close Cavendish Road East for 1939 - every other house on it already has an answer, with Elmhurst and Overdale ticked and blank.

See also [[properties-carrying-two-house-numbers]].

questions.title: A. Hagues read 29 The Ropewalk, and the record holds no odd number on that street at all
questions.detail:
**Among a list of Ropewalk houses read as ticked and left blank, A. Hagues gave 29. The property list has nothing of that number, and nothing odd on the street at all.**

Every Ropewalk house the record holds is even - 2 to 56 - with **2a**, **32a** and **36a** alongside, and one entry recorded only as *The Ropewalk (unnumbered, between 4 and 2)*. The other nine houses on his list were all found and closed; 29 was the only one that was not.

**Three readings.**

- **It is 28 or 30**, both of which he gave in the same breath and both of which are now closed. A 9 for an 8 or a 0 is an ordinary slip in a list typed at speed.
- **It is a genuine odd number the property list has never held.** The Ropewalk is long and only part of it lies in The Park, so an odd side may exist outside the estate and still appear on the same Register page - which is how **Castle Boulevard** turned up in the middle of a Park walk once before.
- **It is 2a or the unnumbered house between 4 and 2**, the two Ropewalk properties still with nothing for 1939.

**Nothing has been closed on it.** See [[the-walk-fails-at-the-estate-boundary]].

questions.title: RMGB schedule 123 carries two households, and the page says which one is right
questions.detail:
**A. Hagues sent the page. Schedule 123 of RMGB is *Ferndene ditto* - the May family, Frederick, Eunice, Geoffrey and David - and Ferndene is on Hamilton Drive. The record holds that household correctly.**

**But the record also has a second schedule 123 in the same book**: John T Fraser Ashby, hosiery machine and fabric designer, with Margaret, Edward M and Louie, at **11 Lenton Avenue**. One schedule number cannot be two households in one book, so the Ashbys' number is wrong.

**The walk says what it should be.** Lenton Avenue in RMGB runs 163 at number 1, 164 at 3, 165 at 5, 166 at 7, 167 at 9, and 169 at 13. **168 is free and 11 is the house that belongs in it.** The record now carries that reasoning in the Ashbys' citation, flagged as in doubt - but nothing has been changed, because a schedule number should be read off a page, not deduced.

**What this cost.** The worksheet built for the Peveril Drive run grouped households by schedule number alone and showed whichever property id was lowest, so 123 came out as *11 Lenton Avenue* and Ferndene vanished from it. The worksheet has been rebuilt to print every household on a shared number. **Any tool that assumes one schedule is one household will get this wrong**, and at least three books are known to reuse numbers - see [[two-books-one-schedule-number]].

**And it moves something else.** On the page, schedule 122 - James and Margaret McCoy - is written with a **ditto in the street column**, and the line below it is Ferndene. If the ditto carries, **the McCoys are on Hamilton Drive, not Peveril Drive**, where the record has them unhoused. Hamilton Drive has three houses with nothing for 1939: **1c, 11 and 24**. That citation is flagged too.

This may be the loose end in the whole Peveril Drive run: nine households with no house against eight houses with no household. If some of those nine are Hamilton Drive, the arithmetic stops being impossible.

---

**The Hamilton Drive guess above was wrong, and the page says so.** A. Hagues sent the Peveril Drive pages. The ditto chain in the street column runs **unbroken from 1 Peveril Drive at schedule 114 down to Park Dale at 130**, and schedule **128 writes it out in full as *Eskdale Peveril Drive***. So every ditto between carries Peveril Drive, the McCoys at 122 included. All nine unhoused households - 118, 120, 121, 122, 124, 125, 126, 127 and 129 - are **on Peveril Drive**, and their citations now say so.

**Which leaves Ferndene standing in the wrong street.** The entry reads *Ferndene ditto*, so by the same chain Ferndene is on Peveril Drive - but the record holds it on **Hamilton Drive** and positions it there, at the far end of Hamilton Drive from Peveril. That citation is flagged. Either the house is on Peveril Drive, or it stands on the corner where the two meet and the enumerator took the Peveril side.

**And the arithmetic is still wrong.** Nine households on Peveril Drive with no number against eight houses with nothing: 4, 5, 7, 8, 10, 11, 12 and Peveril House. One of the nine has nowhere to go unless a house is divided, or unless Ferndene is one of them - which would make it ten against nine.

questions.title: Schedule 13 is 18 Pelham Crescent, and no book will own it
questions.detail:
**A. Hagues read 18 Pelham Crescent at schedule 13. The number is unused in every book the record holds, and none of them is anywhere near Pelham Crescent at that point in its walk.**

| book | where it is around 13 |
|---|---|
| **RMGC** | 11 and 12 at Yorke House, 6 North Road; 14 at 7 North Road |
| **RMGA** | walking down Barrack Lane - 16 at number 12, 17 at 10, 18 at 8, 20 at 4 |
| **RMGB** | the rest of Pelham Crescent, but at **schedules 208 to 221** |

**So this is a fourth book, or a part of one of these that the record has not seen.** The 1939 Register for Nottingham sub-district 26 is held across more than one piece - **RMGB and RMGC are both on RG101/6178A, but RMGA is on RG101/6177J**, a different piece entirely - so a fourth is not surprising.

**The citation says plainly that the ED letter code is not known** rather than guessing one, which is the same treatment given to the households at schedules 26, 77 and 78.

**What would settle it:** the letter code written at the head of the page A. Hagues read. If it is one of the three already known, then that book's walk is longer than the record thinks and something else is misfiled.

Links: [[two-books-one-schedule-number]], [[rmgb-schedule-123-is-used-twice]].

questions.title: A David L Birkin born November 1914 is at Lincoln House, and the name is a known one
questions.detail:
**Schedule 247 of the 1939 Register puts a *David L Birkin*, born 12 November 1914, at Lincoln House, Lincoln Circus, entered as *convalescent after an operation*.** With him is a *James M Birkin*, born 23 April 1912, whose occupation column is a dash.

**The household is Harry Laurence Birkin's** - company director, 67, in the house since at least 1921 when the census found him there as a lace manufacturer with his wife Olive Isabel and six servants. In 1939 the two young men are listed fourth and fifth, after the cook-housekeeper, with four maids below them.

**The record already holds another branch.** Charles Wilfred Birkin, born 1865, and Claire, born 1872, are in it for 1901 and 1911, and their son **Charles Lloyd Birkin**, born 1907 - the horror writer and 5th Baronet Birkin of Ruddington Grange - carries the notable mark. A David Lloyd Birkin born in 1914 would be of that same generation.

**What the record cannot say is whether these are the same family.** Harry Laurence, born 1872, could be father to a son born in 1914 at 42, which is ordinary enough. But the two young men are entered below a servant, which is not where sons usually sit, and a convalescent could as easily be a nephew sent somewhere quiet to recover.

**What would settle it:** a birth registration for David Lloyd Birkin in 1914 naming his parents, or Harry Laurence Birkin's probate, which would name his children. The Birkin baronetcy is well documented, so the pedigree should be straightforward to check.

Links: [[notables-the-two-rounds-brought-in]].

questions.title: Three women on the Peveril Drive pages were in under the stamped married name, not the name they bore
questions.detail:
**The 1939 Register was kept up as a working document into the 1950s, so a woman who married after 1939 has her new surname stamped in capitals over her entry and the old one struck through. The name she bore on the night is the struck-through one.**

Three had been entered the wrong way round, with the stamp taken as the name:

| | the record had | the page has | |
|---|---|---|---|
| schedule 113 | Gwen Hote **Schofield** | Carver, struck, **SCHOFIELD** stamped | now **Carver** |
| schedule 115 | Nellie M **Goodman** | Kell, struck, **GOODMAN** stamped | now **Kell** |
| schedule 117 | Millicent **Taylor** | Powell, struck, **TAYLOR** stamped | now **Powell** |

**The households say the same thing without the page.** Gwen Hote is the fourth of **six Carvers** on schedule 113; Nellie M is the fifth of **five Kells** on schedule 115. A daughter sitting in her family's household carries her family's surname on the night - so a lone Schofield among Carvers, or a lone Goodman among Kells, is a stamp that has been read as a name.

**That is a check worth running across the whole 1939 round**: any person whose surname is unique within a household of three or more sharing another surname, where the odd one out is also held as somebody's variant.

All three married names are kept as variants, and [[the-people-search-now-reads-aliases]] means a search under either finds her.

questions.title: John B Walker JP kept 4 Castle Grove, and the record has never held him
questions.detail:
**Dougal de Havilland's map of the Park gives 4 Castle Grove as the home of John B Walker, a Justice of the Peace. The record holds no such man.**

It holds his son. The 1911 census has **Robert Dudley Walker**, 28, a lace thread manufacturer employing others, with his wife **Helen Main** and their son **John Alexander**, aged one - and that household has now been placed at **2 Huntingdon Drive**, the house built in 1908 that Dudley and Nellie moved into after marrying in that year.

**The record's rounds for 4 Castle Grove begin only in 1921**, with Rudolf Vogel. So the Walkers are earlier than anything the record holds for the house, and the 1881, 1891, 1901 and 1911 rounds for 4 Castle Grove are all missing.

**What would settle it:** the 1891 or 1901 census for 4 Castle Grove, which would give John B Walker's full name, his trade and his household - and would show whether Robert Dudley was still at home. A commission of the peace for Nottingham in the 1890s or 1900s would confirm the JP.

**Two names to watch.** The record already holds a **John W Walker** born 1857 at Cavendish Crescent North in 1881 and a **John D Walker** on Cavendish Road North in the same round; neither is obviously this man, but the initials are close enough to check before a third John Walker is made.

Links: [[nellie-crawford-is-helen-main-walker]].

questions.title: ANSWERED - Nellie Crawford and Helen Main Walker are the same woman
questions.detail:
**Dougal de Havilland's map has Dudley Walker marrying Nellie Crawford in 1908. The 1911 census has Robert Dudley Walker with a wife called Helen Main.**

**Nellie is an everyday short form of Helen** and has been for centuries, so this is almost certainly one woman: **Helen Main Walker, born Crawford, known as Nellie**. Crawford is recorded as her maiden name, and Nellie Crawford, Nellie Walker and Helen Main Crawford are all held as variants, so a search under any of them finds her.

**What would confirm it:** the 1908 marriage registration, which would give both her forenames and her father's name.

**The record holds two Crawfords** - Hugh, born 1873, and Alice, born 1878, both in the 1911 round. Whether either is her family has not been looked at.

---

**ANSWERED on A. Hagues' word.** They are one woman: **Helen Main Walker, born Crawford, known as Nellie**.

The record already held her correctly - Crawford as her maiden name, and Nellie Crawford, Nellie Walker and Helen Main Crawford as variants. **Nellie is now also her known_as**, which matters because the People search reads that field directly rather than through the variants.

She is in the record once, in the 1911 census at **2 Huntingdon Drive**, 26 years old, with her husband Robert Dudley Walker and their son John Alexander aged one - the household Dougal de Havilland's map placed in the house built the year they married.

**The 1908 marriage registration is still worth having** for her father's name, which would open the Crawford side. The record holds a Hugh Crawford born 1873 and an Alice Crawford born 1878, both in the 1911 round, and whether either is her family has not been looked at.

questions.title: prev_house_name is the first place to look when a household names a house the list has not got
questions.detail:
**The property list carries a `prev_house_name` field on fifty-eight houses, holding every earlier name the record knows for them - sometimes two or three, separated by line breaks. Nothing in the working process was reading it.**

**What that cost in a single round.** Three house names were identified from the walk and written up as unproved - **Thorsmore** at 22 and 24 Cavendish Crescent North, **Flixton** at 15 and **Pendower** at 17 - when all three were already sitting in that field. The walk happened to be right. It need not have been.

**What it found when it was finally read.** Two unhoused 1939 households turned out to be strays from households already filed, because the house names matched former names:

| the Register writes | the property list holds |
|---|---|
| **Brightlands (1)**, Clumber Road East | **Adam House**, formerly Brightlands |
| **Edgmond**, 143a Derby Road | **Edgemont House**, 143 Derby Road, formerly Edgmont and Edgmond |

In both cases the schedule was already housed and one person had been left behind and entered twice. Folding them took the unhoused 1939 households from twenty-three to nineteen.

**So the order of work should be:** when a household names a house the list does not appear to hold, check `name`, `house_name` and **`prev_house_name`** across every property, matching the street as well as the name - then the walk, then the ground, then make a new property. Doing it the other way round is how a house gets held twice, which is what [[is-penrhyn-cottage-23-cavendish-road-east]] and [[cliff-house-and-thirty-three-lenton-road]] are both about.

**Beware the street.** Matching on name alone throws up false pairs - *Rock House* on Barrack Lane against Rock House on Peveril Drive, and three different houses called *The Cottage*. The street has to match too.

questions.title: Arthur Carr was somewhere on Park Terrace in 1921, and the record cannot say where
questions.detail:
**Arthur William Carr (1893-1963), captain of Nottinghamshire and of England at cricket, is in the 1921 census on Park Terrace with a household of seven, at an address the record cannot place.**

| | |
|---|---|
| head | **Arthur Carr**, 28 |
| wife | **Ivy Carr**, 29 |
| son | **Angus Carr**, 3 |
| visitor | **Amy Borton**, 65 |
| nurse | **Alice Gosden**, 18 |
| house parlourmaid | **Kathleen Painting**, 17 |
| cook | **Annie Painting**, 21 |

**He had briefly been put at Broxtowe House and has been taken off it.** A. Hagues offered the house from Dougal de Havilland's map and then corrected himself - what the map records there is **the doctors**, the hospital residence that fills Broxtowe House on the same census night. The link is removed and no house is claimed for Carr.

**The household is distinctive enough to match.** Two of the servants are sisters, Kathleen and Annie Painting, and a visitor of 65 named Amy Borton is not a common entry. If any Park Terrace house the record already holds carries those names in 1921, that is his address.

**He is marked notable**, which he had not been - the record held his life and his Wikipedia page but never the mark, whichever house turns out to be his.

Links: [[broxtowe-house-was-a-doctors-residence]].

questions.title: Broxtowe House housed nine hospital doctors in 1921, four of them women
questions.detail:
**On census night in 1921 Broxtowe House held nine house officers of a Nottingham hospital and nobody else.** A. Hagues confirms this is what Dougal de Havilland's map records of the house.

| | age | returned as |
|---|---|---|
| **John Kneebone**, head | 31 | surgeon, born South Australia |
| **Elizabeth Mary Ashby** | 33 | surgeon |
| **John Armstrong** | 29 | surgeon |
| **Olive Sharp** | 28 | surgeon |
| **John Whittingdale** | 27 | surgeon |
| **Arthur Hawes** | 27 | surgeon |
| **Dora Mason** | 27 | physician |
| **Dorothy Jean Gallie** | 27 | physician |
| **Gwennon Mary Griffiths** | 26 | physician |

**Four of the nine are women**, and that is the thing worth following. In 1921 women had been able to qualify in medicine for forty years but were still a small minority of hospital posts, and a residence where they are nearly half the house officers is unusual enough to be worth writing up properly.

**Which hospital?** The General Hospital stood on Standard Hill, a few minutes' walk up Park Steps, and Hart's Hotel - built on Broxtowe House's own site in 2002 - stands on part of that hospital's ground. That is the obvious candidate but the record does not yet say it.

**What would be worth finding:** the hospital's register of house officers for 1921, which would give the appointments and the hospital by name; and what became of the five women. **Dorothy Jean Gallie** in particular is a name that should be traceable.

**The house is gone** - demolished and replaced by Hart's Hotel in 2002.

---

**A woman doctor of exactly that generation was living in The Park and working at that hospital five years earlier.** **Margaret Stote Glen Bott** came to Nottingham in 1916 to nurse soldiers wounded in the war at the **General Hospital on Standard Hill**, and lived at **2 Newcastle Circus** while she did it. She went on to be a surgeon, a Fellow of the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists, the first woman surgeon at the Nottingham Women's Hospital, a city magistrate, a councillor for twenty years, an alderman and OBE.

**She is not one of the nine** - by 1921 she had moved to 9 Wellington Circus. But she makes the General Hospital the obvious reading of the Broxtowe House residence rather than a guess, and she shows that The Park was where Nottingham's hospital doctors lodged. See [[margaret-stote-glen-bott]].

questions.title: CLOSED - the four unplaced house names are not being pursued
questions.detail:
**A. Hagues sent thirty-one house names off Dougal de Havilland's map of the Park. Twenty-six went straight onto houses. Five have nowhere to go, because the property list holds no house of that number on that street.**

| the map says | the list holds |
|---|---|
| **16 Hamilton Drive**, *Morisco* | Hamilton Drive runs 1, 1a, 1b, 1c, 2 to 11, then jumps to **24** |
| **4a Castle Grove**, *Barbican House* | Castle Grove holds 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7 and the house that is also 6 and 6a |
| **6a Park Valley**, *Stuart Cottage* | Park Valley holds 1 to 11 odd and even, then 13, 15, 17, 19, 21, 23, 25 - no 6a |
| **5a Tattershall Drive**, *Palisades* | Tattershall Drive holds 1 to 5 and 17a, and five named houses |

**And one that is held but filed oddly.** *Hine House* is **1 Lenton Road**, which the record keeps under Castle Grove because the house carries both addresses - **1 Lenton Road (6 and 6a Castle Grove)**. It has been named. The name is worth noticing in itself: **T. C. Hine** laid out the estate and built much of it, including the Castle Grove group this house belongs to.

**The four gaps are all suffixed numbers** - 4a, 5a, 6a, and a 16 in a street that stops at 11 and resumes at 24. That is the shape of coach houses, lodges and later infill, which is exactly the kind of building a property list assembled from census returns misses: it has no household of its own in the rounds the record holds.

**Before any of them is added as a property, check prev_house_name** - that field already held Thorsmore, Flixton and Pendower when nothing was reading it. See [[check-prev-house-name-before-making-a-property]]. None of these four names appears anywhere in the list under any field, so they are genuinely absent.

---

**CLOSED on A. Hagues' word.** Morisco, Barbican House, Stuart Cottage and Palisades are not to be chased. The record does not hold a house of any of those numbers and none of the four names appears anywhere in it under any field, so nothing is lost by leaving them: they are written down here, and if a household ever turns up naming one of them, this is where to look.

**Hine House was the fifth and it is placed** - 1 Lenton Road, which the record files under Castle Grove because the house carries both addresses.

questions.title: Dougal's map puts Castle Lodge at 2 Castle Grove, and the record has it at 7
questions.detail:
**The record holds *Castle Lodge, 7 Castle Grove*, with *The Lodge* as a former name. Dougal de Havilland's map gives Castle Lodge as **2 Castle Grove**. Castle Grove is a short street and two houses of the same name on it would be odd.**

**The name has not been applied to number 2**, and nothing has been changed, because writing it in would leave the record with two Castle Lodges and no way to tell which a later source meant.

**Three ways it could go.**

- **The map is right and the record is wrong.** Number 7's name may have been taken from a source that did not give a number, and attached to the wrong house. Its former name, *The Lodge*, is generic enough to have been the whole of what was known.
- **The record is right and the map has the number out by a house.** The other twenty-five names on the same list all landed cleanly, which argues the map is careful - but a lodge is exactly the kind of building to be numbered loosely.
- **Both are right at different dates.** A name can move, and the record already holds one case of it: *Parkdale* is the name of one Peveril Drive house and the former name of another.

**What would settle it:** a directory of the late nineteenth or early twentieth century listing Castle Grove by number, or a census cover sheet for either house naming it.

questions.title: Margaret Stote Glen Bott lived at 2 Newcastle Circus, and the record holds no round that would show it
questions.detail:
**She came to Nottingham in 1916, aged 25, to nurse soldiers wounded in the war at the General Hospital on Standard Hill, and lived at 2 Newcastle Circus in The Park. She had gone by 1920.**

**The record cannot see her, and that is the point.** 1916 falls squarely between the 1911 and 1921 census rounds, and 2 Newcastle Circus has **no round in the record before 1939**. So she is held as a resident with the year written down, not as a census row - and without the Wikipedia article A. Hagues sent, nothing in the record would ever have put her in The Park at all.

**That is worth generalising.** The estate's war years are a hole: the rounds either side are five years too early and five too late, and a wartime household of nurses, officers and lodgers leaves no census trace whatever. Directories, hospital registers and newspaper notices are the only way in.

**What she became.** A surgeon specialising in gynaecology; a Fellow of the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists; **the first woman surgeon at the Nottingham Women's Hospital**; a city magistrate from 1937; Conservative councillor for Mapperley from 1939 to 1958; alderman from 1956; OBE in 1961. She died in 1969, and the Margaret Glen-Bott School in Wollaton carries her name.

**Worth chasing:** who else was at 2 Newcastle Circus in 1916 - she is unlikely to have had the house to herself at 25 - and whether she appears in a Nottingham directory for those years, which would give the household.

Links: [[broxtowe-house-was-a-doctors-residence]].

questions.title: Sir William Arbuthnot Blain is in the record for 1881 only, and he lived in The Park until 1911
questions.detail:
**The record held him as *William A Blann*, a wholesale grocer and magistrate of 50 at 17 Cavendish Crescent South in 1881. A. Hagues gives the name correctly: the surname is BLAIN and the A is Arbuthnot, and the man was knighted in 1897.**

**What he was.** Born at Grimsby about May 1830. President of the **Nottingham Savings Bank**, president of the Conservative Association, acting chairman of the High School, and on the directorate of the Nottingham and District Bank by 1898. *Who Was Who* gives his address as simply **The Park, Nottingham**. He died on 11 February 1911.

**So he was in The Park for thirty years at least, and the record has him for one census.** The 1881 household is his wife **Harriett A**, their daughter **Annie M** of 21 and their son **William A** of 18 - the son a different man who keeps his initial, since the dates belong to the father.

**The question is where he was in 1891, 1901 and 1911.** He may have stayed at 17 Cavendish Crescent South or moved to a larger house as he rose - a man knighted in 1897 and presiding over a bank is not likely to have stayed in the same house for thirty years without the record noticing. **Search the later rounds under Blain and under Blann both**, because whatever misread the name in 1881 will have misread it again.

**What would settle it:** his probate in 1911, which would give his address at death, or a Nottingham directory for the 1890s or 1900s.

Sources: *Who Was Who*, by way of [wikitree.com/wiki/Blain-129](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Blain-129); and *Nottingham & Notts Illustrated, "Up-to-Date" Commercial Sketches*, 1898, at [nottshistory.org.uk](http://www.nottshistory.org.uk/books/nottsillus1898/banks03.htm).

questions.title: Three notable residents the census could never have shown, all found in the gaps between rounds
questions.detail:
**Three people have now been placed in Park houses on dates that fall between census rounds, and in every case the record held both the house and the person and could not join them.**

| who | where | when | what the census says |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Sir Jesse Boot** | Gardenhurst, 5 South Road | **1905** | at St Helier, Clumber Road East in 1911 and 1921 |
| **Margaret Stote Glen Bott** | 2 Newcastle Circus | **1916** | nowhere; the house has no round before 1939 |
| **Arthur Carr** | somewhere on Park Terrace | 1921 | the household is in the census and the house is not |

**The pattern is the ten-year grid.** A census catches a household on one night a decade. A man who takes a house in 1903 and leaves it in 1908 is invisible; so is a wartime household of nurses and officers formed in 1915 and broken up in 1919. **The Park's Edwardian years and its war years are both holes**, and the record will never fill them from census returns however many rounds are transcribed.

**What fills them.** Dougal de Havilland's map - which supplied Jesse Boot, John B Walker, Sam Roper at Rock Cottage and twenty-six house names in a single day. Directories. Probate. Newspaper notices. Hospital and institutional registers. Wikipedia, for the people notable enough to have an article.

**And the mechanism that holds them** is `property_residents`, with `from_year` set and the reason written into `notes` - not a census row, which would be a claim the sources do not support.

**Two of the three were in the record already and not marked notable.** Jesse Boot, founder of Boots and the benefactor who gave Nottingham its university campus, had his Wikipedia page against him and no mark. So did Lady Florence. So did Arthur Carr, who captained England. **The notable marks are worth auditing against who has a Wikipedia URL** - that is a one-line check and it has now caught four people in two days.

questions.title: Forty-four people carry a Wikipedia page and no notable mark, and about half plainly deserve one
questions.detail:
**Marking Jesse Boot notable - which nobody had done - prompted a one-line check: who else has a Wikipedia URL against them and no mark? Forty-four people.**

## Twenty-two with their own article, name matching

These look like straightforward omissions:

**Albert Ball** (1896-1917), **Samuel Bourne** (1834-1912), **Albert Nelson Bromley** (1851-1934), **Charles Frederick Dobson** (1863-), **William Ebenezer Dobson** (1827-1901), **Henry Enfield** (1849-1923), **Robert Evans Sr** (1832-1911, architect), **Henry Farmer** (1819-1891), **Watson Fothergill** (1841-1928), **Lieutenant-Colonel Herbert Herbert** (1865-1942), **Geoffrey Huskinson** (1900-1982, cricketer), **Sir Ernest Jardine** (1859-1947), **Frank Beckett Lewis** (1862-), **Sir Douglas McCraith** (1878-1952), **Sir James William McCraith** (1853-1928), **Sir John Tom McCraith** (1847-1919), **Sidney Shephard** (1894-), **Herbert Durrant Snook** (1867-), **Edwin Arney Speed** (1869-1941), **Edward Strutt, 1st Baron Belper** (1801-1880), **Samuel McIntire Taylor** (1856-1916), **Guy Longfield Willatt** (1918-2003).

**Albert Ball is the one that stands out.** The flying ace, VC, dead at twenty. The record has already had to split him from another Albert Ball this round - and he still carries no mark.

## Eleven where the page is not about them

A Wikidata Q-number, a phone directory, a page about a music venue, a 1970 honours list. These are links to *something*, not biographies: **George Akins**, **Philip Austin Birkin**, **Richard Warwick Bond**, **Edith Cecily Evans**, **Gwenn M Evans**, **Robert Holland Evans**, **James Forman**, **Frederick William Goddard**, **William Goddard**, **Sidney Thompson**, **Frederick A Wadsworth**. Each wants looking at on its own.

## Eleven sharing one page with a relative

Nine Frasers share Edward Fraser's article; two Johnsons share Samuel Waite Johnson's. Sharing a page is not notability - **Ethel Fraser lived from 1882 to 1882**. Only the subject of each article should take the mark.

**Nothing has been applied.** The mark carries `significant_by`, so it is a judgement with a name on it, and twenty-two of those is A. Hagues' call rather than a bulk update. **Say the word and it is one pass.**

**The check is worth keeping.** It has caught four people in two days - Jesse Boot, Lady Florence Boot, Arthur Carr and Margaret Stote Glen Bott - and it costs one query. Links: [[the-parks-war-and-edwardian-gaps]].

questions.title: Colonel Eric Baker was at Castlethorpe, and nothing online can be found to confirm it
questions.detail:
**A. Hagues has Colonel Eric Baker at Castlethorpe, Newcastle Circus. A search of the open web has turned up nothing, and the record holds no Baker who could be him.**

**What was searched, so it is not searched twice.** His name against Castlethorpe and The Park; his name against the Sherwood Foresters and the Robin Hood Rifles, which are the Nottingham regiments an officer of that period would most likely have served with; and Castlethorpe's own history. *Men of Nottingham and Nottinghamshire* (1924) looked the most promising source and its armed forces page would not fetch - **that page is worth trying again by hand**.

**The record's seven Bakers are none of them him** - Elizabeth, Herbert, Ludwig, Bertha Swell, Julia, Alice and a second Elizabeth, none titled, none military.

**But Castlethorpe has a hole exactly his shape.** The house's rounds run:

| 1881, 1891 | the Brownswords, silk merchants |
| 1911 | **Herbert Francis Lancashire**, hosier, alone |
| **1921** | **three servants and no family at all** - Selina James the cook, Emma Griggs and Bessie Louisa Abrey |
| 1939 | Louisa M Riley and the Greigs |

**A house kept up by three servants with no household to serve is a house whose people were away**, and 1921 was a year with a great many officers abroad - Ireland, India, Mesopotamia, the Rhine. A colonel posted away from home on census night is exactly what that round looks like.

**What would settle it:** the Army List for the 1920s, which would give an Eric Baker and his regiment; a Nottingham directory for the 1920s listing Castlethorpe's occupier; or the 1911 or 1939 rounds, in neither of which he appears - which would date his tenancy to between them.

Links: [[which-newcastle-circus-house-is-louisa-rileys]].

---

**The 1921 round probably is not his, and that was my reading to correct.** A. Hagues found Herbert Francis Lancashire in the **London Gazette of 25 February 1916**, given as *of Castlethorpe, Newcastle Circus, The Park, Nottingham*. He is the head of the house on the 1911 census and he is still there five years later.

**So the three servants of 1921 are most likely Lancashire's, with him away** - not a household waiting for a colonel. Selina James the cook was 53 and born at Slapton in Buckinghamshire, a long way to bring a woman, which fits a household that moved her rather than a house held for a stranger.

**That leaves two windows for Colonel Baker**, both narrow: **1916 to 1921**, if Lancashire left soon after the Gazette entry; or **1921 to 1939**, before Louisa M Riley. Lancashire died in January 1928, so the second is the roomier of the two and the more likely.

**The useful next step is therefore Lancashire, not Baker** - when he left Castlethorpe fixes the window. His probate in 1928 would give his address at death.

questions.title: Herbert Francis Lancashire held Castlethorpe from 1911 to at least 1916, and deserves the notable mark
questions.detail:
**A. Hagues found him in the London Gazette of 25 February 1916, given as *of Castlethorpe, Newcastle Circus, The Park, Nottingham*, against the word APPEAL.** The record had him at Castlethorpe on the 1911 census and nowhere after. It now holds the house from 1911 to 1916.

**February 1916 is the month conscription began** under the Military Service Act, and the Gazette was then printing the membership of the appeal tribunals that heard claims for exemption. Whether he **sat on** one or **came before** one is not settled - the extract gives the word and no more - but a hosiery chairman running a works of six or seven acres would have had a great many men to argue over either way. **The full Gazette page would say which.**

**He is a substantial Nottingham figure and carries no notable mark.** Born at Sandiacre about 1869, died at Nottingham on 31 January 1928. Second-generation hosier; chairman and managing director of **J. B. Lewis and Sons**; he led the firm's move from Stanford Street to the Haydn Road works, which were held up as a model factory - a heated indoor swimming pool, bowling greens, tennis courts and a hockey pitch for the employees by 1930, and the Meridian Cricket Club, still playing. He was prominent in industrial relations in the hosiery trade and a Justice of the Peace. He has no Wikipedia page, so he was not in the forty-four that check turned up.

**His father Herbert**, born Sandiacre about 1839 and dead in 1904, was at **8 Park Terrace** - so the record holds two generations of the family in The Park, and Herbert Francis himself at **5 Park Terrace** in 1901 before Castlethorpe.

Links: [[colonel-eric-baker-of-castlethorpe]].

questions.title: The Park's Jewish population was six times the city rate in 2001, and the record shows why
questions.detail:
**The 2001 census profile gives The Park's Jewish population as 1.54 per cent against a Nottingham figure of 0.23 - more than six times the city rate, and the highest of any minority religion on the estate relative to the city.**

**The record shows that is not new.** Households it already holds include:

| | |
|---|---|
| **Hesse** | Stowe House, 6 Maxtoke Road |
| **Weinberg** | Hardwicke House, Cavendish Crescent North |
| **Raflowitch** | 9 Cavendish Crescent North - Miriam Raflowitch, a lace manufacturer in her own right |
| **Goldschmid** | Emil Goldschmid, who turned out to be on Castle Boulevard |
| **Likiernik** | Madge Likiernik at Adam House, Clumber Road East |
| **Hirschfield** | Anna E Hirschfield at Felixstowe |
| **Kohn** | Recha Kohn, a widow of 67 born in Germany, at Pelham Crescent in 1901 |

**The Nottingham lace trade is the reason**, and it is the thread to follow. The trade drew merchants and manufacturers from Germany, Austria and further east through the nineteenth century, and The Park is where the prosperous ones lived. Several of these households are German-born - Recha Kohn is returned as a German subject in 1901 - and the 1939 Register will hold refugees from the thirties among them.

**What would be worth doing.** Gather the households properly, with birthplaces, trades and dates, rather than noticing them one at a time as this record has been doing. The Nottingham Hebrew Congregation's records would give the community's own account. And the 1939 Register's enemy-alien markings, where they survive, would show who had arrived recently and under what circumstances.

**It would make a page.** The estate has a century of continuity on this and the record currently has it scattered across a dozen unconnected households. See [[the-park-in-2001]].

questions.title: ANSWERED - Robert Dudley Walker was named on the address page, just not at home that night
questions.detail:
**The 1911 census has Robert Dudley Walker, 28, a lace thread manufacturer employing others, at the head of 2 Huntingdon Drive. Ten years later the house is his wife's.**

| 1911 | 1921 |
|---|---|
| **Robert Dudley Walker**, 28, head | — |
| Helen Main Walker, 26, wife | **Helen Main Walker, 35, head** |
| John Alexander Walker, 1, son | — |
| | Robert C Walker, 8 |
| | Florence Mari Walker, 5 |
| | Elizabeth Walker, 2 |
| Ruth Holland, 20, servant | Eva Aldis, 17, housemaid |
| **Elizabeth Oliver**, 25, nurse | **Elizabeth Oliver**, 35, nurse |
| | Matilda Gilletle, 21, cook |

**Three more children were born in the meantime** - about 1913, 1916 and 1919 - so Robert Dudley was alive and at home well into the war years. He is simply not in the house on census night 1921, and his wife is returned as head.

**Two readings, and the children date them.** He may have **died** between 1919 and June 1921, which would make her a widow of 35 with four children. Or he may have been **away on business** - a lace thread manufacturer in 1921 had every reason to travel - in which case *head* means no more than head of those present.

**John Alexander, the eldest, is missing too**, at eleven. A boy of that age and that class in June 1921 is most likely away at school, which is the ordinary explanation and does not need a sad one.

**What would settle it:** a death registration for Robert Dudley Walker between 1919 and 1921, or his probate. If he lived, a directory for the 1920s would still have him at 2 Huntingdon Drive.

**Elizabeth Oliver is the quiet thread.** Born 1886 at Ruddington, nurse to this family in 1911 and still nurse to it in 1921 - the same woman in the same house across ten years, three more babies and a war. The record held her twice, as Olivers and as Oliver, until now.

Links: [[nellie-crawford-is-helen-main-walker]], [[john-b-walker-jp-of-4-castle-grove]].

---

**ANSWERED. A. Hagues read the address page.** Robert Dudley Walker is **named on it**, so he was a member of the household in 1921 and simply not at home on the night. He did not die. His wife is returned as head because she was head of those present.

He is now linked to 2 Huntingdon Drive as a resident from 1911 to 1921, which the census rows alone could not show.

**And this is a tool the record has not been using.** See [[the-1921-address-page-names-the-whole-household]].

questions.title: The 1921 address page names the whole household, not only those at home - and it can fill empty houses
questions.detail:
**The 1921 census schedule has an address page that lists the household, and the enumeration pages record who was actually present on the night. They are not the same list, and the record has been reading only the second.**

**What it cost once.** Robert Dudley Walker vanished from 2 Huntingdon Drive between 1911 and 1921, his wife was returned as head, and the record could not say whether he had died. He had not. He is on the address page; he was away for the night. A. Hagues read it and the question closed.

**What it could do next, and this is the useful part.**

**Castlethorpe in 1921 holds three servants and no family at all** - Selina James the cook, Emma Griggs and Bessie Louisa Abrey. That is the signature of a household away from home, and **the address page will name them**. It would settle at a stroke whether the house was still **Herbert Francis Lancashire's** - who was there in 1911 and still there in the London Gazette of February 1916 - or already **Colonel Eric Baker's**, whom A. Hagues places there and whom no search has found. See [[colonel-eric-baker-of-castlethorpe]].

**And it is not the only house like that.** Any 1921 round in this record holding servants and no employer is a candidate for the same treatment, and so is any house whose head seems to disappear between rounds. **That is a query worth running across the whole 1921 round**: households of three or more where every person is returned as a servant.

**The 1939 Register has the same shape of problem and a different answer** - there the empty houses are ticked and given a schedule of their own, so an absent household leaves a mark. In 1921 it leaves a houseful of servants instead.

---

## The thirteen houses to try it on

The query has been run. **Seven 1921 households in this record hold nothing but servants**, which means a family away from home whose names are on the address page:

| house | who is there |
|---|---|
| **Castlethorpe, Newcastle Circus** | Selina James 53 cook, Emma Griggs 29, Bessie Louisa Abrey 18 |
| **1 Cavendish Crescent South** | five, the youngest fourteen - Daisy Sands, Gertrude Annie Hanson, Zillah Spear, Clara Emily Strauther, Margaret Annie Locke |
| **Adam House, Clumber Road East** | Sarah Chambers cook, Olga Frost nurse and sewing maid, Hilda Annie Mildred parlourmaid, Frances Williamson housemaid |
| **6 Western Terrace** | Hannah Rowe 32 cook and Rose Rowe 21 housemaid - sisters, by the look of it |
| **Edale House, Clumber Road East** | Mary Wright 54 cook-housekeeper, Dorothy Harlshouse 18 housemaid |
| **5 Cavendish Crescent South** | Anna Simkin and Lucy Ann Pease, both 42 |
| **15 Newcastle Drive** | Martha Bennett 36 housemaid, Hannah Templeman 58 cook |

**And six more hold a wife with no husband returned** - the same thing one step less complete, and the address page names him:

**3 Huntingdon Drive** (Frances Mary Latham), **3 Clumber Crescent South** (Evelyn Frances Kirkaldy - and her son is **Adam Willis Kirkaldy**, which is the name of a known economist of the period, so the absent husband may be worth more than a line), **27 Newcastle Drive** (Mary Foster), **12 Pelham Crescent** (Margaret Mary Groves), **19 Newcastle Drive** (Gertrude Betsy Knabe), **3 Clinton Terrace** (Alice Maude Coles).

**Thirteen address pages would add thirteen householders the record cannot otherwise see**, and one of them may be Colonel Eric Baker.

questions.title: Clare Valley and Park Valley were transcribed twice, because the first transcription names no street
questions.detail:
**Before transcribing The Ropewalk for 1901 I checked whether the street was already in the record. The check looked for 1901 rows whose address named the street, found none, and I went ahead. It was the wrong check.**

The 1901 round for this enumeration district was **already in the record**, 360 rows across 71 schedules, sourced *"1901 census, Brewhouse Yard and Standard Hill, Castle ward - read from the enumerator's pages supplied by A. Hagues"*. **Those rows carry no address field at all** - only the schedule number and that source line. So a check on the address could never see them.

**It covers schedules 47 to 121.** The Ropewalk is schedules 1 to 27 and was genuinely missing, so that work stands - 165 rows. But Clare Valley and Park Valley are schedules 49 to 72, squarely inside it, and I transcribed them a second time. **Forty rows went in**, each one a person where my reading of a name or an age differed just enough from the existing row that the duplicate guard did not catch it: *Rose Aster* against *Rose Asher*, *Mag Millwood* against *Mag. Millwood*, *Ruth Snell* at 21 against 27. All forty are removed.

**The check that should be run before any transcription** is on the **year and the schedule range**, not the address:

> which schedule numbers does the record already hold for this census year, and from what source?

A schedule number is the one thing every census row has. An address may be blank, unresolved, a house name, or a number the transcriber could not read.

**And it points at a second job worth doing.** Those 360 rows have no addresses. The pages give them - 25 Park Valley, 4 Clare Valley, The Lodge - and the record is carrying a whole enumeration district filed only by schedule number. **Giving them their houses would place sixty-odd households in one pass**, and the pages to do it from are the ones A. Hagues has just sent.
